I do not like Early Access games by default. However, this just came out for free this week only. I figured for that price I would give it a shot. Even with the inclusion of new single player maps, this is not a finished product
Here is what I liked:
1. Sci-fi fps
2. Decent, if dated, looking environments
3. Has typical movements like crouch, jump, etc
4. Has laser/muzzle attachments
5. Stealth options are always fun
6. You can destroy light sources for more stealth fun
Cons:
1. No health, no shield, and 2 hits kills you. On normal.
2. Want to stay alive? Stealth. Always.
3. Some graphics look fairly good, while others look a good 8 years old (such as ground textures and ploygon counts)
4. Not many weapons to choose from
5. No minimap that I could quickly find so sometimes it is easy to get lost or turned around
The game is not exactly bad, but from my understanding it has been in development for a fairly long time. Considering the frequency (or lack of) of updates prior to this recent one, I worry this will be a project that slips into limbo unless a ton of people jump on now. I want to see where this game is headed, but at the current phase, even for less than $7, I will not buy it. As I mentioned, I do not really buy into early access. If there is another free week later in the year with significant updates, I might buy it for the current price of $7

If you have watched Mad Max, then you should really play this game. This game takes a desert world, and let's you play through the entire game in a similarr environment, without getting boring. That is true game design right there. For example, Borderlands: the Pre-Sequel has most of it's environment on the moon, and that game to me is quite boring. As far as the Plot goes for this game, it's nothing too spectacular, however, the overall story is rememberable and enjoyable. Gameplay wise, I think it's a perfect merger of FPS and RPG, as your skill point alloccation really changes your gameplay with new and powerful techniques. Sniping is a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥, however, the other guns are powerful, and the better guns have a rare drop rate that you can farm in certain circumstances; the DLC's have the most availabity,a nd the main game sucks for it. This game is multiplayer, however, when I've played it with a friend, it was laggy, and very precise with the missions (as in you need to be on the exact mission bit to turn in the mission, no skipping).
If there is anything to take away from this, it's that this game is amazing, however,  if you want a great Borderlands expereience, go for Borderlands 2, then comeback to this one, as it can be glitchy, it punches in the face with it's ♥♥♥♥-you interactions (it's very enduring, nbot a bad thing(it's hard to explain)), and I think it gets cleaned up a lot in the sequel. I do prefer this game over the sequel, and I love this franchise so much. 9/10.

Here's the conversation me and my friend had after playing a couple of games of IM:
Dansrage: whats the point of this I can just play Insurgency lol
Arthur Von Winklehammer: Right dude?
Dansrage: let's go play play Insurgency
Arthur Von Winklehammer: aha alright
Visually this game is quite impressive, excluding the endlessly copy/paste assets and environments, the lighting is nice, the weapon models are good, the rain on your visor is reminiscent of Metroid Prime, but there's just nothing under the hood.
There are three game modes in IM, Campaign, Coop and Multiplayer.
In campaign and coop you'll play on the exact same maps, with the exact same bots. There are minor variations of gametype that essentially boil down to "kill all the guys" or "press all the buttons while you kill the guys".
This isn't bad in itself if the gameplay is engaging, but unfortunately it isn't. Bot AI will either run directly into your bullets or stand still and fire at you. The atmosphere with it's excellent sound design and moody lighting is obviously aiming for creepy, but all that ends up happening is that the four players fan out and clobber clueless bots, there's no tension, no real danger besides a bot spawning on you.
The multiplayer is just Insurgency with fewer guns, less varied maps and worse mechanics. It's a bog-standard twitch shooter with the supposed realistic weapon handling counting for nothing when everyone is hip firing in corridors at point blank range. All of the levels look like they're built from a single tileset as if they've been randomly generated. Everything looks the same.
It's pretty much impossible to play with your friends, you can't create servers, the only way to host a private game is to set your preference to "friends only", and then try to join one of the seemingly random servers that pops up while it's still empty, hoping that it's the gametype and map that you want, and that you won't be instantly spawnkilled by somebody who wants this server for themselves. There's also seemingly no way to change map or gametype once you're in the server.
This game uses "Early Access" as a blanket excuse for laziness, this game has been in development since May 2005.
Think about that for a moment.
TEN YEARS! It was originally supposed to release on PC and 7th gen consoles, this current version of the game that you're able to play today was Kickstarted in 2012, and is itself three years old.
This is all they have to show for it. This is the game. If you think the core mechanics and gameplay will improve from here you're optimistic, I'll give you that, because three years of work has given us an "Early Access Alpha" with off the shelf shooting mechanics and about as much content as a Kinder Surprise.
My bet is they're going to tack on more "campaigns" which basically amount to offline bot matches with text-to-speech voiceovers.

Reaching level 110 after almost 180 hours, i think i can say a few words about this game.
I can not recommend this game as it is right now. I miss the game as it was in alpha. It was a fun game. It was quite original (the tier system, the tech tree) but then, with each update it got worse and worse. The "updates" removed the pilot seat, megabots, added the crates, robits currency and the use of more than 1 type of gun per bot. Also the robot factory... It took away all the creativity that was before. Nowdays most of the players have the same robot. Another thing that i miss is the original team deathmatch, the one without respawn, where teamwork was the key to win. It was awesome when you could use only one type of weapon on robots, when players could become healers, snipers, and other classes. The auto-heal is also♥♥♥♥♥♥ Buying distruptors has almost no point.
On the other side i like that they added custom matches so you can play 1v1 with friends, more content such as new guns, movement, cosmetics and again megabots.
There's no real story to it although the second one brings the first nicely into the fold. It's fun and pretty easy to learn. It works well with a controller. Roland's turret sucks though.

The Original Review:
I'm a local Player, so I get games where I can invite some Friends over and play for the whole evening some Games.
As i noticed this Game finaly got his release, I didn't hestitate and bought it.
But... we lost interest in it rather fast. I get why a lot of People loves this Game, and I would be happy if I could too, but there are a few things that kills it for me:
1.) No XP when you play local. Thats really sad, because that means I have to play online with some randoms to unlock some more Characters. But because we didn't want to play with randoms, we had to keep playing with the 3 we had. I want to note Brawlhalla here, where you still earn Gold if you play local to buy new Heroes.
2.) Ok, so after a while we tried to unlock some things and wanted to play online.  So I created a room, just to notice that no one of my friends can join. This means that everyone of them have to be on there Computer and have to buy the Game for themselves to be able to play with me AND unlock things. That's really bad... I want to note here Brawlhalla too. There you can play with e.g. 2 Players on one machine with 2 other random Guys on the Internet.
So we had to play local, without unlocking anything.
Another Problem is the (at least now) poor variety of Maps. It get boring rather fast after playing for ~an hour.
Would love the Game if the Things mentioned get changed. Until then, I will keep it on my Wichlist, with hopes high!
Update:
Ok Guys, I have to confess that my Brawlhalla statements were wrong. I somehow confused that in my head.
But whatever, Move or Die got some nice Updates now.
And one of these Updates made it possible to play online with local Players! Thats just brutal! Now we can play with 3 People, and with one Online Player (and there are plenty) to unlock things!

I remember playing this game way back when in 2010 back when it was released on the PSP. It was a great game then and it doesn't fall short now. The simple hand drawn graphics are still great and the game still holds to the test of time. The game itself in terms of gameplay isn't that great, nor does it standout, yet if you are a competitive individual you will be spending a lot of time with it in order to get a perfect across all the stages, which can take a good deal of time. Unfortunately this is also where the game falls short, sometimes strategy turns into memorization of what enemy comes from where and on what wave. It is with this in mind that the game can become dull at times as you are repeating a level for the third or fourth time trying to get the rainbow and each time takes 30 minutes.
I would recommend this game if you are looking for some time to kill, but I would definitely recommend getting it on sale.

Eve Online is the most complex and hardcore sandbox-MMO out there, but that creates an incredible depth and intrigue. This game has a really steep learning curve and it will take time to learn the basics. Fortunately Eve Online features a lot of player-run corporations (guilds) that is new-player friendly and will help you get started and may even pay for skills/ships. The game also has a decent tutorial and "career agents" that will set you off to a military, exploration, business, or industrial career. Keep in mind that these careers also can branch down to a lot of sub-careers such as piracy, bounty hunting, mining, manufacturing and so on.
This video will give you a good overview of what the game is like:
P.S, Even though there is a monthly subscription of about 15€, all new content/expansions are FREE. This game was launched in 2003 yet has been updated countless times to look and handle better than most of the modern MMO's of today.

This game is definitely a game to buy if your a fan of Borderlands or Telltale Games, if your not a fan of either, this game might not appeal to you.  The game relys on a somewhat understanding of the Borderlands series in order to know what is going on.  The game follows Borderlands 2 and uses the story from that game.  It might also be a good idea to have played through the presequel as one of those characters shows up.
Episode 1: You are first introduced to the characters and some of the plot line which is more towards the end. Contains some action but is more there to introduce you to the characters and the feel of the game. (Exposition)
Episode 2: You are introduced to the main goal of the story and go through some action but mostly puzzles and exploration. (Exposition)
Episode 3: You meet the main villian of the game and are finally getting major set pieces. (rising Action)
Episode 4: The game really kicks off with alot of action story. (rising Action)
Episode 5: The final episode has the most action and is definitely the most sad (emotions) where we finally see the end of the character's adventures. (Climax, Falling Action, Resolution)

I recommend this game to everyone. This is an amazing example of in-game immersion without having to care about a story line, or a certain set of characters...*looking at you "Beyond Two Souls"* But I digress, all of my friends should take advantage of this sale. Proteus has a certain atmosphere most games aren't able to master. Its using the persons mind to imagine what the world "feels" like. Unlike most Triple A games where HD graphics are the norm, Proteus takes gaming back to when you had to IMAGINE what was happening on screen and believe you were in it. Its a certain charm most games lose due to the game screaming at you to go to the next checkpoint, or mission when they really could focus on the environment and setting. Thats why I play FPS's like CoD and heavily critize the campaign for its lack there of immersion. All around this game is not a game, its a statement about modern gaming. I find it to be pretty true and agree with it. :)

The first thing that amazed me with this game was the detailed ragdoll engine used for the Stick Fighters.
Your Stick Figures feel like they have a mind of their own while their limbs wiggle around and you try to shoot your enemies.
Also the maps are cleverly laid out and every map feels "right" and has its own unique tweaks and twists.
For 5$ this game will give you an awesome time, even more awesome if you have some friends to play with.

Gunpoint is among the five best new games I have played in the past year, and I have played quite a few. Everything about Gunpoint is perfect. Well, almost everything.
Gunpoint's art style is great: it has just enough pixels to look contemporary, but just few enough to look retro. With an art style somewhere beyond 32-bit but clearly below 64-bit, the visuals have an attractive complexity and attention to detail, with just the right amount of detail so as not to make finding technology difficult.
Speaking of technology: Gunpoint's core gameplay mechanic is genius. The game uses a tool called Crosswire, which allows you to wire any device of one color to any other device of the same color. This makes for some fantastic gameplay opportunities and unique puzzles. As an example:
A guard upstairs is guarding the exit to a stairway on your floor. Using a button on your floor, you turn out the lights upstairs. The guard sees the lights turned out, and walks over to a lightswitch, which you have disabled. As he fumbles with the switch, you run up the stairs, tackle him to the ground, and knock him out cold.
There are many other gameplay elements that make this game a gem, but I'd like to focus on two: story, and saving. Saving is simple: every five seconds, the game saves. You die? Go back to any save in the past 20 seconds. You got spotted? Rewind away.
The story is much more complex. Every mission contains main objectives, optional objectives, and triggering events. Additionally, each mission is preceded and followed by interactive dialogue. The way you handle all these things gives widely varying story results.
After you beat the final level, Gunpoint pulls one last genius game design idea out of it's fancy hat- but I won't spoil that for you. Just remember to have a functioning internet connection when the game is over.
I have only two complaints- firstly, wall transferring. You can climb on every surface- but sometimes you press a key thinking you'll go to the left of a wall, and you go to the right. You get used to the way this works after a while, but it feels a little abstract. Secondly, the length of the game isn't very impressive- it has vast replay value, and if you're interested in the story, from what I can tell, you can probably get around ten hours out of it, which is good for an indie. There's 42 achievements, and a Final Score too, if you're into those sorts of things. Even so, my first playthrough took me just over 2.5 hours.
Bottom line: Gunpoint is near perfect. It is gaming Nirvana. It is innovative to the point of being unlike anything I have ever played. Buy it. Now.
Final Score: 9.85/10

There is a lot of misinformation about this game being floated around by frustrated people who couldn't figure it out. If you aren't a special snowflake and you don't take dying in a video game too seriously, you can have a ridiculously good time playing EVE without putting in a ton of time and effort. If you want to play a game where everything is handed to you, no effort is ever required, and you can pay to win, then EVE might not be fun for you. WoW is always there if you don't want a challenge. I'll go through some misinformation that unfortunately kept me away from the game for a while:
1) The learning curve is not that bad for most areas of the game. It is a huge game with a lot to learn, but it isn't "difficult" to learn. People just get overwhelmed by the amount of information. For me, learning about everything is part of the fun. I'm a year in and have a ton to learn, and that's a good thing. I'm always improving and learning from my mistakes.
2) You do not have to wait months to skill up enough to do fun things. You can hop in a frigate and have fun in 1000 person fleet battles in null security space on day 1. Two words: ewar maulus. The hardest part about EVE is finding your niche and figuring out what's fun for you. Some people love mining (these pople are crazy), some people love PvP, some people love trading. The people that ♥♥♥♥♥ and unsubscribe after a month of mission running in high security space aren't giving the game a fair chance.
3) You can compete with and have fun with multi-year veterans. EVE is not all about skill points. They will determine how many ships you can fly, and to a lesser degree how powerful those ships are, but if you are smart and have some skill then the advantages are not insurmountable. Each level of a skill takes an exponentially greater amount of time to train than the level before it, but the benefit of leveling up does not increase. So you might train a skill to level 4 in a few days and get 90% of the bonus that a vet got from spending 20 days to train it to level 5 (max level).
4) Everyone is not mean and out to get you. Yes, if you spend $400 on PLEX to outfit billion ISK ships that you can barely fly in your first week of playing, you're going to get blown up, whether you're in high sec or not. People in local chat in trade hubs will try to scam you. Think about what you're doing and ask questions in the newbie chat channels and you'll be fine. You're never safe in EVE (what's the fun in being safe?), but if you're not stupid you can prevent yourself from being a major target. In most ships in most of high security space you will almost never just get blown up randomly. If you're having serious problems with other players in high security space then you're probably being dumb.
5) EVE is not "spreadsheets online". I'm really not sure where this one came from. It has kind of entered the mythology, like the supposedly impossible learning curve and everyone being out to get you. If you're a hardcore market trader or industrialist, or run a giant corporation, then you might want to keep records of things, but in no way does this define the gameplay. I suppose the inventory window is kind of like a spreadsheet because it has sortable columns? I really don't get this one.
6) Getting into a good corporation with fun people is easy. Google Brave Newbies. They are a bunch of newbies who won a 1000 person battle against a powerful group of multi-year vets this week by being smart.
Things that are true about EVE:
PvE is boring for most people and is usually a means to fund PvP. You will probably have more fun with other people than you will solo. You will probably end up with a few accounts/alts. Multiboxers are annoying, but you won't really encounter them much in PvP. The players, not the universe, make things interesting. The lore is mediocre, but null sec politics and wars are endlessly interesting. Some people play the metagame more than the actual game. EVE is challenging, but that makes it fun.

I've been making RPG Maker Projects for years on 2000, 2003, and VX/VX Ace, and this is by far the most user friendly RPG Maker out there. The built in tool tips have allowed me to learn so much more about how everything works without having to resort to google. The Essentials DLC also gives you a skillfully remastered version of the absolutely stellar soundtrack of RPG Maker 2003 to use in your games (the soundtrack was the reason I stuck with 2003 for years), which is a major bonus. You can CHOOSE whether or not to have your game in side view or front view which is amazing and allows you to easily swap at the flick of a switch. Java Script plugins make adding in new scripts and mechanics into your game a lot easier, and is a lot easier programmers and scripters to write new stuff for. But in my opinion, far and away the best new feature that this iteration of RPG Maker has is the character generator. The ability to make my own resources and characters with this program has really opened up my imagination and made the ecreative process a lot more fun (it also creates a battle sprite for side view battles for whatever characters you make, which is fantastic compared to how VX Ace did not as it only featured front view by default.). This one feature has caused me to create characters that have literally quadrupled the scope of my main project, spurring me to create entirely new stories and plot lines just by having the ability to create something new from the vision in my head without having to be an expert spriter or artistically talented. That feature alone warrants my recommendation if you're interested in picking up another RPG Maker, but that combined with all the other pros further solidifies this as currently being the definitive RPG Maker software.
My only complaints concern how difficult it is to add new parts and resources into the character generator, and how it is sparse when it comes to creating non human characters. Thankfully there are a lot of resources out there to help with that, but still, the process to add that stuff in is really annoying and finnicky. MV would be ridiculously amazing if it had Steam Workshop support like VX Ace, and it would help with the aforementioned issues as well.
Overall, it's an amazing piece of software, and I'd recommend buying it. It's currently pretty pricey at $80, but as time goes on the sales on it will just get bigger and it'll be more affordable to most people. If you have the creative itch though and can't wait, I'd still recommend it at full price, it's really freaking great.

Some reasons to give it a miss:
- Skills are bugged. If it's labelled "special" instead of "magic", your characters can't use them. Likewise, if they drain HP/MP or inflict a status effect (or did at one time), monsters can't use them properly. They still inflict status ailments, but they won't follow the damage codes.
-Edit: Damage codes must be ridiculously high (3X or more to whichever damage type you want to use) to inflict damage, and even then they don't do all that much damage.
-EDIT: Characters need to be flagged as using "special" instead of "magic"; I admit to bungling that.
-The much touted side-view battle screen is abominable. You have the cardboard cut-out enemy sprites in the dead center of the screen, and off to the side, often overlapping with them, your character's sprites. This makes it look like the enemies are part of the background.  Maybe this is why the default view is first-person, which always struck me as saying "We can't be bothered to animate our sprites beyond basic walking animation" which might have been acceptable when such a thing would require an extra ten bucks on the price tag and another microchip or two in the cartridge, but now it's just lazy (and it was lazy then too because Final Fantasy 1-6 managed good, long games with deep storylines with side view fighting just fine).
-No adding or removing party members. You're stuck with whatever size of party equals how many "actor" slots you have. If you have nobody in those slots, you still end up with the thing treating it like there's somebody there.
-You can make a fantasy game with some sci-fi or modern bits (deep space, factory, and womb level fight backgrounds; cityscape overworld options, etc), but no option to actually make a pure sci-fi or modern setting game. The basic outfits are variations on "tunics" for male characters, and "dresses" for female characters. Not one whisper of a spacesuit or unigender clothing. The vehicles are a rowboat, a clipper ship, or a zeppelin. No starfighters or space cruisers; no speedboats or battleships.
EDIT: And finally; you need to manually copy DLC files into the program folder, rather than having it do that itself. If I knew how to program, I wouldn't be using an RPG maker. And you can't find them by typing "RPG maker" into your search bar either.

The first part of the Borderlands series was a marvelous breakthrough. Some Diablo fan developers of Gearbox reinvented the way of co-op fighting and looting in a post apocalyptic world named "Pandora". Containing 4 different iconic characters which you can levelup by XP gained from kills or solving quests is still today (6 years after release) a highly addictive game concept. The other thing is the random weapon looting generator which produces practically an infinite variation of all kind of weapons (with elemental damage, multipliers, rarities, weapon classes, character class mods, grenade mods and shields). You can buy weapons from vendor machines but mostly they are hidden in weapon cases, lockers or stashes all over the landscape or they drop from killed enemies. So you cleanout an area in action loaded sequences (the AI is great) and after that you compare stats of dropped and looted weapons.
You better play together with your friends. The game is up to 4 players co-op which is a great experience. Even if there are sometimes loot conflicts or quest solving / achievements asynchronities. Whatever is the reason it still makes fun.
Very innovative was the unique cell-shade graphics at that time which gave the game the perfect comic look. Mixed-up with FoV and depth sharpness effects it felt quite modern and fresh. Today it feels a bit blurry but still nice to watch. Shooting at enemies let drop several damage numbers and criticals hits out of their bodies which is quite funny.
The Bossfights are totally epic. Everything seems very story driven. Other things like quests of collecting things are rather repetive. If you finished the main story you will reach lvl36 but on a second playthrough you can farm enough XP to levelup to lvl50 and lateron with DLCs to lvl69 (max level).   The 4 DLCs content is quite extensive storytelling and new epic bossfights. You cannot miss all the DLCs in the GOTY version which is totally recommended and worth to buy.

To preface this entire review, I hate RPGs. I think they retain a lot of flaws from an age in gaming that was limited by technology and lack of ideas; limitations which modern games no longer have. Xenoverse doesn't even really look like an RPG, but that's what it is. It's an MMO with a fighter skin. And it's not a bad idea really. It was fun for the first couple of days even for me, but around level 50 was when I decided this game was not enjoyable any longer. The gameplay is very simple and between level 1 and level whatever-the-max-is, very little will change about your custom character. Their stats will increase and they'll get slightly different, flashier moves, but you'll still rinse and repeat the same combos or spam the same ki ultimates over and over again. It's essentially the same as mashing the "A" button while playing a Final Fantasy game. Yes, this is a very boring design, but the simplicity was actually enjoyable for me. What wasn't enjoyable was the other RPG elements: grinding and difficulty spikes. Specifically difficulty spikes that shouldn't actually be difficult. A lot of the later quests involve your character and two support characters (or even your character alone) going through gauntlets of Super Saiyans with permanent transformations who never run out of ki and spam energy blasts and ultimates forever. But one Super Saiyan is manageable you say? How about three? Yep, Super Saiyan 2 Goku, Ultimate Gohan, and Super Saiyan Goten fighting you at the same time and hitting you with three Super Kamehame-Ha's and getting rid of half your health is what you can expect in the later levels of this game unless you do the dirty deed of grinding for hours on end. Like I said, I'm not an RPG fanatic and I'm sure the MMO crowd probably wouldn't care much about a few hours of wasted time, it just annoys me when any possible skill the player has is negligible and the fight relies on how much time you've sunk into grinding quests that you don't need to grind. So do I recomend this game to a casual person who likes Dragon Ball and is looking for a fun experience? Definitely not. That person will have wasted fifty dollars and would probably think the game is crap. To an MMO'er or RPG fan, who wants an interesting combination of MMO's and fighting games, they may like it a little bit. Overall, the game is more an RPG than a fighter, but it's gameplay and mechanics are far too simple for it to stand up as either. It won't captivate you for hours on end, but it's a good game to play when you feel like letting your brain melt. It's fun, but it's not that great and it can be a real ball buster at times. I give Dragon Ball Xenoverse a 6/10.

Scourge of Armagon is the first of the two Quake expansion packs. It chronicles the main character taking on a brand new force of extra-dimensional enemies, this time lead by a cyborg known only as "Armagon". It was developed by Ritual entertainment which would later create games like Star Trek Elite Force 2 and SiN.
Compared to the original Quake, Scourge of Armagon has a destinctively sci-fi look and feel to it. A lot of the enemies are footsoldiers and one of the new enemies is this robotic scorpion that shoots nails at you.
However what makes this expansion memorable to me compared to Dissolution of Eternity, the second expansion, is how frantic it feels at times. The map design feels intentionally designed to be a little claustraphobic, and there are many more traps and inconveniant enemy spawning locations. Likewise there are several new enemies that require slowing down a little and being cautious, such as these gremlin enemies that steal your weapons and use them against you.
Unfortunately the final boss Armagon was far too easy, and it kind of made me wish there was an additional episode. I don't think it's a bad expansion pack but by no means is it a must play.

So you telefragged your way to the end of Quake and you want more? Well, you came to the right place. Scourge of Armagon is the first of two "official" expansions, neither of which were created in-house at iD but carry the stamp all the same. This isn't exactly more Quake in the way you might be thinking, but there's a chance you might enjoy it even more.
Unlike the base game whose story could fit on a Post-It, Scourge of Armagon seeks to create a slightly more cohesive experience. In the wake of your victory over the... bad guys, you set out to track down the rest of the... bad guys. This means instead of four disparate episodes to blast through, there's a linear chain of 17 levels that form a story out of their very design. You'll start in familiar tech bases and research labs, gibbing grunts and commandos, before passing through an impressively-detailed dimensional gate and ending up in the gothic castles and hellish mazes of the... bad guy world. You can generally see where you came from when you start a new level (or at least how you got there) which adds a nice bit of continuity to your journey.
It's essential to note that levels in Scourge of Armagon actually look like real places. Bases have control panels and supply cabinets. The hellish cathedral has pews and bookshelves. The mines have cart rails and drilling apparatuses. Every area is far more grounded and identifiable than the insane architecture of the original, though this isn't necessarily a plus considering how much I enjoy the fever-dream ambiance of Quake. You also might not care for how huge these levels are, featuring room and monster counts double or more than the ones you're coming from.
This brings me to the difficulty, which is the one aspect that sours me on SoA. Every level is absolutely jam-packed with enemies, with some absurd mixes of threats in later areas. Normal in SoA feels like Hard in Quake, and I'm not about to try anything harder than that given how much effort each level takes to finish. You'll also run into some devious traps and one-hit kills like crushing ceilings and deadly fans that can quickly end an otherwise promising run. This is exacerbated by the amount of backtracking most levels need, some being so maze-like that the creators helpfully included signs and scripted messages to key locations. Virtually none of SoA's levels are straight shots, and they have a habit of spawning more enemies for you to battle when you pass back through completed areas.
If you can stomach the challenge and the wandering, though, there's a lot to appreciate here. The new enemies and weapons fill in some interesting gaps in the original lineups and are welcome additions. The artistry on display in each level, from the architecture to the scripting, is top-notch and feels pulled from the very best user-created maps. Honestly Scourge of Armagon almost feels like a midpoint between Quake and Quake II, especially in the look of the levels and the new weapons. It's an interesting experience in ways that the original Quake is not, yet features a lot of the same exhilarating combat that you're here for. Any fan of the series owes it to themselves to give it a try.

If the end of the second chapter of The Dream Machine did not emphasise enough that this is a psychological horror adventure game, then this episode will hammer that nail in well. Even the basic premise puts us in an uncomfortable position: our protagonist invades the subconscious of his pregnant wife, which takes the form of an ocean liner where every crewmember is his clone. Here, an investigation into a missing person leads to a few nasty secrets and some… meatier imagery along with the more subtle horror elements.
Since this is the first separately paid episode, it uses a few tricks beyond the longer plot and dialogues to drag out its playtime. The most prominent puzzle type by far is where we have to guess the correct combination in dialogue trees, but a certain pixel hunt may etch itself into the memory as well.
As a whole, this episode is probably the closest The Dream Machine gets to being a standard point ‘n’ click. Even if you had doubts about the start of the game, at least try this chapter, because this is probably the point where one can decide if they want to know how the rest of the game plays out or if this story is just not suited for them.

It's definitely not perfect, but the first in Budokai wasn't all that great which led to the fantastic Budokai 3, and the same happened with Tenkaichi. So if this game is this awesome already, surely if they made a sequel and expanded on pretty much everything, then it's definitely possible that we could have the next great DBZ games that fans argue is better than BT3 and B3.
This game has plenty of things that make me smile, and even more that I find extremely fun. A few things felt cheap at first, like the super armor some enemies would get, but I found myself less frustrated by it the more I played because think about it, in the anime there were a few people with super armor too.
I enjoy the levelling up aspect of it, trying new builds, and all the races are extremely unique. Even the genders have a couple things that make them unique. I would prefer if the armor didn't affect stats though, if I'm honest. In some cases the stats are negligible and you can use them regardless of if they're good for your build or not.
I absolutely love the flight in this game, it's immersive to see your allies fly past you zigzagging or moving up and down like in the anime, and the new camera angles really bring out the action of DBZ, and once again, makes it feel more like the anime.
The combat doesn't have much depth in terms of combos, but that's okay with me because personally I'm not all that great at fighting games to begin with. This game focuses more on timing, positioning, preparation, and keeping an eye on your ki and stamina, while trying to figure out how much of their recources your enemy has left, than memorizing a bunch of combos. It's more of a Smash Bros than a Tekken or Mortal Kombat.
Everyone knows it's a big cliche, but everyone also knows that deep down they want to be part of the DBZ universe. This game does just that, and I enjoyed it. One of my favorite abilities is Destructo Disc, but out of everyone, Krillin has it. So it's used once or twice and that's it, no more usefulness. But in this game, if a weak character has an awesome move, you can give that move the justice it deserves!
The character roster isn't as impressive as BT3, but all of the characters that you really need are here. You can recreate just about any fight in the DBZ universe, and you can definitely recreate all the major fights. But the roster really isn't too big a deal considering you'll be using your custom character about 95% of the time.
People have had two main complaints with this game from what I've seen: 1) The servers. I've seen a lot of people rant and rage over them, saying they can barely play a match and sometimes can't even log on to the single player content. I got this game about a week ago and have had no issues, so either I'm lucky or the servers have been fixed. 2) RNG. Maybe it's because RPGs are my favorite genre, and I've been playing them since I could read, but this game's RNG doesn't really seem all that bad to me. People are saying they'll farm something for hours and hours and never see it, but so far that hasn't really happened to me. Don't get me wrong, I've had to farm for a while to get a certain Z-Soul for a quest, or when I farmed Chain Destructo Disc Barrage, but even then I got it fairly quick, after around 20-25 tries. Then others, like Super Saiyan, I got on about the fifth try. So either I'm lucky, or most people playing this game just aren't used to having to farm for things, which is understandable.
So I say you should give this game a shot if you're on the fence. You'll enjoy it the most if you're a fan of the Tenkaichi games, are a fan of RPGs, and obviously a fan of DBZ. If you're looking for tons of depth in the combat itself, I'd look elsewhere.
Oh, and the lip syncing is horrible, but that's a common theme in most Japanese games.
tl;dr Buy this game, beat things up, get stronger, then beat up tougher things. Much fun. Also laser beams.

Single-Player: This game is really fun in single-player, mainly because there aren't many bugs in SP. It's really addicting and I could probably waste hours a day playing. If you enjoy single player, consider getting this game. The only change I'd like to see for SP is the addition of siege-mode.
Multi-Player: Multiplayer in this game is clunky to say the least. The UI is abhorrent, more-so in multiplayer since you also have to create an account and go through a few extra menus. There are still quite a few bugs, but overall the game is now playable and fun.
Overall: The game is too expensive, the UI sucks, bugs are widespread, early-progression is WAY too slow, and the relic system is terrible! That being said, get this game if it's on-sale because the other aspects of this game are really fun, and most people would probably get a kick out of this game.

I was always more of a fan of the RMXP Style character sets and graphics system, as such I skipped RMVX/Ace. However the RMMV platform is just too fantastic to even compare to any of the previous versions of RPG Maker.
The ease of installing plugins with a fantastic community support makes it easy to really customise your create spark and make a truly original game, taking all the best bits of the games you grew up loving and telling the story you have always wanted to tell. The simple Events manager makes it so easy to do whatever you want that the posibilities are endless.
My only critisism (at this moment in time), would be the lack of visual resources available for the generator. Between the static enemy images and the limited options within the Character Generator, you are slightly limited to what you can do. In my case, I am trying to run an animated side view battle system, which would also include enemies, however short of creating the battler images yourself (54 poses), you cannot have animated enemies, unless they are human. But no-one wants an all human RPG, right?
There is also the issue of DLC's - Although these resources are fantastic, the issue I have found is that they are just files that are dumped into the Steamapp/RMMV directory and you have to manually add these resources to your game folders individually and sometimes these folders are not very clearly labelled, leaving you to do a little bit of guess work. It would be much easier if there was an update system integrated into the Launcher that copied over a set of DLC updates that you want, for example "Copy over all Genertaor Parts", "Copy over all Javascripts" and so on... This would save the user time and a little frustration getting things into the correct folders!
All In all I would still reccommend this software to anyone with a passion for game design / creation because it is so very good. Just keep in mind that it is a work in progress at this point, but I expect some amazing things in the months to come!

Rather than break this down per episode, I'll just swiftly summarize the series (or "season" if you prefer).
I'm someone who actually enjoys the story and characters of the Borderlands games, and I really enjoy it when they take themselves seriously. I had grown fond of quite a few characters. I've also laughed quite a few times throughout both games (I seriously love Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragonkeep, absolutely ADORE it). I'll admit I haven't played the Pre-Sequel, but I do recognize characters who make an appearance from that game.
But this series, this series right here. I haven't laughed this hard this consistently in a good long while. The humor is the kind of humor you'd expect in a Borderlands game, but with the wit, substance, etc., taken to a whole new level. For the serious moments, the emotional impacts made by certain decisions and subsequent consequences hit just as hard. Basically I found myself tearing up both from laughter as well as sadness.
The soundtrack (especially during the intros for each episode) sound superb, with multiple songs taken from the main franchise games that many of you may recognize.
The classic cel-shaded style returns, but the biggest complaint I have is lumped in with a mention of the graphics and visual fidelity: there are multiple graphics bugs, with certain things popping in and out, and certain animations (albeit rarely) appearing clunky and awkward. This and the strangely high-pitched voice of someone in the final episode (that you might not even have a chance of hearing) are the only real complaints I have.
In short, all I can say is... if you enjoy Borderlands, good writing, or simply good adventure/Telltale games, why haven't you played this yet?!
NOTE: It REALLY helps to at least have knowledge of events of the first two Borderlands games before going in.

Possibly the best Tower Defense I've played. But that's subjective, so I'll tell you more about the game:
Whereas in other tower defense games, you build your defenses then sorta sit back for a while, in this game you're almost always on the move. You character has to walk to each tower location in order to build, upgrade and (later in the game) to purchase a tower before it can be built. Never has coin collecting made more sense than in this tower defense, because you're having to scurry about anyways doing other stuff.
The bosses make sense, the levels make sense. There are some frustrations. For one, the game forces you to get a defined number of perfect scores in order to advance to the next set of stages, and this can be difficult. But for a lot of people, you do not want to stop and it's rewarding when you're finally able to unlock a new level.
A tower defense with personality and charm.

I've played close to every mmorpg out there, and Mabinogi is the very single game that stands out to me. It has so many skills, many different classes to choose from, and a rebirth system that allows you to keep on playing without worrying about the level cap. I can sit in the main town (Dunbarton) play my instrument, train some skills, and simply talk for hours to nearest ppl and make friends. Their is probably always a great event going on for players of any experience. They constantly update the game. Ah and one of my favorite features of the game is customization. In this game we like to call it fashionogi haha. Dressing your character in whatever you want, and dying your clothes whatever you want  without any level restrictions. I've even had my character cosplay Kirito from sword art online. I'm always shopping for new clothing! Before Mabinogi I played Runescape for many years. They are somewhat similar in the way the skills work instead of ranking skills from 1-99 its Rank F-1 which costs Ability points that you get from leveling up and rebirthing. I reccomend this game 100% I've stuck with it for 8 years already on the same character!

RimWorlds rare mechanics will keep many people entertained for countless hours. The overall addictiveness and replayability make this a title you should not ignore.
The game starts you off on an alien planet where you and your group of colonists have to learn to survive. You control the colonists by giving them an overall direction and prioritizing their tasks. The game offers a wide variety of choices and really lets you build your own epic story.
RimWorlds Artificial Intelligence is it's highlighting feature. These AI systems are layered and they all work seamlessly together to make an unforgettable experience. RimWorld even lets you select what type of AI you want, giving the title another level of replayability.
Be careful though, the gameplay can be slow and may not be for everyone. Especially if you are more into action games or first-person shooters. However, if you enjoy micromanaging a colony that has the potential for endless hours of gameplay then RimWorld is for you.

Squad  похожа к модификации для Battlefield 2 под названием Project Reality. Тем не менее особой популярности PR не получила — виной тому довольно узкая аудитория игроков, на которую она была ориентирована, и появившиеся со временем достойные альтернативы. Главным конкурентом была и остаётся серия ArmA, для второй части которой даже был выпущен собственный аналог мода (почти мгновенно затерявшийся среди более качественных модификаций для этой замечательной игры), а к нынешнему моменту Project Reality окончательно превратилась в развлечение для избранных фанатов.
Squad — новая жизнь оригинального мода, попытка воссоздать его на современном движке и с более богатыми возможностями, пусть официально прямой связи между ними и нет. В середине декабря проект вышел в Steam Early Access, позволив ветеранам PR вспомнить былое, а прочим желающим — принять участие в тестировании игры.
Разработчики решили обойтись без каких-либо кардинальных изменений, сделав своим приоритетом ориентацию на всё тех же фанатов, которые провели на полях сражений PR не одну сотню часов. Есть две команды (до пяти десятков человек в каждой), различная боевая техника, большая карта в несколько квадратных километров с различными ключевыми точками, за которые и идёт бой, — формула проста и почти не менялась с самых ранних версий. Вроде бы та же самая Battlefield, но пресловутый реализм обеспечивает такие особенности, как наличие у бойцов усталости, не позволяющей весело скакать по всей карте, переработанная баллистика и система подавления огнём, благодаря которым перестрелки меняются до неузнаваемости, и множество других мелочей и нюансов, делающих сражения похожими на настоящие. Оружие смотрится как минимум не хуже, чем в той же ArmA, чего нельзя сказать о звуках выстрелов.
Вообще, нынешнее название гораздо лучше отражает суть происходящего на поле боя. Без своего отделения вы — никто и ничто, пользы от одиночек практически никакой. Напротив, сыгранная команда может с минимальными потерями выполнять поставленные задачи. Здесь чёткое разделение на отряды (собственно, они так и называются — squads), в каждом из которых есть несколько специальностей: стрелок, пулемётчик, гранатомётчик, медик… В угоду балансу некоторые «киты» (kit — набор снаряжения и оружия конкретного бойца) строго лимитированы — например, снайперов не больше двух-трёх на всю команду, иначе большинство занимало бы именно эту, столь желанную, роль.
Меткие стрелки здесь столь ценятся не потому, что у них крутой камуфляж, а из-за всё того же реализма. Заметить врага зачастую не так-то просто, тем более пока он далеко и прячется в складках местности или среди растительности (и того и другого здесь хватает), поэтому нередки ситуации, когда всё отделение стреляет «куда-то туда» просто потому, что в той стороне была вспышка выстрела. Весьма похоже на настоящий бой, хоть и не столь динамично, как привыкли многие по другим играм.
На весьма и весьма неторопливый геймплей стоит настроить себя заранее. Если карта большая, пока дойдёт дело до первого боестолкновения, может пройти более десяти минут, а матч в среднем длится больше часа. Почти как в ArmA, только в альфа-версии пока нет ни наземной техники, ни авиации. Убили — опять пешком через всю карту, если товарищи не озаботились созданием мобильных точек возрождения. Снова реализм — стоит признать, что с этим в Squad всё на достаточно высоком уровне, причём не в ущерб собственно игровому процессу.
Правда, те же любители особо хардкорных режимов ArmA непременно отметят, что динамические метки на карте для каждого бойца (да и вообще наличие карты у всех), подсветка ников у союзников и невозможность подобрать чужое оружие к реализму отношения не имеют. Спорить с ними не буду, но стоит заметить, что тут всё-таки другая игра и у разработчиков были свои причины делать именно так, а не иначе.
Рекомендовать Squad к покупке пока совсем не хочется. Смело брать можно лишь в двух случаях — либо если вы давний поклонник PR и хотите скорее причаститься к новому творению авторов своей любимой игры, либо если желаете не воевать в своё удовольствие, а заниматься именно тестированием. Всем остальным лучше подыскать себе что-нибудь более качественное (взять хоть оригинальный мод версии 1.3, с недавних пор ставший полностью самостоятельным проектом, не требующим покупки и установки BF2), благо жанр сейчас радует разнообразием.

This is a casual Hidden Object point and click adventure game, so ignore the bad reviews because it's not true to the source material!
You are Odysseus and the game begins during the Trojan War with you trying to find a quick resolution so you can go home to your wife. Once the war ends, you begin the journey with chapters covering the adventures you have on the way home, and once you get there, there's a final chapter where you have to take back your home and title from the layabouts who moved in in your absence.
The art style is "cartoony," (which I'm not sure is even a word), the hidden object scenes were tricky, (I had to use the hint button on more than one occasion), and the puzzles range from easy to difficult, but there's nothing there you haven't seen before if you've played other HOGs.
The only negatives I have for the game are the writing. There are no voice-overs, so all the conversations have to be read, and the writing is awful. "Thank you for your help. I would never have been able to do that on my own." And the main character, rather than the warrior and adventurer he should be, is instead, Mr. Goody Two Shoes. Ready to help anyone who asks. (Evil witch transforms your crew into animals .... no problem, how can I help you. Crew sink the ship through stupidity and greed .... he doesn't even lose his temper! ... oh well, you go over there while I look for food!)
Overall, if you are bored of the typical supernatural settings that most HOGs are addicted to, Odysseus is a solid game and a nice departure for a few hours into a very different world.

In summary it is a great game but I would not reccomend it unless you are willing to go through some external workarounds as I would consider this UNPLAYABLE above 60FPS.

Before wrapping up an actual review, I have to declare that I'm literature major. Thus, I have read and reread both
and
more times than I can remember in my years. As being classical epics of Homer, they portray the Trojan War - a tremendously detailed bloody narration of never-ending epic carnages and its political attachments - and Odysseus' journey back home to Ithaca from the Trojan War: both a mythological and psychoanalytical journey of transcendence and growing up. This little HOG, coming from a small Russian developer basically butchers the epic of Odyssey.
The game starts up with a narration of the Trojan War and the presentation of the legendary product of Odysseus' famous wits and wisdom: the Trojan horse. We take on the joy of watching Odysseus and Agamemnon as best buddies. Then, we follow Odysseus through his many journeys, solving his famous adventures through HOGs and basic puzzle scenes. We see him becoming a chef for the cyclops, a friendly visitor for Helios, Poseidon and Circe; and finally, a returning hero who'd use a bee coven to get rid of the suitors of Penelope! Sorry for presenting spoilers on that part, but it really hit some nerve for me.
As you can see, the epic is HEAVILY watered down to be reimagined as child friendly - no violence, sexual encounter or political subtext - which I found to be greatly distasteful specifically for this tale. Any original tale, epic or story can be watered down to be kid friendly. I do not have any major problems with the idea, considering that Disney has been doing so for decades and pulling it off as marvelous work. Yet, the Odyssey is really a bad choice to be retold through a HOG for a new developer. It is an established tale that would create specific expectations - contrary to many other tales from Greek mythology - and picking such cumbersome work without much subtext or experience usually ends up as a disappointment. In my opinion, such was the case for this game. If this would be a completely new tale without the name of Odysseus, I'd probably be at least okay with it.
As a HOG,
isn't anything masterful either. It sure is buggy, works quite slowly and aside the beautiful artwork, animations act so clunky and unnatural that you'd be creeped out watching Odysseus move or Circe talk. There is no voice acting. Puzzles are ordinary - not hard, not easy. HOG scenes are a bit repetitive, using same 2 scenes per act over and over again. There is no map, because there is only 3-4 areas for each chapter and a lazily done audio song swirling in the background.
Over all, I'll pass and give a down vote for the butchered storyline, pretty yet slow display, run-of-the-mill gameplay and distorted animations. There are many great HOGs out there for your enjoyment, hailing from A+ developers or small firms telling original stories.
is not one of them.

Atom Zombie Smasher is a game set in the ficticious South Americian-esque country of Neuvos Aires and pits you as it's leader fending off a zombie infestation. Some of the screenshots made the game look a bit like a grand strategy game, a genre that never really interested me but I picked it up on a sale regardless.
The general premise of the game is that you are given a squad of mercenaries and you go from region to region evacuating survivors. The types of mercenaries vary in their abilities. Throughout the missions your mercenaries gain experience based on their performance (which will be largely dependent on the player's effective utilization of them). The mercenaries that are available per mission vary and which ones are unavailable are at the discretion of the game. This might offput some, but this I felt really added a lot and required the player to use the resources made available in the most strategic way. For me it made it an interesting gaming experience as it required me to think what would be the most strategic action given the resources I was alloted. If players don't like this, there is an option to allow the player to pick the available mercenaries.
Overall I was highly impressed with this game. This game supports the use of a USB controller and local coop, however local coop is simply the single player game with an additional person performing actions.  There is absolutely no change to the game itself besides having a second cursor on the screen.
This game also supports modding and it's all nicely built into the game options. Modding is pretty simple though and is basically just creating a configuration file to tweak behavior and attributes.
One way this game falls short is that difficulty doesn't scale in extended games. I played an extended match and at a certain point it became far too easy. The standard length matches felt a little too short for me, but it seems that the extended matches were thrown in as an afterthought and not given much attention in terms of gameplay balance and pacing goes.

The Odyssey may have lasted long, but this kid-friendly recreation of the story has only a few levels and a bunch of semi-decent hidden object scenes to keep you in the game for 2-3 hours.
Odyssey: Long Way Home was the second attempt by Rainbow Games, a small Russian studio, to create a hidden object game. While they managed to get most of the basics down this time, it is still easy to spot their inexperience.
The story should be familiar: Odysseus outsmarts the defenders of Troy and then spends a few decades on sea trying to get home. Don’t expect to see all of his adventures here though, especially all the gritty and lewd details: this story is 100% child-friendly, including even such famous parts as the dispatching of the grooms. Plus it looks like a story book with the lack of voice acting and cardboard puppet animations.
The hidden object scenes are rather nice, but the item usage feels clunky, showing that the developers weren’t comfortable with this genre yet. On the plus side, its awkwardness is what’s pushing game time over two hours, because there isn’t really much content besides that.

A top down view of the Zombie Apocalypse!
Great soundtrack and effects coupled with addictive gameplay make this a surprising hit for what is a basic top down 2d game with sprites.  Kind of like a tower defense game, but without a fixed base - the people you save are essentially what you are trying to protect!
The Campaign map or strategic view is where you begin.  Every turn zombies (Zeds) take over new territories. From these you choose a territory/city to attempt to rescue civilians from.  This will launch your team deployment phase - placing helicopter landing point etc.
Once each turn or rescue begins, you have a set number of people you have to rescue to be successful - should you fail to hit this number, you will lose that territory.  Should you succeed, it will become neutral.  Rescue during missions is achieved by clicking with the mouse to adjust landing zone for your helicopter in a way that draws the people away from the edges of the city where the Zeds emerge from.  During the daytime when rescue missions begin, this will be from marked entrances, but on sun down, more Zeds will appear from all edges of the city!!
Only people within a certain radius hear the helicopters horn and move towards it - which can later be upgrade - there is a delay until the helicopter arrives and how many people it can carry which you can also be upgraded as you progress.  You unlock new units to assist you as the campaign progresses such as mobile soldier squad, fixed artillery which you can place on a rooftop, sniper team and roadblocks to name a few.
The Zed get scored on how many people they 'convert' regardless of the outcome.  At the end of the mission you are returned to the main map, and scores are added up for yourself and the zed.  At set points totals fixed events occur, such as 'Giant Zeds' etc to spice things up a bit.  Also, depending upon the month/turn, Zed will invade other territories.  The ultimate aim being to out-score the zed in what is essentially a points race - for a large part of which you will be behind in until you discover 'Llama bombs' later in the game ;-)
Overall it is a great little addictive strategy game, one word of warning though, it only has the one soundtrack, so if you don't like it, you may want to turn the music off altogether!

If there's anything that I'm positive this one did better than the original QUAKE, it's the soundtrack. My, my. Pretty badass, of course.

Level design is worse than the original Quake's, and also the second expansion, IMHO. Might be my memory, having played the original QUAKE time and time again even as a kid, but, if I'm not complaining about the second expansion's level design, then I'm pretty sure there's something definitely wrong with this one. It annoyed me throughout the whole damn thing. I know it's meant to be tough, but damn, it's pretty overkill, so much I swear I ragequitted or couldn't deal with something a couple of times, and I rarely do that with single player shooters. Damn.
The new powerups are nice. A welcome break from all the original QUAKE's ones, I suppose. Nowhere near as good, though. I kind of like simple things like Quad Damage and Invincibility better. :P
Also one of them gives you an AI ally. I've got to say, for its age, I understand why they're so terrible at following you, but you're better off leading an enemy to them rather than let them find the enemy. Seriously.
Final boss fight is lame but I understand given the fact id sucks at pulling bosses anywhere outside of games like Quake III. I just spammed rockets at the guy and called it a day. After a handful of attempts, of course. And it was my first time throughout the expansion. Oh, and it was Nightmare. Yeah.
Overall...I'd say it's alright for an expansion, buut...do not get it if you're not that big on Quake. I think. I'm a bit of a challenger-type gamer that always goes for the hard difficulty, so if you're not actually planning on playing on Nightmare, and/or are (maybe even very) patient at stuff like, say, taking a grenade to the face and scarce medkits, then I'm sure this expansion's fine for you. If you get mad at stuff like that and  think this expansion isn't worth the trouble, then yeah, don't. If you are big on QUAKE then go ahead, like everybody else here says.

Basically. I didn't notice much of a difference before using MV and then going to VX Ace.
It was then I noticed that (in my opinion) MV looked... prettier. I also found it more "fun" to use.
MV requires more work but I think that is why I like it so much. Oh and java for those who can use
that.
Now for the thingy.
I started to use VX Ace to make 100 (unfinished) projects that would just pass time really.
Can't remember exactly when I got VX Ace but it was a while after the Steam Release for it.
Now. I was super happy with VX Ace, and when I saw there was a new RPG Maker coming I just
had to get it. I had no choice but to get it. So time passed and I pre-ordered MV right before release.
Release comes around and I fire up the software as soon as I am able. Dear god was I confused at first.
I looked around for the different settings, set up a very basic map and put a man into it.
The first thing I decided to try out was the mouse support and I loved it.
Now being used to VX Ace I was a bit confused when there was not a resource manager or a way to port music in.
I searched long and hard... far and wide to figure out how the heck I would put music in, and soon found out I only had to put the files into the project folder. Apparently that's how you do all of it now.
After being confused for about an hour I decided to start my first project.
I recently decided to open up VX Ace on my laptop again which is when I noticed the difference in how the "graphics" are. VX Ace - Awesome. MV - Awesome. Did you like VX Ace? Doesn't necessarily mean you will enjoy using MV but give it a go anyways. There is a trial version somewhere I believe.
So what I didn't like is the fact that the resource manager has gone bye-bye. I miss that thing.
What I did like is the fact that you don't really start with any preset items/classes, and have to do a lot more of the things yourself. This is very time consuming but also makes me feel like I get more control over how certain enemies will end up being, how powerful a sword will be and so on without having to modify a preset. Nothing wrong with modifying preset items, I just prefer it this way.
I also love the new character generator.
So to answer a question. Should you get it? - Well if you have creativity and really wish to make a story, and if you don't give up 10 minutes into something just because you don't understand it, yes. You probably should.
If you liked the original, this game is very much the same and worth the asking price.

This first expansion pack for Quake is the best out of the other mission packs that were developed (there was a third pack unreleased commercially). The map design is on par to that of id quality, filled with military bases and dark runic/medievil environments, along with having more additions such as more detailed traps and rotating objects. One secret level within the game is designed with Deathmatch in mind and is suspeneded across a black void, something that wouldn't be seen again till the famous Q3DM17. Expanding upon Quake's arsenal is the Mjolnir hammer, great for crowd control, a proximity mine launcher (though not as fun as the vanilla grenade launcher), and a laser rifle that has a higher rate of fire than the one used by Enforcers. While it is nice to have a few extra weapons, they weren't as memorable compared to the base game.
As with ealier FPS titles there is not much story, but all one needs to know is that Quake's general, Armagon, is up to no good, leaving you to eliminate him, along with everything else that gets in your way. Gameplay is the same, kill anything that moves, but still retaining the awesome pixel-hunting secrets (the best ones hidden away by level designer, Levelord), remaining just as fun as its predecessor. Quake: Scourge of Armagon is an expansion pack to the original Quake that introduces new enemies, new weapons and a slew of new levels to shoot your way through. The most noticeable difference from the get go is the amazing new soundtrack added to this expansion. While the original Quake had creepy ambient music that put a sense of dread to the environment the music in this is either heavy metal or some rather dark sounding techno that will have you involuntarily headbanging. This new soundtrack suits the game as the levels are filled with far more enemies at any one time so you'll be shooting more often than not. Unfortunately like the original Quake the soundtrack in this has been cut out of the game leaving it with nothing but sound effects. If you are not willing to mod the music back in I would suggest you skip this expansion all together as it just isn't Quake without the soundtrack. This expansion is far harder than the original game and will require you to put your former experience to the test as they can and will throw tons of high level monsters at you at once.
Enemy placement is also far more cruel and you will often times be face to face with the likes of a Vore (spider demon). It is necessary to keep your finger on the fire button at all times as any delay can lead to your untimely death. This expansion pack is not just a bunch of levels to shoot your way through as the level design is also quite different in that it has an Adventure game like feel to it. For example you will be running from falling boulders, trying to squeeze your way through spinning grinders to press a switch and a few narrow steel beams you must cross over bottomless pit. Most of these environmental hazards that differentiated it from the base game are only found in the first few levels and then it's mostly shooting bad guys in your face with the gun of your choosing. A new weapon added is a grenade launcher that shoots grenades and won't detonate until someone steps near it, whether that be you or the enemy it doesn't differentiate and may cause your death if misused. The next weapon you will encounter is a laser weapons that fires bouncing balls that is very useful for shooting enemies around a corner. Last but not least is a mighty hammer that will electrocute any surrounding enemies though it does take up cell ammo.
You will need all the help you can get as the new enemies are equally as deadly as your new found arsenal. One of the first new enemies that you will meet is a giant robotic scorpion that shoots nails at you. It is a very deadly enemy as these nails move quite fast and are hard to avoid. The next one is called a Gremlin which leaps at you and will steal whatever weapon you are holding. It also has the ability to chow down on corpses and spawn more Gremlins so taking care of any you see should come as a priority if you don't want a small army of them after you. Lastly is a floating hunk of meat called a Spike Mine that will explode in your face if you let it get close enough. It sounds like an easy enough task to simply not let it close to you but these guys are pretty sneaky and while they do emit a distinct sound it is rather hard to hear, making it too late once you see it flying overhead like a deadly piñata. One hit is all it takes for these guys to kill you so while they are the weakest enemies they are also the most dangerous. All of the monsters from the base game are back and ready to rip you in half though thankfully the Slimes are only encountered once in this expansion. You will be facing a lot more of the grunts and Rottweilers as the entire first episode is set on Earth.
There are three episodes overall and it is quite a lengthy expansion pack considering it took me about 6 hours to complete while the base game took me 8. The story is as unimportant as ever and involves a creature called Armagon taking control of the hellish forces after the demise of last game's bad guy and attacking Earth yet again. It is up to you to go into hell and take him down. Thankfully there is an actual final boss fight in this unlike the underwhelming ending in the original. The story is as minimal as ever and will only give you a few lines of text at the end of an episode. The environments you will be exploring are pretty interesting and range from a church, some type of building floating in pitch black darkness and some levels with rivers of blood. Some environments can now blow up in certain set sequences and annoyingly enough the debris from the wall can still damage you for some unknown reason causing you to wait around until they disappear so you can walk to the objective safely.
New items include the Wetsuit which will allow you to breathe underwater and reflects electric type attacks. A rather strange shield that reflects half of the damage you take back to the enemy and last but not least a horn that summons friendly monsters. These monsters will follow you around until they die and what monster you get is up solely to luck. Secrets are plentiful and as difficult as ever to find though it does help to keep an eye out as ammo can be rather scare at times. Running out of ammo is a death sentence as the axe does little damage and has very short range, even if you are lucky enough to have the hammer it has the same range as the axe and it is a rather bad idea to face someone with a chainsaw for an arm or a giant scorpion in melee combat. When all is said and done this is quite a meaty expansion pack with all that we loved about Quake but cranked to 11. If you didn't like Quake the first time around there is nothing here that will convert you though for those that loved the original, Scourge of Armagon definitely lives up to the standards set by the original developers ID and may actually be even better given that you prefer pure action and more difficulty. Why they took away the soundtrack is unknown to me but if you are willing to put in the little effort to get it back this will definitely give you more of what you loved about Quake.

My experience with the game:
For me this is one of the best tower defense games ever made.
I used to play it on PS3 (Encore version) and often co-op with friends and family.
Got it on sale for Steam for a price of 1.19€ which is a steal.
About the game:
Trial and error tower defense game where you need to think ahead, and strategically plan your defense.
The game appeals to casual players and hardcore tower defense fans alike.
The good:
- Fluid relaxing gameplay, nice graphics, zen music, awesome towers, playable character.
- Most of the levels has it's own gameplay feel to it.
- Buy, place, upgrade and sell towers in order to match incoming attacks.
- Can be hard and a bit frustrating, but at a level where you just want to do better the next playthrough.
- In co-op you can actually plan and work together. It's fun.
- Good replay value.
The bad:
- It doesn't have a map/level editor or Steam workshop.
Verdict:
If you like tower defense games, even just strategy games, I can only recommend it.
It is worth it's original price. 9,5/10.

I've been playing Mabinogi for roughly six years, starting just after Closed Beta ended. Over these fine months, the game has grown from a somewhat-playable glitch-fest to a nicely polished MMO. A few of my friends even dubbed Mabinogi "Runescape done right".
The community involved in Mabinogi is one of the best you could ever get. Most players are friendly, and many are willing to help new players with anything and everything. It does, however, have an odd learning curve.
When I started playing, the beginner quests were somewhat lacking, and hard to find. All players will be taken on a "Generation 1" quest line, in which they will be introduced to the enormous plot and equally enormous world. Thankfully, they've added a merciful transportation system in the form of moongates and mana tunnels, which used ot only work during the night and day, respectively.
Once the player gets through the first three mainsteam quests, they will generally feel quite strong, usually ending up to be around level 300-400 by that time. Levels are handled with a continuous rebirthing system. A play may choose to rebirth into a new life, setting their character's age between 10 and 17, and resetting their level to 1. Their previous skills, stats, titles, and accomplishments are retained, however, effectively increasing a player's ability to level up without losing anything.
Skills in Mabinogi are vast, useful, and the main focal point of "Fantasy Life". Each skill set is separated into tags ranging from Life Skills to Warrior, and so on. This does not mean you are restricted by their use, either. Effectively, every player can play as any class at any time without the need to change. For instance, in a Warrior's primary slots, he could have a pair of sharp, deadly blades, and in his auxilary slots, a wand and book to increase his magic potential. The game calls this combination 'Spellblade' in the form of a "Talent Title". Generally speaking, so long as you train the skills and obtain good equipment, you are able to switch between any fighting style at almost any point of your career. If at any poiunt your are stuck in obtaining or training something, there is a user-run wiki readily available with very few advertisments from J-List.
The most common complaint about Mabinogi is that the publisher, Nexon, charges insane bills to those wishing to venture through the cash shop, but the player is never REQUIRED to use it, and why should they? They can get the same, if not, better things by playing the game. Events will generally drop free, usually valuable and strong items that cannot be bought from the shop, or obtained anywhere else. Players will always sell event items they don't want or need. Sometimes DevCat also gives everyone a free month of Premium, or double AP weekends. The advantages of premium don't take away from free users, either. Basically, premium players get cheap items once a week, they get about 10% more EXP, and a bit more inventory space. There's also a daily VIP mission that gives more gold and EXP. The only thing extremely worth paying for are pets, and if a player uses the pets they get from Generation Quests, they won't even need to buy those.
In short, Mabinogi is a great game, and surely worth checking out. Nexon has a very minimalist hand in what DevCat does, so that complaint should not be the first thing that comes to mind.
