There's not many games that I get giddy about, and almost no indie titles.   Gunpoint might actually be the only one in that list.
The entire game is a stealth puzzle game in a 2d world.  There's an overarching plot and everything but honestly, none of that really got my attention.  What got my attention was the levels, and the ability to really tackle a level, and feel that you didn't just "survive" it, but you beat it.
And I feel that way after I beat each level in Gunpoint, not just a sense of moving on but a sense of mastering the level.
The core of the game is being a spy who is able to jump around (pouncing) and use a gun, but the whole game pretty much revolves around using stealth rather than violence.  You can shoot a guard if you need to, but the goal is more to avoid it as it can create an artificial time limit on your current mission.
Instead you can use your skills, and the skills are what really shine.  You use a wirejack system which allows you to create elaborate electrical grids which changes the use of items.  For instance you can wire a switch to a door that normally requires a hand scanner, or remove the wire between the hand scanner and door so the enemy can no longer open it, or wire someone's gun to a trap door right under them.   Each of these add to the feeling of a puzzle of the level.  Often you are limited in what you can wire, until you wirejack more and more access panels, and over time you unlock almost everything in the level.
Of course if you want to just kill everyone, you have the ability to pounce them and punch them to death, shoot them, or kill them with environmental features (rarely) .  It's your choice.
But the thing is, no matter what you do, the game just has a great fun feel to it.  With 2d pixel graphics, it wasn't going to win an award for them.  However what it does with those pixels and all the gameplay modes is impressive.  I felt more immersed in this game, than most of the big budget games that came out just because of the actions and abilities that required me to really look at what I'm doing rather than shoot and run.
One blessing for this game is the save system.  You can save the game, and you can restart the level.  But any time you want (or are forced to by death) you also get alternative saves.  3 saves, usually about 5 seconds apart. While sometimes this fails (I've had situations where the newest auto save is right before someone shoots me.  Most of these auto saves are "safe" moments, that rewinding to will give you a fighting chance (Before you set off an alarm, or shot a gun and was heard, or so on).  Overall the game allows you to rewind after a bad decision and change it.  It really enhances the puzzle aspect rather than punishing a risky move.
That only allows risky play.  Want to jump up on the ceiling to see if a guard will miss you, try it out.  The worst you'll lose is about 5 seconds of progress.  Want to jump through a window but didn't notice guard in the room.  Don't worry, you can try something else next time.
Overall the game just shines in that it rewards unique play styles rather than punishes the player.  Even better, there's a few really awesome moments in the game, but every level shines.  While it's a bit short (about 3 hours) it also is exactly the length it needs to be.  If it was 5-10 hours, I probably would have gotten bored of the repetition.   It is pricy for the time but it's also well worth the money.

Before I tell you about RimWorld, let me tell you a story that happened in RimWorld. It’s about that girl up there, drinking a beer. If you’re not convinced to jump in by the end of this tale, then we have nothing more to talk about. We can’t be friends. Everyone else: we’re still cool. So here it is, the story of Min, a pop star with a privileged upbringing, who is about to come crashing down to earth.
Min slept with all her animals around her. Since the crash, the 16-year-old pop idol was finding it hard to adjust. She would not help with heavy lifting, or farming, or pulling up weeds. The only thing she would do is take care of the colony’s animals. Rabbits, dogs, tortoises. She loved them all. She even formed a close bond with a rat, whom she named ‘Illness’.
But she wasn’t alone. In this game, you can create your own scenario before crash-landing onto the planet’s surface, adding or removing starter items (wood, steel, pelts, gold, widescreen TVs). You can also set the number of colonists and tweak dozens of other small rules, like compulsory character traits or rules about the planet’s climate. The game let’s you mould your scenario completely, right down to the flavour text.
As you can see, my five colonists had all escaped from a crashing party yacht. They were all rich, famous or both. A jeweler, a wealthy businessman, an ace fighter pilot, a star surgeon and (of course) Min the pop star. They all landed with severe hangovers. I am not kidding, this is a setting you can change.
Fast forward some weeks. The colonists had settled in. They had even survived their first few pirate raids. During one of these raids, they captured a large pirate with a low IQ called Ferdnand. This man was physically capable of nothing but sculpting statues and communing with animals. He was like Hodor with a paintbrush. FERDNAND! Eventually, we convinced him to join the colony.
I set him the task of taming a Megatherium – a huge and powerful ground sloth – so that the colony would have some extra muscle. But Min the pop idol was not having it. She had always been the colony’s animal trainer, and she had little ‘Illness’ to prove it. Spurned, she decided to take on the job herself. She left the safety of the village walls and approached the huge beast with some corn in hand. It went mad.
Ferdnand was already on his way to train his new would-be pet when he saw Min being savaged. He took out his Uzi and started firing with surprising accuracy. FERDNAND! Every shot landed. But the Megatherium turned and charged. By the time Ferdnand started to run, it was too late. The animal ripped him to pieces and he died on the spot.
The other colonists formed up. They lured the beast into the walls, where they riddled it with bullets until dead. The colony’s nudist surgeon (who weeks ago had experienced a mental breakdown and now did everything naked to keep himself happy) rushed out to rescue Min, who was lying in a bloody heap, writhing in unbearable pain. He took her to the clinic, wrapped her in bandages and made sure she got everything she needed – medicine, food and rest.
Well, maybe not rest.
You see, I had already scheduled the clinic’s floor to be renovated during this time. And as Min slept (or tried to sleep) my other colonists were busy ripping up planks and replacing them with shiny while tiles, sending sparks and wood chips everywhere. The noise was unbearable. Min snapped.
Crazed with pain and lack of sleep, she went berserk and chased everyone out of the clinic. She terrorised the dinner guests in the common room, and pursued them into the garden, where she chased them around. When she couldn’t catch the colonists, she turned on the animals – hares, pigs and rats – punching the poor creatures to death in her rage, ignoring the scratches and bites she got in return. Ignoring her old friends.
Finally, a colonist stepped up, walking up to the rampaging diva and knocking her out cold. When Min came to, she was back in the clinic. It was completely refurbished, clean and presentable. But the same could not be said for Min.
This once beautiful pop idol, who people would fall in love with before she even started to sing, was in tatters. She now had no nose, no left ear and no right arm.
Over the next two weeks she locked herself in her room and fell into terrible moods. She stopped handling the animals and was assigned to work only on sculptures. Her first work of art depicted a chicken vomiting on the shoes of a lawyer. I put it in the centre of her workshop.
One day, a ship appeared in orbit. They had items to trade. Among them was a prosthetic limb called a “power claw”. After some thought, I decided it was better than nothing. And besides, these rich castaways could afford it. The nudist was scheduled to do the surgery. Min was getting her arm back, even if it was a claw.
When she woke this time, she went straight to her room and locked herself in. I wondered what was wrong. It wasn’t until she was back at her post, carving new statues that I realised what had happened.
We had amputated the wrong arm.
Now, not only was Min a noseless, earless, armless monster, she also had a terrifying claw instead of her only remaining hand.
Welcome to RimWorld, where stories like this pointless tragedy are commonplace. It can probably best be summed up as: “the game for everyone who wanted to get into Dwarf Fortress but couldn’t because ASCII.” That’s not say it doesn’t have its own share of confusing menus. Supposedly there is a fluid teaching system but it seemed more to me like hints handed out at random. In the absence of a proper tutorial, it takes a lot of clicking and umming to understand why everything functions the way it does.
Let’s look at the colonists, for instance. For the most part, they run around of their own volition but you can still take direct control in a number of ways. When I said that Ferdnand took out his gun, I meant that I clicked on Ferdnand and clicked the “draft” button, putting him into military mode – something you’ll need to survive raids and attacks. But when I said he was already on his way to the gigantic animal, I meant he was heading to it autonomously, because it had been assigned to be “tamed” and he was a designated animal handler.
There’s a task grid that gives some order to it all. You can select which jobs you want each individual colonist to do and which jobs you want them to ignore. An advanced version lets you organise these even further by priority, fiddling with the numbers until you have each person specialised in a strict set of tasks. This is hidden away under “manual” control but it is something that soon becomes essential to learn.
It looks far more complicated than it is. And at any time you can just click on a colonist and right-click on something you want “prioritised” to have them commit to this instead of their job. It’s a bit fiddly but comes in useful in a pinch, for example, when someone insists on milking a cow in a burning barn instead of putting the fire out.
Building your settlement is a lot more straightforward. Prison Architect is the obvious inspiration for the way much of RimWorld’s construction and furniture placement works. You drag lines of walls made of wood, steel or stone until you have what you want, filling it with nice floors, beds, billiards tables, lamps and so on. Power is supplied by solar panels, windmills, wood-burning generators. And electricity is stored in batteries and disseminated by carefully laid power conduits. Sometimes these power cables like to explode, sending your whole colony into darkness and spoiling all the food in your freezer. Sometimes the batteries get wet and go on fire. Sometimes that fire spreads to your sleeping quarters and burns everybody to death. How whimsical!

Great game. No handholding beyond what is absolutely necessary for a tutorial. No catering to one particular type of player. No centralized economy (other than the currency, everything is regulated by other players only). Good enough players can play for free, though admittedly I've never been rich enough ingame to buy a PLEX (1 month of free game time to be used whenever you want). The GMs are actually fair, explaining things to new players and, in my case, personally messaging them to see if they need help.
Grinding is virtually nonexistant. Newer players will need to focus instead on getting player contacts and choose their skills, which are trained in realtime even while not playing (up to a week of being offline).
Older players can and WILL be knocked back to newbie status if killed and they haven't cloned, so the game isn't always dominated by the same guys with big guns.
Just pick your battles wisely. Death isn't the worst thing that can happen, and that's saying something, considering it's possible to lose months' worth of training for one death if you don't clone.

If you are sick and tired of reliving the same old sagas over and over again in other Dragonball games, then consider giving Xenoverse a try. The storylines have enough twists and "what if" scenarios to make it feel fresh. Is it the best Dragonball game though? Not necessarily. The AI kind of sucks and the character roster is smaller than other DBZ games. The game also plays more like a situational MMO instead of a fighting game. You have a main hub, then you go to different stations to pick up and participate in quests to level up enough to take on the next bit of the story. I didn't find the MMO-like gameplay an issue, but for fans of the DBZ fighting games, this may take some getting used to.
Despite the flaws, there are many good aspects about Xenoverse. The character customizer is awesome and having your character be an integral part of the DBZ story is very rewarding and satisfying. The character roster, while limited, still contains some good characters with fun movesets to experiment with. The voice acting is amazing, with most of the show's actors reprising their roles. Finally, this game is riddled with fan service that fans of the show will definitely enjoy.
Here's what I would like to see: TEAMFOURSTAR DLC!!! If you don't know these guys, they edit and redub DBZ to get the story across but in a shorter amount of time and with funnier dialogue. They have done an amazing job adapting DBZ into their DBZ Abridged series, so I would love to see what they would do using the alternate universe storyline in this game! I think it would be hilarious, and the actors who work at TeamFourStar deserve a lot more credit than they get.

Squad: Did you think that Project Reality was too janky? Here you go.
Realism is something that most first person shooters struggle with, attempting to balance it between "John Woo madness" and "PTSD inducing realism". And if you feel like having to duck from HMG fire and getting murdered by every flavor of AK rifle is fun, Squad is for you. If you've played Project Reality, which at this point at least 40% of PC users have given it's from 2005, you should be right at home in the mag pouch bedecked chest of Squad.

It's a game that gets past a lot of the janky movements that plague other realistic shooters like ARMA or PR without getting too small scale to forbid you from driving any of the vehicles that get parked in Insurgency. Back in the mid-90s I used to spend a little time in a "virtual reality" chat program called Alphaworld, which I suppose was a sort of early Second Life, but I rarely ever wanted to talk to people, instead preferring to wander around and look at creations and just explore. A few minutes of "playing" Proteus gave me exactly that feeling again; a sort of lazy and relaxed exploration that's enhanced by the otherworldly music you help create by walking through or near objects.
I found myself just spotting something in the distance and lazily wandering in that direction, idly coming up with a theory and then meandering off to some other interesting thing I saw on another hill. I'd love to see what this game would be like with something like the Oculus Rift; I expect it'd be wonderfully immersive and relaxing!
I'm recommending because I found it a beautiful, stress-relieving and thorougly relaxing experience that reminded me of something I used to do that I'd almost forgotten about. It's not something I'd "play" for hours, but a half-hour or so or meandering through beautiful, surreal scenary once in a while sounds great. Glad I picked Proteus up!

The title is as literal as it comes, perhaps second only to NZA 2 (read my review on -that- for more details) in terms of "It does what it says on the tin". Atom Zombie smasher is a variant on those old-school top down "Zombie outbreak simulator" programs that would show lots of little dots rushing around, some were coloured as civilians, and others as zombies, over time you'd watch the infection spread throughout the city, often leaving a small clump of survivors holed up in a dead end praying to survive just another few moments.
This is the logical conclusion of that program, it's a game and a campaign structured around the outbreak simulator program, with you tasked as the last remaining commander of the available defence forces, attempting to save as many lives (and smash as many zombies) as you can. To this end you're provided with a default escape helicopter, and gradually introduced to the toolbox of mercenaries that accompany you over the course of the campaign.
The game runs two distinct "beats", the first is the strategic map, a somewhat procedurally generated vision of a large city with lots of sub districts. This map operates on something of a turn based mode, so at the beginning of a given month, the zombie AI places outbreak counters on various districts, you then select a district to fight in, and depending on the outcome the district is either still infested, cleared out, or reclaimed and made safe for humanity. So far so normal, it's important to note however that whilst you only get ONE district to fight each month, the outbreak AI gets two, and eventually three counters to use, you're fighting a losing battle overall.
However, on the upside, you -do- get some tools at various points, in the strategic map the two major events are access to a prototype cannon (Elephantbird) that allows you to utterly eradicate a district in the tactical mode (more on this shortly), and llama bombs, which essentially decontaminate a bunch of districts in one pass, buying you much needed breathing room. Outside of this, you'll be assigned a squad of mercenaries (randomly selected from the available pool), and you'll get to choose a district to "go tactical" on.
This is where the outbreak simulator program is most visible, in the tactical mode you're presented with a moderately simple top down view, with civilians represented in a sortof beige yellow, zeds in purple, and your forces taking up various other colours. Left unchecked, the map will play out much like the software in question, and eventually all the survivors will be gobbled up, but you've tools to prevent this!
Before the tactical map kicks off, you designate your initial landing point for your rescue chopper (equipped with foghorn that automatically attracts nearby civilians), and you set up your various mercenaries. These range from single shot items like minefields, to ongoing and mobile defences such as infantry and snipers. Effective use and the setting up of choke-points can, if done right, result in you demolishing all the zombies before nightfall and scoring a hefty bonus (indeed, these bonuses, and saving lots of survivors is your path to victory).
The game really livens up once you've got explosives, with the map turning from an often pristine cityscape into a big brown muddy pit. Zombies exploding in clouds of green as your artillery rains down, remote dynamite detonations at key junctions reducing swarms of zombies into kibble, and your infantry protecting choke points and keeping the zeds away from the ever dwindling number of survivors. Once there are no more survivors to rescue, the scores are tallied up and you're returned to the strategic map. Learning how to adapt your tactics to an ever growing outbreak, and racing to the victory of humanity before the zeds inevitably take over forms the core of the campaign.
For a simple pick up and play title, it offers an excellent level of depth, combined with an offbeat and catchy soundtrack. The graphics are not much to look at, but they do the job functionally well (think of a 3D version of that outbreak simulator and you're pretty much there). It's very easy on the system requirements and provided you don't suffer any hiccups at launch, you'll have little complaint from the game. As a cheap impulse buy, it's hard to find fault and as such, comes very much recommended.

To be honest, I am just entering a review for for a giveaway contest entry.
With that out of the way, you probably know that RPG maker MV doesn't require programming knowledge, but it comes in handy, and also provides things such as a character maker to help you get started. (Said character maker is also much better looking than VX Ace's.) Also, native side-view battling is a new plus, and although enemies are not animated, I can understand how much development time that would eat up. You can publish your game for multiple platforms, not just windows. Basically, it's the RPG Maker everyone has been asking for, for years.

The plugin system is top-notch. It makes it incredibly easy to implement scripts that people create, and to temporarily disable them to bug-test. For those of you who hated the Rubyscript in RPG Maker VX and XP and etc... rejoice! Now it runs on the more commonly known Javascript. Also, the special plugins made for launch day are very nice.
On the other hand, as a very personal opinion, I hate the 'intuitive' mapping. You cannot control the layers, they just happen. The first tile you put done is layer one, second is layer two. You can't go back to change layer one without overwriting layer two. It's slightly improved from VXace, in that you can go three layers, but really I prefer how RPG Maker XP did things, with three layers and you switched between them on your own for maximum control and doing things that the tilesets were not intended for, but looked cool anyway.
There is also the assets themselves, the music is great, and character sprites and other graphics are pretty, however the tilesets are very blocky due to how autotiles are handled and leave much to be desired. Which, makes it stand out like a sore thumb against all the much better in-battle graphics, character portraits, and animations.
Lastly, making your published game into an android app is not too simple, but it can be done if you have the patience to make a game in the first place.
If you can get over those negatives, go for it. It's a solid engine.

This is the good ol' days, back when mission packs and DLC actually meant something! In fact it's almost as big as the original game itself!
Scourge of Armagon boasts new weapons such as the laser pistol and proxy launcher - useful tools when faced with limited options in some face-off scenarios. Example: you might be having trouble with scorpions. Answer: mine the corners with proxy grenades! And while the laser pistol is frowned upon by some (the kind that can't aim properly and end up shooting themselves with reflected shots), it can be a godsend on Nightmare difficulty, where enemies often start shooting as soon as you see them, and keep shooting ceaselessly, regardless of their gun's clip or shell capacity. Shooting reflected shots around corners could save your bacon.
As with Quake, you'll need Ultimate Quake patched in to enable the in-game soundtrack, and the tracks are good enough to be worth worrying about. They help to evoke a sense of atmosphere that the graphics may not be able to accomplish on its own.
All our favourite foes from Quake return (except its boss, for obvious reasons). New enemies include the gremlins and aforementioned scorpions, the latter of which will probably grief you the most. Other odds and ends include force bridges and shields, an actual boss

Crayon Physics + Peggle + Auditorium
Pleasant atmosphere, tricky but forgiving physics-based ricochet puzzles.
Droplets fall from a spawn point, and you must place straight lines on the screen to bounce the droplets toward the goal. Once a line has been placed, you move it around or fine-tune the angle by just moving an endpoint. There's no time limit, but you have a limited number of lines to draw per level, and you must hit the goal several times in a row to cement your success. Each zone adds a new twist (gravity effects, etc). Successfully completing a level adds to your stock of "golden lines" which can be used once-per level if you need more than the provided number of lines. Many of the levels can be beaten "under par" for added challenge.
I'm a sucker for the glowing crystal aesthetic used here; the visual & sound designs are clean and pleasant, and the ambient background tones make it a relaxing puzzle experience.

I'm not a big fan of the tower defense genre, but PixelJunk Monsters has a unique appeal that kept me coming back for more.
The system of unlocking, building, and upgrading towers is simple, but not so much that it becomes boring. All necessary information is clearly conveyed to the player, which is very helpful. In addition to currencies and remaining villagers, you can see upgrade statuses of all towers, and their ranges. You can even see which type of enemy is attacking next, and how long you have until they do.
Unlike many tower defense games, enemies never attack your towers, they only go after your villagers. This makes the game less stressful than other tower defense games.
Towers get experience from kills and from you dancing under them. This experience will upgrade them over time, or you can spend gems (which drop from random enemies) to skip to the next upgrade level. Each tower starts at green, and upgrades to yellow, red, purple, and finally black.
The campaign is fairly long; it took me around 20 hours to complete all levels on the three main islands. Replayability is decent, with challenges, Steam achievements, higher difficulties, co-op mode, and a fourth island that includes randomly generated maps.
The downsides are the occasional difficulty spikes and the clunky tower selection spinner. The game also doesn't do a good job of explaining how towers are upgraded, which is why I explained it above.
Don't let the cute characters and pleasant music deceive you, this game can be tough.

Back in the mid-90s I used to spend a little time in a "virtual reality" chat program called Alphaworld, which I suppose was a sort of early Second Life, but I rarely ever wanted to talk to people, instead preferring to wander around and look at creations and just explore. A few minutes of "playing" Proteus gave me exactly that feeling again; a sort of lazy and relaxed exploration that's enhanced by the otherworldly music you help create by walking through or near objects.
I found myself just spotting something in the distance and lazily wandering in that direction, idly coming up with a theory and then meandering off to some other interesting thing I saw on another hill. I'd love to see what this game would be like with something like the Oculus Rift; I expect it'd be wonderfully immersive and relaxing!
I'm recommending because I found it a beautiful, stress-relieving and thorougly relaxing experience that reminded me of something I used to do that I'd almost forgotten about. It's not something I'd "play" for hours, but a half-hour or so or meandering through beautiful, surreal scenary once in a while sounds great. Glad I picked Proteus up!

PROS:

TL;DR --
If you like to meditate, but you have trouble doing it the old-fashioned way 'cuz you have, like, ADD or something (like me), or you end up falling asleep instead, THIS IS FOR YOU. Quake Mission Pack 1: Scourge of Armagon is the first official expansion pack for Quake, developed by Hipnotic, aka Ritual, and released in 1997, few months after original. It focuses on single-player portion of the game, bringing not only new levels but new elements as well, making it the first id software related expansion that doesn't suck.
Like original Quake, Mission Pack uses CD to play it's own soundtrack. And since Steam doesn't include it, you will have to go and find it somewhere. And then you will have to go through trouble of implenting it properly with _inmm if you have Windows Vista or higher, so music properly loops.
As usual, game allows you to choose if you want to play with software or OpenGL rendering. You probably should stick with software one, as it kinda looks less muddy and OpenGL one has some bugs. Like no overly-high lighting or no full-bright textures for light sources.
When you launch the game, don't forget to write "+mlook" in console, to enable mouselook.
There is also bug of sorts where you will not be able to select game's new weapon - hammer. It's supposed to be on "0" weapon slot, but it doesn't seem to be binded to any key. You can fix it by writing "bind 0 "impulse 226"" in console.
Plot of Scourge of Armagon goes: You arrived back into military base after defeating final boss of Quake. Yet it's too quiet and you read from console that base was sealed as reinforcements of Quake still keep coming through portal. So you decide that you should travel to another dimension once again and put a stop to it, somehow.
Then again, wasn't "Quake" a codename for final boss you just defeated? It confuses me slightly. But I guess we can blame all these monsters on surviving member of Quake's order.
Anyway, proudly and couragely, the mission pack throws atmosphere and abstarct level design into trash bin, instead bringing more realistical approach. You got to play through 15 levels or so divided into 3 linear episodes. Futurustic base one puts improves on original base levels of Quake, which felt a bit wasted. More looking like real places and it adds a new enemy for sake of variety too. Then come nest two episodes down in strictly medieval and then "ancient-runes" themes. And this is where I think that game drops the ball. Not only themes aren't that much interesting, but more realistical level design means less interesting level layouts.
It's kinda funny. Times ago when I did a walkthrough on Quake games, I prefered this approach over original. Maybe was more interesting this time around. But as I rebeat game recently, I was missing more abstract and complex approach of Quake.
Not to say that level design is completely flat. No, it's quite good. Got interesting pieces. Like graveyard theme. When you also have to enter coffin to exit the level.
Engine also got updated to allow things like rocks rolling down the slope, trying to kill you. Or force bridges. And levels use some scripted levels here and there. And sometimes they are build in such way, that you are very likely to get hit without ability to avoid it. Like, spawning thunder-throwing monster in open area.
As said, it also doesn't have same atmosphere. Now with brighter maps and with new rocking soundtracks, it's call for action. I don't get the same grim feeling. Something that made Quake unique. Not sure if I dig new music, but most people do.
And yes, it introduces new monsters and new weapons. Weapons are gimmicky thigns that weren't needed to begin with. Like, grenade launcher that throws mines that stick to the surface. They are quite weak for mines and it's more fun to just shoot into face than expect for monster to find a path toward place where you are hiding. Or it got laser cannon and hammer, that waste same ammo as Lighting gun of Quake and once again, seem to be not-so-needed variations. Laser can bounce off walls, but it's mostly there to hit you back. At least hammer is useful without ammo as it can gib zombies.
And yea, new monsters. Scorpions, tough enemies that increase variety in base levels, strafe here and there and shoot nails at you on the floor level. And gremlins, who behave like monkey and just have some gimmicks like stealing your weapons or spawning more of them by ripping corpses apart. Shame that they killed faster to really consider those things. And new flying organic "mines" don't make sense. They increase speed when you aren't looking and are usually put in such way that you will be unaware that one is behind you. Just no idea aside from making you reload a save.
Oh, and it got a new final boss. Who isn't gimmicky and is proper one, unlike final boss of Quake. So it's better. If forget that he will die under half a minute from all the ammunition that player was given by that point. Still better.
Actually, if you wished Quake to have more of Doom atmosphere in grey-brown setting while having more realistical level design, that majority of gamers prefer over abstract, then this mission pack will be better than Quake itself. But if you liked original Quake, then eh, it doesn't get all things in same way.
I am actually surprised that I didn't like it as much in recent walkthrough as I did years ago. But oh well.

Atom Zombie Smasher was one of the more addicting experiences I have had in awhile. Each mission was intense and more than not, brought you to the brink of barely surviving.
The gameplay mechanics are solid, and your selection of power ups are your saving grace in most cases, though I found the basic setup strategy to still be key. Many missions however felt as though there wasn't a lot of room for experimentation on your strategy, but rather one particular set of placements would be the only route. This may have just been a personal experience, but it was observed anyhow.
My only complaint, or maybe this was intention, so instead should be a compliment was the Over Map and the constant "Won the battle, losing the war" feeling you got. It was incredibly difficult to determine which event to tackle next as you always knew that even if that battle was won, the odds were stacked against you overall on your return back to the over-map.
I would still recommend giving this a go if you're a hardcore strategy fan. Although the graphics and presentation aren't awe-inspiring, the atmosphere and stylization work for this game.That coupled with solid mechanics make this a good title to round out your Steam Library.

I have only played a fraction of what this game has to offer so far. And already, I think its fantastic!
Do you like the Wild-West/Sci-fi universe of Firefly?
Do you like base building games?
Do you like stories that dont all have a happy ending?
Do you like a good mix of combat and base building?
If you answered yes to all or any of the above, you will enjoy this game.
And that is this games charm... Its more flexible than an Olympian acrobat. You can go down the almost exclusive route of base building. Or you can go down the dark and perillous route of death and destruction. And there are even in-betweens.
Also, you have different AI storytellers to choose from each with their own way of introducing story elements (random events) into the game One, eases you into things, makes you complacent before bashing you over the head. Another, plays it cool and lets you chill, build your base, and enjoy the occasional event. And then there is one who will be completely random. You will never know what your gonna get next, if anything. And all of these AI's will tailor their stories to the difficulty level you choose.
And be under no illusion, you will get a story. There will be cheers of joy, tears because you lost Beatrice your best sharpshooter and more than I could ever write.
And each time you play, you will get a different story.
This game does something else well, people. Your characters, their personalities show. And there are a plethora of personalities. When i say about losing Beatrice, above, I mean it. if you play long enough, you start to get attatched to them. You will want them to survive.
Then there is playstyle. This game offers something quite fun. A decision about what sort of settlement you want to run. Do you want to be wandering traders? Heartless bandits? Peaceful townfolk who just want to live their lives? Or nomads?
You can do it. All of them. Pick who you want your faction to be.
Because, you see, you're not alone on that planet. There are many other settlers. Many other factions. Some will hate you some will be okay with you, some may even think your awesome. And then there are bandits who generally hate you to some extent.
And the planets, oh the planets. When you begin your game you will choose a planet 'seed'. It will create a randomly populated planet. You pick where you want your settlement to be and then generate your settlers.
But that planet is not generic. You can change it so its a desert like planet. A tropical planet. Or something more temperate. And these planets have ecosystems. Some places wil have differing growing seasons for planting crops and the like. Some places will differing populations of fauna. and so on. And it all makes sense. The equator has hottter regions. the more north/south you go it gradually gets temperate, then colder. Until you meet the ice-caps.
But enough gushing! Does this game have its negatives?
Well of course it does.
The system, the controls do take some getting used to. And the tutorial is okay, but finishes too quickly, leaving you with so many questions.
Some things rely far too much on you looking them up either in the in-game help bar. or the Wiki. I'm not against wiki's at all. But I feel like i shouldnt have to looks some of these things up. They should be in a tutorial, if not
tutorial.
There are some things that will not quite make sense, from a logical point of view. A recent one I discovered was steel being used to create sand-bags.
That being said, this is still an Early Access game. I know, i know, people are tired of hearing that. But in this case its warranted. The game is fully playable with no bugs that i have encountered yet. If all i have to worry about is a few odditites, then it can't be that bad.

Lowglow is a tale about restoring light to the world. As the last surviving member of your species, you must traverse an area, bringing light back to it, while harnessing the lowglow. At the end is the Darkness who must be defeated at all costs.
Lowglow is a very relaxing puzzler that takes you on a journey of physics while introducing some fun mechanics along the way. The music is very calming and can even bring you out of a rage after playing Linea, the game. :P
Music: Extremely calming and relaxing. For a change, I didn't put anything else on in the background. I was very soothed by it and even when I was having issues getting the puzzles right, I didn't mind because the sound effects and music were just so peaceful. This was right after playing Linea, which is highly rage inducing, so that is a consideration in how calming the music is.
Graphics: Fairly simple, but well designed for what it is. Not much more than what is presented is needed. Nothing is too intense, and it also helps to create a rather peaceful atmosphere.
Story: Pretty simple. Not very deep or exciting, but then this is mostly a puzzle game. I would have been fine without a story to be honest. But that it has one at all, is just a bonus.
Controls: Mouse driven. Nothing else is really needed. Easy to work and is intuitive.
Gameplay: Pretty simple, bounce the light to the end goal. Using physics and some mechanics you'll get it there. The game slowly introduces new ideas in each chapter and they are fairly easy to understand, but a bit harder to master.
Overall: 7.5/10 - Seriously as a nice calming puzzle game, this game is really good. I thoroughly enjoyed myself over the course of several hours. While I haven't 100%'ed it yet, I have beaten the main story and look forward to going back and mastering the rest of the levels. Once you complete the game, there are extra bonus levels to complete. The base price of $8 honestly isn't a bad thing. I mean, sure you could get it on sale for cheaper, but it's not a bad way to spend your money, just know that it has been bundled before.

So after spending 20+ hours playing the game over the past few days and working my way up through the game with a friend, I finally reached level 150 and decided I should review the game. (Excuse the terrible grammar, I'm half asleep)
Characters:
There are 12 possible classes/characters to play (5 of which are locked as they're DLC) and each of them feels very different from the last. If you want to play a melee character, you can choose between Viking, Fallen Paladin, Nomad, Samurai, Demon Hunter and Redneck (I may have missed some), each feeling nothing like the last. Every class has it's own set of skills and abilities that drastically alter how you play and make each character feel like a new experience.
Progression:
Although the game doesn't have any noticeable story to it, it's still a lot of fun to play through Classic mode and slaughtering mobs and bosses galore. There's 7 acts, each with 5 stages and a boss fight, dungeons to explore, quests to complete and so much more stuff to do that adds plenty of replayability. Upon beating all 7 acts on Normal, you unlock the next difficulty and can play through it again to continue leveling. If you don't like the repetitive "grinding" from beating the acts over and over, you can always break it up by playing Siege mode.
Siege mode:
Now as great of an idea as Siege mode is, the devs went about the execution of it quite poorly. If you want to level up a lot faster, slaughtering endless waves of mobs over and over is a great way about it, which is where Siege mode shines. But my issues with it are how as soon as you get beyond wave 20, the game feels like someone just slowed it down by 75% and it becomes really annoying to play. One of the ways I found to counter this (though not by much) is to collect all the money and items that drop, reducing the amount of entities cluttering the screen and hindering performace. (Suggestion to the devs should any of you ever read this: have items be removed automatically after 5 waves, as 100 inventory slots is nowhere near enough to push high waves AND collect everything)
Multiplayer:
First off, I'd like to say I'd still much rather play Multiplayer despite all the bugs than single player, as I can understand why it is so buggy, what with a small 3 man dev team and it being an indie game. The game has an excellent multiplayer mode that I'd reccomend playing over single player to anyone new to the game. There's regional chat rooms (all be it spammed with racist, homophobic, degrading, sexist comments and just generally spammed way more than it should be), simple to use server listing and a fairly good multiplayer experience. When you start playing with a friend and you're not the host is when you start to see issues though. Things like taking considerably less damage than the host (to the point me and a friend with almost identical stats play together and what 1shots me barely even scratches him), desync between host and players during dungeon puzzles making it so almost every puzzle has to be done individually, problems with passive skills not working properly if taken when not host, item drops being hugely host biased and giving them much better drops than others.
Overall, I'd give this game a 7/10. If you love playing Diablo or similar loot based ARPGs, Hero Siege is an amazing indie game that costs next to nothing and still provides enough content to easily play for 1000 hours. Although the multiplayer is buggy, it's still fairly new and only has a small team of people working on it so it is fully understandable. My only issue with the game is how DLC is almost essential for endgame. I've enjoyed my first 22 hours, I'm looking forward to the next 100+ and I can't wait to see what future updates bring.

Move or Die is a simple enough concept. However, it still goes beyond my common nature to not stand still when I’m safe in a platforming versus game. I had managed to “hot potato” the bomb away from myself and it seemed like the other three were very content with passing it back and forth between each other. I was fine with that too and then it was down to myself and the last guy. I was on the opposite side of the screen and got to the highest perch in the level. Knowing he didn’t have enough time to get to me, I sat back and laughed at my all-to inevitable victory… and then I lost. I exploded because I stopped moving. I then face-palmed myself because that is what the whole point (and name if you didn’t catch it) of the game.
I believe the worst part of all of this was that I was showing the game off to some friends and explaining how you play when this happened. The game doesn’t stop there though. While you may lose health if you stand still, you also can’t get health back when jumping. You still need to obey the laws of the levels too! I'd like to preface this review by reccomending the Borderlands Advanced Configuration Tool, this allows you to tweak the settings to make the game look even better than it does, as well as allowing for FOV tweaks, command console, etc.
This is the game that started it all, something about all the loot you can pick up just tantalized an entire group of gamers who felt like Pandora was a second home. This game isn't as story rich as Borderlands 2, and is a little rough around the edges in some spots, but it is still such a great game that everyone needs to play.
The little bit of story there is is that Pandora is home to the Atlas corporation, who make the crap planet even crappier, and there are legends of "Vaults" around the planet, and this draws in Vault Hunters looking for them. You essentially compete with the corporations to open the Vault, you get all the pieces of the key and open it, that's as spoiler free as I can make it.
This game's claim to fame was the absolutely obscene amount of guns it has, I've heard this game talked about as more of a experiment to put this many guns into a functioning game, and as such is why the story is as lightweight as it is, and Borderlands 2 was a more proper game utilizing the technology. You have a choice of 4 heros, a Berserker, a Siren, a Soldier, and the Hunter, each of these classes have their own traits that make them unique, but no class is restrained to a certain weapon type.
When I said the game can be rough around the edges, I mean that in that there are some bits of the game that are poorly executed and pretty frustrating, they are mainly little things, like the lack of checkpoints in some areas, forcing you to run back through the empty area to get back to the boss, and the game forcing you to kill bunches of enemies before you can pass through an obstacle you could have passed through easily. One last annoying bit is how Claptrap seems to infinitely remind you that there are new jobs available on x Bounty Board.
One of this games strongsuits is the humor, most every character has some sort of thing about them that makes them unique and funny. My personal favorite is Scooter the car guy.
All in all, out of the 3 main series Borderlands games, this is the second best. Better than the dumpster fire that is the Pre Sequel, but not as good as the masterpiece that is Borderlands 2, overall I give it a 9/10, do yourself a favor and play it now.

PixelJunk Monsters Ultimate is a tower defense game. But it has a few interesting little catches. Along with the standard assortment of enemies that have varying characterstics and towes to counter those characterstics, this game has you playing as a character. You character moves around the screen and must be in position to build towers. You build them over trees, so there's a limit to how many you can have and where they can go. By standing on them, you can slowly uprade them over time. So is it worth it to stand on a tower for a long time, or run off to build another? Which tower is important to upgrade first? How much should you upgrade it? It makes for a more frantic, involved experience and a new way to strategize. You can also upgrade towers with gems that enemies sometimes drop. These can be used for instant updrades to tower, or can unlock more bonuses and tower types by going back to your base and purchsing them. More strategy to plan out. Fallen enemies also drop coins, which you use to purchase the towers you build. Sometimes running through trees will have them randomly drop coins or a gem.
Another cool feature is multiplayer. This allows each player to have their own pool of coins and move about on their own to cover more ground. You share your gems though, so be wise with them. This is a nice mode to make those trickier, more frantic levels a little easier to handle. And basically, you have another body out there to camp on tovwers to upgrade them.
The problems I have with this game are the waves, the difficulty, and the art direction. The waves are nonstop. So you never get any time between waves to rest, collect fallen items, or set up towers. You have to do it all on the fly. And if you had a rough wave prior, you'll be starting the next wave before even a moment's rest. It's just not the kind of tower defense I like, but I assume it's to account for standing on towers to upgrade them. Still, they could've disabled that betwen rounds but... maybe it's for the flow. The difficulty seems to ramp up really fast. You need to make new strategies I supposed, but I was getting destroyed a few levels in. Maybe I'm just bad, so consider that as well. And the art direction is... nice at first but samey after a while. Seems like a lot of reused stuff copy and pasted around. Not a big deal but can wear on you spirits and your eyes after a bit. At least the music is cool and soothing to help counter that a bit.
I'll honest, I got this game in a bundle for free. I kept it and played it for the trading cards. I don't mind the single player, but multiplayer really made me enjoy this game a lot more. It is worth the ten dollar price tag? I'd say not. Maybe wait for a sale to get it cheap. A few bucks wouldn't be bad but... I think at most you'd want to look kat about 3. Just my opinion though.
PixelJunk Monsters Ultimate gets a 5/10 for being a decent tower defense game with a few neat features, but lacks a bit of effort and polish in areas. Worth checking out if you're into the genre.

This is a game where you slowly walk around while soothing electronic noises sedate you.  If that sounds interesting to you, you should try it.
Proteus has garnered a lot of praise as an art game, but the "art game" genre is so young that virtually every entry in it is guaranteed decent reviews.  Personally, I suspect that this is because game reviewers, who are more accustomed to reviewing the sort of conventional pulp titles that built the industry, are afraid that giving a negative review to a game like Proteus might make them look stupid.
But honestly, this game isn't some kind of artistic masterpiece on any level.  The player slowly walks around in a simplistic, dull, and mostly static landscape while sleepy electronic sounds are dynamically generated by the player's surroundings.  Sometimes, the season will change, and new sounds will play.  It feels more like a palliative treatment for patients recovering from severe brain damage, and it is difficult for me to believe that even its most ardent supporters have honestly enjoyed playing it for more than 30 minutes.  Personally, I checked out around 12 minutes.

Atlantis: Pearls of the Deep is a match 3 game which uses physics. Much like in another game by the same studio, League of Mermaids, you clear boards by dropping coloured pearls on top of existing pearls. A match of 3 (or more) will clear it and gradually empty the board.
Boards are not just rectangular pits but are of very different sizes and include obstacles such as gears, rotatable platforms, or balls which must be unlocked first. There are multiple upgrades, which have to be earned by clearing boards with 1 to 3 stars, 3 being best. You earn stars by doing optional objectives on each board which range from clearing it within a specific time, clearing all pearls instead of just the ones containing items, or collecting additional star objectives.
Every five levels the gameplay is broken up by a simple hidden object game where you need to find shells, sea-horses, gems and the like.
There is a story, which is told by static images. It didn't interest me at all but it doesn't hurt either.
Copying from my review for League of Mermaids here:
If you're still not sure what this game is like, think of a cross between Bubble Bobble, Peggle, and a basic match 3 game. Add some relaxing music and cute graphics, and you have Atlantis.
If I were to have to pick between the two, Atlantis currently gets my selection since it has more variation in gameplay than Pearls.

TL;DR: If you want to make an RPG, this is the latest and most flexible offering from the RPG Maker series. But its going to take some work.
I've been using RPG Maker since RM2k, and while changes have been made with each iteration, some for better some not so much, I have to say, RPG Maker MV has made a lot of changes for the better, as well as brought back wonderful things from the past.
Pros;
Simple but powerful database system.
Decent selection of RTP Resources to get you started on your first game.
Multiplatform Capabilities [Windows, Mac OSX, Android/iOS Windows Mobile, its all possible, though Mobile platforms take some extra work.]
Wonderful and supportive community!
Cons;
Deceptively Difficult, yes, I said it was simple in the Pros section, but without your own creativity, you will get stuck. It's easy to use, the hard part is, what are you going to use it for?
Somewhat limited base engine, but this isnt a brick wall limittion.
Database is pretty barren to start.
What to expect; Expect to spend considerable amount of time testing, planning, writing, sketching, doodling, dreaming, talking, laughing, crying, yelling at the computer, wondering wtf went wrong, wondering wtf went right, reading the documentation, asking for help. AND MORE!
Things to help you get started;
Join the community: No seriously, we exist outide of steam, and have existed for a long time. MV specifically has a budding and great comunity happing at htt[://
[yes .co]
Once you've joined the community, talk to us, we're here to help.
Get on youtube! Seriously, there are TONS of videos on youtube for this thing already.
And personally, id like you to understand from the beginning Yanfly, and Akashics are going to be your favorite people, and quickly.
go there, see what he has, for you, for free, for RPG Maker MV plugins. Watch his videos, play with the stuff he is releasing, and if you like it, and have a few coins to spare, seriously, support him on his patreon. Akashics is an artist working with yanfly releasing free to use art assets currently in the form of enemies, and I hear theres even more on the way. You can find his stuff at
If you decide to come join us, welcome aboard. We hope you enjoy starting on the road to making your own RPG.

Move or Die is a party game for up to 4 players, it supports both online multiplayer, and local multiplayer. The game
is the best party game I've ever played, and here's why:
The game has a completely unique mechanic, which is also the title of the game: Move or die. You have a health bar on the bottom of the screen, which depletes
when you do not move, and will result in your death in the moment of it reaching 0%. as long as you move, it will not deplete. The mechanic is really fun
and changes gameplay entirely, because you have to move all of the time, resulting in you having to be careful in various game mode to keep moving, but don't
get killed by the various hazards.
There's currently about 10 Various game modes in the game, with more planned in free content updates after the game gets released.
I'm going to give a small summary of the game modes:
Sugar Rush - A few candies (Always smaller by 1 of the current players. Ex. 4 Players, 3 candies) spawn in a random part of the map, and you have to get one as quickly as possible, otherwise the candies will be eaten by other players, and you'll die. To get to the candy, you can either use the routes through the map, or the various teleporters to get somewhere quicker, you kind of need to be strategic to know which path will be the shortest to the candy.
Chainsaw Backstab - You have a chainsaw and you need to backstab someone using it. If you hit someone else's chainsaw, both of them will fly towards a wall and you'll have to get it back. If you do it quickly, you can do it before the other player and be able to quickly stab them.
Vertigo - All of the platforms are falling, and you need to keep jumping on them to not touch the red death tiles on the bottom of the screen (There's a variation of the map where the whole map is surrounded by red death tiles) The longer the round goes on, the quicker the platforms will fall.
Color Craze - Color as many tiles as you can in your color. If a player touches a tile which has already been colored, the color will be overrided with the one of that player. You need to be strategic in order to make a lot of the blocks the same color as yours.
Jump Shot - You get a shotgun which you have to use to shot the other players. But you can only shot when you're jumping, and your jumps are complete flips, so you have to get the timing right. Or just stand near a player and keep jumping and shooting and hoping for the best.
Cleanup Crew - The wall behind everyone is covered in color, and you have to clean as much as you can in order to win. You need to be strategic and take the best path in order to clean the most.
Bomb Tag - The Friendship Ruining Game.
Stomp - Jump on the head of another player in order to stomp them and kill them. Can't get much simpler than that.
Ghost Scare - You and the other players are transparent. The only way to know where the other players are is their steps GFX effect, and you need to scare them before you in order to win. You can actually scare someone here by taking an unexpected path, and scaring them.
Rocket Run - A rocket is chasing you, and will explode just a few short moments after you get close enough to it.. You have to use the gravity in order to get away from the rocket, or use the teleporters which is more riskier.
All of the gamemodes, as simple as they sound, are changing the way the game is played completely, and they're all completely fun, and guaranteed to ruin lots of friendships!
Another great addition to the game level up system. When you play an online game, or do the daily challenge, you get some experience points, and after you get a set amount of it, you level up and get a completely random item, it might be a gamemode, it might be a new character, maybe even a Pumpkin! If you play TF2, think about it this way: The Crates being opened without having to waste real money, and you not having to be disappointed that you got something bad which is worth less than 3 cents.
All of the items are tradable and marketable, so for example if you got a duplicate character, you can sell it on the market, or trade it with a friend for their pumpkin.
The LVL system is a really great thing, and gives yet another reason to play this wonderful game. The only negative of this in my opinion, is the EXP required to level up after reaching level 12. The amount of XP required after getting LV 12 is always 120, which is quite a lot. You need to play a match lasting 30 minutes to just level up a single time.
In Local Games, all Gamemodes are unlocked for the start, which is great for the players who don't like playing online, but only with real friends or family.
MoD is also really easy to mod, depending on the thing you're doing. You can easily make a map with the Level Editor, create a new character using the provided resources. The game has already a few great mods at the moment of writing this, and it will only become better!
The developers of the game were actively taking user feedback, and changing things basing on them. In other words, Early Access done right.
TL;DR: The game has a lot of various gamemodes where each changes the way you play completely, while keeping the base formula of "Move, or you will die" intact. The developers are nice and will put free content updates for the game, a nice level up system to get various characters and game modes, and it can guarantee a single thing: It will ruin friendships! :Djoe:
I cannot recommend this enough, if you like playing party games, this one will be definitely perfect for you, and you'll definitely have lots of fun, and lost friendships!

Lowglow is a very interesting laid back affair that caught me by surprise.
This is a puzzle game in which you draw lines and that's... basically it. Each stage is set up so that there is a max number of lines to be drawn in order to accomplish the goal. Which in the case of this game is to get a glowy bit into a blackhole repeatedly. It's not enough to get just one you need to get multiple in and additionally they need to be successive.
The lines you draw are bouncy and they fling the glowy bits relative to their polarity. There are gems. Lets call them gems, I'm not really sure what they are called. But they exist as obstacles in the stage. Their color has great significance as everything starts as blue. Pulling the glowy bits toward the bottom of the screen. The glowy bits adopt the last color gem and its properties that they have touched. There is also yellow, red and green. Yellow, as you might have guessed pulls the glowy bits up. Red, cancels the or destroys the glowy bits. Green however, not seen until later stages has no arc and go strait. So as stages get more intricate you must take into account the changing properties of the glowy bits.
There is also some strange narrative thrown in the form of gods being left in the dark and some pylons needing to be re-lit to recover the city or world. These are told in the form of some, being honest, creepy faces that float ambiguously in the sky and speak in very low incomprehensible dulcet tones. Of course that is on purpose as there is text directly underneath.
I found the game to be extremely relaxing as there is no timer or no penalty for moving, changing reshaping or destroying lines. As the glowy bits recede and cascade across the gems into the night that make it a very ambient “wind chime in space” effect that is rather pleasant in that when making minor adjustments to your lines is very soothing not not all taxing. The game is instead scored by how many lines you use to accomplish your task. There are on some stages the chance to obtain “golden lines”. There are a finite number of these and should you use one of them in a difficult stage you lose it forever. The game says something to the affect that they remain there forever which scared me to use them at all because I didn't think I could readjust them but you indeed can. However once the stage is complete you loose the golden line. The only real loss is that these golden lines are also used for unlocking bonus stages outside the city.

This can be counted as all the more surprising since it was made out of Borderlands, a game series well known for having little story and almost no dialogue driving you through it.  While the game uses Borderlands as a IP to base its world off of, it requires no knowledge of the IP.  In fact, I'd encourage someone with no knowledge of the FPS games to play this one, as their ignorance of it will leave them more entertained and surprised by what happens.  The dialogue and presentation are flawless, the choices you can make keep playthroughs fresh and are funny and interesting enough to encourage you to replay the game without making it feel like a chore.
The gameplay follows Telltale's signature system of making decisions which then influence dialogue and further choices you can make later in the game.  I feel this game highlights this design best as the way the characters and world are written make you feel like everyone's ambiguous feelings on morality frees you to make any of the decisions at a whim.  This encourages replayability and you don't feel you have to make a decision you'd regret or feel bad about to see some of the game you never seen before.  So, you're more likely to see, and not be told by someone else, what consequences x or y decision had on the rest of the story.
Beyond that, puzzles are not difficult and involve exploring the screen for the next thing you click on to move, going through a dialogue tree, or finishing a quicktime event.  The mechanics are not there to challenge you, just provide a framework to express the story and cement the choices you make.
The world remains light-hearted even though the characters acknowledge how crap-sack it is.  This light-hearted tone makes serious tragedy hit you harder and have more of an emotional impact than you would otherwise expect.  You need only look to the other reviews and forums to see what everyone says about Loader Bot, Scooter, the protagonists to see how far people were drawn into these characters.
I've been invested and entertained enough to play through the story twice through already to see several of the decisions and dialogue choices I didn't make the first time through.  At no point while I was replaying did I feel I was forced to go through something and there was always enough new things to keep me playing.  I can not recommend this highly enough as Telltale's finest example of how they make their interactive fiction.

Well I was hoping it didn't come to this.But here is my review on Dragon Ball Xenoverse.
Overhyped,but only for PvP.Single player brings you to a story like nothing DBZ has seen before and for fans this is a great splash of refreshing story to the face.Allowing you to make your own character to protect time from distortions and villians that you may have thought only Goku has dealt with.Reality check:Wrong.
Goku fights some people but there are way more out there,way stronger than Goku.Some of which are coming for you.
I'm gonna do a simple list of cons and pros for this one as I don't want to explain in detail.I'm abit on th negative side but I'll be bias.
Pros:
-Great Story Line.Well thought out and utilizes the past DBZ story to it's advantage.You'll have to play to see how since anything I say would be a spoiler.
-Simple yet complex combat.Very easy to learn,yet very hard to use.
-Ki blast aren't as dodgable anymore.No more "ki attacks are all flash" or "line between noob and pro" when it comes down to it.
-Rush attacks must be done by you.They don't autolock and deal massive damage anymore.You even choose when you cancel some of them.Your opponent sometimes won't even know if your meleeing him or using a skill.
-Game doesn't advertise your attacks like it did in previous games.You truely have to pay close attention to your opponent to get a ege or for them off the edge.
-Colourful environments,with blending characters and textures.
-Your character is custumizable from clothing to skills or even colours (only some clothes though).
-Co-op is fun and well optimized.The ghetto open world allows you to split up to tackle some missions tactically for faster times.
-Tons of skills to go through.Literatly skills from every character in the game that can fight.Even Ginyu Force moves are usable.
-Loading times where?Game loads very very fast.I don't even get to sip my drink in most cases.
Cons:
-PvP is terribly unbalanced.
-laggy super sayian can easily spam ki blasts ultimates(cause super sayian gets endless ki)
-If the opponent is lagging and you get hit on their screen you are hit.Even if you clearly missed.
-Host has superior connection.Sometimes your blasts won't come out leaving you wide open.Only in PvP though.
-seemingly abyssmal droprates because why not?This game will make you farm for stuff until you quit.Mimicing a MMO's fustrating low drop rate over massive content.When you finally get what you want you'll ether quit or just abuse it in PvP for cheap wins.
-Ki blasts rule the game.NPC rarely to never dodges Ki-blast except GT saga,which still get hit often.Players usually die in 2-3hits from ki blasts.
-Defencive is a priority in this game.The loser is usually determined by the one who fails to space/run away and outgun the opponent with ki blasts or skills that zoom in close.Most fights are completely 1 sided because Just guarding,steping and dashing are far more effective than attacking and breaking guards or tricking you opponent.They get Super Armor when dashing on start up so they can literatly move out of the way of anything and out beat you by only punishing what you do.Aggression is actually the worse thing you can do against a defencive opponent.
-3minutes on the clock influances players to net a hit and play coy for time out on ranked and player matches alike.Like I said.If your agressive you'll spend all your time chasing and getting punished for trying to attack.Player with the superior spacing/zoning  is MORE LIKELY to win.Not promised.but high chance.
-Stats or style?Style gets thrown out the window when you realize that your cloths can dramatically boost your stats.It gives you 1/5 of your max stat usually toward  2-3 things.So endgame if your out for power you'll be aiming for effectiveness not style.Leaving all players to be wearing the same outfit for their type:Ki or melee.
-Race difference doesn't change much more than your stats and afew of your strong attack effects.Sadly this brutally effects your characters stats as well.Making you pick a certian race and gender to do what you like most.
-HUB world whoever designed this needs to be hung upside down.You run slllooooooowwwwww!Everything is so seperated and far apart.Everytime you do a mission you get thrown in the mission area the farthest away from the count that you could be.This wouldn't be a problem if you didn't run extremely slow.
-Last but not least [skills] will often be thrown out the window because power/effectivenes.Once you reach endgame you'll realize getting the skills you like won't cut it unless they are effctive.You'll always be butchered in PvP and the late game PQ will eat your soul because your skills aren't good enough.Skills like Gravity Impact will always be stuck on your set up because you don't just want them...you need them.This game's saddest downside is this.Skills I loved and wasted long periods of time farming became useless because they don't have good enough perks and effectiveness.So in the end you'll probably be using the same skill set as everyone else because those skills clearly outplay the other skills.
Trust me I wish I was being sarcastic.
In the end though I suppose I have to rate it.I give this game a 6/10.
Clearly less than the other dragon ball games in combat,it butchered its grogous history in that field for a rich,amazing storyline and co-op play.It's downsides don't appear very early on but as you progress the game slowly begins to show its true colours and it's a ether g cheap or go home scenerio.The fun of the game gets sapped away between the excessive day long farming and the fustrating abuse you'll cross playing players and ai alike.In which alot of scenerios heavily imply the abuse of Ultimate attack spam over actually learning to play the game and fighting smart.
This is a prime example of swallowing too much pride.Alot of people might rage at me for this review but in the end this is my opinion.I played all the races through.I tried out tons of skills and tactics posted online.I gave the game a competitive shot but it in the end became a Penthouse for 1trick ponies and unsatifying gimmicks.Such as "You'll be my first Victim" Z-soul,Super Vegeta 2 transformation and spamming Super Electrical storm,or any Z-soul with invincibility frames with a Super Sayian.
As for the good things I thoroughly enjoyed playing co-op with friends.Even farming with them was fun.Tons of fun twists and possibilities in story and quests alongside with having a master who gives advice and pulls you side for training after you fight alot.I heavily suggest this game for co-op/story of it because it's pretty well done despite the flaws I presented.
Much like it's little brother,Dragon Ball Z:Battle of The Z,this game has a potential I hope to see reached in the future.Until then,this is my review.Have fun :)

It's a neat concept for MMORPGs but the always-on PVP (PVP is enabled on every server and in every location in the game, even "newbie" areas) makes it virtually impossible to "break in" to the game.  Joining corporations (guilds) does help a little but the war system means that other corporations can declare war on yours and you're fair game everywhere meaning that, until you've spent a very long time getting higher-end spaceships (even if someone gives you one  it takes weeks of training before you can fly it), you're stuck sitting in a station because you can be destroyed the second you exit.
Even outside wars, people sit at gates (how you travel between systems) and just destroy people randomly and, as a new player there's no way you can stand up to them.  It's not a terribly newbie-friendly game but if you don't mind spending months being completely outclassed by your attackers before you have a chance to fight back you may enjoy it as the mechanics are good.
If there is one thing about Gunpoint that can be legitimately scrutinized it is the fact that there is simply not enough of it to play.

I sadly cannot recommend this game, especially at its current price.
While I enjoy dragonball a great deal, and the game has a lot of offer in terms of story, characters, items, and combat, there is just too much wrong with it.
First of all, always online.  Even single player requires online, which causes lag spikes occasionally, and slow transistions.  Once I was able to play offline when the server was down, and there was a VERY noticable difference.
Next the meat of the game is the PQ or Parallel Quests.  These are where you will battle and grind up, and try to get hidden objectives to unlock special fights.  While I don't mind grinding, these are esentially broken.  More then half the time, the hidden objective that you worked so hard to obtain will not activate.  No better rank, no better chance at items, just level end with you very upset.
Last but not least is the production values of the game.  Some cutscenes have flubbed lines, your character has no speaking lines save for stock grunts and yells, and worst of all if you are playing a female character everyone referse to you as male.
These qualms will probably never be fixed, so if you want to spare your time and money, I sadly would suggest letting this game pass.

A game makers for those Brand new to Rpg Maker MV and using a Mac.
First before downloading it, I made sure my avast was turned off after reading about how some people had issues when they used Advast. After it was downloaded, I permitted Rpg maker mv to Avast  then turned it back on and have had no troubles at all with Avast or RPG Maker MV since I did that. I am unsure what would happen now if one did not do that but it's so simple to do, why not be sure?
I love to create things and RPG Maker MV is  the motherload of being able to create almost anything you can think of or imagine.
It's interface is simple to use -- I downloaded it, then jumped right in, not reading the help files.. and was able to start
a simple rpg game (one I call the Trials of Finding as I learn how to find and make the most of the tools provided by the game).  As I continue to build on this 'starter' game, I am able to improve my ablity to program events and it's easy to see the progression to simplicity  from complex beginnings. (I told you, never did this before.)
Always doing things the hard way (ie programing my first innkeeper and shopkeeper before I realized the game provided simple quick inclusion of these features) has improved my ability to problemsolve event building. I have so much more to learn and I am eager to do so.
The game comes with many sample maps found in the map creation interface under LOAD which I found about a week after beginning.  The tool tips at the mouse curser are very helpful but the Game Help file (located on the top menu bar) I didn't notice until I was directed to it and then actually used it. (it appeared non-functional to me at first glance) As I said, noobie at this sort of thing.   During self instruction, I tend to focus on items I want to know immediately and then branch out as I get more familiar with terms and proceedures.  I also watched many youtubes produced by folks willing to share their knowledge, and that was very helpful. Honestly, before I bought this game maker, I watched about 6 hours of youtube on this product and became more and more excited about what it could do.
RPG Maker MV appears very stable on my Imac and runs without lag  generally. I have found if I run it a long time creating many events and or very detailed maps, that it begins to lag (by long time I am talking 8+ hours without quitting from it)  HOWEVER, this lag vanishes if I just quit both RPGMaker and STEAM  then reopen both.  (Sounds like Ram to me).  I have had no other issues besides the ones I create myself attempting to add items or change item's names in the file program itself and then it's easy to undo what I just did as I keep an alias of the game files on my desktop.
If you are creative, and need an outlet, this program allows you to explore your sprite making, your storytelling, your ability to problemsolve, create art from tiles, perform and record your own music files/sound files and more.  I can't do even  half of what it's capable of yet but I am still planning ahead!
My only issue at this time is how to add the weekly additions to my my RPG maker. I have not been able to add to the character generator, but all other things are not difficult. My pathway does not seem to be the same as for a windows machine. I am not discourged, but I am still learning and it's not stoping me from creating for the sake of creating and my enjoyment.

After completing the original QUAKE, you may think you're the biggest bad♥♥♥♥♥this side of QUAKE-con. But after you play the first level of Scourge of Armagon, you realise you're wrong. You're actually just getting started.
This mission pack is lengthy and difficult and so is an absolute gift to QUAKE lovers and masochists alike. More challenging enemies, such as the brutal Scorpian robots and the weapon stealing Gremlins, combined with a handful of new and interesting weapons, like Mjolnir (That's Thor's hammer!) and a Prox-Mine gun, this mission pack injects new elements into a game that you may think you have mastered.
The long levels are a true test of the player's ability, especially on the Hard and Nightmare difficulties. If you are wanting to brave them, be ready for attrition against a rabbling horde of 180 enemies a level that are ALL more deadly than you.
It'll leave you sweating and battered, but no game is quite as rewarding when finished as QUAKE: Scourge of Armagon.
Recommended for Quake veterans and/ or people who want a challenge!
