One of the only Sonic Games that isn't a broken, Buggy mess, SASRT is a Kart Racer, And a rather unique one at that. You play as racers who operate vehicles that can transform into Car, Plane and Boat all depending on the area of track you are racing on. Tracks change over time, For example: A section of track that was traversed via Car previously may have been completely destroyed by the time you get to it on Lap 2 forcing you to transform into a Boat to traverse an entirely new section of track. Changing tracks aren't the only thing this game has to offer though, It features a Level-Progression system for characters that provide "Mods" at each level that provide single stat or multiple-stat boosts depending on which you choose. Mods aren't restricted to Racer Level though, You can unlock certain mods by playing through the game's Story-Like mode upon which you gain Stars depending on the level of difficulty you choose for certain set events, Meeting the difficulty requirements will net you stars and as you progress through the Story Mode you will come across Gates which unlock additional paths to progress in and Unlock Pads where you can unlock Story-Exclusive Character Mods and entirely new Characters to play as.
Having played this game on the Xbox 360 for an extremely long time i can safely say it's one of the best Sonic-Brand Games out there and while it has Bugs (As expected of a Sonic Game) it's nowhere near a state that i would call unfinished or broken.
It still remains my all-time favourite Kart Racer and with over 5,000 Hours logged on the Xbox 360 i doubt i'll ever grow tired of it.

200+ hours of play prior to adding to steam library. Overall the game is good but as all early access games it still needs balancing. There are a lot of misconceptions in these reviews so here are some tips that will hopefully help you.
Win or loose you still gain reasonable experiance and recources. Low power score matches are not ment to be super ballanced as this isn't an MLG game. It is about building cool stuff and having fun with it. Each match is only 3 mins or less so don't stress it. if your match is bad make some changes and move to the next match. It is just 3 mins and there is no loss of rank for loosing. So feel free to build some silly vehicle and have fun! In higher power scores ranked and clan options are available if you want a more compeditve match. If you are getting mad over lost matches you are playing wrong.
One of the largest mistakes new players make is asuming you should put every piece of armor on your vehicle that you have available to you as you level. The problem with this is this ramps up your power score to quickly before you have the weapons that are apropriate for that power score. Stick to keeping your power score low it will curb your frustrations. Staying below 2500 power score is best for quite some time. Adding another gun over adding more armor is almost always better with current ballancing. Being early access this may change over time.
While people say people strap high power guns on low power builds to fight new players simply is not true anymore. Besides power score matchmaking does take your level into acount now. While this can sometimes still happen as you level you will discover that if you try to build a low power score vehicle with a high level gun you will end up in a match with other people doing the same thing. It becomes a whole new game type almost. The people complaining about this one have out of date info or two take the non ranked matches to seriously. In fact keeping to low power score matches usually insures faster matches which equals faster gain in game.
The game is not pay to win it is pay to advance. Just like many other games out there the game requires you to grind to get good gear. Some people have limited time to play and choose to spend money to get into higher teer matches sooner. This is how they provide the game for free to everyone else. While this can be frustrating at times it is not in any way game breaking. As long as you take my above advice and keep your own power score low you will avoid situations were you are massivly out gunned. Your low rank will limit the chances of this happening. If you are getting wrecked lower your power score. I have seen well organized teams wreck people with high level guns builds if they play wisely and learn to target key vehicle parts. Fancy toys don't make you a good player. Anything over 2500 power score and you risk getting out gunned until you can aford better weapons. Brawls are the best way to earn money fast. Win or loose you walk out with a lot of scrap.
As it stands blue and below items are cheeper to buy than to craft. Don't waist you hard earned curency on crafting them. instead sell the resources and buy the Item. Just keep an eye on prices this will likely change with time.
The key to enjoying this game is to ditch any preconsptions that it is a compeditive game. It isn't at least not until you get much higher in the ranks. They are still working out the kinks on making ranked worth it. Give it some time.
Side note: pay attention to how fast certain items trade in the market. Often under bidding is only screwing yourself out of currency. open the actual trade menu and hit refresh a few times. Quick selling and buying is usually a bad idea. It can make a big difference in your profits if you have patience. You can play matches while you wait. Many items move so fast you are only adding seconds to your wait time.

This is a tower defense game that has each map consisting of one screen. The basic plot is that you are an island native that has to defend your babies from monsters that will eat them. In each level / stage you have 20 babies, meaning no more than 20 enemies can get to your home base. how do you stop them? You have the ability to turn trees into towers. Arrow towers are quick and shoot far. Cannon towers do damage to a lot of enemies, but they are slow and short ranged. Anti-aircraft towers will take out flying enemies pretty quickly from a distance.
Enemies drop money and jewels / crystals. You can use the jewels to research three more towers, such as the tesla coil that will zap several enemies at once in a shot range. The laser tower that will shoot several flying enemies at once and finally some sort of giant cannon tower that will destroy a big radius, but it is super slow. With the crystals you can also use them to upgrade your towers, but you don't really micro manage upgrades like I'd prefer. Each tower can only be upgraded a certain way, like arrow towers can only have their firing radius improved. Cannon towers can only have their power improved. You can also upgrade each tower by standing next to it and you will see a bar go to 100% when its done with the next level upgrade. It is a nice feature and fills any sort of idle time with work.
Waves of single enemy types arrive, mostly spiders, natives and flying pods. There are different varieties like giant natives, fat bee like creatures, and stronger glowing enemy alterations. You see how much time you have before the next wave along with what enemy type is coming next, so you can sell your towers for coins to buy more towers. This is a must in some levels.
You can't really block the enemies. If you get hit, all of your coins will go flying ala Sonic from the 90s. Coins fly in the water and disappear in time. It will really keep you on your toes. The controls are nice and extremely basic. I think you only need to use one button and the thumbstick or mouse. Super simple and easy to use. If you want to research, just return to home base. If you want to build a tower, click a tree. That's really all there is. Oh and at the end of each level is a giant boss, but they seem less threatening than 100 spiders.
The levels are long and meaty. Each level will take a while to complete and there is always a chance of failure. Your 20 babies get eaten and you have to restart the level. The world map is broken up into several different levels and there are different islands to explore. The levels are clumped together and to progress, you need to have a certain amount of rainbows to leave the level cluster. To get rainbows, you need to complete a level without losing babies. Its more difficult than it sounds on regular difficulty.
Its a really nice game that you can sink a lot of time into, but if you're not into tower defense, this game won't make you want to play tower defenses. I've always liked PixelJunk games and they make this one stand out in a sea of tower defense and micro transactions.

If you LOVE Ico, you'll like this.
Gamplay? Not revolutionary by any means. Story? Also not revalutionary. But the way the story is told makes it memorable, and Iearning in the credits that this is this studio's FIRST game - it's phenominal, and there is a lot of heart in it.
It took me about two hours to beat, start to finish in one sitting, but it felt like four hours. Is that a bad thing? Not at all. The length had everything to do with my focus, and not with the occasionally tedius parts. (Basically, don't be like me and try to experiment by jumping off of things. The game is NOT kind when it comes to checkpoints - except for the final boss. Then it is very forgiving.)
Speaking of the boss - If you're like me, you find the majority of endings and boss fights disappointing and lackluster. This case isn't epic of awe-inspiring, but they were incredibly appropriate for the game. It feels like a complete package, with no strong points, no weakpoints, just a consisten experience throughout. It's a good think-piece too.
None of the 'puzzles' are particularly difficult - there's one that comes to mind that was a bit irritating. But the boss fight lived up to being a challenge - using what the game taught us throughout, as well as a bit of thinking and mix and match. You'll try the first thing that comes to mind, to find that it didn't work how you expected the game to operate. I had a very happy moment when I figured out precisely what to do. Maybe I'm slow or easy to impress, but I play a lot of games.
The visuals aren't particularly stunning, but they're imaginative, and the music alone is awesome! If you look into the game and think it isn't for you, I would urge you to maybe get it just for the soundtrack.
Would I recommend this game at full price? Not really. Wait for a sale that puts it at $5 or under, and I promise it'll feel worth its salt. Unless you're someone who delights only in unique gameplay or freedom of play. Then maybe skip over this one.
Does it have replay value? Maybe if the visuals streike you hard enough. As-is, I have all but two achievements, so if I play again, it'll be explicitly to collect those. I'm certainly curious as to where I skipped or missed things!

If you are a fan of perma-death, upgrades and robot jokes, look no further. Clone Drone is very well made (with a few issues) and can soak up your time. Be warned, however, you will be frustrated during your journey into this game, but not due to any glitches or technical issues.
Your human-bot is fragile.
Any significant damage to your head will kill you.
Lost both arms and have no kick? Dead.
Take an arrow to the wrong area of your chest? Dead.
Shot an arrow at a level 3 sword-bot at too close a distance? D-e-a-d.
Lost a leg to some jetpack-bots and can't move far? Might as well be dead.
Some people hate that kind of thing, but I'm a glutton for punishment, so I loved it.
The next thing you should know is that there are several ways to play; there is the Story Mode, the 'classis' Endless Mode and the Challenge Modes.
Story Mode is unfinished as of this review, but the developers are currently working on it, and it is a great way to introduce yourself to the concepts of the game.
Endless Mode is just that, endless. Each of your human-bots are pitted against an endless supply of more and more difficult arenas that you have to survive (or die and use a clone to survive).
Challenge Modes will put you through a set amount of arenas with restrictions, such as bow-only, hammer-only and kick-only. There is also Steam Workshop support, so if you're into creating challenges to torture others, you can, or if you're a masochist like me you can take on those challenges.
The gameplay starts simple but complicates in varying degrees. You start with a lazer sword and the movement speed of a Jazzercising grandmother, but each successfully completed level grants you one upgrade. You can choose to make your sword a fire sword which gradually burns away bits of your enemies for a bleed-like effect, or give yourself a bow, which gives you a slow-moving but effective projectile at dispatching enemy archers and flame raptors (No, that's not a typo).
Alternatively you can use the upgrade points to create 'clones' of your human-bot. These serve as your extra lives, and you are limited to 5 total per run. Period. Recently the developers added a 'repair' function as well that you can spend your well-earned point on.
The upgrade point system is where some will get frustrated, and others intrigued. For example, do I risk not having a clone for the start of the Gold-difficuty levels and buy the booster-style jetpack, or do I play it safe in case I get ambushed in the next level and die? The wrong choice could end your run, but then again, your personal skill will do you in just as quickly.
Since this game is Early Access, I can only imagine that things will expand and get better as time moves on. There aren't many gamebreaking glitches to speak of, so the real make-or-break factor for this title is taste: The concept and gameplay of this game is a love-or-hate ordeal, so watch the gameplay before you buy.

RPG Maker MV, is easily the very best of them all. There is plenty of negative reviews out there, and truth be told - even after reading a couple of them, I honestly do not know why they posted negatives.
Anywyas, let's get to my own feelings about the program :
I absolutely love it, pretty much everything has been improved on and moved into right direction. The changes for many aspects are pretty subtle, but quickly turn out to be a major time / stress savers.
That being said, among many and many pros of MV, absolutely the very best part are user-made plugins. You may ask, why would I give developers credits for user created content, and I'll respond with : It's the same as with the game supporting modding, and the one that does not. Sure you do not review mods when talking about the game, but you surely list modability as a (huge) plus. And in this case, they not only gave means to create plugins, they did all they could to find and contact very reliable and knowledgable people to work on them (eg. Yanfly whom already created 20 very helpful plugins)
The only thing you have to watch out for, before buying RPG maker MV is the fact it does require a bit better PC than the older versions did. The games created in the program are greatly optimised and working a lot better, but the RPG maker itself is visibly bigger strain on your PC. - But well, as long as you meet the requirements, you'll be fine.
I've been only working with MV for as few as 9 hours, but I haven't encoutered ANY bugs nor crashes to happen in this short time. I also have a feeling that I have already progressed further than in 70 hours spent in Vx Ace.
Where the work didn't quite go like I wanted to before, now it's pretty much a pleasure, because everything is a LOT more user friendly.
If you have been using older versions of the RPG maker, and are wondering wether to buy MV - Go for it. You will need to do some tinkering to get your old projects to work on the new system, because it uses different coding language, and different resolutions, but it's worth every second spent on converting.
IF you are completely new to RPG maker series... well you should probably see some review about the RPG maker itself before, but as long you feel you are motivated enough to create an actual game, you should definetely buy MV over other versions. And well, if you want to create 2D RPG games, I also claim RPG maker series being the very best, and cheapest of the programs you can use to create such games (at least counting these you can work efficently in).

This software has been getting an undeserved amount of flak in these reviews; in my honest opinion having played around with VX Ace and XP (not all on steam however), this is probably the most powerful RPG Maker yet.
-Javascript. I know a lot of people are upset about it having very little compatibility with Ruby like the last RPG Makers, but these new Javascript plugins are insanely powerful. Earlier today I met someone who was able to get their project sending data back and forth to an online server, something no RPG maker game has *ever* been able to do in the past. It may be far too taxing to develop an actual online RPG Maker game, but online features to some extent are a definite possibility now, and that's great. Moreover, Javascript is a much more commonly-used language than Ruby ever was, and there are no more hidden classes limiting the scope of scripts, and far fewer hard-coded limitations.
-Plugin manager to easily import and control your plugins. Keep in mind that script order does still matter, but the only way to move plugins up or down is to cut and paste them elsewhere in the list. "Move Plugin Up or Down" buttons are not included.
-All of the same features of VX Ace, plus larger tile size and screen resolution and a smarter map-editor. Or, if you don't want the larger sizes, you can go back to 32x tiles and the smaller res of VX Ace with some of the preorder javascript plugins,
-Clarity. This is the biggest reason for the number of negative reviews. The developers of the software have not been as clear in communicating their product's features as they could have. For instance, they advertised android/iOS porting, and people assumed they would be getting an automated tool that did everything for them. However, this is not the case, and falls on both the end user's expectations and the company failing to clarify that only a simple step-by-step guide would be provided for this purpose, rather than an automated too.

In Proteus you awake, walking on the water for some reason, on a randomly generated "garden of eden like island. You open your eyes and find yourself floating in a beautiful, serene ocean, colored a vibrant blue. The sound of waves grace your ears while you swim to a delightfully candy-colored island. There you find structures, wild life, and an engrossing journey that pleasures the senses. Let the bright color palette of the island and its inhabitants lighten your day and have the music lull you into a relaxed state of "the day can wait, I want to feel good".
Proteus is a simple game. There are no guns, no bad guys, no rounds or goals. There is simply you, the island, and anything you find. It is likeable to a relaxing walk through the park; and rightfully so, as that is essentially what you'll be doing for a large portion of the game.
Is that boring? Maybe. Is it pleasant? Absolutely. It's nearly therapeutic. Proteus' is nice to look at and even better to listen to. Its soundtrack composes of myriad tunes that morph as you walk around the world. It brings to mind the masterful works of Journey and Flower, as seen on the PlayStation Network. If you've played and enjoyed either of those games, you'll feel right at home with Proteus.

Proteus is an interesting game that challenges its medium. Although void of clear objectives, player abilities, or direction, the game feeds off of the curiosity of the player. As you explore the procedurally generated island you are placed on when the game loads, scampering creatures, beautiful fauna, and a rich tapestry of colors and sights all generate music as you come into contact with them. Each time you play is different, and each play-through can be as reinvigorating and relaxing as the last. The changing seasons morph the environment's landscape, and the music and sounds with it. Long summer days and cold winter nights are vastly different from each other, and each iteration of the game ends in a grandiose finale. If you are looking for a puzzle to solve, another player to outwit, or some other thing to keep you busy for 40 hours, this isn't the game for you. However, if you want to wash away your worries and explore a beautiful world, you should give Proteus a try.

Here at Retro 101 we are long-time fans of just about everything that the Pixel Junk team has produced. They just seems to have a way of taking a genre that has been done to death and then adding something new to make it fresh and vibrant again. Now Monsters is making its way onto the PC and we are absolutely delighted to have it around for those lunch time sessions.
What we have here is effectively the original game and the extra content added through Monsters Encore and the PSP version. The game also has online multiplayer modes and a lovely higher resolution graphical style. The island that lets you create random levels by typing in words is also unlocked right from the start. So if you’re a fan you can stop reading this review right here, log into Steam and purchase it.  For those that want a bit more detail then read on.
For those new to the series this is a tower defence style game where your little Tikiman must run around the screen upgrading trees into different types of defensive structures. And yes, you do still move the Tikiman around rather than just point and click on trees with the mouse. Wave upon wave of monsters then pour into the level from various points and head towards the village hut (normally located in the middle of the stage).  Around the hut are a number of baby Tiki’s and once the monsters have made off with all of them you lose.
It’s a concept we’ve seen many times before but it’s hard to remember when it has been accomplished with so much style and flair. You start off with three basic towers which covers attacking land monsters, air monsters and one that does both. The towers all have different damage outputs, speed of fire and targeting radius. Once a monster enters the targeting radius the towers will fire on them automatically. Killing monsters provides gold to upgrade more trees and gems which are stored in the village hut and can be used to upgrade the strength of towers or unlock new types to use.
The extra towers do all sorts of weird and wonderful things. You can get ice towers to slow monsters down, mortars to cause massive damage, lasers to knock flying enemies down and electricity pylons to hit creatures with area effect attacks and the list goes on. It’s with these towers that the game begins to come into its own as you will need to know the strengths and weaknesses of them all in order to succeed. You can’t just lay out your defences and hope for the best here, you have to continually move around the field and change the type of towers to win the day.
PixelJunk Monsters can be a bone crushingly tough game, especially for newcomers to the genre. It takes time to learn that you really should be selling certain towers at certain times and changing from anti-air to ground and back again for certain waves of attack. It’s the sort of game where you may be stuck on a stage for ages but then have a breakthrough and clear three or four in one go. You have to constantly think about what you’re doing and constantly keep an eye on what the next wave of marauding nasty’s will be.
One memorable level ended with a frantic scramble around the stage to clear all the anti-air guns as the final boss stomped on and proceeded to be able to almost walk straight to the babies without taking a hit. Stress like that is what you’re going to have to deal with to come out on top and it’ll happen all the time.
Away from the main game there are a host of other options and things to do. You can play Co-op in online modes and this allows two Tiki men to run around to defend the village. There are also tons of challenge levels which require you to complete stages under certain conditions. The criteria is always different and can range from anything from only using a certain type of tower to making sure you don’t let monsters cross certain parts of the level. As if the game wasn’t difficult enough this will test even the best strategy fans out there.
We’ve established the game is hard, but it always fair and the funny thing is it doesn’t really seem to matter. The sense of achievement from completing a level will always have you coming back for just one more go. You’ll find yourself thinking about levels in your everyday life and coming up with strategies while you should be doing other things. Then you’ll return and try it out and maybe it’ll work and bring you onto the next challenge. It’s perfect for formulating a strategy during the morning and then testing it out in a lunch break.
Overall, this is the definitive version of an already excellent game. The core mechanics are strong and work wonderfully when added to the flair and charm of it all. There is very little reason not to recommend it to fans of genre and gamers looking for something a little different. The difficulty may be too much for some but it’s a great version of a great game and it should really be in your collection.
Overall 8/10

I love Proteus. I love it so much I'm thinking of buying it a third time for the Vita.
When I walk in the country I am not following an explicit objective, I'm not out there to "achieve" anything, I’m simply there for the experience. I want to take it all in, let it wash over me with no distractions. I am there to absorb the sights, the sounds, the smells, the feel and the atmosphere of the places I discover. That is the point.

Ok so I've spent a little time playing this game, and so far, it's pretty good.  You have no idea what kind of game this is from the title though, right?  I mean, you know it's a PixelJunk game, you know it's got monsters, and it's apparently the ulitmate for some reason.  So what is it?  It's another Tower Defense game!
So what makes this game different from any of the other thousand tower defense clone games out there?  Well for one thing, you've got a physical avatar/character to move around the map placing towers.  That's interesting I guess.  You're limited in what you can do by how fast your character moves.  That can be really challenging (and really annoying).
Another feature is that the path is pretty much already laid out for you.  All you have to do is build towers out of the trees in the background on the maps.  If you were hoping for a more free-form tower defense game, that would be disappointing, but considering there's often just one optimal path anyway, I don't really mind.  You're really limited enough by the fact your character doesn't move that fast.  No need to make it even harder by allowing the monsters to rush straight for the base.
Most tower defense games I've seen allow you to pay to upgrade your towers, but this game gives you three ways of upgrading.  1) Experience through kills 2) Paying "gems" to upgrade and 3) Your character does a little dance that gradually adds to the experience bar of the tower, eventually upgrading it.
So these gems I've mentioned... when you kill a monster, it drops some coins (usually) and a green gem (rarely).  You use the coins to buy new towers and you use the gems to either upgrade your existing towers OR apply those gems to unlocking a NEW tower for the level.  Sometimes the new tower is more valuable than having upgraded towers and sometimes an upgraded tower means you actually survive the level.
Oh and one other thing I forgot to mention: You have to pick the coins and gems up, however you're powerless against the monsters so you can't touch them at all or you get stunned and you drop some money that you have to pick back up (think sonic the hedgehog's rings).  I don't think it's possible for your main character to die but I haven't tried really hard.
The graphics are what I would call "quaint".  Nothing super fancy but it seems to fit in with PixelJunk's style pretty well.  The music is OK, but kinda forgettable.  Nothing stuck in my head after I closed the game, so that's neither good nor bad.  The sound effects are passable too but again, nothing memorable about them.  You get some cannon boom sounds, crossbow "thwack" sounds, etc.   The sounds your character makes while upgrading a tower sounds like a native dance, but that totally fits because your character looks like a stereotypical  witch doctor.
You can use a controller with the game, and in fact, that's all I've ever used.   I don't know if mouse/keyboard would be better since you're moving a character around on screen to do all the building and upgrading. A cute, fun, and challenging tower defense game about a Tiki man protecting his 20 Tiki kids from the hordes of monsters that traverse the forest aiming to make lunch of Tiki man's kids. 20 kids, whew! Perhaps the monsters in the game are after Tiki man for overpopulating the forest with his spawn. Anyways, Monsters offers multiple modes and difficulties. Difficulties ranging from Casual, Regular, and Hard-core (once the game is beat on Regular) provide hours and hours of entertainment for anyone from the newbies to the veterans of tower defense games. There's single player, local co-op, and even online co-op. Complete levels in single player or co-op and unlock up to 24 Medal Challenges in the Tiki Hut, which upon completion of each level will net you an achievement if the challenges restrictions/rules were met. Completion of special levels will unlock various rewards like the Speed Potion, Bomb, and things that must be purchased during levels like addition towers or bonus interest between waves.
Once one finishes with Tiki Island, Toki Island, and Gati Gati Island, there's Tum Tum Island which generates a random level based on an up to 5 character word, number or combination of letters & numbers.
Monsters has high potential for replay value thanks to Tum Tum Island, but out of the dozen or so words I've tried I ended up with the same stages too often, most of them very easy.
Highly recommended, even to those that have played the original release of Monsters as there is enough new content to keep the game feeling fresh.

Let me begin by saying that Age of Empires II is a classic for lots of good reasons. There is a huge variety of maps, cultures to be played with different styles, several campains for singleplayer fans and many possibilities for people, who'd like to play with friends - offline as well as online. You can even create content with an in-game editor. What I always appreciated about aoe 2 in comparison to many other rts games is the slower build-up and the fact, that you actually learn something about history. But still, I won't recommend the HD Edition.
So, the HD version has better graphics, it's true. But the difference is so minimal, that I don't recognise it as long a I don't look at a comparison picture. And even then I couldn't care less about the change. I assume that no one, who hasn't played aoe 2 due to its graphic, would play the HD version because of it. The developers implemented modern resolutions, so we don't have to play a blurry game. But thanks to the community this was also possible before the HD version.
Now it is possible to choose between the original and a HD AI. I have played with and against both and I would say, that the HD AI is more challenging. The probably most obvious change is that the HD AI doesn't build walls. This is clever, because the original AI tended to harm itself more than to protect itself with walls. On the other hand, it's disappointing. The developers didn't want to or couldn't get the AI to arrange walls in an useful way. Adding to that, the AI struggles very hard, when it has to face walls of yours. Instead of breaking through a small hole it tries to destroy the whole wall in a very inefficient way.
Furthermore, there is a huge difference in behaviour of the AI whether you play an "open" map or a map that has solely a few land bridges. In case of the latter the AI is very passive and builds mostly naval forces and is never a real threat to you. It doesn't help, that there seems to be a limit of points, after that the AI doesn't grow anymore or only very slow. If you survive the first wave, you have almost won.
In conclusion, the graphics aren't a plus in my opinion, the AI is not better, just different and the HD edition does not support lan. On the contrary, the steam integration is comfortable. It would have been a good service, if the features of this edition had been patched for the original aoe 2. but taking quite a lot money for such small advantages it has to be seen as bad customer service. Thus, I do not recommend this game

Proteus is a brilliant idea that only excels in its visual execution. It perfectly captures the kind of world once portrayed using just a few, two-toned pixels displayed from an Atari 800. A world that you, the viewer were forced to imagine rather than witness in high definition glory. The problem is; there is literally nothing to do within that world expect to wander its hills and valleys scaring off groups of animals while listening to the whimsical but unimpressive, procedurally-generated music.  It is best described as a tech demo and it would make a fantastic screen saver akin to the classic Windows 3D maze. The one thing it is not however, is a game.
24 hours inside of Proteus would offer no more enjoyment or depth than simply watching its 2 minute long trailer video. And that is possibly the saddest thing I've ever written in review.
While most indie games leave you wanting more for their own good reasons, Proteus leaves you to starve on an empty island for want of anything at all.

Toren is a great bad game. Or maybe it's a bad great game. I'm not really sure.
The art is gorgeous, for one thing, and there's an enthralling dreamlike quality to the entire experience. The narration, delivered mostly through text, is obtuse but doesn't quite veer into purple prose, so that's a plus. And again, holy hell, these people know how to set up a few beautiful scenes. Wow. On paper at least, even the combat and the puzzles are well-done - just straightforward enough to figure out without too much failure or frustration, and fittingly used and reused throughout the game.
On the other hand, the animation is janky as all hell, which is a shame since the stuff being animated looks so great. Most of the time it looks like props are just being shifted up and down on a sine curve. The camera is atrocious, too, which is a problem given that your character always moves forward relative to the camera. You basically have zero control over it, and getting the character to go in the right direction can be tricky, especially when the camera is constantly moving without even warning you first.
That said, it's really short, and I think that if you're willing to put up with some jankiness, it might be worth a shot anyway, for the art and the atmosphere. Hopefully this studio's next game will be a bit more polished, but I'll keep an eye on them.

As time passed, it became increasingly clear that this was a pay-to-win, even moreso than in the past. The price of pets was rising to over twenty dollars. That was alright, I could still play. It wasn't as much fun, but I still had the friends I made in the universe of Mabi.
After a while, I started to have trouble launching the game - sometimes it would crash after a few minutes. Not long after, it started to do that every time I tried to play. I tried reinstalling it; at this point it quit launching altogether. I submitted a ticket to nexon, which was automatically canceled since it fell under Tech support; the automated message told me to post in the Tech support forums. I was a little irritated, but I did anyways. I had sunk a lot of time into this, so I didn't want to give up so easily. I didn't get any help, just a few useless comments and one or two people saying they had the same problem.
I found the game was on steam, and all was well for a time. However, when I helped my Guild mine stones for a castle we'd won in an Auction (it would only be ours temporarily) and we completed it, I found that I needed Premium service to actually enter the dang place. I was less than pleased. I still played a little, just dinking around and talking to my friends now and then, working an undeveloped character I happened to have when I had some time to kill. (I avoided playing it unless I KNEW I had a lot of time; many of the quests require a maddening amount of running back and forth to two NPC's who were often on different ends of the continent, or at least a few cities apart. This game is impossible unless you drop some cash on pets to get around without going insane. Even then, travel takes longer than is fair, and with the increasing size of cities, much of which are empty and with a handful of NPC's spread over something that can take half an hour or more to traverse on foot...) Then, after a while, it started crashing after a few minutes again. At this point, I begrudingly cut my losses, deciding that it wasn't worth the effort and the frustration I was getting from the worsening pay-to-win environment and rising costs.

Over The Moonlight let's players witness an enclosed, magically changing environment. Blank canvases surrounded by colour-changing flowers are waiting to be painted on. The game's atmosphere is enchanting, but its execution sadly falls flat on delivering that experience in an undisturbed manner.
Visually abstract but still homely due to its warm colours and soothing music, Over The Moonlight aims to offer a refuge for the mind. Unfortunately though, the game feels unfinished partly due to its underwhelming performance but most notably because of many little problems regarding its gameplay. The hitboxes and controls don't feel accurate and some graphic phenomena are simply irritating. The brush strokes while painting are too unwieldy to be enjoyable, which, in a way, degrades the act into rough colouring. Amplifying this is the lack of ingame options, a menu or even a means to freely close the game: Over The Moonlight only closes itself as soon as the player reaches the end.
The intentions are good, but stripping a game down to its bare gameplay essence requires an overall polish, which Over The Moonlight unfortunately doesn't provide. It may be worth a try, but I ultimately can't quite enjoy it to the extent it's intended.

The core combat gameplay, itself is quite good, if a bit stiff.  Timing and positioning is extremely important, which is fun.  And how easy it is to die adds to the tension.  But I'm sick and tired of the "roguelike" trend that seems to think that unbalanced difficulty is a substitute for longevity, content and a good game design.
If this game would embrace is core combat and expand on it and add depth to it, and at least partially mitigate the "get hit once and start all over again" roguelike element, I would definitely find it easy to recommend it.  As it is, I would only recommend it conditionally - if the person I was recommending it to liked roguelikes.  It doesn't have to be limited to people who enjoy roguelikes, it has a lot of promise - if it would embrace what's best about itself.
Add depth and features (more maneuverability, more weapon types, co-op) and true replayability (more procedurally generated content, multiplayer PvP, more levels, more modes) and it could realize that potential, IMO.

What can I say about this "Thrill-Ride" of a F2P game? Sorry for the ovbious sarcasm, but let's take a look at Mabinogi:
This game first off immediately tries to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off by playing super-loud music at the start screen that you can't change until you've made a character. Now I know what you're thinking: There's a mute button stupid, but at the same time an experienced friend of mine is trying to teach me the basic stuff about the game. To add to that, the game is impossible to figure out unless you have a friend guiding you the whole way. Also, the game is ridiculously slow-paced and boring with just everything that you do. The combat system is ridiculously tedious and annoying to use. When you first create a character, you instantly discover you can only have one character per account and VERY limited customization options. If you try to create a male character, it will always look like a female. The pay to win system is unbelievably bad and stuff costs way too much. The resolution isn't even optimized for all screen resolutions so it looked really sluggish to me. Everything in the game looked horrible and low-res. There is tremendous lag on every server and channel even though I have way above the recommended system specs for this game. The worst part is, the customer support for the game by the publishers, Nexon, are unresponsive and couldn't care less for the community. The servers are practically barren and the few people I find outside of the 2 friends that tried to guide me through the game never leave me alone and spam the chat like crazy. The first guy you meet, Duncan literally tells you that: "All of these jobs may seem boring to you." So heed his warning. The only things that are nice about this game is that it is a bit different from other mmos and the story is set up well. But other than that, this feels like a boring, tedious, annoying, and a confusing experience the whole way through. This game is slowly dying so I advise not to get in to it. The sad thing is, I hear from lots of dedicated players that the game was decent when it first came out back in 2003, but then Nexon screwed it up significantly. The worst part is, there are way better Free-To-Play MMOs like Planetside 2, Warframe, SWTOR, Rusty Hearts, Cosmic Break, and so on. This game was so bad that my testicles committed suicide due to the lack of testosterone considering that no matter what you do to customize your character, you'll always look like a female! Not being sexist or anything, but I want to look like my own gender please, come on now Nexon!
To sum it up, this isn't just a bad F2P MMO, it's probably one of the worst F2P MMOs I've ever played. Just do yourself a favor and just play a different F2P game unless you enjoy grinding for several hours just to earn or do anything that is cool or fun at all.

The majority of people disliked my review, and I would like to guess that it was either because they figured out a way to easily export games to iOS, or because I sounded rude and dislikable. If the prior is the case, I would enjoy a brief comment to prove me wrong; for the latter, I apologize but I was greatly disappointed and I ensure that I have been an RPGMaker fan and continue to be. Anyways, to the review:
I don't recommend it... not yet, at least. The exporting functions clearly need work, as stated by many, many other reviewers. Obviously, things such as the character generator and side-view battle system were improved, but the main grab to this program compared to RPG Maker VX Ace was the ability to "easily" transfer your games into a smartphone, show your friends, and all that jazz. I was a perfect test subject, as I had no experience with exporting to iOS, and I have to say it was not "simple enough for a child." I couldn't even get it to work after two hours of confusion, even with the tutorial on the community hub. You apparently need some certification to create the app, and if you don't, I haven't found anything which says otherwise. So, if you just want to create a classic RPG and learn the fundamentals of RPG Maker, you should check out VXAce for now, since it has a lot more community help and advice. Until these problems with exporting are fixed, I am going to take my $72 and spend it somewhere else. I'm sorry, even as an avid RPGMaker fan, I don't think I want to start on this one until more support is established.

There's right ways and wrong ways to release a 2D platformer on Steam.
The right way is to combine great gameplay with real artwork and a contemporary instead of pitching a low effort deal and not reverting to the old and dead "retro" look to avoid having to hire an artist.
The developers of SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect decided on the latter.
Gameplay - Terrible platformer with a clunky engine
Artwork - None - they opted for a slightly japanese looking 8 bit motif - it's old, tired, done, and dead but here they are rehashing it again as if it's somehow still cool and hipster to be retro.  It's not.
Engine - Some special comments on the game engine.  They decided to use an arcade emu for the game without permitting widescreen or even 4:3 graphics - so if you own a PC, this game will look terrible on it, and not just because of the terrible 8bit style.   You cannot change the engine and the controls aren't by default mapped to a keyboard or joystick, it expects a gamepad, which would be great if this was a console game but it's not.
A whole series of things are wrong with this entry into the overcrowded cesspit of "me too" retro platformers.   I'd have a hard time recommending a good entry, and this most certainly isn't one.  Avoid.

Reviewing MMO's is hard. Having people pay attention to those reviews is even harder. Yet I'm going to write one anyway:
EVE is around 10 years old now and is showing no signs of slowing down. If anything, it is (probably) still expanding its player base. The reasons for this are many, but one thing that can certainly be said is that it is unlike most other MMO's out there due to the fact that it is a "sandbox" rather than "themepark" MMO. The latter-type of MMO, which includes most other MMO's out there (World of Warcraft being the most obvious), EVE is not about dungeon crawling or loot hunting or any of that sort of stuff. The "sandbox" of this game allows for an absurd, and honestly frightening, amount of options for how to play the game. There's PvE content for solo and groups, though admittedly this is easily the weakest and least interesting part of the game. The PvP environment is, on the other hand, arguably the most vibrant and violent of any other MMO out there. Fight scale from arranged one on one duels to massive battles involving thousands that have been noted by gaming and even mainstream news outlets on more than a few occasions. And then there's the market, full of complexity and opportunity in equal measure.
In other words, this game isn't very good solo. It's far better in groups and even moreso if you choose the right one for what you are wanting to do in the game. It is worth noting however that these groups have a double-edge to them not usually found in other games. Aside from hacking the game, RMT, and stuff like botting, there are virtually no rules on player content. This means theft and scamming are perfectly legal, which scares people away from this game but the reality of it is that you can only really get conned if you are careless or too trusting of bad people. I personally have never fallen for a scam, though some of the cleverer ones almost grabbed me early on. People can't just go into your hangars or wallet and steal all your stuff: You have to either put it in a place accessible to other people, like Corporate (Guild/Clan) hangars (think Guild Banks in WoW), or you have to actually hand your stuff over to someone else without realizing you are falling for a trick.
The other side of this lack of rules is that this game has a metagaming scene unlike any other. The individual scams and steals from hapless victims, but the corporations and alliances have full-blown intelligence networks. Espionage is a very real thing here, and the great heists you may have heard about where someone steals gigantic amounts of stuff are, more often than not, agents of another group specifically sent to spy and eventually take everything that isn't nailed down. Or it can be a high-ranking officer who decides to rage-quit and just steal stuff on the way out. Eiher way you only will personally lose stuff if you allow it to happen.
This game does have flaws. The potential for theft with few consequences creates a culture of paranoia that some might find really annoying to deal with. The spaceship gameplay is often boring, with the PvE content being the worst offender. The public channels, like every other MMO, are often filled with idiots who just spam garbage. The learning curve is notoriously high, and the sheer amount of things there are possible to do can easily overwhelm a new player. The game's skill training system, while good in that it lets a player make progress even while not playing the game, makes it take some time before you can truly get to where you want to be. And lastly, as with all MMO's, tedium and grindy activities are inevitable. This may be an MMO unlike most others, but it is still an MMO. You should think long about whether or not to jump into this game, because it  can become extremely difficult to pay proper attention to this game and others at the same time.
But, I like it. If I was forced to play an MMO, it would be this one.
So if this overlong review didn't make you flee, you can check out a free 21-day trial. Speaking of free, it is entirely possible, if you make enough in-game currency on a regular basis, this game can be a free-to-play MMO. Perhaps not for the first few months, but it is very possible, once you are established, to never have to pay real money for this game again. I haven't since early 2012. :3

Disclosure: I spent 700+ hours in RPG Maker VX Ace, and I pre-ordered via the official website.
So, I've been developing a game in VX Ace; and now I decided to move on to MV after pre-ordering it (forgive me), and I gotta say; this is actually a great program. Awesome to see sideview battlers integrated within the game, although I wish enemies had their own sideview animations so it's more like Final Fantasy VI.
Pros:
-Great first program.
-Awesome, more improved generator.
-Pre-order DLC is glorious.
-A higher resolution.
-Move to Javascript, which means no more using an unfamiliar language or having to learn a whole new language. This will certainly welcome in some new developers who are also learning Javascript.
-Plugins. You can still edit them with Notepad/Notepad++ but I find the plugin system nice, as you can now edit things without worrying about editing this one line of code ♥♥♥♥ing up your game or making it do a CTD.
-Same interface RM users are very familiar with, which means RMMV is welcoming for newcomers and veterans alike.
-More things to spice up.
-Great base/DLC soundtrack and graphics. Some songs even give the Hotline Miami/Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon vibe.
-Addition of an options menu, even featuring the ability to turn down music and sound. Yanfly also made plugins for customizing controls, thank god; as WASD > Arrow Keys.
Cons:
-Smaller database than VX Ace. This should be a non-issue if you like building things yourself. (UPDATE: You can download the full database here:
)
-Character generator gradients kinda suck. You can edit the gradients with
which I've done later on. Non-issue if you plan to use custom graphics.
-Lack of native true Linux support. Granted, Android is based off of Linux and Crosswalk exists but still.
-Older computers should stay away for now.
-VX Ace to MV converter is kinda not worth it, I just converted some of my databases over and started from scratch.
-Removal of formula generators when setting damage.
-No exiting to desktop integrated, but
- Fixes this issue.
-Some plugins need to be installed to fix some flaws.
-Lack of FLAC and MP3. MP3 is no longer supported but you can convert to OGG easily with Audacity.
Score: 9.0/10. MV is, despite its flaws improved over VX Ace.  I do hope more is added but I'm pretty satisfied with it; and I hope to see it improve as it develops.

The main issue with this game is randomness and lack of information. The paths the monsters follow are really not well defined and even will be different between waves as they go up and down in the lane. This means towers that worked for you perfectly might just not shoot anything the next wave. The ranges of the towers are circular, combine that with the strange monster pathing you'll see towers aiming to shoot a monster but never actually fire just because they didn't enter the range long enough. What do upgrades do exactly? What are the base damages of the towers? How much range is each? How much damage does the upgrade give? This information as well as the monster pathing itself I suppose you're just supposed to learn through a lot of trial and error, which in a tower defense game where you can't directly interact with the monsters a calcualted defense is all you have. Bloons gets away with this by simplifying the "monster" hp, everything dies in one hit, pop it and it will change color or turn into more. In this game the monster HP doesn't even have the decency to stay consistent, the same tower that just killed a monster might leave the next in the same wave at low hp. The mechanics that trees will randomly have coins or gems as well as dancing to slowly upgrade towers, and needing to collect the coins to get money. to give you something to do really just make the whole experience feel more drawn out.
Just... yuck, there's very little redeeming this game, play ANY other tower defense, and likely it will be better than this.

Short version:
4/5. If you're a puzzle collector, get this. The simple interface and simple concept but challenging puzzles make for a nice, approachable game.
Long version:
Lightbender is a good way to spend 10 minutes or 2 hours, solving incredibly mind-bending puzzles. Such a simple concept, just mirror, reverse, break or combine light; and yet it is very challenging. Sometimes you'll solve the puzzles by accident when you're trying out something new, and that's not necessarily a bad thing. It'll teach you to think. There are also user-created maps, as well as a whole plethora of maps on the developers' part, so you won't be speedrunning this game.
The critical things that I would have to say would be that the music could be a bit better-ish. It's not bad but it can start to irritate you after repeating over a same puzzle for a long time. Fortunately, as always, you can turn it off in the options if you don't like it. Other than that, I can't really think of many bad things to say. If the game continues to be what it has been so far, it should be a nice, small little puzzle-game. To be honest, it might not be one of the most memorable ones because it doesn't seem to have a plot of any kind, but it's overall very tidy and nice game.

Lets get the elephant out of the room: yes, Proteus isn't the most traditional game, but it is a game. Hear me out here:
Do you like exploring in games? Do you like wandering around and seeing all the details the level designers and artists placed so delicately in the game?
What if I told you Proteus was a game that randomly generated experiences like that?
Proteus randomly generates an island for you, each time you play. And each time you play, new events can happen, and you can see new things, and explore an entirely new world. And take that world and add simple, but beautiful art, and music that reacts to literally everything you do, and swirls around?
Sold yet? What if I told you that the ending is something that will stick with you forever?
Proteus is something special, just give it a chance to change your mind on what you define as a game.

Quite a difficult and highly unforgiving tower defense game. Even on Casual difficulty and borderline cheating by using two controllers, I still had major difficulties. Things have a tendency to very quickly get out of hand. You might think you have a well-planned defense, but the game will throw a wave of monsters at you that you're completely unprepared for, negating ten minutes worth of work (no, there is no fast forward feature in this TD game).
One particular point of frustation is that the game absolutely forces you to perfect levels in order to unlock progression, unlike most TD games where you can always go back later to improve your score. This leads to a situation where you'll feel compelled to restart if you lose so much as one point (even if you've already put ten minutes worth of work into a level), as there's little point to finishing with an imperfect rating.
I'll recommend this, but with the caveat that this is really for those who are interested in a co-op TD game, or those who really relish a challenge.

Dispite the enjoyment I've had with this game thus far, I find myself horribly frustrated more often then not. Ideally, your experience with this game will be a Mad Max inspired deathrace with other players in custom built and modified vehicles, painted and decorated to one's own style; but this is an online video game, so f*** you. There is a clear and unstoppable meta in this game, which are drones. Remote controlled, weaponized drones that can be deployed and left to do the damage for you. Here's the kicker though: They do more DPS than pretty much every other build in this game, and do not require your physical presence to attack things. You can roll up to a point, drop off all 3-5 of your automated warcrimes, then run away. They have an okay ammount of health post-"nerf", but still do an asinine ammount of damage and are pretty much inpossible to hit with most weapons due to their speed. These types of players are in every single game you will play, in every single BR from starter to endgame. Nothing is more infuriating than dealing with players that you can't hit but can shred even the largest, tankiest vehicles in a matter of seconds. Cancer comes in many varieties, from the most toxic builds such as Sidekick drones to the least deadly but still terrifying Fuze drones, which tend to kill themselves but take a large chunk of your health with them (if you catch my drift).
Other personal gripes I have with it are some unbalanaced parts, such as hover-like chassis that allow you to strafe at Mach 5 (making you nearly impossible to hit), weapons that are just clearly OP, and some fairly high-tier weapons that are somehow possible to bring into super low-tier matches. Imagine bringing a military APC to a carfight against a small fleet of Honda Civics.
Also grindng. Lots, and lots, and lots of grinding. Most of the fun pieces to use are late game. Don't expect to have tank treads, spider type legs, hovercraft, mortars, (actually viable) missiles, lasers or cloaking devices until at least 50-100 hours of grind. You're stuck with a rusty Ford Ranger covered in Nerf guns and old school lunch trays for a long time unless you fork out that sweet cash.
This game has some great qualities to it though, being that you can build almost anything you can think of. I literally saw a guy driving what was essentially a go-cart with two 57mm cannons strapped to each side. He did a backflip every time he fired his guns, it was purely awe-inspiring.
This game is just too unbalanced to call good right now, though. It needs some serious work before I'd consider dumping more time into it. I absolutely believe that in a more balanced state, this game could be great. You can defend it due to the "beta" title, which is fair. Have you ever played a game where the mechanics were so rich you felt like you could refine the entire thing into one concept and it would still be great? That feeling may work for many games but most of the time you won’t find out one way or the other. Most designers and gamers alike understand that games are an amalgamation of many ideas rather than a thoroughly impressive one-trick pony. This understanding seems to have evaded the creators of Proteus, or maybe they thought their game was exempt. Proteus is a one-concept tech demo that might’ve been neat if it was part of something bigger but what’s there isn’t enough to keep your interest or justify the seemingly inoffensive price.
The concept of Proteus is relatively brief. You control a first-person character that starts off in the ocean with an island in sight on the horizon. Once you get to the island, your only source of interaction is what you walk next to. The game reacts to your presence by playing different music depending on your location and occasionally there is a sprite animal or insect that runs away from you. That is the entire game. There is “progression” and an “endpoint,” but not in the way you might hope for. Endings are usually synonymous with finales or closing thoughts. Proteus’ ends a lot like a High School final project. They probably could’ve kept prolonging it for a better grade but the class already lost interest and the teacher gave a glance that implied what they had was good enough.
That’s not to say that “good enough,” is actually any good. Proteus’ quality hinges on the music and visuals, neither of which is very impressive. The artwork may be appealing in screenshots, but the environment remains completely static during gameplay. There are occasional lighting effects which add a bit of variety but nothing to make up for the overall stiffness of the game. As a result, the world feels very lifeless and the lack of interaction from the player doesn’t help.
The music doesn’t add much personality either. Proteus’ concept of “different music plays depending where you are” certainly works but the sounds you’re hearing sound like placeholders rather than actual music. Most of the tracks sound like someone pressing buttons to see if the instrument is working rather than playing actual music. This blunder contributes to the feeling that Proteus is an undeveloped tech demo, not an actual game.
If you somehow “finish” Proteus, you won’t be getting much more from the experience than the person who loads it up for five minutes and closes it out of disinterest. This game may be the latest discussion in the “are games art” debate but I’d argue that Proteus offers absolutely nothing to the player. There is no interaction to speak of, the music is amateurish, the visuals are mediocre and the experience is pointless. There is no message or mood established in Proteus, it’s the definition of wasting time. Proteus may serve as inspiration for a mechanic that’s a part of a bigger game, but on its own there’s nothing worth playing.

- I didn’t find the story too interesting, maybe because the game is overloaded with spiritual/philosphical bits which just went over my head. Some of them don't even stay on the screen long enough for me to read.

Toren is not a fun game to play and I can't recommend it.
I wish I could. It's an absolutely gorgeous game, the screenshots don't even do it justice. Palettes pastel and traditional abound, the environments are pushed to their absolute limits and a few of the dream sequences (some optional) are absolutely insane. Character designs feed into that, apart from one brusque fellow near the end who got lost on his way to a different game.
An ambient soundtrack that builds into high notes supports all this. It knows when to be silent and when to keep it pumped, it's not an all or nothing approach.
The story itself is beautiful, mixing allegory, mythos and literal to such an extent that I don't even want to talk about it beyond what the blurb does. They took the time they had to tell it and ran with it - a 100% playthrough ran me 2 hours, with some time thrown in for card idling.
The problem with Toren is not that it's short (in today's age of eternal backlogs, that's honestly not a bad thing). Or that it's buggy, including a set of hilarious bugs that saw me flying off a cliff at mach speed when I pushed a set of statues. Or that everything clips into each other and it never quite figures out how to put decals on things.
The problem with Toren is that it's not fun.
Base movement control is jank beyond measure, with the Moonchild being completely unable to comprehend any turn without moving forward, and at its worst controls like a bumper car that half-listens to you, with terrible animation wait times. At its best you're still just waiting for the animations to play themselves out while thinking of all the fun things you could be doing.
It's cranked up to 10 during the platforming, where Toren will struggle up every step for a good 10 seconds, float in the air for another 10 seconds, and then recover for a final 10 seconds when you figured out exactly where you need to go and do in their extremely simple levels in about 10 seconds. It's turned up to 11 during the stealth/avoidance sections where you'll just be waiting there for what seems like aeons for the arbitrary wind or petrification beam to just go away and let you continue.
Combat, actual combat, controls even worse than just walking around. Forget hitstun, forget hit sfx, or more than one enemy type, or any sort of mechanical aptitude, you'll limply slap at the mook or the dragon that serves as a sort of puzzle boss.
The puzzle is waiting. Waiting for it to charge up a beam or waiting for your ally to catch up to you. The climax of this game turns into a wait-em-up, that ends with some more waiting as your wait for camera angles to change. This is on top of already bad mechanics, a mere 2 hours and Toren manages to feel like it's wasting your time.
It's not fun. It's not remotely fun. And it's hard to appreciate beauty in a game when you're not having fun.
Harder still to recommend it to others.

But I certainly wouldn't recommend it to anyone else.

Adopting a retro arcade 8-bit art style, the SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect, or Sword Justice Deluxe Selective Memory Erase Effect plays as a 2D platformer where you move your character, a mechanical android cat through different layers of fear clusters in order to reach an end terminal to log out and return to the real world where his link partner, M1Mi resides in.  Along the way, the cat meets many parts of the operating system that take a physical form as enemies.  In order to progress through the game, players must complete each level by moving their character from the left to the right; killing enemies along the way which will increase your score.  The developer has taken an extra step, whether intentional or not to bring the complete experience of a CRT arcade cabinet by featuring in-game screen brightness control for CRTs’, three button layouts found on cabinets and of course, infinite continues.
SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect follows true to the standard cabinet platformer.  To give an idea of how the game is like, think of the original metal slug, except your default weapon is a blade instead of a pistol.  Jumping, ducking, dodging, button mashing all the good mechanical components of cabinet games are retained in SWR JST DX SMEE and mesh really well to play a fun to play game.
SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect’s visuals are extremely well done.  For a game with only 256 different shades of colours to work with, this game manages to bring colourful visuals with unique background design for every chapter.  Although enemy mechanics and attack patterns were used in more than one type of enemy, each chapter of the game introduced new and special looking sprites for all the enemies.
The difficulty of the game increases at a reasonable rate.  The first few chapters introduce players to the mechanics, and slowly become more demanding, such as throwing daggers while dodging and immediately air strafing in the opposite direction to slash an incoming enemy.
The plot is based off of a good concept which actually revolves around an inner conflict that appears within the player. Taking a step back, you can see there are two sides of the story.  One of which is really evident to the player, the cat’s drive to log out of this nightmare and return to M1Mi.  But in order to reach the terminal, all the operating system enemies’ have everything that they longed for destroyed.  Looking back into the dialogue between the main characters, reveals that the main antagonist isn’t even truly evil, but just someone whose ideals sided with the OS components.
Let’s start with the game itself.  Mentioned earlier, I’m not sure whether or not the developer decided to bring about the whole experience of old arcade games including the problems, or was just simply limited by the game engine they are working with.  Please note, at the time of writing this review, the game cannot save, meaning each time you start the game up, you have to start from the very beginning.  The argument may be that the game is short and can be completed in one sitting, but it is just a poor excuse that a save function not be implemented, if high scores can be recorded.  SWR JST DX SMEE also has problems shutting down properly.  The window may close, but it hangs on steam locking you in-game.  In order to play your other games again you have to shut down steam and restart the client.

Level design is not the best, and is very evident in the ice chapter where you utilize the same run and gun strategy.  Progression between levels can be spontaneous and abrupt with no warning narrative as seen by the mine cart stage. The result is a lot of gimmicky level designs that force you to lose a life no matter what, unless you’ve played through a second time.
The game itself is contradictory as to the scoring style.  2D side-scrolling platformer games like these usually are fast paced because they provide you with a ranged default weapon and unlimited ammunition.  Since SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect gives you a sword as a default weapon, you will often find yourself kiting backwards and staying just outside of the enemy hit range.  Anyone who has played a 2D side-scroller knows that going back the way you came from breaks the tempo of the game and since scoring is widely based off of number of enemies killed, you are forced to kill your enemies, making pacifist and speed runs totally redundant, not to mention impossible on some of the later levels.
The plot itself is pretty shallow and leaves a lot to be desired.  Yes, the writer may have been going for a hero vs villain scenario, but nine lines of text between levels is not enough for the player to connect with the characters, leaving an empty and hollow characters.  It really is not enough for the player to judge the scenario correctly, and is hard to sympathize for the other cast of characters that are being antagonized.
As a complete package I rate Sword Justice Deluxe Selective Memory Erase Effect at 4/10.  This game is just too large of a hassle to get up and running and an even bigger annoyance when it comes to shutting down.   If you look at just the game, I would personally score this game at 6/10 just for the amazing visuals and good controls.  The reason it isn’t higher is because the game really falls short in terms of level design.  But if the game’s art piques your interest and your computer successfully passes the
, give this game a try.

Mabinogi is quite possibly the most unique MMORPG I know, comparable to Blade & Soul.  Literally anything you want, you do.  Want to murder things with the most intimidating equipment?  Beat things with a stick?  Send meteors on your foe?  Go ahead!  There is an open world to explore, a variety of skills to master, and exceptionally well-done storylines across multiple generations.
An active player community, an active economy, and much more.  There's also music.  From Lute, to Flute, to Pianos and electric guitars, make your music and play it with impunity.  Getting bored with the game?  Here, have an event to spice things up.  Finished all the storylines?  Here, we've been working on this new one for a while.  Mastered all the talents?  Let's toss another one in here.  Mastered that too?  Let's combine them into a new one we call an Ace.  Not to mention are the three races, Human, Giant, and Elf, which specialize in whatever they do, but nothing really limits you in becoming Grandmaster anything, except maybe archery for Giants.
It's an experience to play, but the learning curve is oddly shaped.  Familiar to some, hard for others, but still odd in its own way.  It soon becomes second nature over time, though.  Other than that, I give this game the highest of scores, and encourage those interested to play, and hopefully stay long enough to enjoy the fun.

Just going by the screenshots, SWR JST DX Selective Memory Erase Effect may seem like a fairly unimpressive and milquetoast retro throwback, but in all actuality it's a solid little platformer with a cyberspace-tinged storyline that really goes places and enough variety and charm to make it well worth recommending.
Firstly, this game looks wonderful in action. Screenshots really don't do the lush backgrounds and fantastic digitized-looking sprite work justice.  The interstitial animations also look great, and there's a fairly memorable soundtrack backing everything.  This is a game that does not drop the ball at all with its presentation.
Gameplay-wise, it's about as arcadey an experience as you can get. As a cute little robot ninja cat, you'll run, jump, slash, and throw daggers to overcome most of your obstacles, but the game's strength is the staggering amount of variety it manages to pack into all of its stages.  Nearly every world has a unique set of gimmicks and challenges to overcome and it's always shuffling you in and out of new situations so you never end up doing too much of the same thing for long.
Each level is a fairly bite-sized affair, lasting roughly 30 seconds, and nearly all of them are fairly challenging (except the bosses. They're all chumps), but there's nothing that can't be overcome with a little persistence.  There are however a couple gimmicks that feel like they needed a bit more work.  The stages that drop your character into a boat with only a sword and some daggers to defend yourself don't feel properly balanced at all, and this is only emphasized later in the same world when you're able to equip your boat with a proper projectile weapon.  The mine cart stage a bit later in the game, though fairly short, is a nightmare of randomly generated nonsense that can create many impossible situations and was really a low point for me.
Other than those niggling flaws, I had a blast with the game.  It'll take you just over a couple hours to see it to completion, and even though the overly easy boss encounters kind of make for an anti-climax, the storyline and stages leading up to them are definitely solid enough to stand on their own.

My recommendation comes at a strong maybe. I'm going to try and list all of the pros and cons for me and you can base your decision on that. Overall it was a fun way to pass 2 hours and definitely worth what I paid for ~3 dollars on sale but in no ways is it so good that its an instant recommendation.
Pros
- Very Easy on the computer, very well optimized.
- Creative
- Responsive Controls (I never did something I didnt intend to do)
- Amazing camera work. Even though it has the option to use your mouse or right analog stick to look around the environment akin to any open world game, thats usually very limited. However the camera is more similar to early 3D games like Mario 64 or the first few 3D sonic games where the camera follows you and switches its angle based on where you are. Theres no glitchy back and forth that makes you lose sight of where you're going and overall is done very well.
- Impressive visuals and artstyle
Cons
- The environment can be a bit clippy
- The screenshots definitely make it look better than it actually is. Its by no means a bad looking game and ingame looks very similar to what they show you. Its just a little bit worse. Wasnt a deal breaker for me but I did notice it
- It's actually horrendous to play with mouse and keyboard. Granted they do recommend using a controller but I figured I'll give mouse and keyboard a try for 20 minutes before I used my controller and I hated it.
- There wasnt really anything that captivated me to enjoy the gameplay. It's too short to have a deep story and alot of the gameplay was just simplified platforming and walking around. For those of you looking for a great piece of art from a small studio I'm afraid this isnt it.

There is a lot to this game, but ultimately, it's a game with so much you can become, so much you can collect, so much awesome for you to achieve, but only if you sell your soul to it. Most of the game revolves on making yourself LOOK cool, with special clothing, pointless weapons, micro-transactions from hell, etc. It dangles skills, weapons, armor, trinkets, and whatever neat stuff in front of your face saying "Hey, this stuff exists! And you can get it! But only if you spend 300 hours grinding the same action over and over again!"
This game is also very buggy, both for and against you. It can be VERY unforgiving in certain missions, making you start completely over if you fail. The in-game store for micro-transactions has some items that help you quite a bit in surviving, but your spending can quickly add up if you aren't careful.
However, if you DO put enough effort into it, you can get a lot of really cool stuff. And I do mean A LOT. They do a good job rewarding you, even though it often feels like you will never make it. Also, the community is surprisingly helpful. There are rarely people that exist just to give you a hard time, and most people will help you if you ask for it. And playing this game with a friend can make for some really fun adventures.
I recommend this game to people with a lot of time on their hands, and not an extremely critical way of looking at games. It can be very enjoyable, but it will eat away at your soul if you let it.

THE GOOD
In many ways, RPG Maker MV is a great upgrade from Ace. The RTP visuals are of incredibly high quality and the tracks and catchy enough to listen to on loop for hours. Thanks to the inclusion of plugins, users will no longer have to fumble around with Ruby/RGSS3 to get custom scripts to work. For someone like me who has very little programming knowledge, this is a godsend. The inclusion of sideview battles is welcome, and they play splendidly, even without plugins.
A great new feature is the ability to remove unused assets before exporting. No more reliance on a beefy run time package!
THE MEH
No encryption tool. Datamining is far too easy now, so I guess this make sense.
THE BAD
The file sizes for projects are absolutely massive. An exported project with the default RTP is over 400MB. The lowest I was able to reduce this to was around 100. Your project’s exe file is around 50MB on its own. This is a little worrisome, and if you are looking to make casual projects that are easily disturbuted, MV is not the engine for you. Stick with earlier versions if file sizes worry you. I also havent played with it much but the iOS/Android/HTML5 export options have been described as incomplete.
I like the engine overall. A definitely upgrade for more-invested developers, but more of a sidegrade if you only use RPG Maker casually.
