I had a lot of fun on Lightbender and there are a lot of puzzles ranging from very easy to very difficult. You have to get the light to change to the correct point whilst changing colours if necessary. There are also a lot of rules behind the game, as to what changes colours and what mirrors can move. In fact it’s probably wise to have a notepad with what happens to which colours and what makes it change to what colour. This can make the game a little scary. I just played the game blind and got pretty far and enjoyed what I played. I’m not the smartest of people though so I did get stuck quite often. Here are the positives and negatives:
Positives :
+ Great audio
+ lots of content
+ really good price
+ Level editor
+ Graphics are really good with the lighting effects
+ Gamepad Support
Negatives:
- No Audio sliders
- No Windowed Support
- No Mouse Support
- Lots of rules to colour changing which can be hard to memorise
Changes:
- No Audio sliders  (Audio sliders have been added 20th December)

Hot-Fix:
For those experiencing crashing or freezing when trying to change the parameters in the traits-window; there's a bug related to the software not being able to distinguish between the "," and the "." properly which causes some sort of havok.
You'll need to alter your computers "idea" of what the decimal symbol is like, and make it correspond with "." in RPG Maker MV since it thinks the decimal = "." and not the ",".
To do this, flip up your control panel and click "Formats, Location, Keyboards and Languages" or "Administrative". Choose "Region and Language" and "Additional settings". Then change the "Decimal" from "," to ".".
After this gets fixed, you can revert back to normal to avoid any further problems with software designed for European computers/input methods.

Edit: Great and fast response and patching from the devs, only thing missing now is mouse controls. Would definitely recommend! Worth the price! :D

With approximately 80 hours in game(when this was written), I am no master, but I've had enough time to really feel it out, and think it deserves a review.
When I started a few days ago, the first thing that I noticed was a very "Mad Max" feel to the game. I can appreciate that, and adding great grafix, music, sound effects, and smooth gameplay, I think we have a winner here, and they are not even finished yet.
I have not suffered from lag, or glitches or bugs of any kind, and if I really had to pick something I did not like about this game, the only thing I could really say is that they might have to work on matching powerscore a bit better, although, I think this may work itself out as more players join, making the pool of players to pick from for each match larger and therefore closer matches.
I have no doubt that the player population will rise for this game. It's already becoming more popular for Twitch Streamers, and once more people see/hear about it, the players will flock to this Gem of a game.
Some talk about parts of the game feeling "grindy", but I haven't felt that way, since the matches are genuinly FUN, which takes the grind out of it, for me at least.
Also, and a Massive Plus for me, is the fact this is a TRUE free to play, NOT pay to win game. Everything in game can be bought with in game currancy, except maybe some visual perks, and every free to play player, that has not spent a cent, can acquire everything they want, in time.
A couple things I would have liked to know when I started.
- As soon as you possibly can, install a fuel can on your truck, as every winning match that you survive till the end, you'll get 5 fuel, which you can save up and either use for Raids, or sell for profit to buy that shiny rare gun you've had your eye on. Only add one can, as they do not stack, although, once you have some money to spend, you can buy a rare fuel tank, which stacks with the can, for a total of 5+10= 15 fuel per winning match (as long as you survive it).
- Personaly, I sold scrap, copper, fuel, wire, and any extra gear that I did not need as I was leveling up doing missions. It did not take me long to get a decent build, and I was able to try several weapons, cabs, etc. Everyone will have their own preferences, so I will not say what I feel is best.
I hope, since I took the time to share my experience and how I feel about the game, that you'll give it a try. It cannot hurt, it's FREE! I definitely recommend this game. Hope to see you all inside.

A lot of the negative comments about RMMV are from people who haven't taken the time to work out how to use the new engine. The character generator is excellent, much improved over VXAce, and allows you to quickly and easily make a variety of faces, field sprites and animated battlers with a few clicks. Furthemore, these graphics do not clash with the default resources (most of which are in a separate folder in DLC, to keep the file size of new projects down). the Database now starts off with only a handful of default weapons, skills and enemies, although all th animations are still there, and there are still a variety of reources included, they're just in "BaseResource" your DLC folder by default, something which a user can easily remedy by moving them to the "NewData" Folder, essentially allowing one to create a custom RTP with all the files one normally would import into any new project.
Instead of RGSS Scripts, a new Java based plugin system is used. As someone with no programming knowledge, I much prefer this, as you can customise these much more easily. The included bonus plugins for the english release add a wealth of new features and optional tweaks, and are likewise incredibly customisable, using easy to understand menus rather than having to search through walls of code to find out how to change the size of a window or make a character move around the screen in battle animations for example. There are more than 40 plugins included in your DLC folder FOR FREE with every copy of RMMV, and the amount of things you can do with them is mesmerising. Now you can easily have skills cost HP, alter the menu and save screens, upgrade weapons, limit items, increase the default maximums, have text boxes that word wrap (FINALLY!), make the battle camera pan and zoom, have enemies chase you round the map, and just SOOOOO much more. My one criticism is that not inluding all these resources in each new project folder does mean that some people can get the impression that they don't exist. This is the best and most flexible version of RPG maker yet, and I've been using it since XP came out.

This is a pretty good game. Probably the best of its genre of the 5 that I've played.  The vehicle building isn't as sophisticated as say robocraft but the outcome and game play is better.
The problem this game has is the matchmaking balance is not well thought out.  They have a power score system where for the most part everyone is in the same range of power score.  The problem is that the weapons don't reflect what their power score should actually be.  There are 5 tiers of weapons, but primarily 3, Common, Rare, and Epic.  Each tier has a cost per energy system however the difference is very small between the different tiers. This allows players who have been able to play a lot and acquire the more expensive and rare gear to play with those who are just starting out.  Because of this it creates an illusion that the game is pay to win causing many new players to leave uninformed reviews trashing the game.
TLDR Its not P2W its poor matchmaking and power score system that allows for players who have acquired the better gear to get matched with players who have common gear.  Essentially making it common to find yourself with T10 opponents when you are in a T6 vehicle.

To describe my excursion with Proteus and attempt to use it as a cause for you to play or avoid it would be a rather disingenuous waste of time. This is a title that exists outside the spectrum of a traditional critique, and is not something that is easy to recommend or dismiss as the experience will differ vastly for different players.
Like a piece of abstract art there will be those that fall in love with it and are able to recall in vivid detail just what they found so amazing, and an equal or greater amount that shrug it off as pretentious and insubstantial. Regardless of which side you fall on, Proteus is almost certain to draw a strong emotional response, from infatuation to downright anger.
Dropped onto an otherworldly island, your only objective is to take in your surroundings through four seasons. The primitive graphics and bizarre soundscapes are in no way ideal for first impressions, but ultimately are integral pieces of the game that wouldn't be at all the same without them, that if you allow them can be surprisingly engrossing. The developers clearly had a vision how Proteus looks and sounds, and there's no doubt in my mind they managed to achieve it.
If I was to level a complaint at Proteus, it's that in the end it wound up feeling like something that belonged in a gallery, not in my steam library. I want others to experience what I did, but also expect most would feel cheated to have paid what it currently costs, or even anything at all. Thus is the case with most things that aspire to be considered art, which for better and for worse, is the only way to describe Proteus, a love it or hate it affair if ever I saw one. I'm sure this hasn't helped in the slightest for you to decide if this is worth your time or money, but no matter how many words I type I couldn't tell you. If you have access to a copy then I wouldn't hesitate to tell you to play it, but otherwise I'm afraid it is a risk you have to take for yourself.

Toren is interesting, but it is certainly not for everyone. It is a narrative driven, platform/puzzle/adventure game that evokes a "Legend of Zelda" aura, in that it has a dark-fairytalish atmosphere and, to be honest, kind of feels like a Zelda temple/dungeon, for any of you that know the series. For those of you who are unfamilliar with this reference, allow me to provide you with a more detailed explanation of what the game is and how it works, since a list of pros and cons would not suffice in this situation, considering that many of the cons other people have listed were pros for me.
First of all, the story. Toren places you in the role of the "Moonchild," an unnamed girl with no recollection of her identity, born in a world where the sun never sets, that is tasked with ascending an immense tower in order to defeat a black dragon. The plot is framed as a sort of legend/myth, providing you with fragments of the story as you move through the setting, by completing small challenges in the form of beautiful dream sequences that also function as platforming puzzles. The game does not narrate the plot in a straightforward manner, which is something that is listed as a con in some reviews I read, instead allowing the player to piece together the lore of the game in order to understand what is happening. For me, this was a plus, since it immersed me into the world of Toren much more that it would have if the story was handed to me without any challenge. I will say, however, that not everything in the game is explained, requiring some brainwork from the players as well, in order to fill-in a few gaps that are left at the end.
Moving on to setting, Toren takes place almost exclusively in and around the large tower I mentioned before. The environment is beautifully rendered and detailed, with rich, vibrant colors fleshing it out and making it a delight to explore. Other than the tower, there are several dream sequences that completely change the setting, from endless deserts to the depths of the ocean, providing diversity and interesting platforming challenges. It is not an open world, Toren being a fairly linear experience, but there are a few secrets that require you to stray off the beaten path in order to discover them, so this adds a bit to the exploration.
In terms of visuals, the game is beautiful. Even in low graphics it still looks wonderful, being a combination of, both, realism and comic/pixar graphics that are easy on the eye and work wonders with the fairytale/legend framing of the game. The colors are strong but not irritating to look at, with the game featuring lush woodlands, deserts, run down and decaying towers as well as underwater segments, proving that the color pallete is demanded to be diverse and impressive. It is also well-optimized, meanind that low end pc's will probably be able to support its best graphics.
Gameplay wise, as I said before, the game mostly focuses on puzzles and exploration, which means that platforming takes center stage here. Most of the platforming requires the player to make accurate jumps over dangerous crags and precipices, and most puzzles are a combination of said platforming and, most of the times, pushing or pulling environmental items in order to progress through the setting. Other than that there a few fighting sequences that I actually found quite refreshing and a welcome break from the overall plarform segments, but those are mostly found in the few boss fights that the players will come across. In other words, if you are looking for an action adventure, look elsewhere. As I mentioned previously, this is mostly a narrative-driven game for the players who enjoy exploring a small, forgotten world and slowly piecing the story together, an experience similar to games like Shadow of the Colossus.
Finally, perhaps the only thing I sort of considered a con was the game's length. It took me a bit above two hours to complete with every achievement, meaning the game is quite short. It would be hard to recommend at full price, but it is quite worth it during a sale, since I got it for 2.49 during the 2016 Winter Sale.
In conclusion, yes, I totally recommend Toren but, as I said at the beginning, it is not for everyone. If you are someone who enjoys narrative-driven games, where exploration and discovery take center stage, then pick it up during a sale. Its world is hauntingly beautiful and evokes a nostalgic sense of solitude, the story is quite interesting to discover, the platforming is adequate and the action sequences are quite enjoyable. Those of you looking for an action experience, or those with small amounts of patience when it comes to finding out the plot, look elsewhere. The rest will discover that Toren is actually a small gem in the rough.

"Simulation" should not be a four-letter word. Just because Proteus happens to communicate the joys of exploration and nature through a digital medium doesn't mean that it has any less merit than taking a walk in the real outdoors. Still, it is impossible to deny that it is a separate experience and akin to a poem in its presentation and tone.
The game sets you down just offshore of a relatively small and uninhabited island with a variety of flora and fauna. You can walk around and observe your surroundings. There is no obvious objective or even an air of secrecy about the whole thing – it is purely a game that exists to let you wander. Eventually, you'll find out how to change the seasons and find certain landmarks that trigger heightened moments of reality. You can choose to investigate any of these moments for as long as you choose to let them linger, or let them fade away by wandering over to another point of interest.
It is in these specific visuals of nature afforded you that set Proteus apart from a walk you might experience in real life; Proteus is an artist's rendition of a walk. In the end, my experience playing this game does boil down to that possibly vague distinction, but if you're someone who likes stumbling across that one huge tree, or seeing clouds drift overhead, or eavesdropping on the smallest sounds of nature, I'd highly recommend looking at Proteus. It is a refreshing change of pace to take a walk in someone else's walk.

Dragon Ball Xenoverse... the name is... odd, to say the least. However what lays under Xenoverse's strange title, is a game that I'd awaited for literally, years.
My personal history with Dragon Ball games goes back to the early 2000's, playing SNES rom's of the fighting games and RPG Super Saiyan Legend. As well as the Playstation 1's Ultimate Battle 22 and Dragon Ball Z Legends.  Of course, Xenoverse has more in common with the later Tenkaichi games than with say, Ultimate Battle 22 [which is of course a great thing.]
The prior game in the series that even comes close to Xenoverse gameplay wise, is Ultimate Tenkaichi, which was released for the PS3 and Xbox 360. Where Ultimate Tenkaichi had a relatively minor create a character ability, allowing one to create a custom male saiyan, Xenoverse throws it to the wind, and gives us a full host of 5 races, 3 of which have 2 genders, and each has different, underlying stats. Xenoverse offers up the ability to create Majin's [buu's race], Saiyans, Humans, Namekian's[only male], and Freeza's race [only male, and named Freeza Race].
These create a characters are the bread and butter of the game frankly. With a host of customization options, including super moves, ultimate moves [the big attacks], and various clothing pieces, scouters, swords, ect. You're able to create damned near anything you want, from re-creating a character that may not be in game from Dragon Ball lore, to your own special snowflake super saiyan 2 god.
The combat in Xenoverse is about the level of the prior Tenkaichi games, with some refinement in my opinion. The controls feel good and the camera decent, while wonky in some aspects, leads Xenoverse to be a fairly fun action fighter.
However, not everything is sunshine and rainbows in DBZ land. Apon launch, Xenoverse saw a huge influx of players, that the developers and publisher had no idea was going to hit numbers far exceeding the ability of the servers to handle.  While this was remedied in a fairly timely fashion, Lag is a continual issue in online battles. Speaking of online battles, the Multiplayer of Xenoverse is, especially on PC, full of hackers. With the decision to house player data locally, players have been able to utilize various cheating tools to give themselves outragious statistics [100 in everything, which is impossible.] As well as access characters and content not even available to the average player. And god mode hackers have been seen topping the leaderbords in PVP.
The other shortcoming of Xenoverse lays in it's loot system. Which awards you on a pure RNG system. You could play the same mission 20 times and get Raditz boots half of that time, and never see his chest piece. As an example. And while this isn't a huge issue, for those of us who wish to get complete sets of gear, it does tend to be rather tedious, especially when some things don't trigger properly, or are not explained in the most helpful of ways. And even if you trigger the ultimate win conditions, you could STILL not get the item you're attempting. And be awarded nothing but XP.
Despite Xenoverse's Shortcommings. Dragon Ball Xenoverse is a solid entry in the long line of DBZ 3rd person fighters, that has it's roots in the Tenkaichi series over all others.  All that's holding Xenoverse back, is a relative lack of some playable characters, and a rather tedious RNG system that seems almost punishing at times. However, the storymode is solid for a DBZ title, and the customization is decent for the first major title with customization.  I have to give them points also for, well, offering this iteration up on PC, as this is the first Dragon Ball title, outside of the now defunct Dragon Ball Online, to have been offered up on PC.
Dragon Ball Xenoverse rates a solid 7/10 in my book. A damn fine dragon ball z game, but lacking as a game on the whole. Despite that it's a solid game that's worth the buy.

The Bad:
The game is repetitive. Now, a lot of game are repetitive - the whole of Half Life (an absolute classic everyone should play) is variations on a theme, when you get to gameplay. The same holds true for other incredible classics across many genre: Metroid, any given SHMUP, all the Diablo-Likes ever made (including all the Diablos), the LoZ series, and so it goes.
There's a distinct difference between good-repetitive and bad-repetitive. Good-repetitive has strong narrative, vast variation, or an intrinsic value in the repeated mechanic (think Tetris).
Toren is pretty awesome, but it doesn't have that - it has Bad Repetitive: the same goal, mechanic, and so on repeated ad nauseum. So why do I reccomend it? Well...
The Good
Beautiful. Don't get me wrong - it won't kill your gaming PC. Hell, I can play it on my laptop, which is not... you know, fantastic.
That having been said, the design is fantasic, and clearly optimized. It won't kill your PC, but it will look as intended, and that look is great.
The controls are perfect for what they're meant for. Never once did I accidentally do something other than what I meant to do. Now, I'm a klutz and I literally can't play Parappa because I can't keep the locations of particular buttons in my head... and this still applied. The controls are as close to perfect as you can get.
Also, the intent probably isn't challenge. It's an adventure (akin to the old Sierra games like KQ, SQ, PQ, and AQ), not an action title, and there's nothing in the game that's not pretty clearly meant to be solved within a few attempts.
So, what you have (when you get right down to it) is a blend of point-and-click adventure, exploration game, and walking sim. It's interesting, captivating, and, as far as I can tell, unique.
If you don't mind a game that's low on action, high on visual art and exploration, and isn't really challenging, then this might be your thing. I know it's mine.

Mabinogi is definitely one of the most interesting kinds of MMORPG's I've ever played. It's packed with things to do both combat and non combat related. The community is great depending on what server you're on (I'd suggest Alexina if you're a beginner) and is truly one of Nexon's crown jewels in the F2P Market that holds up with new content even after 6 YEARS. The style is friendly, warm and inviting. The music is also calm and relaxing in my oppinion. The skills are a point and click with a skill hot bar system which may turn off some people if they're tired of that kinda thing like I was, but the combat animation looks so cool I barely cared at all plus some skills require you to press buttons like the martial artist talent which I found pretty sweet. However I must explain the cons, The game's Rebirth System maybe confusing to some people. Basically it's the system that replaces traditional "Level Up, Up a few of your skills". Mabinogi has a ranking system with each and every skill and you rank up these skills by spending a certain amount of "AP" which you get by Leveling Up and Doing quests that reward AP. So for those that feel at one point that they need to get more AP they're free to "Rebirth" which means resetting back to Level 1, BUT you keep all of your skill ranks so you're able to increase them further by leveling up. (NOTE: LEVEL UP YOUR WINDMILL SKILL FIRST, IT WILL BE MORE DIFFICULT TO LATER ON) Next on the Con List is the steam version..I've ran into so many problems with the steam version that I just up and decided to un-install everything and re-install it from the actual site. In fact you'll probably get the best performance from just installing it from the website. Last on the con list is Nexon, Now I do love some of their games but I dislike their company mainly for my poor experience in Customer Support. I don't know about you but I expect AT LEAST average to good customer support whenever my money is being put into a company (You can purchase additional content not required by the game in the Nexon Cash Shop for Character Customization, Different mounts, and Pets). Nexon's customer support is poor, so poor that it's almost insulting so buyer beware. So in short, I do recommend this game just not the Steam Version :/

Sometimes, you must slaughter a few cows to save the herd, and in this game some deliberate collateral damage will be a virtual necessity.
Basically, you fly out to a bunch of rather urban-looking towns populated by civvies (yellow dots), where zombies (purple dots) start pouring in from the outskirts. You, from a high-flying bird's-eye view, direct efforts to airlift the civvies the heck out of there while using snipers, commandos, barricades, dynamite, mortar fire, and more to hold back or redirect the tide of zombies. Infection spreads FAST, and there's no penalty for getting a little, uh, extreme with your methods, so... yeah. Sledgehammers for nails. If you're quick, you can blow up all the zombies and win that way, too.
There's also a strategy element where you choose upgrades for your troops, direct research focus, and pick which town to try to evacuate based on your current (random) assignment of weaponry and tools. Still, the meat of the game is evacuating towns.

It was one of those rare days; I'd woken up sober for a change, my head a bit muddled from the unexpected absense of corn whiskey and pain killers.  The pain killers were still there, but the fog had taken a vacation that day.  I was awoken by the post man, he only rang once, but he left a package.  They were my new enhanced pants; they fit nice, tight across the seat showing off what some say is my best asset.  I didn't care how they looked though.  They let me jump.  They let me jump high.  That counted for a lot in my line of work.
I hadn't been in the pants for long before the doorbell rang again.  I figured itt was the drab UPS man coming back to check on the fit of my order, but instead I was hit with a dame charging in without waiting for an answer.  Her hair flamed red, fell down over the shoulders of her severe over coat with her fedora pulled low to hide her eyes.  I stood looking her up and down; it was quite the sight.  She stood avoiding any attempt at eye contact, though I noticed my new pants caught her attention again and again.
"I don't have time for games," she spat as she opened her coat and reached a steady hand into the shadows inside.  I tensed for moment thinking she might be going for her piece.   That thought didnt' last long though; if she had come to rub me out, she would have done it by now.
She threw a folder on my desk, finally looking me in the eye from under the brim of her hat.  Her eyes, they were brown.   "I lied.  This is actually a game.  But it's a fun game, so you're going to like it.  You're going to figure out how to get through all of these buildings, then you're going to hack some computers, maybe punch a few guards.  It's going to make you think and it's going to make you get creative.  And the whole time, you're going to get a jazzy soundtrack that's pretty great to push you along."
I snagged the folder from the desk, flipping through the pages.  The thought of playing a game, a game that was part stealth, a game that was part puzzle; it sounded like a tough nut to crack,  I knew I was the man for the job though.  After all, I was having a good day and I've got these new pants to try out.
"I'll do it," I said, looking up for the folder.
As abruptly as she'd entered, the flame haired dame and vanished, leaving me alone with nothing but a case load and the promises of puzzles to solve.  I was going to find my way back to her; after all she'd never mentioned how she planned to pay for the job.

Fair warning: it took me in excess of three months begin to appreciate the game and more than 2 years to start playing it properly.
It's worth it.
I fear there is little I can really tell a new player, other than the mechanics of how to play (don't use WASD), in order to get them up to speed and having fun.
EVE is a sandbox MMO and it's a long-term game. There is unprecedented freedom, yet anyone looking for an easy, on-rails experience needs to leave quickly. You will make decisions that will take months to complete and may not be profitable nor pan out for you. You will learn, slowly, and you'll adapt.
The major battles (the fun stuff) are player-based and do not depend on the whims of developers (CCP tried and we barely took notice). Nigh all of the items in-game are made or otherwise harvested by players. Don't play this game if you do not like the concept of PvP as you will be forced to face it, whether flying in space or tackling the markets. Play with friends or learn how to make them fast. Some will want to run background checks on you. Most find this normal. Those who don't are spies.
You will find yourself making spreadsheets in Google Docs and using the API to your advantage. You might find yourself shooting lasers at rocks, you might find yourself shooting lasers at other ships, you might find yourself staring at endless items and modules for hours on end, trying to eke out as much function out of your ships powergrid and CPU limitations.
And it will be fun.
If I have yet to scare you, you may have what it takes to be a capsuleer.

Just excellent. Ever been bothered by predictable A.I, or games that are 'set in their ways?' Up to now, there has been little predictability in this game, which makes it the most interesting shooter I have ever played. Camping means countermeasures by very intelligent A.I.'s, which work together constantly to close in on their target: You! Which means you must do everything you can to convince them you are not there. If one cannot learn to work as a team and understand how much communication, routine, persistance, adaptation and covering each other is needed, well, the adversary does! And that is just part one of this still developing game, which is promising indeed. Up 'till now, I have only played against the Combat Robots. You will fear them. You will grow to hate them. Their sound, look and zombie-like behaviour. That's ok, they really seem to hate organic intelligence too. You will thoroughly enjoy gunning down each and every one of them, which is another thing you have in common with them. In fact, it doesn't feel right to leave one standing. Even though you are a badass marine, somehow you will understand and appreciate a certain BeeGee's -song. You will scream, you will run, and you will cry, which is why this game is best played with friends in CO-OP. After all, aren't friends the people you share laughter, despair and your vulnerabilities with? And just to be clear, this game is not for people who believe in 'health-bars', cool guns vs. effective guns, or fair game. You're the game. Fair enough. This will make you experience the future of shooter games. Because that is exactly what it is. That, and the end of noobism.

Inspector Gadget meets film noir meets Bugs Bunny's brand of fourth-wall-breaking sarcasm. "Gunpoint" is an action-strategy-puzzle game, where the goal is to infiltrate secured buildings and put a stop to various nefarious happenings, usually by reaching some sort of computer locked away deep within the building.
"Gunpoint" really shines in its application of new mechanics, where you manipulate power systems and electrical wiring to accomplish your objectives. The storyline is intriguing and has several different branches to explore, putting "Gunpoint" ahead of some RPGs, but the game is rather short. You can beat the campaign in about three hours, but the game has greater longevity thanks to a built-in level creator.

Proteus is a very, very pretty... erm...
interactive- well, no, not really...
Well... I guess... Um...
Proteus is a very, very pretty walking simulator.
Don't get me wrong: I like Proteus. It's a good ga- walking simulator. But there's not really much to /do./ As you walk around, night slowly falls on the world. If you walk up to certain things, certain things happen. At midnight-ish, you find a certain thing, and the seasons change. After all four seasons of the year, the game ends.
The world is randomly generated. That's something, I guess.
Really, though, I only completed Proteus because I was curious if it ended.
I guess that's kind of the point of this simulator though: curiousity.
"Look, there's a bunny. What happens if I try to touch it?
Oh. Look. It runs away. Just like every other organism in this bloody 'game.'"
If Proteus was $2.50, I'd scream
"Go! Buy Proteus! It's magnificent! It's wonderful! It's a splendid work of art!"
But this game is TEN DOLLARS.
Ten dollars can buy me 1,345 different steam games (as of October 20th, 2013).
There are 60 different games on steam with metascores higher than ninety for less than ten dollars.
Why spend ten dollars on Proteus, you may ask?
Don't spend ten dollars on Proteus, I reply.
Do not.
If Proteus goes on sale- buy it. But do not spend ten dollars on it. I beat the game in forty-two minutes.
$9.99/0.7 hours = $14.271/hour = 23.8 cents/minute.
Keep your money.
Buy yourself a sandwich.

Quick summary: A cart racing game with Sega characters that doesn’t hold your hand about gameplay mechanics. If you’re a casual racing game player like me, you’ll probably want to play this on easy mode for a while.
I’m not a console gamer and I’m not a racing game aficionado either, so this review is from the viewpoint of someone who has played the first Mario Kart game, and not much else in terms of racing. In many ways Sonic and All Stars Racing is very similar: cartoony carts driving around helmed by video game characters and shooting weapons at each other in a family friendly way. However as I mentioned before, this game is challenging even on medium mode. You will need to master “drifting” to beat the later levels of the world tour, and you really, really, should be using a controller. I used an xbox 360 controller and it was great. Also, if you’re going for Steam achievements you’ll need monster skills to get a really high % because there are a lot of requirements for beating missions on Expert difficulty.
Good news though, the game is a lot of fun. Especially when you’ve got a great run going, drifting around corners to build up booster speed, and smacking down your opponents with various random weapons. The world tour game mode is probably the equivalent of the single player campaign and it’s made up of about 50 different levels of varying types. From the basic no-weapon races, to drift challenges, traffic challenges, and even boss fights (kind of).
Each level in the world tour can be played at easy, medium, or hard, and you get a “star” for each difficulty you beat. For example, beating 2 missions on medium gives you 4 stars (2x2) or beating 5 missions on hard would give you 15 stars (5x3). The stars are used to “unlock” further playable characters and levels. If you play every mission on easy (like I did at first) you won’t be able to progress to the end of the tour because you won’t have enough stars to unlock some of the later missions. Beating everything on medium will get you through just about all the levels, but won’t be nearly enough to unlock all the playable characters. I beat the world tour on medium with about 110 stars out of 200+ possible.
Who should get this game:
People who enjoy cart racers and have some skill in handling them. If you play the “time attack” mode to try and get the fastest possible lap times on specific levels, you will be facing off against the “ghosts” of people with awesome speed/skills that seem to make no mistakes. There are just so many ways that experts shave a second or two off of their lap times and leave you in the dust.
People who want to battle their friends on the various multiplayer modes. This includes arena battles like the ones in Mario Kart that aren’t about racing, just hurling weapons at each other in large free-for-alls. Bear in mind though that not too many people are playing the online matchmaking. If you’re not playing with friends you may have nobody to face off against.
Who should NOT get this game:
People who rage quit if a game is hard.  This isn’t like Mario Kart where the person in last place gets a bonus speed boost and better weapon drops. If you’re in tenth place in Sonic Racing, you’re probably going to lose horribly and everyone will laugh at you.
People who expect to just drop in and learn everything quickly. There’s no real tutorial in this game and the hints on the loading screen disappear too fast for you to learn some of the things that you really should know.

I wish i could give a mixed rating. While i somewhat enjoyed the game, it has a lot of problems. While those could be fixed, the developer didn't update the game for over a year. This fact and the 'jankyness' of the game are why i tend to the negative review.
Toren is an (action-)adventure game sometimes and a third-person walking-simulator at others. You are thrown from sequence to sequence with a hint of a story that doesn't make all that much sense in the beginning. You climb a tower by walking and jumping around. There isn't much substance to what you're doing. The artstyle and the music are beautiful though.
Strangely enough i enjoyed the last parts and the ending of the game the most.
Sadly the game gets bogged down by a myriad of things. It feels like it's in beta and needs way more polish. All of these problems could be fixed.
The animations look silly and janky most of the time. Your jump is floaty to the point where you at one point are slowed to a crawl but still can/MUST jump 4 meters from a standing position. There are points where you have to jump somewhere which looks like you can't reach it - but in the middle of the jump the game boosts you upwards so you can make it. The main antagonist looks menacing at times but plain silly at others.
The graphics themselves are pretty blocky with washed-out textures.
Your weapon is sometimes as big as you and sometimes it's the size of your arm.
There is a dark sequence where you can only see where you have to go when lightning strikes. But the screen lights up for such a small amount of time and the lightning-strikes are so far apart that you can't make out anything. Also, the camera-angle changes all the time. It got to the point where i just took a screenshot to find out where i had to got.
The advertised 'rich puzzle-solving' translates to pressing X at one spot so you can press x at another. Example: There are 3 torches, 1 is lit. You have papyrus in your hand (and you are told to burn it). You go to the lit torch, lit up the papyrus and light the other 2 torches with it. Done.
The necessary subtitles (i think they speak in a made-up language) sometimes are on the screen for way too long and sometimes they are gone extremely fast. (There is a textlog though).
The combat while existent doesn't feel good.
The camera sometimes shows great angles and sometimes mangles it completely (i'm looking at you, MERCY...).
If you can look past all of those problems and are still interested - grab it while it's on sale! Otherwise: you aren't missing much.

DBXV is a mixed bag.  The fighting side of the game is a lot of fun, and controls very well compared to older DB-series fighting games.  The movements are fluid and attacks are aesthetically pleasing.  There is enough variety in creating your skill-sets to keep the combat interesting and unique.
However, the rest of the game has it's issues.  The scripting/acting in the story leaves much to be desired. Cut-scenes are laden with bugs and visual glitches.
Single-player (offline) quests run smooth enough, and don't have the netcode issues plaguing the online versions of the same quests.  Oftentimes you'll find yourself stuck in a quest, waiting for the timer to run out because an NPC failed to spawn.  Other times, your character will be stuck in-place, unable to assist your teammates.  This can happen even when it looks like everyone's latency is acceptable.  Yet, it happens far too often.
Drop-rates on items and skills are a mixed bag.  Some people farm entire days to finally get something to drop, while others will get it on the first try.  There's a lot of RNG praying involved.  Would it not be better to put the drops on the stores after you Z-rank a mission, perhaps?
The "secret" goals on missions keep it fun, but it's difficult to coordinate with online players without using voice chat.  This is an online game - Why not open up typed chat, rather than using pre-scripted chat options?
The interface in the hub city could use some work.  But once you find where all the menu options are, it tends to flow.
PvP is unbalanced, and there are cheaters taking advantage of bugs that make them nigh unbeatable.  There is no in-game report function.
I find the experience is far better playing offline until the netcode issues are resolved.
If you're a fan of the DB series, it's probably worth playing when it goes on sale.  The character variety and fun combat will keep you entertained for many hours.  But if you're not into the series, it's probably not worth your money as a fighting game.

In this abridged review (I could easily complain about a lot more) it's a very mixed bag of a game to say the least. It's crammed full of fanservice for fans of the anime, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired. It's a real time action rpg at heart with fighting game elements, only with limited ways to play the game that are actually effective.
If I were to sum up the story in the game in one sentance it would probably be something like:
The Saiyan Race to say the least is basically easy mode for the game with ki related moves being basically the games version of magic. They have access to a transformation which basically allows them to endlessly spam ki/magic moves. Couple this ability with the strongest ki attacks in the game and the AI barely becomes a threat in most instances anymore once you have the stats to back it up. There are also majin (buu), piccolo, human, and Frieza races, but none of those except the latter are really as clearly defined as saiyans with what they are good at.
With how the game grades your completed missions it seems clear they only had saiyans in mind with that also, since the game only seems to grade you on speed, damage taken and most importantly how often you finished off enemies with a special finisher (which basically gives a ki spamming saiyan a free pass to high scores in most cases)
The skill and leveling system is very loose, with not many restrictions (though some classes are more naturally inclined towards certain builds than others *cough*saiyans*cough*) and it's fairly easy to rebuild characters which is something I like compared to the grind fest of other games.
The problem lies in that the majority of the the unlockable attacks suck compared to the better ones in the game rendering them near useless in the long run beyond their novelty of "HEY LOOK IT'S THIS MOVE FROM THIS GUY".
The game is also a console port at heart, which means it suffers from the same problems as a console game, such as simplified menus and an online system designed more with console gamers in mind.
In short I felt like playing saiyan was required! Since it makes unlocking the content for all your characters to use so much easier for you to try more challenging tasks with melee characters later.
The max lv of a character is 80, once you reach that exspect to spend countless hours at the mercy of random item and skill drops, replaying missions endlessy to get whatever elusive item you're after, and tweaking and changing your loadout and stats until you find a build that works for you (which shouldn't take long because there are very few builds that seem to work well in this game)
There's a PVP too, but I've seen so many hackers and cheap tatics it's hard to recommend if you take competition too seriously. It's also worth noting that you can play as not customisable characters from the show on any mode other than story mode (which is also odd because the entire game is done through a hub world with other players rather than game menus) but once your created character reaches max level, you will be stronger than most of the other characters in the game! So to use them instead would be actually giving yourself a handicap
All in all, this is one for the fans only! or at a push for those who want a more casual action rpg, rather than the hardcore crazy "goodbye social life" stuff

As my first Lego game, I chose this one because many people told me it was the best.  I was never really all that interested in the series, but I'm looking forward to playing some others after this one.
Gameplay is typical Lego, using the abilities of various characters to solve puzzles and find collectibles while you progress through the story and explore the game world.  There are a ton of characters to collect as well, some I don't even remember from the books.  This one follows the Lord of the Rings movies, and the majority of the voice acting is taken directly from them so it is very high quality.  Cutscenes are thankfully skippable, especially considering you are forced to replay story missions in order to find all the collectibles.  If you are a fan of Lord of the Rings, you will probably enjoy this game.
I personally found the humor pretty weak and often forced, though it is generally considered one of the high points of the series.  A few areas in the game really made me wish there was a way to summon a horse so I could move around faster.  There are a number of bugs and though most of them thankfully minor a few can be quite annoying.  One in particular makes a couple platforming puzzles in the game extremely difficult.  When juping across these platforms, the game  slows you down in the air so you don't jump too far and fall off.  Unfortunately in certain locations, it always slows you down too much, causing you to not jump far enough and fall no matter how far you actually try to jump.  This makes it extremely difficult to actually finish what should be trivial puzzles.  I have also heard reports of a bug preventing 100% completion though luckily I did not run into that one.
For the technical aspect of the game, it runs mostly smoothly except when loading a new area in the overworld and is very stable; I only experienced one crash in my playthrough.  The graphics are nothing special but it's a Lego game, not Crysis.  The game does not have mouse support like all Lego games so I would highly recommend playing with a gamepad rather than the keyboard.
I enjoyed this game a great deal, more than I thought I was going to.  I can definitely recommend it to anyone who's a fan of Lego games or Lord of the Rings.
My wishlist for future Lego games:
- A minimap (I believe this was added in Lego The Hobbit)
- Proper mouse support with free look
- A way to move faster later in the game
- The ability to skip in-game cutscenes in addition to cinematic cutscenes.  Blacksmithing is quite tedious in this one.
- Better autotargeting.  This game likes to loose the target when you hit the button to act on it.

This game is excellent. The gameplay is similar to Another World (aka Out of this World), in that you're a weak individual exploring a hostile environment and trying to find items, avoid traps, overcome obstacles and solve puzzles. Meanwhile death is around every corner and there are endless things that can kill you and gory ways in which you can die. People who are writing negative reviews clearly don't understand this game: death is not punished, you have infinite lives, you respawn immediately and checkpoints are given frequently (and there's even an "easy" mode). Quite often I jump into a trap or monster's jaws on purpose just to see what happens and to watch the death animations. Otherwise the controls are tight and the fixed camera angle was reminiscent of Alone in the Dark or early Resident Evil games.
Aside from the gameplay, the atmosphere and environments are beautiful and creepy.. the game is mostly black and white, and we explore a surreal ruined nightmarescape of blood, gore and cracked tiles, etc. It feels a lot like Eraserhead. As you progress, you unravel more of the story and the game spices things up by awarding you with new abilities and constatly surprising challenges presented by the environment (including boss fights). You control the protagonist, a strange little mammal creature who looks a bit like Ren (from Ren & Stimpy) but also a bit like a tarsier. He looks so scared and vulnerable in that awful environment and that, along with the excellent sound design and fixed camera, create an atmosphere of tension and horror. The graphics look a bit like goofy 3D from the early 2000's but that adds to the charm and it kind of suits the surreal, cobbled-together found-footage feeling of the game.
I generally don't review games but I felt I needed to speak up about this game. It really is something unique, something special and you can tell that the developer has poured so much love and creativity into it. This game won't be for everyone, but it's not trying to do that. If you've got love and respect for the original Alone in the Dark and also Another World, or if you like your games a bit weird and difficult, then you're certain to adore this highly underrated gem.

With several side missions, wacky outfits and gear, and kooky craftable items, this hilarious comedic mash-up of an otherwise serious fantasy adventure is fun for the whole family.  It'll make you chuckle every time you play it!

Lithium: Inmate 39 is developed and published by Canu Arts. I honestly expected more from a company that’s just getting started on Steam. Their first project is clear flop.

It’s almost amusing how misleading screenshots can be, even for (in my own opinion at least) a trained eye. I could have never guessed just how bad the game I was about to start, can actually be. Sure, I could have read the reviews already posted by I try to judge a game from my perspective alone. It’s not that I might not trust others, it’s simply a habit. I don’t even read other folks’ reviews for the game in question until I thoroughly playtest it myself. Luckly, the times of doctored “in-game” screenshots are about to end. I’m glad Valve is finally stepping in and trying to deter such misleading actions as some developers were presenting almost fake (or at least taken out of context) images that did not reflect the finally released game. Now onto Lithium’s creepy story. At least this part delivers what was promised. Our tormented lemur-like silent protagonist (inmate 39) must escape what looks like the worst kind of mental asylum I’ve seen in recent video games. That’s not really a compliment, even if we’re talking of a horror game. The atrocious camera controls and equally abysmal key bindings (in terms of actual response), make traversing the booby-trapped hallways even harder than it already is. After sufficient trial & error and some degree of repetitiveness you think you’d be treated with something else, but no. It's always the same thing. Key retrieval, trap avoiding and the rare moment in which you can fight back instead of just running away.
Terrorized lemur has an alter ego/buddy. A less than convincing zombie of sorts which for a very limited time frame, can help you destroy other pseudo-zombies or to break away some obstacles in your path. Don’t expect me to go further into detail regarding a coherent plot, since I never found one. At least there weren’t any cheap jump scares and for that I am grateful. Now, if only the developer would have specified that his game is ideally played on a controller...

As far as graphics are concerned, they are fairly subpar. Low-res textures are aplenty and even those seem to have trouble loading from one room to another. I dare not imagine what would Lithium have looked like, in full color spectrum. Mercifully, we are treated with a grey scale setting and the occasionally shade of red and yellow. I cannot complain of its sounds though since there’s not much to say at all. The in-game options are fairly limited and simplistic to a fault, no doubt as a result of the legacy it shares with consoles. 1080p the maximum supported resolution, really? Seeing comments in different places and Lithium being compared to Limbo seems closer to a blasphemy than anything else.

+ Interesting chromatic choice
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- Texture loading issues and other glitches
- Troublesome control scheme
- Overpriced for its current state
I might have still recommended Lithium if it was priced at about 5 dollars/euros and not a cent more. Asking 10 for so many technical issues, is just too much. The story is half-decent I’ll admit, but it's far too broken for me to continue playing, even less so to encourage others to give it a chance. When and IF some of the issues I mentioned above may be fixed, you should consider purchasing it when found on offer. At a substantial discount, naturally.

For fans of Jedi Knight 2: Jedi Outcast and Jedi Academy. You will find that the combat is very similar in this game. For anyone who wants a game with solid melee mechanics, I wholeheartedly recommend this one.
Pros:
♥ Very challenging at times. You will need to make the correct decisions about upgrading in the challenge modes
♥ Some funny dialogue from the commentators
♥ Fun upgrades, particularly for the sword and bow
♥ A lot of fun enemies to fight
♥ Great and reliable combat system
Cons:
♥ The story mode gets a bit repetetive. I get that's the point, but going through the early levels again & again is a bit tiresome. To be clear, once you clear a certain number, you do get a "checkpoint," so no need to go through the WHOLE game again.
♥ Some upgrades feel more viable than others, which tend to just go ignored. For example - the hammer, despite its cool ability, feels supremely inferior to the sword.
♥ Some higher level enemies (such as the raptor or hammer bots) don't feel very challenging. Probably dependent on playstyle though.
♥ A bit more music variety would be nice, as the combat track does get somewhat repetetive after a while.
All in all, well worth the money, in my opinion.

There is no doubt in my mind that you need this game, if you're into tower defense games.
If you don't like tower defense games, then avoid this at all costs, because that's what this is, but that's not /all/ this is.
A set wave of enemies will spawn and attack your home base where your children are helplessly hoping they make it alive from the Monsters, but not unless you save them, then peace will be restored (a typical layout for a tower defense game, but Pixeljunk takes it further than that). You get a large variety of bad-a$$ towers to choose from like fire towers, ice towers, laser towers, arrow towers, cannon towers, and much more to take down your enemies. Around half the towers you use are to be unlocked by beating other levels. A rewarding experience to unlock the new towers and watch at how powerfully you can blast through a previous level to try to obtain a perfect score, unlocking new levels to ultimately, unlock even more content. The amount of replayability to this game goes on a whole 'nother scale of "awesome". What Pixeljunk Monsters does, is it gives you a standard tower defense game layout, and create an enlightening charm, creative ideas, and personality that cannot easily be replicated.
Just like I like to tell people about Serious Sam (very unrelated game) is that the enemies and sheer creativity given to them makes the game memorable. Another trait that both games have in common is that you learn to acknowledge the sound of your enemy. Whether it be knowing what's coming (Serious Sam) or knowing what you've just killed (PJ Monsters) hearing the sounds of your enemy is only accomplishing if you begin to love the characters you're decimating.
This Steam release does feel rather lacking, now here's where things get more in-depth.
PJ Monsters feels more like a Steam port than an ultimate HD re-master. There's a new map that "randomly generates levels", but this is actually nothing more than the game on "shuffle" as it gives you a random map from the game and changes few things like enemy spawns and location textures. The maps are exclusively the same otherwise.
The game does look remarkable in HD on a monitor, and saying this without playing the original PS3 version, I feel as if it's probably not too different from how it looked on there. In fact, the game being in "HD" should be a given, and not an announcement. The game isn't old. Regardless of their showing off "High Definition", the game looks nice, plays nice, plays right, and plays fair.
They do give you Steam trading cards, which is probably the best feature added to this Steam port. They include descriptions of what you're fighting, and if you collect them all you can share your love of the game to your friends by showing off your pride with your PJ Monsters badge.
Did I mention co-op though? The co-op feature to this game on Steam is undenyably the best way to play. Get a friend to buy the game, or purchase the two-in-one bundle and blast through these baddies with strategic planning, mapping, and basically any other skill you can accomplish in a game of tower defense, with a friend! (I think the maximum was eight players at a time, but I don't have enough friends who play this and the Steam page doesn't explain co-op for the game too well as of this review, so I cannot say for certain).
Overall, I feel like with this release there could have been a little more content (I think if they revised the randomly generated levels to actually be randomly generated that would be enough for me) would have been nice. The game delivers what you'd expect and the charm of this game is enough to play it alone. It's not scary, it's not hyper, it's not angry, it's just happy and fun.

PixelJunk Monsters is a tower defense game set on tropical islands in which you play as Tikiman who is tasked to defend his home from the onslaught of various monsters. While this sounds very appealing, PixelJunk Monsters is riddled with a myriad of serious problems that will only frustrate and bewilder you.
It pretty much plays as a classic isometric tower defense game, the only notable difference being that you only directly control Tikiman, so you have to use him to do pretty much anything. Tikiman has the ability to cut down trees and build towers in their place. The tower selection is abysmal and the game will force you to use three or four towers most of the time. To unlock a few towers more, you have to collect gems which are randomly dropped by defeated monsters. You can also use these gems to upgrade existing towers.
The first thing you’ll notice is that the controls are surprisingly wonky. Tikiman will almost always sort of slide just off the point you designated him to stop. Unfortunately, a small thing such as this becomes a major problem simply because Tikiman has to be in the exact spot of anything you need to interact with, be it a tower or his home. When you finally do get him into place, you will find out that you usually have to click several times on the tower before the game registers your command. This becomes a huge problem when there are several towers very close to each other. He also has to manually collect every single coin and gem dropped by the destroyed monsters. All of this leads to incredibly monotonous, frustrating and completely needless micromanagement.
The true incompetence of the developer failing to understand the appeal of tower defense games is best evident in the game design. When you fail a map in a superbly designed tower defense game, you always know why and how you failed and you can devise new tactics on your second try. That’s what makes you keep going and repeating a level until it is perfect. In PixelJunk Monsters, you will repeat levels because the game will punish you for not being psychic. Most maps have multiple routes, but you have absolutely no idea which one the monsters will take, you cannot affect or change paths in any way and you don’t know anything about the upcoming monsters and their abilities until they actually show up.
Speaking of monsters, the difficulty spikes are absolutely insane. All bosses are incredibly slow and boring making them complete pushovers which makes each and every final wave disappointingly anticlimactic whereas you will get completely trumped by a random low level monster wave. All of these bewildering design choices result in constant soul-crushing trial and error effectively destroying any semblance of strategy so inherent to the tower defense genre.
The game looks nice enough. It sports simple 2D graphics, but the art style is vibrant and colorful. The tower and monster designs, however, are rather poor. Upgrading the towers will only change their appearance when they reach the final level and even then it only adds a golden outline. Until then, the only way to differentiate them is by looking at the ugly colored flags. The animations are pretty bad and the sound effects are lousy. The only redeeming quality is the lovely and surreal electronic soundtrack.
Considering the stiff competition within the genre, PixelJunk Monsters Ultimate has far too many problems for it to be considered anything but a complete and utter failure with frustratingly poor controls and absolutely awful trial and error design.

It started with apprehensive curiosity, then uneasy comfort - the sensation of discovery and uncovering secrets. The euphoric happiness turned to a sense of nervousness, worry and despair as Fall set in. I don't think I can accurately explain the sense of dread, lonliness and fear I felt as I trudged through the snow and twisted trees of Winter. Mabinogi is without a doubt a diamond in the rough.
Anime inspired MMORPG's have a stigma of being boring and generic, Mabinogi offers much to break this stigma. At first glance the game looks simple enough though it's not till you've entered the world of Erinn will you truely appreciate the games mechanics. Graphically the game is not anything to marvel at, using the excuse that the game is old and dated does little to soften the blow. I remember playing this in it's early days and even then the graphics weren't up to the top tier MMO's out at the time. That being said the game's graphics are unique enough to not get completely washed away with what is offered today though it is evident that it's graphics won't be a big selling point in whether someone would play this game or not. The sound direction in the game is nice and cheery for the most part. Whilst exploring you won't find many out of place sounds but at times you won't hear anything at all, though that's not a bad thing. By not hearing anything at times you gain a sense of loneliness which inturn brings you to make choices that ultimately benefit your experience. Grouping up with others is where the game truely shines. Being an amazing fighter means little if you have nothing to fight for, Playing beautiful music means little if there is noone to listen to it and the mabinogi experience offers little if one has noone to share it with.
Mabinogi was a game I played back in it's first year of release and till this day I have tremendous respect for it. The overall game design works in perfect harmony with the games mechanics and it is evident that the design choices were made with a set goal in mind which I think they accomplished.
A small issue I have with Mabinogi isn't an issue with the game itself but with it's steam integration. Unlike some of the other nexon games currently found on the steam F2P section, Mabinogi seems to have the most troubles being integrated with steam. If you want to play the game then I would highly recommending downloading the game directly from it's website which can be found published under Nexon.
Mabinogi is one of my favorite MMORPG's of all time, it's unique and very memorable. Anyone who has never played it but has some kind of interest in it should definitely try it out as this game is really an experience to be had and a marvel of excellent game design.

The game is about fighting different kinds of robots in various arenas.
After each won round you get an upgrade point to put into a skill or weapon and their upgrades - so far sword, hammer and bow. But you can also use jetpacks, kicks, flame breath... That being said, you can defeat any level without a single upgrade, in theory.
Upgrades help, add to your tactics (some weapons are better against some opponents), but you can use just a basic sword and environment to your advantage - sawblades, spikes, lava... Having Kick ability can be very handy in that regard. But the environment can be used against you, too.
Everything is voxel based, so you can dismember (and be dismembered) during fights. It's cute to see those huge hammer bots skipping after you after you cut off one of their legs. And it's oddly satisfactory to cut off legs of spider bots bit by bit.
Completing challenges unlocks additional weapon upgrades (fiery weapons), which at first look just like a visual improvement, but in fact make them much more powerful.
Also, Steam workshop levels added, brings in some freshness to the game.
In short: buy it, try it, you won't regret it.
One thing it lacks - multiplayer. Devs, please add multiplayer, would be awesome.

I purchased Toren on sale after reading the reviews and it is definitely worth playing for the experience but if you are looking for a game with replayability, complex gameplay, open world interactions and long hours to log in, this won't be the game for you.
Toren has a very cyptic way of telling its story, even after just finishing it -- not even sure if I was able to fully comprehend what had happened.
Strangely enough, even with the cons outnumbering the pros, I still ended up enjoying my experience.
Those hiccups and annoyances are very small and it never actually comes off as being immensely frustrating unless you are impatient. I had moments where I thought, "I should stop and do something else", but then the screen would load and I'd just start playing again.
Toren does a great job of at least keeping you interested in the environment and that's probably what got me to stay every time I swayed.
And when I say "simplistic gameplay", it really is as simple as it gets. You have your interact button, that also doubles as your attack button. And then you have your jump button. Literally. That's it.
I only had a couple moments where the interact button didn't react when I wanted but, like I stated before, it was never annoying since the game is very gentle in your mistakes or when you falter. I only died a few times and it was only when I was figuring things out.
If you come close to an edge, your character will react and give you a chance to step back.
If you still fall, she will manage to grip the ledge and give you a chance to climb up again.
It will only be unforgiving when it comes to attacking the dragon (not really a spoiler, I mean, he's kind of there a min into the game so...). If you don't attack the dragon and just stand there, you die. But that's just common sense, you know?
But I feel like I should end with a good note and that has to be the orchestral soundtrack and the art style.
Really, really beautiful. And I feel like they have such a great vision, I really want to see more from these developers becuase of it.
The art style is bright, beautiful and vivid. Though I feel like they could have incorporated the different medium they illustrated in two of their cutscenes in the whole game. When you play, you'll see what I mean. One of those moments where I was like, "Wow, that's really interesting" and yet you only see this style being used twice. In addition, the ending credits are just downright gorgeous, and I felt slightly bereft that this was not something they could have included in the main game either.
The soundtrack is definitely worth a listen even if you don't play the game. Reminded me a lot of Journey and Shadow of the Colossus and how the music really enhanced the experience of the game rather than just being there.

There's an interesting and beautiful game deep down in here, but the execution fumbles at nearly every step. The controls and animations feel laggy, you jump through about 5 or 6 different environments in the first 10 minutes, none of which feel connected, and you're guided to sequences before you have any idea what you're getting into.
The first time I died, I was taken to a location I had never seen before, and the first interactible location took me into a dream sequence in yet another disconnected environment. After a few deaths from experimenting with things in this dream, I could no longer jump, thus completely preventing me from progressing at all. When I exited from the pause menu, I had to wait through the splash screens again so that I could exit from the main menu. Even getting out of Toren was unintuitive and frustrating.
Again, there is a great game here, but the number of technical and design issues prevent it from being a really good experience - or in my case, playable at all. I may have gotten particularly unlucky, but general QA should have picked up the issues I ran into.

Old Review:
I joined the game originally as a closed beta tester, there was almost nothing to do, but the interesting combat/skill system caught my attention and I continued to play the game. Since then they've added a ton of free content- such as singing, piano playing, dual gunning, farming, commerce, shadow-missions, etc.
There's weeks worth, if not more, of storyline content to play and they're still adding more. The leveling system makes it so you can always play any 'class' you want and have any and all skills or equipment you desire. You do have to rebirth once in a while to reset your level and get the ability points required to level skills efficiently, but fortunately it was made far easier when they somewhat recently added a conveniently free rebirth every time you hit age 21 in-game, which takes 3 real-life weeks after a rebirth to the maximum age.
There is also quite a bit to choose from in ways of character customization, and if you don't fancy the anime style there are a few more neutral choices, as well as different races to choose from. You can also edit your characters height, and gain or lose weight and muscles depending on what you eat. There are also tons of clothing and armors to choose from, as well as dyes- although some colors are somewhat difficult to achieve, but there are always fixed-color dyes available from rebirth, gachapons, and other players.
They're currently giving out a free Holiday pet, along with the two free mounts you get for joining the game. Unfortunately a lot of the older pets have been retired and may or may not be re-released, but there are still a decent amount currently available. There's still a lot more to experience in the game, but you should try out the rest for yourself. If you ever need more information about the game you can always go to the mabinogiworld wiki, which although fan-made is pretty in-depth, active, and well-written. All things considered, I do recommend the game despite it's flaws and old age. It's definitely a unique experience and still pretty fun if you can get into it.

So here's the thing, I like this game.
+ It's a pretty simple formula. Build a vehicle piece by piece, strap on some guns, go fight. Blow off all the pieces other people put on, try not to explode on the way.
+ Different factions lean towards different play styles, and you can change which faction you want to level up every 24 hours, so you can mix and match the pieces you want.
+ Most games are bite sized 3 minute max PvP fests, win, and you get new parts you use to upgrade you vehicle, scrap, and probably some fuel to do raids.
+ Raids are the PvE element that last longer than the the PvP battles, and award you materials to make upgraded versions of the parts.
+Combat is really satisfying. Cannons will let you hit hard, machines guns will let you pick apart another car piece by piece, shotguns will shred parts and guns in short range, and melee can be devistating. More powerful weapons often have a limited range of motion as a trade off. The mix really helps make it so every round plays out differently, and helps it feel rewarding to play the style you enjoy over chancing the loudout others use, as is so often the case in PvP.
+ Balancing in game is pretty good consindering how many combinations there are out there.
+ Getting into battles or raids is quick. Rare to wait more than 30 seconds to be dropped in a fight, and often with battles it will be almost immediate.
Its not perfect by any stretch:
- Can feel grindy. While it does appear they are working to add more content, the core of the game is playing the same mix of maps and 2 modes to get enough base items to eventually craft them into better ones. Since the parts can be fairly random, it can definitely feel grindy if you are trying to upgrade a certain piece.
- Exchange Rate through the in game store seems a little jenky.
- Arguably ugly micro transactions --- This takes some explaination. You can, in theory grind out everything and not spend a cent. The part I find ugliest is to upgrade your parts you need to purchase limited use work benches from the respective faction that cost credits, something like 25 credits for 5 uses. The credits are the main microtransaction in game, which in turn are used in the market. To my knowledge, there is no direct way to earn credits in game, other than selling items on the Market. Now, most common items will only sell for about 0.25 or less, so in theory, to be able ot unlock that workbench, you're looking at 3 or 4 hours of grinding, and not including the materials you need to then make the item.
45 hours in, and I've only spent 10-15 bucks on it, with enough credits left to last me a while. Personally I'm more than happy to spend that on a game I can sink that many hours into. The money sink being the only way to upgrade your weapons does put a bad taste in my mouth, but the game is still enjoyable beyond that.
Now, there are complaints about it being pay to win. I don't know if that is completely true. The number of parts are still limited by your level, which you can't buy. Buying better parts may give you an edge, but by no stretch are a guaranteed win. Buying parts definitely can skip a lot of grind, but is definitely not as stark a contrast as in some games.
Ultimately, it's an enjoyable game, and up until Level 10, you probably won't even think about money in game, probably a little longer. Its free, play it, and if you like it enough to keep playing, support the devs.

Its a semi fighting game thats also a semi dragonball simulator. Definitely a must buy for Dragonball fans. Its presentation and gameplay its just good enough and enjoyable enough to keep bringing you back. Although its not as technical or challenging as something like Budokai 3 or Burst Limit; its definitely in my top 3 all time favorite Dragonball games.
Now, on to the negatives...
PVP is literally busted. Yes yes, Z-souls are busted, a lot of them have been nerfed or fixed but Z-souls made PVPing absolutely terrible in the first weeks. But what also makes it busted are things like the Stamina Drain or Blue Hurricane or SSJ players who as soon as the match starts, charge up, go SSJ and start spamming you to death with ultimates. Most of these people also put 100 points in ki blast and ki energy. There are ways to stop this, but its extremely annoying when coupled with the fact that some people are extremely laggy and you cannot stun them or break their guards. I had one match where I constantly dash charged my opponent to get a combo going and they werent stopped once or took any damage. But they were able to land every single hit on me and crush me. Lord help you if you try to do a 2 on 2 PVP battle and one of them is an Ultimate Ki spammer. Or even both. Anything more than 1 on 1s with people you don't know is a bad idea, unless you're very organized with a friend who can play a specific playstyle while you use a different one.  But honestly, PVP just feels like more of a chore than it feels like just having fun. Another negative aspect to this game is RNG. Everyone on the forums will tell you just how awful (or for some wonderful) it is. You could grind your heart out for hours on end for Ultra Fighting Bomber and it will never be guaranteed that you will get it regardless of achieving all the hidden assignments/goals. Its all random but your chances are somewhat higher when you play online with other people.
I already made a review on this but next is DLC. The first pack is terrible, its about 30 minutes of content and 3 PQs to grind... for weak stuff like the Devilman outfit? Like who really was aching for the Devilman outfit to be in this game? As DLC? It would have been fine if it were in the vanilla game but this trivial stuff theyre including in their DLC is lame. Not worth 10 dollars at all and the coming DLC also does not seem worth full price. But thats what happens when you buy a Japanese developed game: The studio doesn't listen to what the community wants they just pre package DLC and release it as time goes on. They really need to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together when it comes to "DLC" as they call it. Because their definition is very jaded to what would normally contest as DLC.
Overall, if you disregard PVP in its current state; this game is probably a strong 8/10. With it, its a 7 or even 6/10. Its kinda funny to see so many people say PVP is the end game. Well its a pretty terrible end game if all PVP consist of is who can out stamina or out ki blast spam you. Customization could be better, I'm fairly displeased with the fact that going super saiyan, your hair is the exact same as your base form but just golden now. Also the lack of certain Saiyan hair styles. (Vegetas, Cell Saga Trunks [the pony tail], Gokus instead of a wig, Gohan, Broly, Paragus, Goten, Trunks). Also disappointed to find that no other race besides saiyans were balanced to get special transformations. Xenoverse is like the blueprint to a dream Dragonball Simulator game. You will get hints and touches of what it could truly be but for a first attempt its valiant. This is the first Dragonball game I was excited to be released and greatly followed its progress and development. I'm one of those guys who only really liked the classic side view 3D fighters... The original budokai games, Shin Budokai and Burst Limit. So I took a risk with this, a risk I hadn't taken on Dragonball games in a long time because I was constantly disappointed with the direction they were taking the fighting games, starting with Tenkaichi.
Ultimately: Buy it if you like Dragonball, but don't PVP.
