The game itself is good. I just have 2 main problems with it -
Nothing is explained. Nothing.
There is no tutorial, no pop-up boxes, nothing. You have to figure out everything yourself. I understand that people don't like it when a game babysits the player and holds their hand, but this is the complete opposite. You create a character, and nothing is explained. You have to figure out all controls and buttons by yourself, you have to figure out how the items menu works (and the items menu is GOD AWFUL, atleast I think it's the item menu. Its just a bunch of random sized boxes and one has a chest, and if you open it its just 6 more random sized boxes appear.) The skills menu is okay, because its obvious. It tells you what skills mean and you already know what mana, health and things such as that are. You start the game by spawning into a village, and thats it. I literally went around and talked to every single person. Nobody told me anything. I got an acheivment for joining a Coffee club, though... cool?
After the beginning, which confused me for 5 whole minutes trying to figure out what to do, I realized I had to walk into the Act 1 Portal all the way to the left of the town. I tried standing on the pedestal next to it for a whole minute trying to get in before realizing that the pedastals in front of it are useless and you have to walk into the actual portal. There were about 6 circles and one had an insignia on it, I thought that was me and I had to step on it. Anyway, I start the first act and enemies jump out at me on all sides. Spiders, rats, skeletons. I start holding down left click and firing, and eventually killed a lot of them. After this I got the hang of a little bit, but I still don't understand how items and specific things work. Nothing is explained to you, you have to figure all of it out on your own.
My second problem with the game is this: It gets boring, very quickly. VERY quickly. Usually in a game such as this, there are ways to keep the player excited and interested during waves and battles. For example, Orcs must Die or Dungeon Defenders add towers, and you want to keep fighting to keep getting better towers. Something like that, just something special to seperate the game from just running around and fighting...thats basically what this game is. The game (or Atleast Act 1 as I played it) Is literally just running around in circles in a very small, boring map while holding down left click and occasionally going to my stats to click some buttons after I level up. I assume the game gets fun when its more fast paced, but it starts off so slowly, I don't understand how somebody could have fun trying to get into this game. I greatly enjoy games of this genre (Hack N' Slash enemies coming in waves), and I will play this game farther to see if it gets more interesting or helps me out, but so far, the game has a tedious and boring start and the rest of the game doesn't look very promising. I got this game on sale for .99 cents late last year, so if you really want to see if this game is alright, pick up during the summer sale or something, maybe you'll get your money's worth.
Oh yeah, I should probably say this too, you get a few classes when you start. About 6-7. The rest (about another 5-6) are locked behind a paywall. Not just .99 cents per class, nope. Each comes with a DLC pack. So if you want all the classes, you have to buy all the DLC, and all the DLC together is about 30$. There is quite a bit of content locked behind a paywall. So if your okay with paying 6$ for the game and 29.92$ for the missing chunk of content, be my guess. This game is like looking at the Mona Lisa (We'll say this represents the video game genre) and asking if you could have another painting like that for a cheap price. You pay 6$ and get a nice painting of a man, but its colored with such vivid strangeness you can't tell what your looking at until you look it up. After you look at the painting a bit, you realize that the top right corner of the mans face is missing in the painting, and you have a giant hole in the middle. You ask for the middle and they charge you 30$ For it.
That sounds stupid, but that's basically what this game is. A decent game with a fair chunk of it locked behind a greedy scheme to take more money out of you, and such a poor presentation that it can be hard to get into, especially if you're knew to this genre. If you want to play a good game in this genre, try Orcs Must Die (2), Dungeon Defenders, or just play Zombies on Call of Duty. I hate Call of Duty, but I would probably enjoy playing Naz' Zombies with my friends doing 4 player couch co-op then being restricted to only 2 players with no introduction or assistance to the player.
Edit: Something I forgot to mention, I hope the whole game isn't like this, but Act 1 is very...dark. The screen is very dark black and you have a small ring of light around you. That kind of thing just doesn't seem right with me, I feel like having a dark room and you can't see anything but the enemy's health bar just doesn't work for this type of game.

I'm rarely an impulse buyer when it comes to new releases.  In fact I more resemble a certain XKCD comic about delayed enjoyment of major releases.  Somethng about Gunpoint though grabbed me right off.  I threw my $9 down and let the chips fall where they may.  They... uhm... I'm not sure how to finish that metaphor.  It wasn't $9 wasted, let's just say that.
The entire thing is a wonderful mix of retro-puzzle-cool, with visuals in the vein of a 386-era platformer but with that modern twist of ingenuity and "hey, you're a spy now, cool!"  The ambiance is great, very 30's hardboiled/gumshoe/spy but with a pseudo-modern setting and sci-fi gadgetry.  As a kid, did you ever wish there was an awesome "be a super spy" game that you could play?  This is that game, except designed by an adult with rather good development sensibilities.
The gameplay itself is that perfect mix of "easy to pick up" and "takes practice".  All your gadgets have their obvious uses, but after you spend enough time playing around you start to learn all the other cool things they can do... and the other cool trouble they can get you into.  You can generally get through the game if you take your time, but after you do you can challenge yourself to do it faster and possibly with certain restrictions, like never knocking out a guard or even being seen by one.  Yes, you will want to play it again.
Gunpoint's plot is satisfying but somewhat short, leaving you wanting more.  As I said above you can get some of that satisfaction from playing the game over again, or even going back through old levels with your new gadgetry to completely break the intended puzzle aspects.  There's also a level editor and the ability to load custom levels, which can further satisfy that need for more.  The only downside is that they can't (as far as I can tell) be arranged into a plot-based progression like the main ones are.
The last thing I'll say in this surprisingly long recommendation is that the game really reminds me of Deus Ex, of all things.  That's hardly surprising though given that the game was designed by Tom Francis, a self-confessed fan of the game who's written articles on it for major game publications as recently as 2010.  Gunpoint definitely has that "multiple solutions to every problem" thing down, and it tickles that same part of my Game-brain.
In short, buy this if you like Deus Ex and/or puzzle platformers and/or spy coolness.

Commenting on a game like this almost requires someone with a proper sense of poetry, because artful words are necessary to communicate the experience.  Proteus isn't a "game" in any sense of the word but rather a literal experience to discover and explore.  To that end I encourage you to play this in a manner which best allows you to immerse yourself and let Proteus BE your world for a little while.  Play in the dark with headphones on and toss out your preconceived ideas for what you should see and do.
If you can approach Proteus in this way you'll find a tangible sense of wonder and intrigue as you are presented with details that are both familiar (land, trees, mountains) and unfamiliar like pixel presentations that alter your perception of what's normal along with an everpresent sense of music and interplay as your participation in the world changes the experience.  There are sights and things here to capture your imagination if you spend the time to take the world on its own terms.
With that being said Proteus is rather short and repetitive.  The whole world is procedurally generated which in theory means that every time you play you'll be greeted with an entirely different island than you ever visited before, but there are certain rules about the lay of the land which remain consistent and so the wonderful sense of new discovery can fade over repeated plays.  This doesn't diminish the enjoyment of the game any more than repeated trips to your favorite campground at a national park can make you tired of going back, but one of the primary appeals is that sense of discovery where you're confronted with a world that's simultaneously familiar but alien.
...so despite playing the game several times now I still feel like there's more yet I haven't found.  I'll come back again.

Its a pretty good game and I really recommend it, But your not in the reviews section to look at reviews, Your here to learn a ravioli recipe, so I gotchu covered:
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Interstellar Marines is a very nice, atmospheric FPS.
It's got good graphics, phenomenal sound design, and a cool movement system that comes together to create a very immersive, fun experience that feels well-polished, even in an early state
Co-op & singleplayer missions are incredibly tense and scary - they don't use any typical horror tricks like jumpscares or flickering flashlights. In the current ones you're up against some simple, melee range robots. However, their erratic, unpredictable behaviour makes them very uncanny - hearing their footsteps in the distance is an unsettling sound.
Team versus play is also a lot of fun, and the dynamic weather, lighting, (and even dynamic terrain on some maps) keeps matches interesting. Lighting has a big deal in the game - if things get dark you will often have yourself thinking about your actions, shooting out lights to stay in the dark and keeping your flashlight to a minimum so you don't  give away your position. It really is a unique experience.
Interstellar Marines is a good game, at a good price. While updates happen around once a month, each update is quite a big one and there's obviously going to be continued support from the devs.
Simply put, it's free and it's fun. Worth playing.

I'm so disappointed. The trailer for this game promises a sort of ICO / SotC game with it's own story and art style.  It seemed really polished.  I was really looking forward to this.
The first thing I noticed is just how unpolished it feels.  Some locations are actually quite beautiful, but angular polygons and blurry textures make everything look either rushed or ameteurish. Toren herself also turned out to not be as well done as she seems in the trailer.  She seems very angular, rough around the edges (3D modelling-wise) and poorly animated.
Eventually the very shallow story lost me, it seems like it's spending too much time trying to "feel" like Shadow of the Colossus and not actually making sense or captivating you in its own way. Take SotC, you notice he has a dead girl with him and is asking for her to be revived - you're instantly caught up in his story, and hope to see the girl revived.  In Toren, some old dude mumbles (and I do mean mumbles) something about only one special girl can kill the dragon or something.  Alright... whatever you say.  Dragon is just a big meanie, you know the drill, no special motivations or anything.  Oh and something about people being arrogant and building stuff was thrown in there but doesn't seem to have any bearing on whether the dragon came or not.  Seems to be thrown in there to make it seem more poignant than it really is.  If I seem harsh, well, this aspect of the game really makes me cringe.
But there are a few really cool stand out moments which were to do with mind-bending puzzles and aesthetically pleasing locations.  I feel they got these individual "scenes" right (except for the unpolished modelling) but not the game as a whole.
I'm probably going to try and finish it one day out of curiosity and on principal, but I'm not in a hurry, that's why I can't give it a positive review.  I think they had a noble cause but got lost in trying to "feel" like SotC instead of trying to make the game compelling in its own right.  As for the artwork, I guess they ran out of time?

The game is good.

5,99 € without being on Discount is a fair price for a game that you can enjoy for quite a while.
Summing up the way you will play this:
You start playing and get realy confused at first but thats fine because items and relics keep you interested.

A single point on strength is good to start off and it makes a difference but when you get 1000 strength on a single item later you be like... *why?*
Further into the game you will learn about the relics and find out what they do, afterwards you stop picking up every single relic you find because you can remember some relics being realy bad or useless and thats not a bad things it is great, because it gives you a good feeling once you find a powerful relic.
When you get to the point where the difficulty becomes hard and you wonder how you die you are probably almost level 150. You finaly become level 150 after grinding that low tier monsters and you can continue on the higher difficulty.
It could happen, that you find a super rare red item and get hyped but guess what.. It is very likely worse than your low level item for some reason.

RANDOM INVISIBLE DAMAGE SOURCES - Yes, you just die and get realy confused.

I first watched Dragon Ball when I was eleven.  DBZ had an automatic fan since the first episode I watched.  More than a decade later and I'm still a huge fan.  Fighting games generally leave me bored and button mashing my way through them.
In short:  This was a game that could have failed  hard like most of the DBZ games out there and I'm predisposed to be disappointed and bored in this case.  So, when I say it's one of the best games I have ever played, there have been myriad bars set *reaaaal* high that it hopped right over.
It starts out seeming a bit sparse.  Fighting gamers may not care for the very straightforward combos, but that's only because they've failed to explore the other customization aspects, the very unique defensive/evasive/RPG mechanics, and the excellent speed and visciousness DBX excels at.  To top it all off, there's a high skill ceiling and strategic considerations to master.  Race and gender even change how you play dramatically.
The story is pure DBZ ridiculousness and had a definite nostalgia drawing me through it every step of the way.  Parallel Quests and their hidden requirements affect character skin unlocks, item / ability drops, score, experience, zenni, etc...  Hiring NPC versions of players to be your minions on your adventures is pretty fun.  Having other Time Patrollers/Players appear randomly in your Parallel Quests to give you the chance at a dragon ball, which you earned from an embearded mini-me Friezan named IzyerFriezaRun'n? or a myopic elder called MasterNoshit is downright hilarious at times, and lets you test their layout against your own :)
I've never cared to perfect my mission scores in other fighting games.  However, this game gives you excellent benefits and rewards for doing so.  And, it's a joy to play through old matches.  You know what is required for a perfect score, you've had epic battles and close calls and, if you choose not to don OP gear on your alts - there are no restrictions of any kind except the odd race / gender item-, then you can have an honest to god challenge on your hands.  This game is very difficult if you are not built right, or if you do not know how to manage your Ki / Stamina, or a thousand other consierations.  The first real missions will likely frustrate 90% of players, but I doubt any will complain.  It's all part of becoming the strongest in the Universe.  See you all in the player World Martial Arts Tournament.  Which is a thing.
Buy it already!  Get Goku's hair, now comes in SSJ, or Master Roshi's beard, or Yamcha's bandit sword, or a signature move from a master like Big Bang and Gallic Gun.  DBX almost perfectly weaves MMORPG aspects into the fighting archetype.  The poses and animations and canned chat make for some bombastically funny moments in town.  So many fans, and no manual chat system make for a far friendlier and entertaining environment than pretty much every other online game ever.  And, really, there's a World Martial Arts Tournament.  For us.  What fan could resist throwing their wallets at the chance to compete for real?

I'm rarely an impulse buyer when it comes to new releases.  In fact I more resemble a certain XKCD comic about delayed enjoyment of major releases.  Somethng about Gunpoint though grabbed me right off.  I threw my $9 down and let the chips fall where they may.  They... uhm... I'm not sure how to finish that metaphor.  It wasn't $9 wasted, let's just say that.
The entire thing is a wonderful mix of retro-puzzle-cool, with visuals in the vein of a 386-era platformer but with that modern twist of ingenuity and "hey, you're a spy now, cool!"  The ambiance is great, very 30's hardboiled/gumshoe/spy but with a pseudo-modern setting and sci-fi gadgetry.  As a kid, did you ever wish there was an awesome "be a super spy" game that you could play?  This is that game, except designed by an adult with rather good development sensibilities.
The gameplay itself is that perfect mix of "easy to pick up" and "takes practice".  All your gadgets have their obvious uses, but after you spend enough time playing around you start to learn all the other cool things they can do... and the other cool trouble they can get you into.  You can generally get through the game if you take your time, but after you do you can challenge yourself to do it faster and possibly with certain restrictions, like never knocking out a guard or even being seen by one.  Yes, you will want to play it again.
Gunpoint's plot is satisfying but somewhat short, leaving you wanting more.  As I said above you can get some of that satisfaction from playing the game over again, or even going back through old levels with your new gadgetry to completely break the intended puzzle aspects.  There's also a level editor and the ability to load custom levels, which can further satisfy that need for more.  The only downside is that they can't (as far as I can tell) be arranged into a plot-based progression like the main ones are.
The last thing I'll say in this surprisingly long recommendation is that the game really reminds me of Deus Ex, of all things.  That's hardly surprising though given that the game was designed by Tom Francis, a self-confessed fan of the game who's written articles on it for major game publications as recently as 2010.  Gunpoint definitely has that "multiple solutions to every problem" thing down, and it tickles that same part of my Game-brain.
In short, buy this if you like Deus Ex and/or puzzle platformers and/or spy coolness.

Looks can be deceptive - the simple style and mechanics can hide some surprising challenges. This game truly proves that in a solid fashion.
The idea is simple - the player has to aid a blue cube named Qbik in navigating caverns. In each level the winning condition is the same - succeeding in making Qbik eat all the yellow cubes in the cavern. Each level is different and might require quite a lot of planning at times, especially when there are new elements to the environment such as switches, clay or teleports. Fortunately, it is possible to rewind time which definitely helps in correcting mistakes. This makes for a very relaxing atmosphere to play a couple of levels in between something. I think this game just begs for a boss key (although it would be weird to implement it since the game's on Steam and I'm pretty sure it's not allowed to put boss keys in games anymore anyway).
There is only one thing I can count as a drawback so far. I think that Qbik eases the player into new gameplay elements a bit too slowly. Though I suppose it can be excused given the fact that there is a total number of 63 levels AND a level editor. Speaking of the editor - it's very easy to use. Potentially anyone could sit down and create something, even your beloved grandma.
I can definitely recommend Qbik for anyone who likes cute, little, honest puzzle games. Oh, and did I mention it has Steam cards? Because it has Steam cards.

I'm noticing a trend in the reviews section here.
Well, I for one haven't played this game or that, nor do I own them. I was handed a key for free by a friend, so here we are. I had no high expectations, nor any low expectations, I was just given a game so I played it.
And, well, it's pretty cool. I mean, it feels okay. I don't really like that you can't customize your crosshair, it's white, you see, and in a game which makes a heavy use of 'white' in it's colour palette, well, it'd be nice to be able to change it.
So first things first, opening up the game, and OH GOD it's VERY APPARENT that it's another Unity game, because the Unity engine has a lot of very noticeable things that just very clearly define it. But what is nice is that this one's actually the first actually well made Unity game I've played, so that's not even a detractor this time around.
So lets talk story. There isn't one. THANK GOD. The last thing we need is for a game to come along, say it's this one thing, this nice, cute little idea, and then go all philosophical on us, or something like that. Just not cool. Tick Tock Bang Bang has no story. I love that.
Graphics are lovely, surprisingly. A bit too much bloom, explosions are super annoying when they're in your face because they render you blind, and then it's just blind (haha) luck whether or not you're going to take a hit, and die. This is a pain because this happens every now and then, and usually you've got no choice except to pick a direction to go in, and deal with it. But I digress. Lots of vivid colours, bright, sharp colours that you look at and go 'wow that's bright'. It's a good thing, too.
Gameplay is simple and self-explanatory. There is no tutorial. You get some basic buttons, and that's it, and like it when games do this... if they can actually pull that off. And this one... well, does it. The black hole generator needs to be used once or twice before you figure out what it actually does, but that's okay. Anyway, you just hop into a level, shoot flying robots with this taser thing, or maybe a gun. Everything, no matter how big it is, dies in just one shot, if you can place that shot correctly. And this is one mechanic I really really like. Nothing is more satisfying than seeing something that looks like an upside down space ship from Starcraft or something explode into a million pieces after being shot once in a sensitive spot.
I don't really have much more to say, the game's pretty fun, it is what it is, in a good way, and I surprisingly managed to place pretty high on more than a few of the maps, especially the last one, so that's cool.
Also, I spotted multiple references to certain other indie games, and that's really awesome. I found the Aaaaaa!!! one the most entertaining, since I remember playing that way back in 2011 briefly.
There's one or two levels in this which kind of annoyed me, but pretty much everything else was awesome. There were a lot of really great moments. Lots of pretty explosions.
I can't think of anything bad to say about the game. It's pretty cool.

In my last scene i was walking through what I thought was water. I seemed to be walking for ages, leaving the island behind me, I started staring at the clouds. Soon it seemed as if I was moving up through the clouds and into a nothern light show. As I looked down at the clouds hiding where I was, falling stars signalled my experience was over and "my eyes" closed and it was then over. It Left me agape. First, they put all the main LOTR movies in one game, so there is very little padding (un-like say in the Star Wars Lego games).  The main story goes through most of the major plots points in well designed, fun and most importanly non-frustrating levels/missions. Final word, get a decent gamepad, leave your cynicism at the door and have fun.

I think it is a good game, that I am very bad at.
Think of the principle of minecraft, or RoboCraft if you played that, but instead of using tiny blocks, you use entire car components.
A door, a bumper, half a van side, what have you - all of that can be used to build a vehicle you might take into combat.
There's no rhyme or reason to the way the components are chosen, you get individual doors as well as an entire backside consisting of two doors (welded shut).
It's easy to build something that rolls and can be brought into play.
It's hard to build something that will survive more than a few minutes.
You get a few predefined designs, more when levelling, and players can publish their designs (which is, at first, mainly cool to look at, but not useful, since you will lack all of the higher components).
Matchmaking is troubled, as with many similar games. A good player will succeed even with low quality items. A mediocre player with high quality items will crush a bad player with low quality items, making it harder to grind your way up.
Usually you'll find all three kinds of player in the same game...
PVE is available, although the number of plays per day is limited (the limit increases with level, and you can grind the resource needed in PVP, if you're good).
It's not just "rush in, destroy", but a few nice game modes, some of them requiring a minimum of teamwork and strategy, like having to transport a cargo to a destination while defending yourself or the carrier.
I think it'll be more fun if you play with people you know - at least you can define a strategy during play, making sure everyone understands the rules of the current game.
As always, since it's a free game, just give it a try. At worst you lose some time and download.

I'm just going to list the bigger gripes I have with the game. Don't let my play time fool you. I've played hundreds of hours on PS4, and on the stand-alone client from their website.
First thing, the grind people complain about. And you'll see why:
Although the game is not Pay 2 Win, it is Pay 2 Skip. As in the grind can be unbearable at times. You have to dedicated a good chunk of your free time every week to make real progress at times. Scrap, a vital resources for crafting, has a weekly limit. Which is 2800. Each basic Rare (Blue) weapon cost about 450 scrap alongside other White (Common) Weapons.
The white weapons are no problem, that's like 6-10 matches and tend to be traded at equal price. The problem is that you only get 15 scrap per match minium, plus a little extra for how well you do. Usually around 18-20 if you are doing well. That doesn't sound bad, it's like 30-50 matches per Blue. That would mean 6 Blues a week. Keep in mind you have to dedicate some serious time into this. But you also have to level up the faction to unlock the blueprint, not to mention the most criminal thing IMO, the fact that you have to rent workbenches.
The most efficent price for a Blue Workbench lets you craft 15 pieces for about 67 Coins, the Premium Currency. You have to sell stuff to get that coin, but because you are working towards that weapon, you have to sell some of that scrap. 100 pcs of Scrap averages for around 10 percent of that 67, so 6.7. So that's around 1000 scrap for renting the workbench.
So that leaves you with around 1800 scrap per week. So that's actually about 4 blues a week. Sounds alright, but it gets worse when we get to Purple. Yet, I haven't told you about Copper, a raid exclusive resource that is limited by the fact that you can only go on raids if you have fuel. You get 200 fuel a day. 20 for easy raids, 40 for normal, 60 for hard. And 40 for Leviathan raids. You get tiny amounts of scrap. Fortunaly Scrap is cheaper, so if you use all your fuel, you can always sell more of that scrap and buy what you need. The higher the difficulty the more copper you earn, but good luck if you are just starting out.
If that sounds bad, it gets worse with Purple parts. To craft a Purple, you need an average of 5-7 Blue, 250 scrap, and 150 copper.  The worse part is the new resource needed just for Purple, Wires. You need 750 pcs. You get wires from playing from a different reward pool. This reward pool doesn't give you any scrap or White at all, just wire. You get 10 pcs from each match you WIN. There is no pity rewards. So that is an extra 75 matches + Plus the ones you will lose in.
You get the gist of the problem, so I wont talk about Orange which introduces another resource just like purple, but you also need Wire along with it.
The second thing, something a good chunk of players seem to suffer from, the connectivity issues:
A rather large amount of players seem to suffer from connectivity issues. This isn't a small amount of lag, this is unplayable, I don't even know where the real me is at type of lag. And it seems to come in waves to random people. You can have the best internet connection, but if the Gods seem to be extra spiteful one day, you will have bad internet. It seems to be a gamble at times, you are fine for a week or two, then you can't play at all for 2-3 days.
It's a good game, I enjoy it, obviously. It's just that this stuff pushes people away. There are some other issues here and there, such as some weapons being unviable completly at higher Power Scores and such, but I'm sure therea re other Steam Reviews that go much more iun depth into that than I can.

Mabinogi is one of the greatest MMORPGs out there. Very Unique and Very Fun.
I was recommended this game by a friend and I told him that I wasn't very impressed by its 'looks'. Sure enough, I at least gave it a try...and From that point onwards, I have never stopped playing it. That was about a year or so ago. That's how amazing this game is!
Mabinogi is one of those games that doesn't require you to complete EVERY SINGLE quest and task; it's all completely up to you to make the choices and do what YOU want to do.
One of the main things that makes this game so unique and fun is its combat and leveling system. The combat in this game requires more stragetic choices and as well as good timing of skills and attacks to do some damage against foes, rather than just pressing the skills button to do some extra damage. Also, the leveling is very different to other games. There's quite a lot to explain but to put it shortly: There's no level cap. You can just keep on leveling.
Another thing is the gaming community. I promise you, that this game has one of the most friendliest communities I've ever played with and that is what keeps me playing. Simply just asking for a little assistance and someone, who hears it, would usually come by and help you out.
Last main thing is the story and updates. The story of mabinogi is very unique and it is separated into 'Generations'. Each generation can pose quite a challenge and usually isn't something you can just rush through. The story overall is a very interesting one with its twists and turns. Each update is always something that I can look forward to as each one usually has some sort of event with it, giving players the chance to win great and useful prizes.
There are alot of other great things that I can say about this game, as well as a few minor problems. But overall, this game ROCKS! and I recommend it 100%!

I played the first Borderlands right up until the very end, but just didn't quite finish it. I never bothered with Borderlands 2 or the prequel or anything else. I am tired of Telltale's gimmick, which lasted through the first Walking Dead, half of the second Walking Dead, and Wolf Among Us. And then . . . I was done. Fed-up. Frustrated. Not even interested in giving Telltale any more consideration going forward.
Then, Tales from the Borderlands went on steep sale and I was bored. I played an episode per night for a week and was very satisfied. This is probably the greatest accomplishment of any of their titles in this style. It improves on a lot of the "game play" gimmicks they use in other titles, massively improves on the humor (the game is truly funny and not in a trying-too-hard way), and I actually care more about the characters than in any other Telltale game since the first Walking Dead.
I'm not sure what more I can offer than to say it is a fast-paced, action-heavy, humor-heavy game that is compelling from the first episode to the last. Fantastic characters. Great art-style. And again, this is coming from someone that lost interest in Borderlands and was sick of the Telltale "thing" a long time ago . . . and they still pulled this off.

Having given up on the daily review writing game,  I have come to realize that this means I can actually take time to play and enjoy games that I really wouldn't have been able to sit down and enjoy had I continued.  It's actually surprising now how I can open up one or two of these new games and find myself enjoying playing them far more than I would have if I had a too-short deadline in front of me.  I guess this means that when I write new reviews, they will probably be much more authentic.
Hero Siege is no exception to this statement.  I opened this up a week or so ago, thinking I would find a fairly simplistic top down bullet hell-ish bore, and i found myself actually surprised.  Surprised enough to not realize five hours had passed and I had finished my first playthrough of the base game, and with enough relics to make me effectively unstoppable, and I still didnt really want to put it down.  This, to me, is the definition of a truly good game, one that keep s your interest over time, even as you get to the end of it.
Now I will say, that officially I have 'completed' the base game in that five hours, but that doesnt mean I stopped playing.  The game is basically an odd combination of bullet hell, tower defense, and binding of isaac roguelike, and for all its entertainment is actually fairly short.  What you get by playing a character however is the ability to play the same levels over on harder difficulty levels, though with your massively overpowered character dealing hot death to scores of mindlessly wandering foes.  The characters are simple enough to control, use your base attack most of the time then deal massive death with special moves when the cluster of baddies gets to dense for your base attack to be worthwhile.  As you progress, your experience grows your levels and base stats, and you also get random powerups which add unique powers in a binding of isaac like fashion, which you lose if you die, meaning you have  an increasing sense of protectiveness of your character the more difficult the game becomes.  The intent behind this I have to assume is that it keeps you on par with the difficulty level, which unfortunately it didnt seem to have done.  I was basically unstoppable until half way through my playthrough on the third difficulty level, whereupon I happened to hit a brick wall in a particular boss that apparently doesnt seem to understand that exponential difficulty increases only work if you go up one exponent at a time.  Afterwards, I lost all my relic powerups and quicly realized that my character though quick at reaping destruction before, was apparently not as powerful as i had been led to believe.  Curse you Hero Siege for such slanderous lies.
All that being said, do I recommend this game?  Basically the answer there would be yes, though I will say that it doesn't have a lot of things that make it unique among the roguelike genre, and if you are already knee deep in things like isaac or Enter the Gungeon, it may be best to give a pass on this one, at least until you get sick of those and want to try something slightly different but still the same.

Wow let me first state that i have been watching dragon ball since the mid 90's. This game, Dragon Ball Xenoverse had good potential to do something entertaining. Instead the game overall feels like a combination of all previous games with a failed online mode. Let me break the game up into 5 categories. Presentation, Gameplay, Story, Value, and Fan experience.
For presentation graphically speaking the game is overall good while fighting. Characters look sharper and more like the show than any previous game. The movement of the characters and fighting appearence is pleasing to the eye and immersive. But when it come to the maps there is a bit of a let down. Maps in general are large, yet for any real dragon ball fan knows the show has lots of interactable destructable terrirory on the maps to slam or crush the villian into. For some reason, developers decided to make less slamable targets and also the animation of the interactions to be rather lame. Targets that recieve blast damage also show pretty pathetic craters that dissapear faster than it takes the character to get up. Toki Toki city which you will be forced to look at for at least 20% of the game, looks like something you might see in a Nintendo Gamecube princess rpg. Quite dissapointing for the heafty $50 price cost for a game you download and cant even resell. Score wise for presentation of this dragonball z game is a 10 out of 20.
The gameplay of this game is very simular to past games.  Combos and attack moves are easier than ever to produce and it sometimes feels like the game was dumbed down for the masses. What the game does well is it makes an experience easy to pick up and quick to start to enjoy. There are NO new battle features really, just a recasting of  all previous game titles minus a few features.  In terms of game play the only new thing that i have not experienced before was a 3 vs 3 atmosphere where all players are on the map at once.  I would be lying to say i was not dissapointed to see more creativity by the developers of how to attack and fight. Where are the grab and slams in to targets like Broily does againt the Z fighters, Why does hitting a surface cause no damage.  Why cant i transform in stages like the show does and all previous games have done. No im forced to play only 1 type of Freza character, no im forced to pick only 1 Super Sayain  transformation. LAME really really LAME. If playiing online or not, fighting more than 1 target on this game is pretty weak. its almost like the cpu is just waiting for one to move out of the way before making his attacks and when fighing online cycling your attacks between 2 or more targets is not fluid and is very non authentic to the Dragon Ball series. In the first clip in the game you play Raditz attacks Goku and Piccolo with a double attack, why cant i do these sort of things more often. Ki battles like Gatling gun vs Kamehameha are Very rare if non exsistant. I have played over 40 hours and have still not experienced one so i dont know if they are available.  I could say more about gameplay not so much good but this i guess is enough to make my point. I would give gameplay for Dragon Ball Xenoverse a 5 out of 20.
The story aspect of this game does better than average. The alterered history and future story line is refreshing and new. Add ability to create your own character and seeing him in the story was nice too. There is no difficulty setting so its pretty easy to go though the entire story mode solo as long as you lvl up along the way. Call me crazy but i would like to see a dragonball z game go from start to finish through the entire series without skipping huge chapters. At one point this story line goes from killing Frieza directly to the Cell games. Where's anything from the 30+ episodes skipped by going directly to the cell games.  If we are going to see anyting it will most likely be in the form of a DLC the get more money from the wallets of gamers.  I would also like to see in a game the times gohan in in the wilderness training in the Sayian Saga in minigame form or something. Exploring heaven and hell though snake way and searching for dead Vegita as you fight you way out of Hell are some good ideas too. A strange non feature in the game is your character has no voiceover even though you choose one at the start of the game. Overall for a story they didnt do a terrible job but i would have liked to play the original story in the game along with the altered history story or just a much longer altered history as this current one is too short. For the Story of this game Dragon Ball Xenoverse gets a 12 out of 20.
Value is something that would justify most short fallings in games. If you are only charging $10 and get a great experence though fun gameplay but the graphics are a little weak it is acceptable. In this game Dragon Ball Xenoverse, we are currently forced to pay the HEAFTY price of 49.99 for a downloadable non tradeable game so it would not be too far fetched to have some high exspectations of this title. The game does deliver an experience you could get more than 100 hours out of. With its custom character feature the story mode is replayable through the 5 races which should last you at least 8 hours per race if you rush though. Online game play (if it even works) allows for tournaments, up to 3 vs 3 battles and coop quests which are pretty fun when they are challenging. For the heafty price however the game has far too many tech issues. My expereience with the gamehas way to many in game crashes during missions and battles online. Currently it would be conservative to say that my game crashes every other match online. I sometimes go 2 or 3 retarts crashes in a row. It is Rare to find a match where the game is not hit with a lot of LAG SPIKES thoughout your fight and it doesnt matter if your online or not dont exspect to see your ki blast or any energy animations half of the time you play because they just dont display.  This all means that 2 out of 10 online battles will run as the game intended. VERY BAD. This level of error should have been fixed or at least the game should have been release as uncomplete and at a discount.  The game feels like a 29.99 title. Its not super stellar or detailed in any aspect of the game. Dragon ball Xenoverse preforms around average in each of its features and sometimes takes a step back. An interesting experience to say the least. Mabinogi brings a lot to the table, from open world exploartion, a dyanmic combat system, and one of the widest array of life skills I've seen. To call this a game is an understatement, hence it truly is a "fantasy life". People of all ages of any play style can enjoy this game. It's array of skill sets cater to a wide range of interests, and the best part of it, there are no classes! You can literally mix and match any skill you want. One of the most unique features of Mabinogi, the rebirth feature, which allows a free rebirth every 3 weeks and an OPTIONAL paid rebirth every week allows one to reset their level whilst keeping ALL of their accumulated skills. With this you can truly pave the way you play. If you aren't a combat oriented person, then have no fear. With Mabinogi's life skills which range from cooking to blacksmithing theres plenty to do, and of course having more crafters in the game will be helpful, they are hardly looked down upon. Not a fighter or a crafter? Well do you like music? Mabinogi has one of the coolest music systems that I've seen so far, literally being able to COMPOSE your own musical scores to be played in game from a wide selction of instrutments. Mabinogi truely is an interesting experience, if you're looking for something new or fresh, than I point you in the direction of Mabinogi.

I have not completed the game yet, I am writing the review as a "first impressions" kind of thing.
Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed. I recently acquired the game on a sale, as it looked like a fun little racer. I went into the game pretty much blindfolded, not sure of what to expect.
Tons of special modes like VS-Mode, drift-challange, boost-challange, etc.
Unique and beautiful tracks, which can even change inbetween laps.
Lots of choosable characters with different strengths and weeknesses.
In-depth risk and reward boost-system (boost for stunts and drifts).
Many fun powerups to use.
Surprisingly difficult on harder difficulties.
Options for touch-inputs and different sensors. Not something I'd use, but that is a very rare feature to see.
All PC-Related settings, like graphics and controls, have to be set in a broken and cheap-looking launcher.
How the AI uses powerups can be very frustrating at times, ruining the flow of the race.
Some characters feel very out of place. Some are more cartoony than others.
Drifting + Braking/Reverse use the same key, which makes sense on a controller, but not on a keyboard.
Shadows look kind of grainy, even on high graphics-settings.
Nitpick: Default keyboard layout is horrible (can be changed in the launcher tho).
Ingame, only some gameplay and sound-settings are available. When you get the launcher to work (running as administrator), you have lots of graphics settings to your disposal. Every resolution seems to be supported. The launcher is just not clear on what kind of anti-aliasing it uses (spoiler: it's FXAA).
This game performs beautifully! Surprisingly, I was able to get it running on my Windows-Tablet (Intel Atom, with integrated graphics) at 640x400 with 15-30 FPS. Would not have thought that it would get anywhere near that. So feel free to try this on a low/mid-spec PC, it's very well optimized.

If you like arcade-racers like Mario Kart and you are searching for an equivilant on PC, Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is for you. Although it might be a little hard to get into if you are new to the racing-game genre. Definitely give it a spin!

It was hard to get into the character, not knowing anything about the game and just being tossed into the world with barely any knowledge of ... well anything.
Character cards are ridiculous and make no sense.  Allowing a person to make one character per account or card is just silly and was a big turn off at the beginning.  Then suddenly I'ma  horse running around attacking spiders and wolves but unable to talk to anyone and no idea what was going on.  It's basically a game for older players.  As in, people who have been playing it for a couple of years and have gotten to know one another rather well through the game itself.  Which is fine, if you're looking for a social game.  I was looking for something with more adventure.  This was not that game for me.
Although it does have combat, it's tedious and slow.  With numerous combat progamming issues such as slow to no response, it get boring and annoying very quickly.  If you want to be with your friends from the beginning you have to make the same type of character.  Unless you are one of the players who has played for some time then you're aware of how to get where and what exactly you're doing.
I was enticed by the farming, cooking, trade skill aspects only to learn that those are the main skills you pick from the beginning.  While you're welcome to learn other skills or professions, if you picked cooking then cooking would be the only thing you truly excelled at which gives the game another annoyance factor for me personally.
I'm not going to say anything about the graphics because I believe that graphics do not make the game no matter how beautiful or up to date it is, if the game play is awful it is awful and god rays won't save it.  t's dated to be sure but it works for what (I assume) the game is going for.  After awhile I got tired of children players running around and elves with large breasts giggling constantly and decided to try something else.
It's a charming thought but all in all this game left me more confused than with the feeling of enjoying a real role playing game.  If you have extensive amounts of time on your hands, do not like social interractions in the real world or are one of the few serious fans left of the game, enjoy.  Otherwise, I would try something else with better, more responsive controls and doesn't rely on extreme amounts of beauty shop items in order to enjoy the "game".

This is a one of a kind game that everyone should give a chance. Mabinogi is a fantasy anime MMORPG with a rich character development system, unique combat system, and a rich story that separates it from other generic MMORPGs. As you dive into the world of Erinn, you can do a variety of things. From fighting monsters, performing quests, and leveling up to fishing, jousting, dressing up, and even playing and composing music. Each time a player gains enough experience from doing these kinds of activities, they will receive an AP (attribute point) that lets them distribute it to any skill and rank it to make them stronger or more efficient. There is a rebirth system where a player can reset their character's level in order to easily acquire more AP. This means that there is an infinite amount of levels so you can create a character that will suit your own play-style. Since the amount of content Mabinogi has to offer, the possibilities are endless. This is a game I can see myself playing for many years.

I played the first Borderlands right up until the very end, but just didn't quite finish it. I never bothered with Borderlands 2 or the prequel or anything else. I am tired of Telltale's gimmick, which lasted through the first Walking Dead, half of the second Walking Dead, and Wolf Among Us. And then . . . I was done. Fed-up. Frustrated. Not even interested in giving Telltale any more consideration going forward.
Then, Tales from the Borderlands went on steep sale and I was bored. I played an episode per night for a week and was very satisfied. This is probably the greatest accomplishment of any of their titles in this style. It improves on a lot of the "game play" gimmicks they use in other titles, massively improves on the humor (the game is truly funny and not in a trying-too-hard way), and I actually care more about the characters than in any other Telltale game since the first Walking Dead.
I'm not sure what more I can offer than to say it is a fast-paced, action-heavy, humor-heavy game that is compelling from the first episode to the last. Fantastic characters. Great art-style. And again, this is coming from someone that lost interest in Borderlands and was sick of the Telltale "thing" a long time ago . . . and they still pulled this off.
Absolutely worth buying and playing -- and an excellent game to watch other people play, too.

DBX has an interesting take on beat em up genre that I've personally not seen since the late 1980s where an RPG developement element has been added to the beat up portion of the game. Most of the modern day beat up games like Street-fighter, Tekken, Dead or Alive you potentially unlock additional characters and costumes. Within DBX you also unlock additional moves from various quests you can repeat over and over, this leads to a fairly large element of grinding for a particular move. There is also a level system and with each level you get a handful of points to assign to your character to impact the effectiveness of your character.
Word of note, to potentially get maximum benefit from the game, I personally recommend either reading or watching either the manga or anime of the Dragonball series, you can probably skip GT, but definately see the first two series. The game plays on the events of the series and how they have been altered and its the job of your character to fix the timeline... Although you do not need to watch or read the DB series, it does help you to know how events pan out in the series to unlock "hidden" events.
The game itself is enjoyable in the sense it does things quite simply but fairly well. It doesn't not have the combination move depth of games such as Dead or Alive, Streetfighter; however it does give you a much greater customisation of your character in terms of which super moves you go into a fight/quest with. Although not really an MMO, if you use the multi login of your character, you will be thrown into a sort of Pseudo MMO lobby where you can see other players/  Interaction is very limited through preset emotes and messages. You CAN NOT customise the messages in game.
The game consist of a single player story element, a group element both pve and pvp. I've not tried the pvp as I generally stay away from online beat up pvp due to heavy dependance on have an amazingly awesome connection, you're better off getting a few mates around to play on your console than to play online beat up pvp. The difficuly of the game is very unusual because there is no consistent difficulty curve, you can easily go through several story missions without too much trouble to be stumped by one mission of significantly greater difficulty for a long time, then when you are past that you are back to some fairly easier missions until you hit the next mission wall... Many of the difficult missions/quests are often ones where you have to make sure an NPC companion stays alive or you are facing several chain stun locking Super Saiyans at once.
The server deserves a mention, connecting to the multi lobby can at times be a little annoying as you may depending on the time of the day need to make several attempts before you finally connect to it. Apparently this was a lot worse at launch. When you do have to do attempt multiple logins it can take several minutes. So be prepared for that.
All in all a fun game with some frustrating elements here and there

I keep coming back to Proteus in my mind. It's just that good.
I haven't actually replayed the game since my first time playing. I intend to do so at some point, but it was an experience quite unlike any other, and I would rather not spoil it by letting myself experience it too often.
Yes, all you can do in the game is walk around. No, that is by no means boring (though you may need to be in the right mood for the game to "click" for you). For one, there is more to it than just blindly walking around without a goal. There actually is a progression system in the game, and a big part of what I enjoyed here was discovering that by what felt like accident and being surprised by it. It's not challenging, but it fuels the game's exploration and gives it a purpose beyond curiosity. Which is great.
Secondly, the game is a work of art. Now, art is subjective, and you may prefer realism over the abstraction Proteus offers. Fair enough. Just don't judge the game by screenshots alone. Give it a shot, and play it. Let the gorgeous, ever-changing colour palettes pull you in, let the reactive soundtrack (walking past certain objects or characters will yield various sounds) become it's own distinct melody.
But what Proteus succeeded at most for me personally, and why I keep coming back to it in my mind is this: It is a game that loves nature, and it's love for it is infectious. It appreciates the seasons and the changes they bring. It knows the power of a beautiful sunset and the serenity of a summer night's soundscape. It understands the dread and beauty of autumn leaves signifying the passing of time. It's familiar with the romance of a melancholic winter's eve. It manages to capture the essence of both nature's biggest hits and the underappreciated details and distills them into this simplistic, impressionist pixel painting. The fact it goes for abstraction rather than realism is part of it's power, I think. It lets you fill in the gaps, pull from your own pool of memories; supports reminiscence. It lodges itself in your mind and after having played it; it will make you recall it, remember it's sounds and the feelings it brought up when you encounter that which it portrays in real life. And then, you will learn to love the game even more than you might have loved it when you played it.
Proteus is an amazing achievement, and I cannot recommend it enough.

Mildly amusing and a fairly entertaining romp, but there are many issues that let this game down. Overall, it's a very sloppy port to PC.
1) It's a PC game that doesn't support the mouse, despite several game mechanics being ideally built for it - for example aiming ranged attacks brings up a reticule that must be placed over a target. The game does not support the Playstation 3 pad, so if you want to play it, I'd have to recommend picking up a 360 controller.
2) It's buggy. Characters will frequently get stuck in walls and other such similar annoyances. Thankfully if you move far enough away, they'll teleport behind you when you're not looking, but this isn't always an option. Mercifully, I've not found myself unable to continue at any point. Rendering errors are frequent - and I've found myself unable to continue past the Nazgul attack in the moors, as some sort of ground overlay is floating around in the z-axis meaning I can't actually see the gameplay area. From what I gather, the console version of the game have been patched, but the PC version has been neglected and abandoned. Reading online also indicates that there are bugs related to white blocks that can potentially make it impossible to finish the game.
3) The overall design isn't great and the game has it's problems. Some of the character interplay towards the mid-game is nice and it may get better later (though I may potentially never find out as I'm unable to continue), but the level design is shockingly poor. The majority of the game is entirely linear, including the puzzle sections which have components that illogically have to be completed in a certain order rendering the puzzle section little more than a waste of time as you go through the required motions. Large parts of the game seem to take place on hills and slopes, but the player is tasked with collecting studs which are represented with rigid bodies - as a result you'll spend a lot of time chasing them down hills to collect them, only finding they have rolled into water or off a cliff and are therefore unobtainable. Some levels have too many playable characters - one level has the entire Fellowship of nine characters, which makes selecting the correct character a chore - it doesn't even fit on the character wheel any more. Some of the character icons, particularly those of the hobbits, are difficult to discern from one another, compounding the frustration. In some cases areas of the levels are enclosed and too small (such as structures in Rivendell), meaning that the camera is obscured by outside walls of the structure, meaning you cannot see what you are doing. Lastly, some of the lighting and choice of colour palette can make some things in the environment very difficult to discern, particularly during levels that take place at night.
Overall the game is entertaining, but frustrating due to issues, and I cannot recommend it.

It's "OK", but not even the fabled 10.0 overhaul feature list puts it close to the Arma3 feature list and thus I wouldn't recommend it. A bunch of shooters spawned for the new generation of folks that just want their game tightly defined with a ruleset: DayZ, PUBG, this, etc. IE easily digestible candy. If I can make an Arma 50vs match with the game mode of Squad, then it's comparable to a narrow Arma3 feature list and all that's left is the actual delivery of that game mode. Given the Squad forums are wanting new animations, new weapons, new vehicles, it's as if they are trying to build it up to Arma's spec which sits there with all those features and a tonne more and isn't limited to the UR4 engine. I find it impossible to recommend where you make a choice between the two, but if I just pretend for a few seconds that Squad and a specific Arma game were in comparison on their own then I should rightly point out some bias towards Squad as follows:
Engine and graphics: Squad has an edge for standard boxed affects that you would need a combination of mods to achieve in Arma. Especially firing and under fire effects, explosion effects and particles. Arma needs JSRS, Blastcore and some others to be in line and still not as good as the effect of Squad.
Scalability. Performance is optimised for a specific small map PvP experience. Arma will not perform as well with bots on the same engine, or on the 270 square km Altis map. But should it? Should it compare to a 68km squared map? The level of detail is higher. Perhaps it's an advantage for Squad. Nevertheless I think Squad probably does better for FPS in a like-for-like.
Much of this adds up to an apples and oranges review based on a faulty comparison, but I cannot pick a canned game over something I can adapt, has a longer and more successful pedigree, has community developers, greater variety and depth and is at least finished. There's a reason A3 has 4x the players in game, and is two years earlier than Squads release date.
I find a typical review from players stating: "But the cooperation level is so amazing, i'm learning to play with other humans". Wow. I think that's a sad shame on our internet culture, at any given time you can join and cooperate with groups around the world who have been doing the same since the internet was born in every multiplayer coop game. What the issue I have is that it's down to luck if you have a good experience or a bad one, I've had both, leaning very much in the direction of bad. Should I review a game that needs luck to find good cooperation in a public game? Or should i look for a group that plays together well (more sensible approach). Thus again, go play milsim with a military simulator, not what is in effect a public matchmaker of random experience.
Unfortunately that brings be to the negative part of the game as is. You have no choice. Games are matched, you spend ages trying to get your friends onto the same team due to side balancing, only to dfind you are playing versus the server hosts and getting nailed. You have no option to play with a moving target and practice, the firing range is just ...ugh. You can't even zero your weapons on it, there's no range modelled on the guns and Kentucky windage is the primary method of correcting fires.
People want milsim, but they aren't prepared to cooperate for it or invest the time and discipline to join a group. They want milsim but no keybinds. They want to spawn in a battle, to last 15 mins and then go offline. Then if that's you, I think Squad is your choice, for either a public match or organised group play. It's not a crime to want things your way, but you have to be prepared to sacrifice a lot. If you want to invest in something, get Arma, go milsim and enjoy exactly the game you want. Zombies, dinosaurs, or ridculous simulation levels with campaigns and science, exactly how you want it with an amazingly in depth amount of variation and customisation. Arma3 is all things but not quite champion at the small level, it's an offputting simulator to someone needing to shoot another player in the head, now, please. But quite frankly, I don't see the point in having slighly shinier graphics if I can't make it do exactly what I want. Squad isn't a bad game, it's just not different and less capable in so many ways to others and thus I chose to keep my investment in something more in depth. YMMV.

I am Kiera563 of Alexina, and I endorse this game!
I love Mabinogi: it's a fun MMO that has kept my attention for years.  This is no small feat, because I have major attention deficit and MMOs generally do not hold my attention long.
You explore the land of Erinn as one of three races: Humans, Elves, or Giants (and yes, Giants really are more than twice the other races' sizes).
What is unique about this game is the leveling, aging and rebirth system: your character can be from 10 to 17 years of age to start with, and every week, he or she will grow age a year.  This provides a small boost in stats, but more importantly, once you reach Age 20, you can Rebirth.  Rebirthing allows you to reset your level to level 1, and your age to 10-17.  Sounds pointless, right?  Well, though you lose the stats you got from leveling, each level-up earns you 1 AP (ability point), and you keep all AP and skill ranks when you rebirth.
AP is used to rank up Skills, whether they be combat skills like Combat Mastery, Ranged Attack, or Defense (to name a few of many), life skills like blacksmithing and tailoring, magic skills like Icebolt and Healing, or any of the many other types of skills: the highly-defensive Alchemy skills, the wide-area, dual-attacking Puppetry skills, the buff-providing Bard skills, the massively powerful single-target Fighter skills, and my personal favorite, the lightning-quick, highly offensive, wide-area Gunslinger skills.  A higher-ranked skill will be more effective, and will also permanently boost your stats.
This means a veteran player who is currently at level 1 but has rebirthed many times before could easily be stronger than a newbie who managed to reach level 50 for the first time.  So, the best way to size up somebody is their skill ranks and stats, not their level.
There are also extremely powerful Transformation skills, and they come in two flavors:  Race-specific and Demigod.
Race-specific transformations provide an impressive buff to all stats as well as resistance to certain forms of damage, and most allow you to use a unique skill.  Demigod provides regeneration, increased movement speed, and the ability to fire off some of the most powerful attacks in the game.  They're really cool looking, and once you get them, you have a couple highly effective trump cards up your sleeve to pull out for boss fights.  If you're really desperate and/or going for overkill, you can use both at once!
Another unique aspect of Mabinogi is the ability to play music.  You program a song onto an item called a Score Scroll (or copy paste it from the Internet...), and equip the scroll with an instrument, and voila, you can play MIDI-like tunes to your heart's content.  (Until the scroll breaks, that is, but you can always make another.)  Yes, hearing those tunes from your favorite games, like Mario and Zelda, echoing from the town square is really cool.
This game has a massive amount of content, so if you're just starting to play, you definitely won't get bored, especially if you play with friends.  Mabi is a highly social MMO, and is at its best if you are screwing around with your buddies.  Of course, there's plenty of room for serious play, because the enemies can get brutal in dungeons like Peaca.  Mabinogi used to be much harder than it is now, but its original difficulty still shows at times, especially in early dungeons and story quests at low levels.  But it's never unfair, and having a full party of friends is always enough to even the odds.  *fondly remembers newbie bum rushes of Rabbie*
Mabinogi does have its flaws, and Nexon, its developer/publisher, has dropped the ball many times before.  (Nexon is legendary for its screwups, though in recent times, they seem to be doing a lot better.)
However, I highly recommend this game if you're looking to get into a new MMO.  And I'd be more than happy to show you the ropes if you add Kiera563 on Alexina.

An odd little indie strategy game about the Zombie Apocalypse. It's a bit different from other zombie games though:
1.) It covers the initial mass-evacuation of survivors rather than survivors fighting for themselves after the end. You command both the evac helicopters carrying people out  and the military protecting those still waiting to be rescued.
2.) It takes place in a fictional part of Latin America. I don't know of another zombie game set in that part of the world.
3.) It's 100% strategy. You tell units where to go or where to shoot rather than doing any direct combat yourself.
It presents a fun and unique experience with a lot of customizability - you can add a lot of different modifiers to your game to alter the experience to your liking. It's too bad the bizarre back-story in the game makes zero sense. But who cares? Zombies!

Toren is not an action adventure game. Don't let the sword in the picture fool you. Toren is a game of discovery, that happens to have a sword sometimes. This third person adventure game will take you on a journey exploring the existence of a girl and her quest in a tower against her nemesis: a dragon.
Right the wrongs of the past and restore balance as you play a child/girl/woman, exploring the tower and entering dreams to follow in the steps of great men. Can you slay the dragon and restore order to the universe? Only time will tell.
Story: The story is rather confusing, there were aspects of it I didn't quite understand. One cut scene is repeated over and over and though the text is different, I am not completely sure of the symbolism behind it. That's probably a failing of mine though.... perhaps it's clearer to others. There are times when the game doesn't really prepare you for what will happen next. I almost quit a few times because I thought, "Hey, that's not my fault...." only to discover... that was intended by the game on purpose. Upon completing the game, I didn't get a grand sense of achievement, though I did enjoy myself.
Sounds: The sounds are pretty good. I rather enjoyed it, however, there are times when distance plays zero part in what is happening in the game. There are these critters you can kill and they are just as loud when they are on the other side of a wall as when you are standing next to them. So that can be a little confusing if you're hoping to home in on them via their noises.
Graphics: There's something about the graphics that are both appealing and not at the same time. While great attention to detail has been paid to certain areas of the game, others seem to be thrown together as a last ditch effort to complete the game. Or they intended them that way. If that's the case, I'm not really sure where I stand on the issue. However, there is little graphic smoothing and at one point when you're wearing a cape, and it's kinda flowing in and out of your body, it doesn't really jive and looks a little sloppy. I also wasn't a fan of her hair at certain points. Seemed like they cut a few corners there. Also, there were some areas where it seemed like in order to mask the lack of completeness, they blurred out the edges of the screen, trusting in the setting of the game to make you not question it. But I did.
Controls: The controls are a bit clunky sometimes. If you want her to walk in a different direction, you have to hope she will immediately reverse, but that often doesn't happen, she tends to go off slightly to a different direction. This probably has to do with my major complaint about the game which will get it's own section. Combat is pretty much a joke, and seems thrown in as an after thought. There can be monsters right in front of you, and when you attack, your character swings the sword parallel to the ground, instead of at the monster. Doing a combo of attacks will eventually get you a down stroke which will kill it. This was not pleasing for me or entertaining.
The Blasted Camera: Seriously, I've never had a game screw with me so much just because it wants to move the camera around in whatever way it sees fit whenver it wants. Changing directions can cause the camera to zoom in or out with no real discernable reason. Further, those changes often make it so you're heading not in the exact opposite direction when you want to turn around, but rather, slightly off course because the camera changed where it was and controls are directly related to the camera's position. This was the thing I hated the most about the game. Everything else was tolerable, and I could enjoy those aspects of the game even if they weren't ideal, however, that blasted camera man in game that randomly flies around like a fairy has a sadistic streak and I hope he gets torched by a dragon.
Overall: 6/10 - Base pricing is a little high, in my opinion. I'd probably have no issues paying $4-5 for this game, but I might be grumpy paying $10. If you can afford it, feel free, but I would definitely recommend a discount. There is little replayability, so you're probably gonna get 3 hours of the game tops. You may replay it to finish some of the missable acheivements, but it's not enjoyable. Thankfully you can select which chapter you want to start at once you've completed the game. It's a fun little adventure to take a stroll through, but nothing fantastic.
Hardcore. Get it.

This game is full of beauty and shows it as it tells its story through its bold colors, music, and yes controls.
I'll start off saying the controls aren't the perfect. However, I feel there is a lot of intention and purpose in changing the controls to fit the themes of the chapter you're on. This is a sacrilidge to anyone who things genres are king and any game without perfectly fluid controls is broken and I won't change anyone's mind there. Your character changes over and over and the game grows along with her. She can feel young and weak, or spry, or tired. You feel the growth as you slowly understand how she fits into the world.
Combat is bare but intentional, platforming has tension and failure has reason. My advice is play the game at it's own pace rather than expected it to be something it's not. It has it's own rhythm and rituals. It evokes Zelda and Ico but doesn't play like them.
I appreciated how visual everything is. There's text but it's poetic and reflective rather and obvious like most other games I've played. The world you end up in are shocking and symbolic without being overdone, very memorable. You can see the limits of the tech and budget but in general they don't affect the overwhelming moods of each area.
If you want a small game with huge beauty, mystery, a plot to reflect on, don't wait for a sale. You should give this game a second look and play it.
