Just in case you are wondering, yes. This is the STEAM account of Johan from Ruairi. I've played this game ever since 2008, during Closed Beta testing. In this review, let me summarized for you a short history of Mabinogi.
Enjoy!
Long before I've started my time in Mabinogi, I enjoyed MMORPGs mainly for the communities within. Many early MMOs tend to have helpful communities, which is why I joined in on this joy ride the moment I knew about it.
Mabinogi started off as a simple game of rock, paper and scissors. The three basic combat skill goes with Defense, which blocks normal attack, Smash, which breaks through Defense, and Counter, the skill that allows you to counterattack Smash. The skills are based upon loading time and latency, meaning that if you lag, it is more or so likely that this game will be more difficult for you.
The game evolved from simple melee, magic and archery to the wide spectrum of skills you have today; from sharpshooting to even puppetry, where you make use of puppets to fight for you. The community was welcoming in the past, and the game was fresh, being a half-sandbox, half-quest-and-instance based orientated RP. Events were plentiful, and every day would be an interesting experience for all.
-----
Skills, level and attributes:
Mabinogi is a game with endless possibilities. With hundreds of different skills, you have countless ways to combine and make use of the combat technique of your dreams. Feel like being a gunmage? Mabinogi has that. A spellknight? No problem-o! Perhaps you are a fan of Naruto and you would like to use ninjitsu along with puppetry? Mabinogi has it all.
It is generally one of the most complex, and yet simple, game I've ever played. Skills are trained based on how much you use them, and sometimes it can be quite a grind. However, ever since the Adventurer's Seal Shop update, players can purchase skill seals every Sunday to help with training on difficult skill ranks.
Attributes are mainly gained via levelling up, or ranking of skills. Based off the game's endless possibilities of limitless levels, you can get your character up to insane tiers. For example, the maximum level limit for every "Life" is capped at 200, but you can rebirth to reset that back to zero, gaining valuable ability points and keeping all your skills and resources.
Levelling in Mabinogi is generally easy for the first few steps in the game. The game labels anyone under the total level of 1,000 as a newbie, thus giving them perks and benefits for new players to try out new skill sets, reset their current skills, and even rebirth once every day (After your 1,000 levels, rebirthing will be capped at once every week unless you have rebirth potions). Leveling allows players to take on more challenging aspects of early game due to the amount of attributes and stats it gives. However, in the late game, levels barely give less than 5 to 10% of your kept statuses, and thus becomes less of an importance.
-----
Customizability, clothing and fashion:
In Mabinogi, you are given a wide range of hairstyles, facial features, and even colors to go along. Being my favourite portion of the game itself, the freedom they give to you as to customize how your character looks, fights and lives is incredible.
Ever wondered how old your character is, or how your character might look years down the road? In Mabinogi, characters age once every week and grow in terms of size. From the age of 10, capping out at the height of 17, the game keep tracks of your current age and gives different levelling stats and attributes based on the character's current age.
How about eating? Do you enjoy a good roast beef, or perhaps having a beer or two? In Mabinogi, eating food will actually change your appearances. Yes, that means you can become amazingly fat, buff, slim or even slender based upon the food you eat. Each portion of the body is customizable, based upon the sort of food used. Top, which includes the chest (Or breasts, for female characters) and arms. Bottom, which includes the hips, the waist and the legs. Customize your character to the size you love!
Not just the fact that you can change your height and size, however. Mabinogi also gives you loads of facial features, hairstyles and colors to create the character you love. This is just a little about the character themselves.
What about clothing? In Mabinogi, there are hundreds of clothing available in game in a full spectrum of colors. From light skimpy skirts to full metal body armor, each clothing has a maximum of 3 dyeable slots, giving the player the customizability to make them unique in their own very way.
It's a fact that unless two players intentionally dress up the same, it is almost impossible to find two exactly similar characters within Mabinogi. Why not start your fashionogi adventures today?
-----
Quests, life skills and economy
Mabinogi works itself along side a full storyline of quests, from fighting monsters to celtic gods. Each quest revealing a little more about the world of Erinn. There are a whole bible of quests for you to go along with, each possibily traversing different worlds and dimensions.
Life skills allows players to create pre-determined equipments of their own, from clothing to armor, gloves, boots, hats and even swords and staves, shields, guns and more. There is just countless of things you can find to do in Mabinogi. Feel free to roam and go wild, experience life as never before!
Mabinogi, being an open economy, late-stage game has seriously inflated prices. However, in comparison with most of the MMOs of it's age (Mabinogi is 7 years old now), the items are not really THAT expensive. End-game quest grinding gives around 2 million gold per hour, and most of the equipment price range goes from under a million to a twenty, at a most. Unless you are a perfectionist who will aim for the best possible weapons to squeeze for that last ten damage, Mabinogi wouldn't be too hard to get into.
-----
Actions:
Mabinogi also has many ways of levelling up your character. Combat isn't the only way to get good. For example, mining gives EXP, cooking gives EXP, potion making gives EXP... Even merchanting gives you EXP. There are part time jobs given by NPCs for you to gain EXP from and train your skills, so level your character which ever way you want. Dungeon grinding is just the most basic of them all, but that doesn't means much in a world where everything gives you decent EXP.
Mabinogi also gives you many different ways to do things. For example, merchanting or bartering would require you to bring products from town to town to sell and make money. Farming requires you to tend to crops. Winemaking allows you to create dank brews and more! The possibilities are endless.
-----
Of course Mabinogi sounds all dandy and all, however, like all good things goes, there has to be a con that goes along with it. Mabinogi has quite a few cons, and it is important to know what you can do and what you can't do in the game.
Latency is a huge issue in Mabinogi. If you lag, it is going to make your experience in the game itself worse. Skills might become unusable. For example, Blaze, which is a skill that makes use of magic being in melee range and has a loading time based on how long and how close you are to the enemy. Lagging in Mabinogi WILL cause "rubber banding", a term MMO players use when they jump back in time because of server desync. Several skill sets fail to function at optimum, like archery, gunner and ninjitsu. If you lag, I recommend playing something that gives you a wider range of leniency, like magic, for example.
There are more issues, like as with the community and more, however there is a word limit in STEAM, therefore I will cut this review short.

If at first you don’t succeed then try, try again. This is one of the many lessons that FobTi Interactive have learned from their debut Steam game, Obludia, which received only mixed reviews. Jet Set Knights marks their second attempt on Steam and thus far I have nothing but good things to say about it. Thus far Steamified have been fortunate, to the point of being blessed, to have been able to cover some of the best games in Steam’s early access program. More often than not these have been accompanied by hungry and talented development studios who are dedicated to seeing their final product reach its maximum potential. FobTi Interactive are a perfect example of this type of developer. Hard work and perseverance ultimately pays off and it appears to do just that with Jet Set Knights.
As the Steam description explains, Jet Set Knights takes its inspiration from the likes of Mario Bros. and it shows in every aspect of the game thus far. It’s definitely old school in the way Mario is as well in that it is a rather difficult game. I’ve read that it has taken experienced gamers over twenty attempts to get past the first boss and truth be told it took me about that as well. For the first several games I really didn’t understand what I was supposed to do so when the first boss popped up I was wondering what I had done to really trigger his arrival. I died fairly quickly. I then died a few more times before I got it to pop again – kill all of the mobs. You can build towers and walls to assist you in protecting your princess but if she dies – even if you don’t – it’s game over. My advice to newbies to the game would be to take note of the advice given in this thread posted by the developers on the Steam’s discussion board. When you get tokens it is recommended to use them in the gambling house as they can help you greatly. However, be careful for the triple poop as you’ll lose everything!
If there is one concern that I have for the game it’s that there is no plan to include online multiplayer but thankfully they will be incorporating up to four player local player which is great. However, for those of us who haven’t got many friends who would be able to play that we’ll miss out on an option that would seemingly be a ton of fun is a bit of a downer.
In its current state Jet Set Knights is entirely playable. The devs are just adding the last major components of the game together and working out the bugs before they are ready to launch the full retail version of the game. They anticipate that this will take them a month or so – from the launch of early access at the start of January – so we’re looking for a February or March release. As per most early access games the full retail release will be set at a higher price point than the early access level. I recommend taking the jump if the game appeals to you as a result. There’s more than enough content already present to be worth your ten bucks.  Further, they’re already planning on incorporating achievements (they’re present in the game already but are not Steam-ready) and Steam trading cards.
FobTi Interactive have updated the game 7 times in the less than 4 weeks that the game has been available so you’re definitely looking at a dedicated development team.
Jet Set Knights is the PC return of old school platforming. It’s a difficult game but one that begs to be played. I highly recommend it.

Jet Set Knights is an old-school, arcade action platformer which is currently available through Steam Early Access and is developed by FobTi Interactive. You’re a knight (well duh) and as a knight it is your job to free the realm from evil! Over the course of six different levels you’ll take on several different kinds of enemies as well as a boss fight for each level. The levels are small and often have environmental dangers meaning enemies aren’t the only things you need to be wary of.
Since JSK is inspired by the likes of Mario Bros, it’s hardly surprising that FobTi have gone for “retro-styled handcrafted pixel graphics”. The game does look good, providing you’re a fan of the ‘retro look’, and it does, in my eyes, emulate the appearance of the games it’s inspired by but with its own little twist and with a touch of modernisation. The UI is simple yet provides all of the relevant information while sticking to the art direction of the game.
JSK’s gameplay is more in the vein of Towerfall rather than Mario. Rather than moving through a level you stay in one spot and fight off waves of enemies until the boss for that level appears. The level is complete when you have defeated the boss but failure takes two forms in JSK. The first fail condition is outright death which is, of course, when you reach 0HP (you start with 3HP), the other fail condition is if an enemy reaches the princess on the bottom floor of the level, if she dies the level ends. It seems each level has five waves before the boss fight with each wave having more enemies than the last. To aid you in your fight against whatever enemies the level throws at you, you have a sword (given to you automatically at the beginning) and a bow and arrow (arrows must be collected from chests, you can unlock special kinds of arrows such as ones that freeze enemies). You also have a special attack which is unique to each of the four characters and can be used as many times as you want, though there is a short cooldown period you must go through first.
As well as chests, every so often a special item will appear such as a health potion or a stack of iron ingots (used to build turrets). These items are incredibly helpful to you and it’s important you pick them up as soon as you possibly can. While the princess is pretty much just a damsel in distress, she will offer you special quests to complete, such as drink five health potions or find ten chests. Completing a quest grants you a special token which can be used on the gambling machine found in the Artifact-o-Matic location within the game. The Artifact-o-Matic is a slot machine which, if you win, awards you with artefacts which can be used to help you in some way during the game’s levels. While the quests sound quite easy I’ve found that it’s incredibly difficult, if not nigh on impossible, to complete the quests in the space of one level as the number of times you need to do something is usually unrealistic, for example the chance of getting five health potions is incredibly small. The quests are so hard to complete that I’ve only managed to complete one and unfortunately I didn’t get lucky with it so I haven’t been able to try out any of the artefacts in the game.
Killing enemies not only gets you coin drops (the number of coins depends on the enemy) as well as some EXP. Currently there seems to be no use for the coins but the dev has said you will eventually be able to get Artifact-o-Matic tokens when you collect 100 of them (though the chances of you getting 100 coins in one level is pretty unlikely). EXP is of course used to level you up and once you have enough to level up you can choose one of your stats to increase such as damage or max health.
JSK has a solid foundation, it looks good and the wave-based platforming gameplay is a lot of fun but it only has a few levels and it does have a couple of balancing issues. If you’re a huge fan of old-school platformers I’d say go for it but if not it may be best to wait for a sale.

This is a platformer that just doesn't *feel* right to play.
Your character controls like a brick. Aiming a jump is difficult because you have very little momentum once in the air, and even then, correcting in the other direction is sluggish. You don't jump high, your arc is small, and when you start to fall, you fall fast and pretty much straight down. It's tough to explain with words, but it's easy to feel within the first few minutes playing the game.
Forgive the comparison, but in Super Meat Boy (which is an incredibly good platformer) you are comparatively lighter and can maneuver well. You're fast, you can change direction and accelerate in mid-air, and you can generally get through insanely difficult levels with micro-precision. Electronic Super Joy, on the other hand, doesn't feel precise at all. It feels clumsy and awkward, which quickly leads to frustration when trying to navigate its death traps.
And yet, this is a game that absolutely demands precision. Because you have so little momentum or ability to control while in the air, jumps must be timed *exactly* right when launching. If this timing is off even by a little bit, you will not succeed the jump. This is especially true in the later levels - world 4 from the vanilla game and the Hot Sticky Mess DLC in particular have some punishing challenges that will definitely feel unfair before you succeed. Again, this is par for the course for this type of platformer, but since Electronic Super Joy feels so heavy and cumbersome, it's hard to get a sense of improvement in your own skill as you progress.
To add to the disappointment, a significant portion of the levels rely on infinite homing missiles to keep constant pressure on you. Since these missiles have slow, looping trajectories that are constantly changing based on your position, you will often get stuck amid several of them without any possible way of surviving. They also have a nasty habit of tracking you while offscreen, and you can wind up getting killed by a missile that you could never have seen coming. The game requires you to manage this by taking them out with your stomp ability, but it's not a perfect system, so the mechanic still leads to many cheap and unfair deaths.
On the plus side, there is some really good platforming design. A lot of the challenges combine the traps, projectiles, and gaps in pretty creative ways, and you can grudgingly appreciate the thought that was put into the gauntlets even as they kill you over and over again.
The aesthetic is also decent. The music has that Swedish House Mafia sound that was popular in the late 2000's, and while it irritated me most of the time with its upbeat joyous major-key synth progressions, it's still admittedly pretty well produced and some may like it. Visually, it's pretty much one flavor: black foreground, monochromatic colored background. It would have been nice to see the artists combine numerous colors in more interesting arrangements, sort of like what you would expect to see at a light show for an EDM concert, so this seems like a missed opportunity. The visuals will also deliberately mess with your perception of what's happening, which just adds annoyance to the difficulty.
So in short, while there are some interesting ideas here, laced with a bit of humor and some appreciable effects and artwork, the core of the platforming controls just don't feel good, and it makes the significant difficulty level joyless to face.

Context/Synopsis:
Beat game, 2.5 hours played as of review.
It's a game that wants to be a movie, the story is compelling, but ultimatly the cinematic focus works against the limited game mechanics, while the frustrating game mechanics harm the cinematic delivery.
Buy it if you want what is essentially an interactive movie, with a very artsy, obscure fantasy plotline.
In the end, I enjoyed it, but I can't see many folks agreeing with me.
Pro:
* Great story (although see neutral caveat below)
* Great art
* Great music
Neutral:
* The story is VERY abstract & obscure (think From Software Souls game style narrative)
--- also worth bearing mention is that the game uses some heavy symbolism, and you are probably not going to catch everything the 1st time thru. The story is clearly designed to be replayed to catch all the metaphors & symbols.
* Game is short (quite easily 2 hours or less short)
Con:
* Felt like I was being dragged around by the nose a lot of the time, instead of free to explore the game world
* I was consistently frustrated, not because the game was hard, but because it was compleatly obtuse what I needed to do to proceed.
* you can't really control the damned camera, most of time it gets put in a good spot, sometimes however the angle obscures the area in front of you, has wierd zoom levels, etc.
* it is VERY easy to accidentally miss some content because the game has heavily gated progress, and the first gates occur literally in the 1st 2-3 decisions it is possible to make in game.

I got this game a while ago in a bundle and was very excited to play.  I had heard a lot of good things about it, both on and offline, but to save myself from spoilers I hadn't looked at any videos.  I really wish I had.  Toren was just one frustration after another, leaving me a grumpy mess in the end and causing me to write my very first review on Steam.  You did it, Toren, you broke my silence.
Cons:
First of all, the controls are abysmal.  I used the Steam Controller to play and thought at first that maybe I had picked the wrong setting.  After a few tweaks...and a few more...and then more, I gave up and realized it's not me, it's you.  I reset the setting to default and got on with it.  Twenty minutes later I'm ready to destroy worlds in my frustration.  I cannot tell you how many times I ran off cliffs, or almost did, and had to here "oh!" "ooh!" "ohhh!" as she cartwheels her arms.  I had barley started turning her and she was already falling off again.  Girl, get your act together and just turn around!
There were also odd little moments where I would walk by something, like a tree branch or a whole in the wall and, without my prompting, without me even moving towards it, I would suddenly be walking across the branch or ducking through a hole in the wall.  Why?  Seriously, why?  I was just trying to walk past, and because I got within ten feet of it I'm suddenly going that way?  It was then a case of trying to run around, get off the branch and walk away without triggering it again.  And then triggering it again anyway.  Or ducking back under the wall three times because her turning circle is utter bums.
The checkpoint system I'm a little two faced about.  Possibly the game is trying to punish the player by making them trek endlessly back from the beginning of a 'dream' sequence if they die.  Possibly the game just can't get its head together and play nice.  If the first, fine, it's teaching you to play slow and learn and take baby steps so you don't run off the same cliff you're just trying. to. walk. by.  If the second, then...then whatever, I'm disappoint anyway, I guess I'll just play this same bit of the game over and over and over ad nauseam.
Lastly was the camera system.  My first indication that I was going to have a fair little fight with it should have been the little into movie.  It 'clicked' around.  I can't think of a better word to describe it then that.  It seemed to click, or jump, from one scene to the next, like I had blinked and missed something, but it was just the camera moving.  It wasn't smooth and it just looked weird.  It was the same as I was playing the game.  I would turn a corner, or climb up something, and click! new angle and now I'm falling off a cliff because I'm no longer going up while I'm pushing up, I'm going right.  Right off a cliff.  THANKS.  I struggled with this the entire time I played because it was so unpredictable.
I had to stop playing near the end.  I paused the game, got food, and when I came back my controller was nonfunctional.  By the time I got back into the game, I had to reload from a checkpoint right at the beginning of the board and my sanity just said NOPE.  So off the game went.
Pros:
The music I suppose?  Although it was mostly just soft backround noise, it worked well with the game and the quiet little sadness the game seemed to try and portray.  Woo?
The story was very beautiful, what I saw of it.  And seeing/finding all of the statues and trying to guess what she had been doing before she froze was pretty cool.  While I haven't finished the game fully (sorry my sanity is more important Toren, but I'll finish you when I'm not a huddled mess of grump and annoyance) what I have seen so far is enough to make me want to come back some day and see the rest of it.  So that's good, I suppose.
The art wasn't terrible.  A lot of it was really beautiful, what I got to see of it.  Some of the most beautiful things happened while I was reading the wizard guys words.  I either missed what he said, or I got to see just a half second of something very pretty.  Not enough time to read the story, or not enough time to enjoy the beauty around me.  Like I said, though: at least the story is good.
All in all, while I'm quite sure I will go back to Toren and finish it, I'm equally sure I will never play it all the way through ever again.  I like my sanity the way it is, and would rather not lose what little is left on a game I'm only getting to half enjoy.

You can play solo with bots, but it's gets annoying getting 1-shot across the map by a random sniper that seems to have aimbot.  Barely anyone plays this game, so the "multiplayer based content" is basically already gone.  The only way that I could recommend this is if you don't mind playing a 3rd person team-based shooter with bots on 4 different game modes. The content is very limited and having nobody to play with really limits the game.  The game modes are very generic, FFA, Team Deathmatch, Hero(Where you defend one person and the teammates can only respawn if that person is alive and the goal is to eliminate the entire team), and Supercharge(Capture the Point, but the team that controls the point gets health/damage buffs).  The gamemodes are very lacking and there isn't much content there, but there are a decent amount of maps, 10 to be exact.  I do not believe that there is enough content to justify purchasing this for $10.  The "Fast-Paced Multiplayer Shooter" is dead, now it's just a Fast-Paced Bot Match.  It loses the enjoyablility of going against other players and having a good time with other people.  I'm pretty sure more people play Monday Night Combat than this, and that game died long ago.  That game has had a major spike of 15 people playing at the same time, compared to it's usual 0-5.
TL;DR
It's a multiplayer based game with nobody to play with.  I'm pretty sure more people play Monday Night Combat than this, and that game died long ago.  Only buy this if there is a high discount, 75%+, and if you want to play against bots for a few hours.

This game should be renamed Robot Tazer-Paintball Match: High Latency Mode instead of Interstellar Marines.
The game play reminds me of playing CounterStrike but its you and 3 friends vs 50-60 robots. Each match is played in a predefined arena, each of which are fairly static environments albiet for a couple doors and buttons. The only stimulating thing about these arenas is the dynamic lighting and changing weather (keep in mind 50% of maps are entirely indoor). The robots you fight are relatively boring in terms of combat and have one of two modes of attack: stampede with velociraptor arm♥♥♥♥♥♥or stand awkwardly at a distance firing a gun with either 100% accuracy or no clue you exist (relatively no inbetween).
Everyone's gun shoots tazers for some reason, which gives the whole game a feeling of a giant paintball match. I really did not feel like an "INTERSTERLLAR MARNE!!!" My greatest complaint about this game is the latency though. The robot's movements are janky, my shots and hits are always delayed even when playing solo. Overall this made for a poor gameplay experience. The online experience against other players or with friends is near unbearable, with no consistency regarding who fires first and who ends up living.
Overall: Hold off on this buy unless you can get it for dirt cheap.
Pros: Dynamic lighting, necessity for teamwork and ressing downed players, must listen carefully for tromping robot footsteps, slightly scary and exhilirating with friends for first 1 hour, nice ingame HUD system, options for flashlight, laserpointer, silencer on gun
Cons: Latency, glitchy character and robot movement, poor hitboxes and detection system for firefights, poor match making system/map finder, single player has no save points, checkpoints, or way to gauge your progress.

This game is not worth the money, nor agrivation that it will cost you. The game has a myriad of faults that were intentionally implemented, such as:
AI cheating their stats - A character that has no fesable way of reaching a high speed or boost stat, can out-speed a 5/1/1/5 or 4/1/1/6 character (Max speed, Acceleration, Handling, Boost)
AI ganging up against the player - Many, many times you'll be in 10th place, the very bottom, and instead of the AI throwing their items forward at the other AI to try and get further ahead, they AI throw them back into the players face.
Long, Boring backtracking - After playing through the main storyline, gathering stars to unlock items, at a certain point the hardest difficulty will unlcok, in which you have to go back through all the levels you'd completed once before, on a higher difficulty which just increases your chances of dealing with the above two issues. It feels like a massive grind.
The limited stage variety - All in all, there are very few races to choose from for a racing game. with a total of 20 tracks to choose from, a mere 3 of which were updated from the first game, meaning 17 tracks were original to the game, compared to the Mario Kart, with an average of 16 new tracks and 16 returning from previous games, updated. There are challenge mode variants of the maps, but that only furthers the issue of a lack of variety, as you're forced to play the same maps multiple times to progress, with a different stipulation slapped on top.
For a few extra random complaints: Tornado doesn't effect AI for obvious reasons, and the effets of tornado don't come into effect immediately, a delay between the control switch up. Various items seem to have a minor effect on AI while a greater effect is had against the player.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Of course, there are Pro's to the game, such as
- It's fun to play with a group of people
- The time attacks are challenging
- The character selection is decent, some characters sharing similar stats as to not imbalance multiplayer (Seeing as you cannot choose the same character as your friends)
- The soundtrack remasters and remixes classing music, faithful to the games that the tracks were based upon.
- The racing feels fun. While the controls can feel unresponsive when performing stunts in order to gain more boost, but the game has a charming feel to it, and is enjoyable enough to play when you're not being completely agrivated by the BS AI.
All in all, I wouldn't reccomend the game to anyone unless they were a sega fan growing up, and wanted a similar experience to Mario Kart or Smash Brothers, where you can see child-hood favorite characters (and some you weren't aware of) playing in the same game. But to those agrivated by cheating AI, don't go near this one.

A day later, I'm still not sure how I feel about Proteus. I guess I thought it was great for a while, and then not so great for the rest, but I'll get to that. Like Dear Esther, it involves exploring an island, but rather than using the island to tell a story about something else, exploring the island in Proteus is for the sake of the place itself. As you wander, you can potentially encounter a variety of things at different times and places, some straightforward, some surreal, and seeing what you can find is the experience.
The visual style is very simple, with it clear what everything is supposed to be, but leaving you to fill in the details yourself. The sound is more noteworthy, with different layers of the music entering and leaving as you approach different areas or climb a mountain, and creatures or objects you interact with or pass by plinking or blipping their own bits that contribute to it.
I suppose my main problem ended up being that while it was wonderful strolling around aimlessly and seeing what I could find for the first half of the time I spent with it, I didn't agree with some of the ways it changed as it moved toward the end. I'll be a bit vague to avoid being spoilery, but while the changes to the world did fit with the theme, I didn't like the way the visual changes made it harder to navigate, and it was much harder to find anything interesting going on as a result, which made the world feel less alive toward the end. A+ for the idea overall and the first half, but a B- for the execution of the latter half.

With its postcard feature, you can take a screenshot that has your randomly generated world encoded into it, and send it to a friend, who can then load your world and explore it themselves.
As for whether it's worth buying, it's hit or miss.  This might be the kind of thing you like, or it might not.  Grab it on sale if you can.

Just an incredibly solid Kart racer, with pretty much everything you would ask from a modern kart racer. Online works well and there are always people playing and the game controls extremely well. Most of the tracks are pretty cool (that billy hatcher level sucks), and the roster is so ridiculous and obscure that I can't help but level (I don't know who General Winter is but seeing him race against AiAi, Sonic, Danica Patrick, and Wreck-it Ralph is a site to behold).
What I really love is how the game rewards mastery of its mechanics, in that if you're good enough you'll be able to keep a constant speed with boosts, drifts, stunts, and knowledge of each course and the differences between the three vehicle modes. From here, the items serve to balance the playing field, making it so there's never a guaranteed winner (which can create either a joyful comeback or ragequitting a race).
The single player offers a good challengs and a.i on hard that is only slightly less difficult than actual human beings (meaning they're still pretty difficult). Some of the challenges in world tour are kind of dumb (I hate the one with the tank it is never fun or good), and I personally wish certain characters weren't locked behind some of the needlessly hard challenges, but it still provided a lot of fun, which is something I appreciate from a single player mode in a kart racer.
Again, a really well made kart racer, probably the best on PC. If Mario Kart were on PC, I would still be recommending this as something for any fan of the genre.

It's just another LEGO game, but that's not necessarily a bad thing.
If you've ever played a LEGO game before then you already know exactly what to expect from LEGO The Lord of the Rings.  There are no surprises here.  Having said that, this is a fun and well-made game that fans of
films will enjoy.  Of particular interest is the overworld which allows you to walk from one end of Tolkien's Middle Earth to the other with no loading screens.  Not at first, of course, since certain parts of the map will be locked off until you've completed the requisite story level, but once you've finished the story mode, you can walk from Hobbiton straight through to Mount Doom without stopping.  It's not to scale, so the trip will only take you a few minutes, but it's still very cool, and the sights along the way will be familiar to fans of both the books and the movies.
The individual levels are very enjoyable and contain lots of puzzles and secrets, most of which can't be accessed your first time through since they require the right character, so you'll want to go back and play them again in Free Play mode which gives you access to every character on your roster; however, you may want to wait until you've beaten the game because then you'll have every character you need to tackle every challenge, and finishing the game isn't hard since it's virtually impossible to fail.  If your character dies, you lose some studs (LEGO currency that you use to buy special unlockables) and your character is immediately resurrected on the spot, so even the most ham-handed gamer should have no trouble being able to make it to the final cutscene.
LEGO games are known for their humor, but I was somewhat surprised at just how funny these cutscenes are.  Since they use dialog from the movies themselves, the animators had to be creative, and there are endless visual gags like the possessed King Theoden briefly nodding off while talking and Grimma Wormtongue elbowing him in the ribs to get him talking again, or Lurtz taking down Boromir with bananas and chickens fired from his bow (trust me, you'll never look at Borormir's climatic scene the same way again).  Who knew that the films' relentless severity lent themselves to so much humor?
The game looks good with its colorful, high resolution textures and lighting effects.  We're not talking Arkham City quality, of course, but it does the job, and the music is great because it's taken straight from the Howard Shore soundtrack, so no complaints there.  I did run into several minor glitches throughout the game, such as characters getting stuck in the level geometry or suddenly freezing in place while the game carried on around them forcing me to restart from a checkpoint, but this was relatively rare.  Finally, multiplayer works great with the innovative dynamic splitscreen, and my boys had fun playing through the game with me.  I might even go so far as to say that this is the recommended way to play.
Buy this game if you're a fan of LEGO games and
, but if you've had your fill of LEGO games then move along because there's nothing to see here.

Tales from the Borderlands is the next Telltale game, and the first thing you may think is - boy, another Telltale game. I mean sure, you have played the Walking Dead and enjoyed it, but some of the others have been less than average. Well this game is DEFINATELY not less than average.
Tales from the Borderlands encorporates lore and story/plot points across the 3 main Borderlands games throughout its 5 episodes. While the main characters that you control you have never met before, there are definately some new and old friends you will meet along the way. The game is enjoyable and I ended up playing through its entirety in 1 sitting, taking around 12 hours, give or take a few, because I took time to think about decisions and searched up story points I didnt recognise on various wikis.
While I think the game is great, there are some decisions you have no choice about that I really dislike that you encounter through your adventure.
When you near the end of the game, instead of the usual button mashing or occasional push of a button, you will come across Super Smash Brosesque combos which you can use, which make the game a whole lot more fun for people who tire easily at button mashing.
One of the best things about Tales From the Borderlands is the amount of choice that is available. While there are the usual multi decision points, that drive the story, there are also multi decision points that can make something cool or funny happen, and also, while you collect money throughout the game, new opportunities such as cosmetics for your person or caravan are unlocked, along with some other stuff later which is linked a bit more directly to the story.
While playing this game on keyboard and mouse is okay, I reccommend playing it on controller. I used a PS3 controller with the XInput program on Windows 8, which was really easy to use. To search how to set it up (if you are having trouble using MoitionInJoy, search for an Instructables article on it, that goes step by step on how to set it up)
This story is non linear, and has many twists and decisions that are made that surprised even myself, whereas I can usually guess where a movie or game plot goes before it gets there. While there arent too many surprises at the start, as you get through to the end, when the main storyline and the storyline where you are telling the story to the person that has captured you, things get interesting. While I thought that Telltale would use this plot point to spin off for its next episodic game, Tales from the Borderlands 2, they actually continuted the game, adding another hour that actually closed off many of the questions I had about the plot. By the end of the game, most plot points, if not all, are closed, with a possibility for a second game, but no cliffhanger to entice you to buy the next game, one of the many grievences that people have with Telltale games.
If you have any questions about this game before you buy it, feel free to friend me and I can talk about it, but I would rate this game 10/10, and am hoping to play it again in a few months and make different decisionsto see how it changes it.

Yet more of Telltale's ingenuity shows itself in this series, set on the infamous world of Pandora in the Borderlands universe.
Set after Borderlands 2 this story follows Rhys: A semi-ruthless businessman looking to screw over his new boss, and Fiona: a street-wise Pandoran con-artist after her next big score. By their sides are Vaughn: a pen-pushing accountant and Rhys' partner in corporate crime, Sasha: Fiona's sister and fellow grifter, and Loader Bot: Pure awesomeness.
Through 5 chapters, these unlikely (and unwilling) partners unravel the mystery of The Vault of the Traveller. (Or traveler if you're American).
From the signature comic book styling to the extremely clever storyline, this is another classic creation by Telltale.
Pros:
Great art design,
Intricate storyline,
Signature British-style Borderlands humour (Psychos included),
Relevant choices with far-reaching effects (obviously, It's Telltale),
No technical problems on my (relatively high end rig) laptop.
Cons:
Like the other games you get a list of your choices at the end of each chapter, however to get all of them you have to go through the hassle of making a Telltale account.
General warnings:
If you are not familiar with the Borderlands universe don't play this game, you will not understand it at all,
If you do not have the sense of humour that you find skags being killed at opportunity funny, I advise you avoid this game as you would avoid Boris Johnson on LSD. (Unless you are familiar with British politics then that joke is cruising over your head).
All-in-all I highly recommend this game for the player that knows what they are getting into. It has everything a Borderlands/Telltale fan could want and more besides.

Let me just preface this review with this: any time I write a review, I always try to find as many pros and cons as possible. Let's look at the pros.
Pros:
+ Absolutely bangin' soundtrack.
...
And that's it. That's literally all I can find. Other than the soundtrack, this game is 100% not fun.
Cons:
- I don't get seizures, but one or two levels of this actually made me feel a little sick.
- Collision detection is absolutey terrible on obstacles.
- Some people say the game is "humorous". The only "humor" is jokes straight out of the 2010 "lolrandom" era.
- Checkpoint placement is frustrating, and not in a "this is a well-designed but difficult game" sort of way.
- Tons of particles, explosion sprites, and trailing sprites will obscure the screen. That's not good in a platformer game.
- Some areas have static cameras despite requiring constant movement, meaning you're flung into danger without knowing.
- It doesn't teach you some important things, meaning that some "difficult" areas are only that way because they held back something they should have told you in the first place.
I ended up quitting on a level where you had to open a portal by gathering runes. First and foremost, the level was a BLATANT rip-off of Super Crate Box (arguably a better platformer game), and I was screwed over by RNG.
Yes, you read that right.
Random. Number. Generator.
In a platformer game.
This level had hazards would spawn right over the item I'd need to collect, forcing me to restart the level even when I only had 2-3 items left to collect.
Hazards would block me into an area and stop me from collecting anything.
Horrific collision detection on the lasers meant I would be killed if I so much as sneezed near one.
Constantly spawning enemies that you can't take out fast enough because the jump-slam can't be done fast enough to protect yourself.
That portal level, I think, is the epitome of how much this game just isn't good. Some people say that this is the "dark souls of platformers", which shows me that a) people are abusing the term "dark souls-esque", and b) they don't understand what makes a DS-style game "fun". RNG is not "fun". Terrible camera placement is not "fun". Holding back information is not "fun".
Only thing I really got out of this was a nice soundtrack, but I could've just looked it up on youtube anyways.

It's a nice hallway-simulator.
Which really is infuriating and disappointing, because the assets are all there, but the game never does anything with them. Instead, it's too busy with telling a story that happens somewhere else through abstract sequences that require hardly any input and are so emotionally distant from the player that they mean absolutely nothing. It feels forced and pretentious.
The gameplay is nothing to write home about, either. Like the rest of the game, it could be something really fun and exciting, but it's not. The controls are clunky, exploration is harshly punished and the single one direction that the game wants you to go is not always intuitive to find. The game tries to throw these "epic" moments around but forgets to build up to them, so it all - again - means absolutely nothing to the player. It's not like a whole lot more happens than walking from point A to point B and ocassionally back. If there are any gameplay-mechanics that give a twist to the gameplay, the game immediately abandons them and pretends they never happened (e.g.: Pushing your sword into the ground to not get blown away, five minutes later that doesn't work anymore; you're asked to hold onto statues to not get blown away (which you couldn't do with the statues the first time you encountered them -  but whatever, right?))
And don't even get me started with story-through-gameplay. The topic of ascending and descending a tower could be so interesting and so great to fuse with the gameplay. But no, the designers opted for a railway-experience. Stuff happens, you're there to witness it. Press Button to win.
It's obvious some people put a lot of thought into the game. The style seems promising and a lot of things are already there. It could be something, which is why I was willing to spend money on it. It shouldn't be surprising then that I'm so frustrated. Not only do I feel like I wasted my money, I'm looking at something that is not what it could be. It's so close, yet so far away.
I hate that I don't like this game. But that's just how it is now. And I hope you do better next time.

Thisis a game about agirl who climbs a tower to fight a dragon. It pretendsto have a deeper meaning, but the more words it uses, the more abstract it gets, so let's just stick to basics: girl, tower, dragon. Lofty words here are just decorations.
The game itself is an amateurish attempt at making someting like ICO. From the aesthetic point of view, it's beautiful, though unpolished. If Shadow of the Colossus was a Giorgio de Chirico's painting come alive, this one guides us through a series of dreamscapes more like the works of Yves Tanguy or Salvador Dali. The music matches the visuals, creating a gorgeous meditative experience.
Gameplay, though, falls short. The game is not a "walking simulator", but neither is it a full-fledged action adventure. Puzzles and action sequences are barely there, either taking just a token effort or making you wonder what exactly you did wrong as you fall to you death again and again.
Still, the gameplay, no matter how watery and inconsistent it is, stays bearable and does not interfere with the game's aesthetic experience. Since it's short -- just a couple of hours -- the dull gameplay is forgivable, and the game is worth playing.

Rimworld is a scifi colony builder where you must manage a group of people who have crash-landed on an alien world. It looks very much like prison architect (it uses the same game engine) but plays more like a streamlined version of dwarf fortress and I think I speak for most PC gamers when I say that a more graphical, playable version of dwarf fortress is something people have been wanting for a long time. Rimworlds mood and character simulation is excellent and leads to some very memorable scenarios, the game controls intuitively, the music is great, overall this is a very well put together game, and the mods available through the steam workshop let you tailor exactly the experience you would like to have as well as adding whatever crazy stuff you want to add to the games already decent amount of content. This is a game where a jealous colonist can lure another out into the woods and attempt to throttle them so that they can attempt to steal their spouse. Or have their beloved pet rhino have a heart attack leading to a deep depression that culminates in the colonist hacking their wrists open while cooking and covering most of the kitchen in their vital fluids before being restrained, leading to mass food poisoning because the cleaner was off praying to his god and forgot to clean the kitchen. Or having a town sieged by an immigration of 100 blood crazed panda bears resulting in the town nearly starving because outside the building was a bloodbath as the pandas tore thru the towns livestock. Or having an artist carve a vivid artwork into a bedhead showing when the artist himself captured a prisoner from the fleeing enemy tribals and then making that prisoner sleep in that same bed. Or having a drugged out mayor who shows up to every morning breakfast with a spliff in hand. And so much more, I freaking love this game

Just wanted to throw in a quick few words after getting this in HD recently. I used to play this a bunch, but my AoE2/Conquerors discs don't work because Win 10 just isn't optimized for them, so I got this along with expansions.
Here's my quick verdict:
Pros:
-Everything good about AoE2 is still here in a neat little package.
-Lots of units, huge battles, sieges, etc. Chaos in real time.
-Still super fun to make huge armies, attack enemies, defend your city from opposing armies, etc.
-Music is pretty good, like before. Some new tracks if you haven't played the expansions past Conquerors, like me.
-Plenty of locations, map and game types, difficulty levels, units and civilizations to play around and master
-Lots of achievements if that's your thing. On one hand it's a bit of a con because it seems like there's just an unnecessary amount of them. One for winning as Turks and another for defeating Turks and one of each of those for each civilization along with too many quantity-based grindy achievements which are usually restricted to RPGs. But it's not like it has to be there, so I guess this is more of a fun bonus.
Cons:
-Everything that sucked about AoE2 is still here. The AI is still moronic unfortunately. Like the enemy sending small streams of archers to attack your castle throughout the entire game. How is treating your archers like expendable and worthless units a good strategy? And then the AI will pull a fast one on you and actually send an army to attack you when you least expect it, bucking its previous unexplainable strategy.
-Tracking is still terrible. Oftentimes, your units won't attack the enemy when you send them to a location forcing you to use the command attack. If units they sent somewhere via a regular right click or a gathering point from a Barracks for example, they won't attack an enemy until they get to that point, and often times if the battlefield is busy, they take weird detours and freeze in their tracks for no discernible reason, forcing you to give commands multiple times and hope they comply (they usually don't and get their asses handed to them)
-This needs a separate point regarding AI: When you send your units to attack an area, what will happen oftentimes is they will just attack randomly. So you will try to direct them towards the most crucial buildings like town centres, barracks and castles. After those buildings are destroyed, they will need special commands to attack the next target instead of automatically choosing the most pertinent threat of death. If you get them to attack a building and an army comes and starts attacking them, what will happen also is that they won't bother defending themselves because you've given them the command to attack the building. It's just frustrating that the AI does not have inherent prioritized auto-targeting, nor can you program either your army or individual factions of that army to prioritize certain units, like they should be able to, considering some of them are more effective against certain unit types (and ranged units typically need to stay away from buildings altogether).
-Archers still somehow do damage to buildings. Like, what? And some of the more annoying variants of archers like the Chinese Chu-Ko-Nu or the Vietnamese archers can actually do relatively decent damage to your castle if they gang up. I
-If you play with AI on your side, they are ALWAYS going to be dumber and more useless than the enemy AI, which despite its failings will always win over your computer allies, forcing you to try to do something early on (usually by Castle Age), and if you don't, you will find yourself defending multiple fronts and having to manage too many armies at once. It's a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥
-It really isn't all that HD, but the increased resolution definitely helps when you play in 1920x1080, which is of course a welcome change from the low resolution original game.

I've never been big on racing games, but two prior experiences stand out: Mario Kart 64 and F-Zero GX. The former for the combat aspect, and the latter for the brutally satisfying difficulty (completing it 100% felt amazing). Sonic All-Stars is clearly Sega's take on Mario Kart and fits that first type more, with the familiar nostalgic faces, if you've played other Sega games before, and the items/weapons you pick up while racing to help give you an edge.
That said, this game does have difficulty options ranging from Easy to Expert, and completing races and events on maximum difficulty has proven very satisfying as well. There are a few modes of play, including Time Attack (with ghosts to beat), a Grand Prix tournament, online and local matchmaking, a regular racing mode with AI, and a World Tour where you compete with the AI in regular races as well as several other event types structured like specific challenges. You're given an in-game license that records your progress through the game's modes, and your accomplishments are factored into a game completion percentage listed at the top. The ultimate goal is to achieve a Triple Star rank license, which you get at 100% completion for beating almost everything in the game at the highest difficulty (World Tour, Grand Prix, and Time Attack). I'm most of the way there, and it's been great fun.
The action isn't quite as fast as I remember F-Zero to be, but it's still very quick with constant speed boosts laying on the tracks, sharp twists, and jumps across gaps and over cliffs. The tracks and music are beautiful and representative of the various Sega games they're based on. There also tends to be more than one path through various sections of the tracks. Switching between a car, a plane, and a boat allows for many types of terrain within each track, making it pretty unique. There are many characters to choose from, most of which you unlock by playing the game, and performing well in races allows the character to level up a few times, the point of which is to unlock mods for the character to alter its vehicle's performance.
TL;DR : Lots of nostalgia for Sega gamers, many similarities to Mario Kart, plenty of fast dynamic action, and much satisfying difficulty for the more hardcore gamers.

LEGO The Lord of the Rings is a fun and simple game which does not require a lot of skill.  You take charge of a party of protagonists and work your way through the Lord of the Rings plotline (in the style of Peter Jackson's movie trilogy).  Along the way you collect lego bits as a currency, smash enemies and objects that get in your way, and solve an occasional puzzle allow you to progress ahead.  There are a bunch of optional side quests which allow players to collect/craft various items and have some fun outside of the storyline.
As one might expect from LEGO-branded games, this one seems fit for young or new video gamers who don't want too stressful a challenge.  The only penalty for dying is losing some of the bits you picked up on your current level.
The story follows Peter Jackson's depiction of Lord of the Rings, however it does take a little bit of creative liberty.  The end of Boromir, for example, is more comedy than tragedy, in the LEGO telling of the tale.  This is almost certainly a necessity when making an E-rated game out of a PG-13 rated movie.  The musical score, character voice clips, and scenery right out of the film trilogy really make you feel like you are playing through the films, and not some alternate rendition of Middle Earth.  Except, of course, when creative liberty was taken here and there to cause LEGO-appropriate silliness.

Yet more of Telltale's ingenuity shows itself in this series, set on the infamous world of Pandora in the Borderlands universe.
Set after Borderlands 2 this story follows Rhys: A semi-ruthless businessman looking to screw over his new boss, and Fiona: a street-wise Pandoran con-artist after her next big score. By their sides are Vaughn: a pen-pushing accountant and Rhys' partner in corporate crime, Sasha: Fiona's sister and fellow grifter, and Loader Bot: Pure awesomeness.
Through 5 chapters, these unlikely (and unwilling) partners unravel the mystery of The Vault of the Traveller. (Or traveler if you're American).
From the signature comic book styling to the extremely clever storyline, this is another classic creation by Telltale.
Pros:
Great art design,
Intricate storyline,
Signature British-style Borderlands humour (Psychos included),
Relevant choices with far-reaching effects (obviously, It's Telltale),
No technical problems on my (relatively high end rig) laptop.
Cons:
Like the other games you get a list of your choices at the end of each chapter, however to get all of them you have to go through the hassle of making a Telltale account.
General warnings:
If you are not familiar with the Borderlands universe don't play this game, you will not understand it at all,
If you do not have the sense of humour that you find skags being killed at opportunity funny, I advise you avoid this game as you would avoid Boris Johnson on LSD. (Unless you are familiar with British politics then that joke is cruising over your head).
All-in-all I highly recommend this game for the player that knows what they are getting into. It has everything a Borderlands/Telltale fan could want and more besides.

So where to begin. This game is really fun and offers a lot in what it already has. The ability to slice enemies in half is very satisfying and with the addition of photo mode, you are able to set up really cool shots. It is still early in development and many features are still being added. However, there are still many things that do hold this game back. Some of which are very hard to control. As it is now, I would definitely recommend this game. It is fun and very playable even. I play games in waves and will play a game until I lose interest. This game has been one of the very few that is fun to go back to and play fro a while.
For this review it is important to take in all the factors that may alter the game. As far as I know (please correct me if I'm wrong) there are only 2 dedicated developers who work directly on the game. With that in mind they have lives and deserve to take breaks. Though they did make this commitment to the community they should in now way feel obligated to give up their entire life.
I would also like to say I am just a customer who wants to know what I think. Keep that in mind that everyone has different preferences and you might find something wrong or great about the game that I didn't. I am not trying to tell you to buy this game, I just want to give you my opinion to help with your decision.
Pros:
- Addicting game play that is fun to both play and watch
- Passionate developers that want to help the best they can and want to talk with the customers
- Twitch mode allows for streamers to be challenged by the viewers and adds a bit of unpredictability to the game mode
- The workshop is a great place to see what people are making and adds something different to mix things up. The new update that adds color customization adds so much more. It allows you to make the map truly how you see it.
- The enemies in the game offer a wide verity of obstacles that allow for experimentation with which ones work well together
- The Game play is different from other many other games that gives a unique and clever game that has the violence and fighting as many hand to hand combat games but in a cartoonist and child friendly way
- the commentators are funny and have a wide variety of comments so that it doesn't become repetitive after a while
- flameraptors are really fun. They have a lot of potential and are hard to beat if you don't know their weakness. this leads me to the con though. The bow makes the flameraprots easy. this might have been on purpose but I think it should be a little harder.
Cons:
- There are bugs that are not all bad or that big but do sometime take away from the games experience
- (as of now) story mode is very interesting and has a lot of potential but is still in development and not that long. As of now the two chapters are very similar except with different enemies and a different ending. The ending of the second chapter is interesting and makes me excited to see what will happen next.
- There are still some balancing issues that should be fixed such as the bow. It is a great weapon once you get fire arrows and slow time but at a certain point is still no mach for the sword
- The hammer is great in my opinion and has good damage to wield-ability but doesn't have as much depth as it could. I think there should be more ways it can interact with enemies.

As of now, this is a very simple game, but it's really fun. TL;DR at the bottom.
Players have only two guns for different ranges of engagement (I find this is very balanced and works well, but they'll probably add more guns in the future). You have infinite ammo reserves, and your weapons have toggleable flashlights, quick attach suppressors, and laser aiming modules. Weapons are reasonably accurate regardless of aiming down sights.
I played Survival mode, and I was really pleased with the emergent gameplay.
In Survival, you and your co-op partners are put into a large urban/indoor area with objectives strewn around it. You just have to reach each objective to win. Each objective you reach will change the lighting and/or weather of the area, reducing or increasing visibility indoors or outdoors. Objectives can be reached in any order. Killed players can be revived immediately with the press of a button by a teammate.
The main component of the gameplay is a steady flow of hostile combat training robots into the area. There are two kinds of robots: melee robots that sprint (really fast), and robots that use guns. Both types can kill you in 1-2 hits. You will usually die before you can react, so you have to listen for them and make sure you see them first. Robots will immediately see and shoot at anyone standing or emitting a source of light, such as a flashlight or light source in the environment. Good players will shoot out lights and use their flashlight sparingly in this mode. The gamemode encourages very tactical movement. Good players will practice sticking together, covering multiple angles, avoiding shooting at the same enemy, timing reloads properly, and entering new areas and rooms sensibly.
The graphics are clean and simple, but are likely to be changed as development continues. There is heavy emphasis on atmosphere and lighting that really lends itself to the game, sometimes things get kinda spooky.
The sound design of the game is impressive as it is; most of a player's information on how to proceed through an area will be from sounds far, near, muffled through walls, or in the same room.
My only technical complaints about the game are the framerate instability and slightly high latency overall; the game is totally playable for me. The game is also a long time in development, it's a crowd-funded game before crowd-funded games were cool. It would be a great shame if the game was not finished. The core gameplay fundamentals are very solid and would probably be called "hard but fair" by a lot of people. It's certainly impressive by modern game's weak standards. The devs cite strong influences for this game: Half-Life, Rainbow Six 3, and System Shock 2. Each one of these influences shows. If the devs stick to their principles, this game can be a nice little pinprick of light in the darkness of recent FPS fare.
TL;DR: I recommend trying this game, even in its current state. It's good challenging fun with friends, and despite its simplicity the gameplay does not get old quickly, which is very promising.

I'm not even going to touch on the whole 'pay to win' thing since ye it's all attainable in-game. But the in-game way of gathering things is sooo slow. And yeah, I get it, they need money to actually continue to maintain and update the game. That's fair, that's what you expect in a free to play game with a cash market.
The problem is that the game just feels unbalanced. You can sit there for hours working on building your machine. You can fine-tune it, build it with multiple weapon-types to help cover weaknesses at a specific range, shifting your armored pieces around for maximum protection, and even try to make sure your center of gravity won't leave your rig doing awkward flips on tight turns.
And then you'll get shot down by someone who just built a flatbed of the basic frame 20 feet long, line it with the cheapest gun, and basically just shut you down by force of 'the game is designed this way'. Basic frames can't be destroyed like armor, after all. Put your guns on it and bam, they're far harder to pick off by peppering armor.
But that's rare. Let's move on to the next game. A lot of people with neat designs, some just copies of one-another, and so on. You take your rig into the next game. And then you see it. Is that an unarmed enemy? No turrets, no melee weapon, just charging at you? Why that's an easy- What are those flying things?
Before you know it, you're shredded to pieces, shooting at someone who has to do nothing but drive around and avoid your shots while his drones rip you to pieces. In seconds, your guns are picked off, your wheels fly away, and you're shredded before you can even do meaningful damage.
Next game, rigs packing nothing but double-cannons that can pick your rig in half in a salvo.
Next game, invisible rig lined with bomb-tipped spears destroying you instantly. Well at least he can't do that one again.
Next game, frame shenanigans.
The game just feels AWKWARD, and as though the effort you put in is wasted. And if you get unlucky and picked out of a round early on? Sucks for you! 10/several thousand experienced needed to level up. And if you leave early, you get nothing. Not like World of Tanks where you can basically start another game while your tank is 'left' in the battle to finish it, no. You have to sit there and watch your loss or victory the entire time or you get nothing. Satisfying gameplay, 10/10.
So you think 'I'll drop some money on this game, ♥♥♥♥ it. I'll buy some parts.' Well you better do your damn research on good builds or your money is wasted.
Oh, right, and don't diversify. Just stack as much of one or maybe two weapon types on your rig and go for burst damage. Chunk someone and they probably won't be able to fire back to take advantage of any weakness in your weapon lineup.
It's a shame, too, because the game has potential and is overall pretty cool with mad max-style fighting, but when you actually start playing the pvp you go from 'cool post-apocalyptic cars/tanks' to 'just stacking whatever helps me kill as fast as possible to overcome the ridiculous grind'.

The short review: I recommend this game, but I would not pay more than $4-5 for it. It is short, but beautiful (even more so if you can run the higher settings).
The long review: This is a lovely game with a lot of great potential. However, I was also very disappointed with it. I was expecting a semi-lengthy game and I completed it (and went back through for two chapter-specific dreams) in 3 hours. I would have loved to see the story fleshed out more to give it a fuller experience because it felt there was still some disconnection between the dream stories and the main protagonist. The gameplay was also pretty slow (regardless of the settings). The unresponsiveness, camera switching, and invisible walls not flush with the graphics made moving around a bit annoying and resulted in unnecessary death or the need to restart a puzzle. Despite all of this, I still enjoyed it enough to recommend. I was just disappointed in how short it was. It didn't feel challenging or difficult, but it was engaging. I would recommend this, but only if it were on sale. I would love to see this game developed into a much deeper and challenging game.

2011 was an amazing year for PC games. Sadly, this means a few great titles have been overlooked amidst the flurry of releases. Atom Zombie Smasher is the best of them. Developer Brandon Chung has always been a master of style - even his student game Barista 2 has more spunk than most commercial releases - and in Atom Zombie Smasher that style really meshes with the gameplay. The randomly-selected narrative vignettes are amusing, but this is a game that tells its story almost entirely through its gameplay. This is a real, horrifying zombie apocalypse, viewed with a clinical distance. You will try and save Nuevo Aires. You will lose. And you'll enjoy it all the way.

EVE Online can be best described as one-of-a-kind in the MMO Market today, and has been pioneering since it's release a decade ago.  But if you're looking for a one-word description of this fantastic game, that word is going to be "Emergent".
What makes EVE Online so unique is the player-driven aspect to everything in this game.  EVE players create the economy (it is 99% driven by players); players create the wars and news stories you hear about; players create content through alliances, piracy, industry, and exploration; and most importantly for me, players create STORY through their interactions not only with each other, but with the developers as well, ensuring that New Eden is a living, thriving place that Capsuleers feel a part of.
To say that EVE has a steep learning curve is a bit of an understatement, but the devs have spent the last year or more working on the new player experience, making EVE a vastly more inviting game.  No longer will you be dumped straight into the action with no idea what's going on.  Instead, tutorials and starting missions give you experience and understanding into the core mechanics; new interfaces make ships and progression easier to understand; and active player corporations dedicated entirely to educating the masses are available and easy to get into.  And with dedicated roles that players can start to focus on at any time, even the newest player can give a veteran a run for their money.
Offline progression and the PLEX system ensure that no matter how much time you have available, you'll always be able to fit into New Eden.  Have too much time on your hands?  Then buy PLEX directly with in-game currency to essentially play for free!  Don't have nearly as much time to play because you're constantly working?  Then buy a PLEX from the EVE Store and sell it on the in-game market for a quick and legal way to buy in-game currency!
EVE Online is fantastic for any player looking for a real sandbox-style game with consequences, sci-fi and space sim fans alike, and those seeking gameplay that you simply can't find anywhere else.  Comes highly recommended.

The concept is nothing special, but it's executed extremely well. The career mode is varied and interesting and offers a difficulty-reward balance on every level, though I feel like I've cheated myself if I don't do everything on hard for those three stars. The stars are then used as a meter, which unlocks things when you reach certain numbers.
The actual gameplay is mostly the same as Mario Cart with drift turns, boost pads, item boxes which can give powerups or weapons of varying usefulness and interesting, nuanced level design.
There's a good variety of characters and a good number of them are well-known, a little surprising considering Sega's somewhat-limited roster of IPs. Character choice has a strong effect on stats and, by levelling them up, you can gain access to mods to further customise your favourite racer.
The look and feel are fantastic. Graphics are very well-polished and pretty, I quite like the music, but I think that will be somewhat subjective and the controls feel good.
Now for the complaints. The hitboxes are a bit odd, but I think I've got fairly used to them, some character's voices can be a bit grating (Shadow is just so EDGEY!) and there's no tutorial, so you're just kinda left to figure it all out. Saying that, I *did* place first in my first race, so it just takes some time to learn all the specifics and details, like tricks and the starting boost.
Also, in all star mode, you can press use item again to launch a character-specific attack. It's not *exactly* like mario's star powerup.

Shortly after breakfast a crazed trio of man-eating dromedaries showed up. We all headed into the safety of our bedrooms.
The dromedaries broke down the front door, then headed around back. We could hear their horrible moaning calls through the walls as they hunted us.
Meanwhile, a wayward shipment of muffalo wool dropped out of the sky. Someone else was having a bad day too, I guess.
After breaking down the back door, the dromedaries entered our compound. War, our young cat, was in the wrong place at the wrong time. She got trampled by the camels while Ray shot at them, to little avail. Like War, Ray was downed quickly under crushing blows and violent kicks.
Immediately following Ray’s fall, five heavily armed members of The Razor Raccoons (a pirate faction) took the opportunity to attack.
Wallace pulled Ray to safety, and Kars went into battle with his trusty knife. Bravely, Kars killed one dromedary before being downed by another. Wallace died under the hooves of a furious and psychotic camel.
The dromedaries turned their aggression towards the pirates next. One of the remaining camels was downed by a pirate wielding a huge steel club, and the other was shot dead.
The pirates then came after the settlers.
Kars lost his right leg, and Wallace was beaten to death.
Ray got off easy with just a bruised arm, but started feeling withdrawal from her go juice addiction.
The pirates decided to kidnap Kars and leave, but not without first kicking the walls and starting a fire in our pantry. During all the confusion, an emu wandered inside and got stuck in our crafting room.
Ray recovered enough to go fight the fire, though she was starting to feel the effects of starvation. She finally collapsed from hunger, withdrawal, and fatigue.
A thunderstorm rolled in, so the fire did go out, but not before destroying a pantry wall and the power lines to the refrigeration units. Most of our meager food supply was lost in the blaze.
A radio message came in from The Razor Raccoons… they’re holding Kars for ransom for 1541 silver, which we must give them within 24 hours. We have a whopping 370.
Lightening struck near the house, starting another small fire.
Ray, the only remaining survivor, passed out from extreme exhaustion.
A heat wave struck, adding to her discomfort and pain.
A group of four tribesmen from the “Coalition of Louir” visited. Before they even got to our compound, two of them started fighting each other, apparently over an insult.
They found the unconscious Ray laying outside what was once the front foyer, but didn’t offer to help. They were deeply upset by the sight of Wallace’s body. They ate a great feast at our table, before leaving.
Ray is now extremely malnourished and has heat stroke.
The window for the ransom demand has just expired. Rest in peace Kars.
It’s 108 degrees inside our base.
Ray has died of starvation.

EVE Online or as I call it: Star Trek on Steroids that just ripped your house a new doorway. This daunting giant of a game has been around the internet for as long as most people can recall and this beast still continues to keep tearing at boundaries.
The basic premise of this game is "You are a space pilot, you are in space, you're pretty rad now." but to say that's where it ends would be insulting as there are too many things to even list in a mere review meant for a brief read for some form of idea.
A more accurate description is that you're a space pilot in a constantly changing galaxy that litterally evolves and changes based on what the community itself are doing within it: Sectors can be claimed or lost for factions, mine deposits can be exausted in certain areas, pirates can come for you when you least expect it, you can be a bounty hunter that hunts down other players or be the bounty yourself, making yourself feared throughout the galaxy!
That alone was enough for me to buy into this and yet, more new features are constantly being added to this (already huge) giant such as building your own Colony within a sector or planet, hacking ships to get treasures and even linked play with Dust 314 to assist players fighting on planets with orbital bombardments.
The downside is that since there is so much to this game to even consider doing or even do, it's very mindblowing to any newcomers to EVE Online, putting them off as a whole. Fortunatly, the tutorial sets you off to some basics to help you get some form of idea what you could be doing. Skipping the tutorial altogether however feels very non optional and will not only leave you very confused as to what you should be doing, but make EVE a very boring game in the long run since you'll have nothing to start off with.
If the tutorial didn't help you, there are several players that will gladly mentor you (which to be honest, actually saved me from running screaming from this game and never looking back, so thank you brilliant mentors!) and help you get onto your way with whatever you want to focus on.
All in all if you're willing to put the time and effort into this game, it begins to get very interesting as well as rewarding, such as using in game currency to rebuy your subs rather than using real money instead. If not owning this game, then at least try it just once.
