Personally, for an early access game, it's fairly engaging. However, pros and cons do exist here, and I do feel they should be addressed.
Pros:
1) GREAT atmosphere. Personally choosing which directions to go, what weapons to have out, and what to do seemed more than filled with it's fair share of tension on a solo mission. You know the enemy is dangerous, and taking it out quickly is essential as they can more than easily take you down with their bonzai-like charges or sudden gunfire in your direction. Even frightening at some parts for me, though not too much.
2) Lovely graphics. Personally I was impressed with the graphics and how realistic they made everything seem.
3) From my experience, the community is decent. The first time I ever played a multiplayer server, I actually got great people. They were friends, and we all used teamwork to get past difficult objectives. They were friendly to the new players and happy to lend out a hand.
Cons:
1) Lack of community. Out of a good number of 10-15 servers (Give or take a few), usually only 2-4 of these have players in them at any given time. Admittedly very annoying.
2) Only two weapons? I was hoping for a bit more weapon diversity, as though the two weapons obviously serve different purposes, their usefulness in close quarters combat against these bonzai charging robots can be panic filled when they close in. Not too annoying when your comrades can simply press 'E' to instantly revive you, but when players are fairly close together, this can lead to disaster.
3) Lag. Admittedly my computer is not exactly a gaming device that's beefed up or such. But even when attempting my best to lower graphics options (Which was also nearly useless) I felt that on larger maps my progress was slowed down to a nearly unplayable rate as my FPS dropped to an average of about 15. Bleh.
Obviously not the perfect review, but if the lack of players doesn't turn you off and your computer is better than some windows 8 laptop, go ahead! This game is well worth the buy.

Opening caveat: I am a kickstarter backer of the game, and received this copy as a result of that
A lot of reviews comment on the fact that you're not getting a lot for your money. There's hardly any content, and it's incredibly buggy. These reviews were posted within the first day or two of release, and do not reflect the current stage of the game right now. This is, after all, an early access game. Oni-punks have been releasing near-daily updates, adding content and tweaking bugs since release. Is this a finished product? Not hardly. But what it IS is a taste of what the final game will entail.
You have a grid, you move on the grid, you attack your enemies. Conserve your ammo, choose your targets, and time your attacks properly to avoid reprisal. There are three characters, each with unique weapons and abilities. Each has a set of stages through which they must pass, along with optional side missions. Since that first release, bugs have been fixed, the stages have been improved and organized better, and the game in general just feels better as well. As I said, it's still more of a demo than anything, but it's growing steadily.
In time, you will have helper characters, along with a wider variety of heroes and weapons from which to choose. Sure, it's been a long time coming, but it's heartening to see these basic building blocks, to know that the game DOES exist. As long as the flow of updates continues to be as rapid as it has been, I, for one, will continue to recommend this game.

My firt review I think! I try to be as honest as I can and I still do play this game. But have limited the amount of time I put into it now as I feel there is quite a lot to work with, but I also have had some good times playing it and hopefully will have some more ones if they can start adressing some of the bigger concerns (and a lot of the small ones!) :)
Pro: You get to build your own vehicles!
Con: Takes a lot of levels to start to get enough parts to do the stronger builds and there is a lot of cookie cutter builds.
Pro: Pretty good graphics.
Con: Some glitches / bugs etc, but not that bad considering it is Open Beta.
Pro: Free2play
Con: You will be cannon fodder for quite some time for ppl who played since Closed alpha/beta (They have loads of money as it was easier to get in earlier phases and all the top end gear) and ppl who put real money into this (open beta) game...
Pro: They use bots to help populate games.
Con: Bots are quite bad compared to real players.
Pro: They use a Match Making system based on PS (Power Score) of your vehicle.
Con: The Match Making does not work that well and the PS value of high tier weapons are way off leading to high tier weapons being used to gank newbies. Group up to 4 can que together and will be matched against randoms, this of course leads to easy wins for the side the group plays on.
Pro: Fast paced games, 3 minutes.
Con: If you die fast you have to sit and watch your teammates until the game ends to get rewards (and if you have not managed to get a kill, assist or cap point you will get nothing anyways)
Pro: Get into games fast.
Con: There is an autojoin next game after one is completed, this leads to a lot of AFK:ers and ppl who did not want to leave the prior game early due to the "no reward" thing being part of your games. So you can find yourself 2-3 people short in games.
Pro: You can select a geographic region to play in.
Con: You get forced on servers in other regions even if you selected another one, this leads to unplayable matches (high ping, rubber banding etc. Example, had EU as region, gets forced on laggy RU servers and cannot communicate with my team as none wishes to speak english).
Pro: A lot if different type of competitions, design this and that car etc.
Con: They had a "Starter car" competion, to build the winning car as a new player you need to invest over thousands of coins. (1500 coins goes for 29.99 euro). A good example of the mentality of the company delivering the game.
Pro: PvE and PvP options.
Con: The PvE aspect is limited to "Fuel" that you have a set amount of each day, you can gain more fuel from PvP or buy it on the market. Also very painful when you do a PvE raid and one or two people leave, you will fail the raid and the fuel spent to join that raid is lost.
Pro: .....
Con: Coin seller spam in chat (Think WoW gold spammers), and a lot of profanities, harassment and racial slurs seems to be quite accepted in the general chat.
Pro: ....
Con: UI is a bit, well, not intuative directly. Takes a bit getting used to and hopefully they hire a UI specialist to sort it out.
Pro: ....
Con: A lot of AFK bots around in the late hours when playing, they are of course helped by the auto-join functionality the game has. I have repored quite a few and even contacted their support on the forums to report them again, sadly tho this does not seem to be a priority to get rid of bot / afk macro users.
You can play this game without putting money in or playing since alpha, but you will be in for a long grind to be able to compete. It is fast paced and below level 10 it is great fun (first 4 levels you fight only bots), but at 10 you are released out in the "wild" and will run into the big boys with their high tear weapons just waiting for you. :)
If you going to play I suggest keeping a PS score below 2K when you get to level 10 when you PvP to avoid as many as possible of the high tier weapon ppl who are out to gank new players etc.
A few tips if you still will play:
* Learn the market. (Don't start selling off everything you have etc, you need a lot to craft new stuff)
* Read up on crafting, this is how you will get better gear.
* If you end up vs premade groups, clans, forced on another region server. Just quit and join a new game.
* Don't join PvE too early, there are PS scores to join them, but joining a normal raid with 3K PS is not recomended.
Cheers

This game is one of the best that I have ever played. It can be a real challenge, but it is always very fun. It is a constant struggle to survive, and manage food and resources, and the game gets progressively harder as your colony gets better, so it hardly ever gets to the point where your base is overpowered and nothing is a threat any more.
Even if the base game gets boring, or if you feel that it lacks in depth, Rimworld can be very easily modded, and the majority of mods out there are very well made, and fit in with the base game without unbalancing it, or feeling unnatural. The majority of Rimworld mods add or tweak small things, for example, one makes it so you can make prosthetics, rather than having to buy them from traders, and another adds a recipie for neurotramine. There are a lot of mods that tweak small things, or add things. So if there is something you dont like about the base game, or feel is unbalanced, you can easily mod it out.
Each playthrough is different and memorable: you have different colonists, all with different skills, traits, and backstories; Different events such as raids or toxic fallouts, or cold snaps effect each playthrough in a different way, and make it so that every playthrough has memorable stories. You can see what I mean by scrolling through the reveiws.
Don't let the fact that it is early acess put you off, as the game feels very polished, and is virtually glitch free.
This is an amazing game, with amazing features, and an amazing developer. Go and buy it

I have over 100 hours in this game. For starters, I think any game that nets you over 60 hours for 60 euro (AAA titles) is a good deal, because in my experience I can only get 30 hours at the very most from AAA titles. Rimworld is under half that price, and offers a potentially unlimited playing time - because there's one thing Rimwold has that other games don't - replayability.
Every single game will have a diffferent story. Every colony will develop differently. If you find yourself getting bored, all you need to do is up the difficulty to remind you just how flawed your strategy is. Every Alpha update adds a plethora of new content to enjoy, and it's obvious to see that this game is being loved and cherished by the development team.
With a thriving modding community since it's release, and developers who actively encourage them, it's a no-brainer to pick up Rimworld and enjoy it while in it's still in its Alpha, because I can easily see the price rising for full release to €40 euro - it'd be worth every red cent.

This game is like a bag of potato chips. You sit down and open it, intending to just engage a little bit, and before you know it it's six hours later and you're covered in salt, grease, and tears.
Hero Siege is essentially Diablo re-imagined as a bullet hell game. You select from a large number of different characters, each with their own unique tree of skills. You're then dropped into a field filled with obstacles, traps, and pre-placed monster lairs. Foes pour in from the four cardinal directions; defeat four waves of them and you'll face a miniboss. Every five fields, the miniboss is replaced by a large boss.
An amazing amount of things in this game are procedurally generated. Monster leaders, minibosses, and even bosses can randomly receive adjectives on their names that grant them special abilities. You counter with relics, magical items with a variety of bizarre effects -- summoning familiars, creating hazards, offering special attacks and defenses, adding new effects to your existing attacks, or just increasing your stats.
Make no mistake: this game is really random. Skill is a primary factor, but a bad selection of relics or a particularly useful adjective on the wrong monster can spell doom. Fortunately, unlike most roguelikes you are able to keep your cash, levels, and equipment after dying; only your relics and progress disappear.
There are a few negatives.
First, some of the graphic effects make it hard to see what you're doing; "misty" and "Satanic" in particular get in the way a little bit more than they were probably intended to.
Second, the randomization can sometimes get out of hand -- it's possible for one of the optional dungeon sidequests to be generated with wildly inappropriate opponents, leaving you with no way out but through.
Third, the game is a bit on the easy side. It takes a while to build up a powerful character, but a few lucky equipment drops can give you a huge boost. Completing Normal mode is difficult; from that point on, though, your power increases just as fast as your foes' power does. I'm partway through the fourth difficulty level out of five, and haven't felt at all intimidated since Normal difficulty.
Still, forty or so hours' entertainment for the price is pretty spectacular, and this game is definitely worth a look. (It's also a pretty ideal game to play while watching TV in another window.)

EVE Online is definately not for the faint hearted. The game has a very steep learning curve and a very unforgiving community, but where there is challenge comes great reward if you stick around long enough to learn how to play properly and turn a profit.
Essential Info about the game:
* EVE has no levels or classes. All skills are trained in real time even when you are offline.
* Two free expansions a year
* Once you start earning enough in game cash you wont ever have to pay a subscription fee again.
Gameplay wise the game plays more like Knights of the Old Republic in terms of combat to compare it to anything else. The ship movement is not like Freelancer or Elite, and combat can sometimes be slow paced. Community wise it has both it's ups and downs, there are always organisations and groups to help you out and get you started on the right path. The game features an extensive API that is integrated with dozens of addons and tools accross the web from tracking your in game mail and skills offline, to monitoring star system activity.
The downsides to EVE against over MMOs is that it can be overwhelming. Corporations (clans) have many confusing aspects to them from tax rates to seperate divisions along with titles and roles. The UI is hardly friendly to begin with and requires players to set it up to be their own and how they can use it best. Unlike other MMOs death is a setback and punishment, if your ship gets totaled then you lose all of your equipment and modules on it, if you die then you lose implants and need to buy them again.
The community can sometimes be visceral and real, many players take the game very seriously and do not mess around, but the more casual gamers can be found at it's core. EVE allows for nearly any type of gameplay, from being a lawless outlaw and killing anyone you see, to running a massive corporate alliance manufacturing weapons and starting wars between players.
EVE Online is tied into two other games, those are Dust 514 and EVE Valkyrie (Valkyrie still in development). Actions taken in Dust effect EVE, they share a market and a currency, and battles on planets in Dust are happening real time in EVE. If a player in dust calls in an orbital bombardment then there is a player in EVE online piloting the battleship that carries out that bombardment.
It is a game people should always try once and give it a go, many people who dislike it do not give it enough time and over my years of playing it the game has improved considerably and with the Rubicon expansion, is beginning to change forever.

This is the best Mario Kart clone currently on the market, but it does have some positive points over even Mario Kart...
- The tracks are so varied, with some really good tracks included.
- Content, the game has so many characters to unlock, kart mods, tracks, & a long campaign that get's pretty tricky near the end.
- The campaign is 2 player.
- The AI doesn't cheat, if you're spanking them, you're spanking them. They don't magically get the equivilant to 3 blue shells in a row & take you out on the last 2 corners, despite dominating the entire race.
- The difficulty is fair & has a nice upward slope, meaning you get better at the game as it gets harder, nothing ever seems too hard, unless you jump straight in for the 3 star missions despite never playing before.
- The music and graphics may not stand out as much as Mario Kart, but they do stand on their own merits.
It's not all positive though, the game does have some bad points;
- Character selection, quite a few are pretty bland & won't be used unless you're aiming for 100%. I mean I love the Football Manager series, but I have no interest in driving as some generic manager just because SEGA publish the franchise.
- Shadow's in it.
- Some of the 3 star missions will do your head in, but again, this isn't the game being unfair, it just means you're not driving well enough.
- A few of the tracks are forgetable.

No, I would not recommend this game, it's bad, very bad. The gameplay itself is awesome, but, still, this game was very poorly thought out, it's very disappointing. There's 4 things that make this game really bad:
The first one is the online unlockable requirements. It's really silly that you have to play in online mode only just to be able to earn experience and coins to unlock the unlockables, because there's almost NO ONE online for this game. I only have limited time to play, and waiting for people to show up in the lobby wastes my time (it can take hours for people to show up). That's a terrible arrangement for a game, any game, where you're dependent on playing online only, to unlock things. You should be able to unlock everything in local play, too, because that would make it fair for people that don't like playing online, or aren't allowed to. I don't even like playing online, anyway, I avoid it as much as possible. I prefer local play and playing with my brother or sister, and I think it's wrong when games force you to play online to unlock things, because you should be able to do the same thing in local play. If you had been able to unlock the unlockables and earn experience points and coins in local play too, then the game would have been much better.
The second bad thing about this game (and by far the worst) is the experience points bar. It's UNBELIEVABLE how long it takes to get to the end of the experience points bar, when you earn enough experience points to get two gold coins! The experience points crawl up the bar at a PAINSTAKINGLY slow pace, it takes WAY too long to get to the end of it. It takes so long, you'd be at least 1 or 2 years older by the time you'd be finished unlocking everything in the game, I'm not kidding, that's how long it takes. The bar should have been shorter, or the amount of experience points MUCH less, definitely one of the two, at least.
The third bad thing is that if you want to get x100, x40, or x10 gold coins, you have to pay for it WITH REAL MONEY! What?! You shouldn't have to pay for the coins, because, when you buy a game, that should cover everything in the game as well. And that includes the coin packs in Deformers. It doesn't make sense to pay real money for something in DeFormers when you've already bought the game.
And the fourth bad thing is the dummies in local play. I prefer local play in all games, but the local play in this game is just such a MAJOR let-down, and really boring. Not only do you not earn experience points or coins, but the dummies you pick for your enemies DON'T EVEN FIGHT BACK! They just sit there, and literally do nothing. They should have at least been able to fight back, I mean, really, the local play mode was terribly thought out.
Overall, you're literally stuck in this game: You can either wait a long time for someone to show up in the lobby to play with you in online mode, or you can play with dummies in local play, who don't even fight back, and you don't earn anything. Unless you have a brother or sister to play with, you will easily get bored of this game, waiting for people to show up in lobbies. It'll just leave you feeling disappointed and bored, guaranteed, because it takes a long time for people to show up in lobbies, it wastes your time. Trust me, from playing it, I can honestly say it just gets too annoying to have to wait all the time. While the gameplay itself in this game is awesome, those 4 bad things in this game really make this game bad, and make it too boring and annoying to play. This game is definitely not worth the amount of money that it is on steam, it's really only worth $5 or $10, no more, because there are just too many bad things in this game. It just would have been better if those 4 bad things in DeFormers had been better thought out, then I would have recommended this game for sure. The gameplay is great, but there's so just so many bad things in this game that make it too annoying and frustrating, that's why I gave this game the thumbs down. Don't buy this game, it's not worth it! :(

I really want to get this review right as I REALLY want you to buy this game that is how much I recommend Interstellar Marines! Even if you buy it now and don't like it, which you would have to be crazy not to, this will be an investment. Simply because Interstellar marines is a game to watch, with a ton of future potential and that future isn't far off.
The game, as it is, puts you in the boots of a Marine undergoing training in preperation for combat missions that will take you to the furthest reaches of human expansion in the universe that will lead to first contact with other intelligent life in a very realisitc way.
The developers are fantastic, dedicated, imaginative and have in my opinion (and I know this is a review) have given to us as customers the most brilliant concept for a game I can concieve espically the way they have implemented dynamic environments.
When the lights are on you walk about like you own the place but the dark corners you still avoid, when they go out completely you hide in the corners edging along walls frightened to turn on your flash light because the dark just seems so vast because when all the lights go out it really is pitch black and the dark feels real.
The weather is also diverse with rain that falls on your visor obscuring your vision really giving you a sense of presense and depth like no other game offers.
The weapons feel like tools of war rather than cap guns, the sounds of your boots on the floor make you concentrate on moving forward, the only sound this game is missing to make you feel alive is the sound of your heart beating but then you might be able to hear it but I could not over the sound of my own.
The graphics are impressive when you can see and when you can not. If you look outide at the stars you get a sense of loneliness that not many games give you that take you to space but that might have something to do with what is waiting for you inside. This game may not be for fighting fans, but DB games never have been.
The story of this game is pretty cool for a Dragonball game. Rather than just having you play through the story of Dragonball Z (with a little GT thrown in there in the DLC), your created character has to fix anomalies in time that change the course of the timeline, mostly caused by the villain of the scenario being powered up by the main bad guy. The fixing of said anomaly consists of you beating the crap out of the altered individuals of the scenario until the events play out as you'd expect.
The style of the game appears to be more towards the recent Battle of Z game, but the fighting is imbalanced as all getout.  It boils down to "does my opponent have a barrier attack and/or do they have an ability which lets them not stagger? No? PunchpunchpunchpunchpunchULTIMATE! Yes? Crap. Circle around and blast them for a while, get a few cheeky hits in to buld meter, ULTIMATE!" Once your character gets stronger, even these issues become essentially moot. Often you'll be put into team battles, but the AI is...not exactly advanced. It seems they never use their ultimates and spend most of their time circling the opponent and getting punched.
Where the game really shines is the creation suite. 5 races to choose from, some with genders, all having different base stats. Thousands of different outfit pieces to equip, which boost different stats and in many cases can be color customized. Lots of different Z-Souls, which give you different abilities such as increased movement speed, faster Ki regeneration, powering up certain skills, etc. Items that can be used in battle to regain life for you as well as your teammates, cause a regen effect, revive from a KO, and other effects.
These can be bought in-game in some cases, but are earned mostly through Parallel Quests, where you go through an area of time with a predefined goal, usually just punching people until they fall down. But hey, you can dress up a Frieza Clan member in Bulma's clothes if you want! (Gives a nice boost to basic attacks, too.) You also have the option of being mentored by several DB characters, from Krillin and 18 to Goku and Beerus. This will get you skills you normally can't buy. These areas give plenty of replayability as you try and get your created character absolutely perfect.
All in all, if you're a Dragonball fan, you'll enjoy the customization the game provides and will be able to ignore the flaws with the fighting system as you relive, and fix, the Dragonball timeline. If you're a serious fighting game fan, you still may enjoy the customization aspect, but the simplicity of the fighting system may be a turnoff. I'm in the first group, so I very much enjoyed it.

"Swordtales’ Toren is an imaginative, abstract adventure game that falls prey to its own poor design choices turning what could have been an excellent, meaningful journey into a slow, repetitive experience."
In Toren you play as Moonchild, a nameless young girl destined to climb the mysterious tower all her life, from cradle to grave. The tower, silent and immovable, is your home, your prison and your destiny. Through ascending the tower, the tree of life begins to grow, as do you, through the trials laid out before you. The premise behind Toren is fantastic and its story laden with philosophy and meaning but sadly, fails in the execution of these concepts. I often felt as though the game was telling me too much rather than leaving me to infer meaning from the environment and gameplay. Instead of an experience where you slowly learn the truth yourself by looking around and piecing together the story, you are outright told what’s happening, albeit in a vague, abstract manner. The result being that nothing in the game is a surprise – there are no revelations and the story ends all too quickly. You aren’t left pondering the meaning of the tale because aside from what the game gives you, there’s nothing left to find or interpret. There are some solid concepts on display here, but they are conveyed in a largely linear and boring manner.
Repetition is a consistent theme within Toren, as moonchild is trapped in an endless cycle of death and rebirth, sadly this motif also extends into the gameplay which is largely repetitive and dull. The game contains two major concepts which are recycled constantly – standing behind objects so that you won’t be blown away by strong winds, and tracing shapes with salt, and yes, both of them are about as exciting as they sound. As sad as it may seem, these really are the two main things you’ll be doing in Toren aside from, of course, walking and climbing. There is incredibly little  by way of exploration with only a small handful of trinkets to obtain, while the environments remain sparse, linear and void of interaction.
Not far into her ascent, Moonchild will acquire a sword allowing her to fend off enemies (of which there are only two types, including the final boss). The sword swinging animation is clunky and unsatisfying – moreover enemies can be defeated just by spamming  attack when they jump at you or simply avoided altogether. Platforming is equally unimpressive; seldom requiring any kind of timing or precision, most jumps complete themselves, dragging Moonchild into the correct spot. The fixed perspective camera angles also do little to assist in navigation, often making a short hop resemble a wide gap, and vice versa. The jumping animation itself is slow and floaty with no weight behind it. One nice little nuance is the way moonchild stumbles after jumping – it adds nothing to the gameplay but is an obvious nod to the movement in Ico, which I can appreciate. When examined as a whole, not one element of Toren’s gameplay shines through and the few “puzzles” (and I use the term loosely) that are present fail to be anything more than an inconvenience.
But it is perhaps the less tangible gameplay experiences that makes Toren somewhat endearing. Throughout the game you will enter various dream-like states, each representing an aspect of humanity and manifesting itself accordingly from an underwater abyss to a fiery temple. Visiting these planes is arguably one of the better parts of the game; their environments are unique and varied and help to reinforce the game’s message. Sadly, they don’t bring with them much actual gameplay – these areas seemed like the perfect chance to mix in some new challenging elements and while each one does provide a slightly different slant on the gameplay, they are short lived and lacking in any real challenge or depth.
Toren’s obvious strong suit is its game world – artistically and musically, the game is certainly appealing and may even be worth playing for them alone. Toren isn’t going to win any awards for its graphical fidelity – many textures and animations look pretty poor, but the art style is enough to carry the game despite these flaws. The game draws upon a number of philosophical and mystical concepts in its inspiration but most notably Norse mythology: the Tree of Life (Ygdrassil), The Jormungard motif of endless rebirth, and Toren itself being the Dutch word for tower – nothing is without reason. This theme is pretty consistent and fits the mood of the game’s soundtrack which is suitably sombre and reflective. Sadly, while the original scores for Toren are well composed, the game’s sound design is notably sub-par, doing little to achieve any sense of immersion in the atmosphere as well as multiple actions and events making no sound at all.
There’s not a whole lot more to say about Toren without ruining what little story there is and without highlighting particular instances where the game could be improved – it is what it is – a poor game bundled up in a unique piece of art. Critically, Toren doesn’t know what kind of game it is, it dabbles with a number of mechanics and falls short of the mark at every point, the result is a brief, dull, repetitive experience. And so, a warning – while I am recommending this game I need to make the following things clear. Firstly, do not purchase this game at full price, wait for a sale and grab it cheap, the length and breadth of this game do not warrant the initial price point, modest as it may be. Don’t go into this game expecting the next Ico, any similarities it bears to the PS2 classic are purely superficial, that being said, if you enjoy atmpspheric, abstract stories, Toren may be of some appeal. For an indie studio’s first outing, Toren is a mixed blessing, while it pales mechanically to its forebears, the world, story and art of Toren are unquestionably impressive. Swordtales deserves credit for that at the very least, and hopefully, their next project will address the issues present in this one.

The really pretty art style (marred by the awkward animations) and the ico-esque atmosphere more than make up for the shortcomings of the game... if it is on sale. $10.00 is asking a lot for most people when the game is this barebones and at most 2 hours long.
If you enjoy Team Ico style games then you'll definitely enjoy this, but if you're looking for good puzzles or gameplay elements look elsewhere. While not bad this game could be a lot better with a gameplay overhaul.

It's not really a game as much as it is a 3-d, somewhat interactive storybook with better graphics than you usually get for those. Someone in a video I saw compared it to Ori and the Blind Forest--don't go into it with that idea.
A lot of the scenes and transitions between when you can do something and when you can't are slow, even painfully drawn out. The combat is limited, and fights against the boss--while not quite like anything I've seen before and while they introduce an element of teamwork with the AI--are repetitive and more about solving puzzles and waiting between boss attacks, so I found them boring overall. There is some reading, although not as much as other story games. Considering how crappy a lot of storybook games are with their paragraphs of reading before you can do anything and find an object 2D styles, it is very good graphically and thought out. A few minor glitches here and there, but for the most part, sound bug-wise. Oh, the credits don't let you skip and just when they seem like they will end, more come; I'd recommend just cutting the game at that point unless you enjoy final cut-scenes. t's also relatively short. I think someone not out to explore despite the game's linear nature could finish it in a few hours.
I guess if you're into story games or you're 10 and enjoy pouring sand in shapes in a game, it's fine, but it moved too slowly for me, so I felt bored a lot of the time. I wouldn't recommend it to any of my friends, who prefer more combat-style games.

EVE Online is definately not for the faint hearted. The game has a very steep learning curve and a very unforgiving community, but where there is challenge comes great reward if you stick around long enough to learn how to play properly and turn a profit.
Essential Info about the game:
* EVE has no levels or classes. All skills are trained in real time even when you are offline.
* Two free expansions a year
* Once you start earning enough in game cash you wont ever have to pay a subscription fee again.
Gameplay wise the game plays more like Knights of the Old Republic in terms of combat to compare it to anything else. The ship movement is not like Freelancer or Elite, and combat can sometimes be slow paced. Community wise it has both it's ups and downs, there are always organisations and groups to help you out and get you started on the right path. The game features an extensive API that is integrated with dozens of addons and tools accross the web from tracking your in game mail and skills offline, to monitoring star system activity.
The downsides to EVE against over MMOs is that it can be overwhelming. Corporations (clans) have many confusing aspects to them from tax rates to seperate divisions along with titles and roles. The UI is hardly friendly to begin with and requires players to set it up to be their own and how they can use it best. Unlike other MMOs death is a setback and punishment, if your ship gets totaled then you lose all of your equipment and modules on it, if you die then you lose implants and need to buy them again.
The community can sometimes be visceral and real, many players take the game very seriously and do not mess around, but the more casual gamers can be found at it's core. EVE allows for nearly any type of gameplay, from being a lawless outlaw and killing anyone you see, to running a massive corporate alliance manufacturing weapons and starting wars between players.
EVE Online is tied into two other games, those are Dust 514 and EVE Valkyrie (Valkyrie still in development). Actions taken in Dust effect EVE, they share a market and a currency, and battles on planets in Dust are happening real time in EVE. If a player in dust calls in an orbital bombardment then there is a player in EVE online piloting the battleship that carries out that bombardment.
It is a game people should always try once and give it a go, many people who dislike it do not give it enough time and over my years of playing it the game has improved considerably and with the Rubicon expansion, is beginning to change forever.

This game is like a bag of potato chips. You sit down and open it, intending to just engage a little bit, and before you know it it's six hours later and you're covered in salt, grease, and tears.
Hero Siege is essentially Diablo re-imagined as a bullet hell game. You select from a large number of different characters, each with their own unique tree of skills. You're then dropped into a field filled with obstacles, traps, and pre-placed monster lairs. Foes pour in from the four cardinal directions; defeat four waves of them and you'll face a miniboss. Every five fields, the miniboss is replaced by a large boss.
An amazing amount of things in this game are procedurally generated. Monster leaders, minibosses, and even bosses can randomly receive adjectives on their names that grant them special abilities. You counter with relics, magical items with a variety of bizarre effects -- summoning familiars, creating hazards, offering special attacks and defenses, adding new effects to your existing attacks, or just increasing your stats.
Make no mistake: this game is really random. Skill is a primary factor, but a bad selection of relics or a particularly useful adjective on the wrong monster can spell doom. Fortunately, unlike most roguelikes you are able to keep your cash, levels, and equipment after dying; only your relics and progress disappear.
There are a few negatives.
First, some of the graphic effects make it hard to see what you're doing; "misty" and "Satanic" in particular get in the way a little bit more than they were probably intended to.
Second, the randomization can sometimes get out of hand -- it's possible for one of the optional dungeon sidequests to be generated with wildly inappropriate opponents, leaving you with no way out but through.
Third, the game is a bit on the easy side. It takes a while to build up a powerful character, but a few lucky equipment drops can give you a huge boost. Completing Normal mode is difficult; from that point on, though, your power increases just as fast as your foes' power does. I'm partway through the fourth difficulty level out of five, and haven't felt at all intimidated since Normal difficulty.
Still, forty or so hours' entertainment for the price is pretty spectacular, and this game is definitely worth a look. (It's also a pretty ideal game to play while watching TV in another window.)

Here is a game that has great promise and if any other publisher was involved, would probably be one of the top games in it's genre.  Unfortunately, the developers use broken game systems and everything is pushed toward spending real money for a "free game".
In its current state, the game is so broken as to be totally unplayable.  There is a huge variety of weapons to chose from and the sheer number of designs is about the only positive thing I can say about this game.  You design your own vehicle from available parts, each part having an inherent power-score and stats.  At a powerscore of 2500 or less, the game is totally dominated by what is called "open-frame" builds.  These  are raft-like  designs using nothing but framing, wheels,  cabin and a weapon.  The frames contribute to the vehicle's health and, as a result, these builds easily exceed 1200 points at a level where a "normal" build will have 400-500.
In addition to the open-frame design, the players have found that the "best" machine-gun in the game is the Caucasus, an auto-turret, controlled by the AI, with now 300 health.  But you'll find these frame builds using two of these guns and in my last and final battle, one of these designs destroyed 6 of the 7 vehicles on my team.  Other possible choices are multiple drones which hit harder than your normal weapons, or multiple cannons, which can more or less one-shot your 350-health build.
Matchmaking does not take into account the quality of the weapons used in the match.  If you can fit a "legendary" weapon on a 2500 power-score vehicle, then you're in the match with other low power-score players.  Which encourages  new players to spend real money in order to buy their own legendaries in order to compete.
Another factor is player level.  Leveling is not the same as in other MMORPG's.  You level with one of the 4 "factions" in the game (a 5th faction is planned) in order to acquire better parts for your vehicles and to have access to build better weapons.  One of these factions, Steppenwolf, has what would be the equivalent of modern armor parts.  So there you are with your brand-new 1800 powerscore car, got yourself 3 machine guns on it...and you run into one of the high-level players with his 1800 powerscore car with upgraded parts and you get decimated, because he has 3 times your health and his parts can take twice as much damage as yours before being destroyed.
I know this sounds like whining.  Fine, perhaps it is.  But the game quickly became "not-fun".  Between the other players who appear to deliberately interfere with your combat, to the open-frame builds, to other similar in-balance, this is easily the most frustrating example of a first-person shooter I've seen in a very long time.  Totally not worth the aggravation.

I will rate this game based on the following things:
Content
Mechanics
Art/Graphics
Music/Sound
Story
Content - 7/10
The story can be completed in as little as a few hours and there isn't much replayability. There is a simple level editor, but it was difficult to share levels until Steam Workshop support came out. Even then, a lot of players (myself included) cannot even play the game with the newest patch.
Mechanics - 10/10
The main mechanic, the Crosslink, allows you to rewire electronics and it is just a fantastic concept. It creates fun puzzles and constantly adds new devices to rewire. You can also by upgrades, like being able to rewire guns or boobytrap electronics, which adds a lot more fun. The whole way you play as a spy, climbing on walls and hanging from ceilings, works well and the game would not be the same without it.
Art/Graphics - 10/10
The style of the art fits the theme of the game very well in my opinion. The animations are great and the background city landscapes match the tone of the game fantasically. The only problem is that characters can be floating mostly in mid-air when they are unconscious on the ground, but this doesn't happen constantly and can be overlooked most of the time.
Music/Sound - 10/10
There isn't much to say about the sound except that it's present, which makes the game better than if it didn't have any sound, but the music is what is beautiful. The jazzy sort of songs make the game feel very alive and fits the tone of the game so well. There are many tracks, so it doesn't get repetitive and most of the songs are kind of catchy, anyway.
Story - 8/10
The story is very linear for a freelance spy, as you are involved in an ongoing murder plot throughout the whole game. The story is very basic, but well written except in a few places where it just seems uninteresting (to me at least). There are also no major plot holes, as far as I can see.
Total - 90/100

There's some nice humour in this interactive movie. Some great humour! It's not often you burst into fits of laughter. You've made a new friend! Eww gross is that a face?
The music is top notch.
The cinematics are varied, interesting and for the most part are seamless.
The voice acting is superb, and feels like they fit right in to the PAndora/Borderlands world.
You care about the characters - and they are all very individual.
You may shed a tear. You may squee.
If anything the 1st/2nd eps are a little slow to begin with, and aren't without their flaws, but if you can get through those the pay offs in terms of the story and pure entertainment are huge.  This might be one of my favourite casual games because of the way the stories were weaved in.
Episode 4 was an absolute treat from beginnning to end.
Episode 5 was an amazing finale, and well worth the 10 hours it took to get there.  It's rare I catch myself smiling through a game, but I definitely did it in this one.  I never knew a Quick Time Event  could be that much fun!
Negatives (minor):
Using voice actors who sound remarkably similar to other iconic characters usually doesn't work well
(e.g. one of the main protagonists sounds like Lilith from the Borderlands series).
Where's the skip dialogue button?
The first 5 minutes made me want to uninstall.  That's not a good way to start.
The main antagonist, in my opinion, was made too hateable and unredeemable in the first 2 minutes.
This is on my "Highly recommended" list for seasoned hardcore gamers and casuals alike. Enjoy!

This is not for the faint hearted..  SQUAD is modern warfare.
SQUAD is sitting in a Forward Operating Base, you just built,mortars raining down, being yeld at to get moving, while APCs push in from the west, unleashing a firey hell on your postion.
SQUAD is getting shot at while sitting shotgun in a truck full of supplies, Driver asking you, 'is it the next right or one after it?', trying to find yourself on the map, cause the Corporal is chewing you out for going at 'Granny Speed'.

I downloaded this for the free weekend and will be buying it momentarily, but i wanted to mention a few things for new players. First, the "minimum requirements" are a little high. What i mean by this is, my computer shoulod not be able to run this game, but it does, albiet on low settings, but i get a consistent 50-80fps in almost every map/situation (with a few settings at medium) and i run a xeon quad core (with hyperthreading, but from 2009. comparable to a 1st gen i7) and a gtx 950, 10gb 1066 ram, and sata 1 hard drives. you won't really need a computing powerhouse to enjoy the game.
Second, the gameplay and your enjoyment depends pretty heavily on your squad leader. Having a leader that has played the role before and knows what he/she is doing makes an enormous difference in your success as well as your fun. This is a given, since teamwork and coordination is the primary premise of the game, but it stood out to me a lot in the last couple days playing.
Learning curve as a normal player isn't too bad, there is a lot of stuff to keep track of in the begining but once you get the basics, the rest comes fairly easily.
Gameplay can vary between being constantly in the front line fighting for those adrenaline junkies and sitting at a FOB waiting around while the rest of the map is lit up constantly. But, a lazy guard position can easily turn into a hectic, massive battle, complete with artilery strikes and armor very quickly.
all in all, worth the purchase.

A game that shouldn't be good, but is.
First, some basic points:
Graphics:  Very poor.  The best that can be said about them is that they are functional.  In fact, they would be considered poor in the days of 8-bit computing.  Developers seem to compete to see who can produce the worst graphics in this genre so I'm not surprised.  But I am disappointed.
Sound: Atrocious.  The worst soundtrack I've ever heard.  Instead of going for an ambient, mood-enhancing backing sound, we have repetitive made-for-tv quality tripe.  Apparently you can buy the soundtrack seperately. "Expect plenty of copies to be available," as the saying goes.
Theme: wild-west meets sci-fi, supposedly.  It bombed for the excellent Firefly (leading to its cancellation in season one), and Cowboys and Aliens was a dreadful movie.  Yet, for some reason, the theme of cowboys in space gets revived time and again despite being proven many times to be a bad idea.  What's really strange is that the pioneering West was driven by trade, capitalism and greed - whereas Rimword is arguably more Communist than Capitalist.  An odd, bad choice of theme.
Gameplay: Gnomoria-style.
Everything I've listed makes it look like an unexceptional game and first impressions are not good.  But if you turn the music off it suddenly gets a whole lot better.  The top down approach is far better than the isometry of Gnomoria, and the awful graphics do at least allow you to grasp quickly what is happening.
The gameplay has a moreish quality to it, like Gnomoria, but the graphics are easier on the eye and clearly the developers have learned a lot from similar games that have come before.  The GUI is exceptionally streamlined, tricky things like roofing are cleverly handled, and the options for creating a challenge are varied and work well.  Also, there is no tunnelling, with exploration going 'wide' across the planet, not underground.  This makes keeping track of things much easier.
In short, it gets more things right than wrong.  The sound may be unforgiveably bad, but there is the option to turn the music off.    Use that option.  You won't regret it.  You can't do much about the cowboy theme, but the good news is that (other than Cowboy hats) the theme is underused.  If you just think of them as regular colonists and not cowboys'n'cowgirls you'll enjoy the game much more.
I like it.  Overpriced and over-hyped, perhaps, but undeniably a good game.

Hello folks!
So, you might be wondering about buying Toren but you are kind of skeptical about doing so. Well, allow me to give you my feelings on the game to possibly help you in your decision.
I have 2.3 hours on Toren, and I'd say about 30-45min of that is because of silly mistakes I made. This brings the total time it took me to actually "beat" the game and solve the puzzles it had to a bit less than 2 hours. If you are looking for a long game, this isn't for you.
However, if you can get past the short length you'll be met with unique graphics, that I personally enjoy. But, there are plenty of graphical issues like clipping textures, being able to see the ground under a texture because it doesn't conform to the terrain, and your character's dress ocassionally going through your legs. So it is by no means perfect.
The story is most all text based and the voices are in a made-up language (i'm pretty sure). The story is somewhat interesting, but it isn't anything majorly exciting or engaging really.
Since it is an adventure game, we gotta talk about the combat. Or actually the lack there of. For the most part, you only have 3 main battles. The other monsters, which i would compare to Facehuggers from Alien die in one hit, but can also be easily avoided. You also might have to swing at a passive deer or two. The combat is just pressing the same button, so it isn't anything special.
The other MAJOR part of the game is the puzzles. Most of the game is puzzles, to be honest. How to find a path to climb the tower basically. There is a decent variety of puzzles though, which is fairly great and nothing is too challanging that it will make you quit, but not easy enough that you can get them all on the first try.
The last thing I have to mention is the concept. A girl who climbs a tower while aging in the process. It is quite interesting and I would have liked to see it done in a longer game over the course of a longer time. You get basically 4 ages: infant, child, teenager, and adult. The first two go by really fast, however.
I'll go ahead and sum things up with some pros/cons.
On a scale of 1-10, I'd give it a 6/10. I would love to rate it higher, but the combat wasn't the best, when there was any and there were many noticable graphic glitches.

Once you obtain a certain combination of weapon and shield mods, the combat becomes alot easier (almost too overpower). There are many side missions and DLCs for a change of pace. But you are better off to just proceed to Borderlands 2. Overall: 8/10

Crossout is a build-your-own-car-and-then-blow-up-other-cars game, kinda similar to Robocraft. Where in Robocraft you build from blocks (where you then lose to the exact same meta defining bots every game), Crossout has you build a vehicle that looks straight out of Mad Max to...lose to the exact same meta defining cars every game.
I hate that I have to put a thumbs-down, as I feel the game has a ton of potential and is still in Beta. However, after spending a decent amount of time on it, I don't know if it's something I can recommend at the current time.
Graphically, the game looks good. The enviroments have a good amount of detail and the cars blow up nice and good. Performance runs fine on my rig, never encountered any framerate issues.
Sound wise, music fits the theme but isn't anything special. Guns sound great, and there's a lot of explosions. One thing I'm not a fan of is that the explosions near you mute your sound (shellshocked and all) for a few moments, and that happens a lot. Outside of that, sound is fine.
It's easy to build a car, and you can come up with some very interesting designs with some clever thinking. Cars require a frame, cabin, and wheels. Then you use a set of specific parts such as walls, doors, and roofs to customize and armor your vehicle. Then, finally, you strap on the guns and other support parts. Support parts range from radars to rocket thrusters.
You have a limited amount of Energy to equip things like guns and support parts on your car, and that is the big limiting factor on keeping the power of your car in check. At the end, your car is judged on it's "Power Level", which is used for matchmaking.
The game will give you basic parts just for playing, but beyond that, you have to craft, or buy the parts you want. Crafting is the usual grindy affair it ususally is in most games, and you have to wait for a specific time before the part is available to you. Depending on the quality of the part, this can take a day. That's, of course, after you purchase a workbench for Credits (premium currency) which can only craft a limited amount of parts for you depending on how many credits you spent, and--There's almost no reason to craft anything.
Crafting is made more complicated as you are restricted to one of four factions, each of which have their own unique craftable parts. One faction you're always a part of, the Engineers, sell some useful items but you'd have to balance between leveling all these factions to get all the parts to craft.
Or, sell all those resources you gather such as Scrap and Fuel, and directly purchase the parts from the Market. It's instant, doesn't require any materials outside of cash, and you can get any part in the game this way. When I switched to this method, I found it a lot easier to get better gear for my car without having to spend real money...Which is of course an option when it comes to Credits.
Early game, I found myself having a great rip-roarin' time tearing through the wastelands and blowing things up. However, when I got to 3000-4000 Power Level after buying parts from the Market, things change. Seems that I'm always up against enemies with multiple drones. Drones are, as of this moment, the most broken weapon in the game.
These drones will automatically attack enemies for you for pretty heavy damage, given what they are, and you are given multiple on a short cooldown. You can shoot the drones down, but that takes quite some time. Some weapon types really struggle with shooting down drones as well, such as shotguns and missiles.
You can equip a lot of drones at once: Seeing an army of 3-4 drones surrounding you just from one car is not uncommon, and that's only one: Multiple cars can have drones and have them basically play the game for them.
I tried many other weapon types to deal with this, and there is a good variety, but at the end of the day, drones seemed like the way to go. If you can't beat 'em, join 'em. The autoaiming terrors dominate the battlefield. Just get a heavily armored car with 2/3 of these things and just casually drive in circles as they mow down foes.
The game is in beta, and there's a lot of time for improvements to be made (as well as much needed balancing changes). I will happily re-do this review at a later time once changes are made. At the current time, however, I think it's more fitting that the game is titled, "Drones Out" due to the prevalence of the effin' things.
Still, keep an eye on this game, as it leaves beta maybe a lot of things will change!

all in all, worth the purchase.

So. After a while I decided to give this game yet another shot. The last time, my review was not that kind and it was a downvote. You can clearly see that this it is not a downvote this time.
However some points still stand. If not all. Seeing as I deleted my old review without thinking much about the content of the review and saving it I will simply say what I still think is a bad influence when it goes to playing the game.
Overall the idea of the game is simple: Survive. You can choose different characters which have different attacks and skills. Some are ranged, some are close combat. And from here it goes directly into the first part of the game. You play on a randomly generated(?) field where there are 4 gates, 1 on every side of the field. The monsters move mainly into the field through the gates and it is up to you to defeat them. Sometimes, you can even find Monsterspawners which will spawn Monsters until you destroy them. Over time, and by random chance, mini dungeons can spawn or you can enter shops. The Minidungeons are varied and contain a good amound of stuff that keeps you on your toes. Some stuff can only be reached by walking through spikes that hurt you and on a low level that will kill you pretty fast. But this, walking through spikes to reach what you want, is optional. Because most of the time the dungeons themself have a beginning and end point. Everything in between is either optional or required to move further into the dungeon. And when you reached it one out of two things will wait for you. A miniboss, with the reward when you defeated him, or a direct reward for reaching the end of the dungeon.
And what happens when you leave the dungeon? The game continues on the field as if nothing ever happened. Go and survive until you reach the sixth wave. Because on the sixth wave, your spawnpoint will spawn a servant of Hell (as I like to call it) that tries its best to kill you. But dont worry. Most of the bosses can actually be defeated easily when you are standing next to the spawnpoint when he spawns. Put one of your abilities down, wait for it and he is defeated. Or you can do it the hard way and maybe get killed the first times you play it with a new character. And if you killed this boss you get rewarded with a special item and a portal to the next field.
But before I forget to mention it, there is also another thing that happens. Item drops. And I waited until now to mention the reward for killing bosses or clearing dungeons. During your gameplay you will be able to collect items. These items can be special items from bosskills or dungeons or regular Armor to stuff out your character. While I dont see a big difference with armor I can see it with the special items. They give you abilities or just enhance your current stats. Like a Burger that gives you 7k health. Pretty good if you are struggling with the monsters. Or you get the Shiv, which is a active Item that shoots out Daggers(?) and damages enemies in their way. So it is similar to Binding of Isaac. And yes I am making this comparison for a reason, because this game reminds me of Binding of Isaac atleast in terms of Special Items and what they can do for your character.
But now we have reached the point of where my old review comes into play. My old review was about this game being bad, a game that I wouldnt recommend at all. While I still stick with, "I dont really like it that much", I cannot truly say that this game is bad. It may, or may not be enjoyable and for what you get, there is a lot to do. But now lets head on to what I have said before and what is still a problem for me in the game.
1. First Timers Death
The first time you will play this game, and that means that you have never played it before, you will die fairly quickly. Even going back in you will die fairly quickly again. Of course this has to do with figuring out how to play mostly but some of it doesnt. For a person that never played this i was a bit frustrated at first because of the sudden deaths of mine. Mind you that was in an earlier version of the game but it hasnt changed. The game is difficult, which is good and bad at the same time.
2. Difficulty = Hitbox
When playing this game, the hitboxes of Monsters, and yourself seems off. I am saying this because a Skeleton or Rat have hit me when I was 10 pixels away from them. And this varies. Mostly downwards, yet it happens. I have died multiple times to a skeleton hitting me while it was not even able to reach me. And that is a problem. A problem I am sure they will take care of.
3. Difficulty = random
The game is difficult on its own, but it also is spawning in various traps and objects over time. I have noticed many times as to how new traps like Autocrossbows fell from the heavens down on the field. And if you dont pay attention because "THERE IS LIKE 50 OF THEM! WAAAH!" it can end up killing you.
4. Difficulty = "Watch out"
Every enemy in the game, if big or tiny, if boss or elite can be killed fairly quickly. But as mentioned above, if you are a first timer you will die fairly quickly. Especially when reaching the second field. One of the enemies is a maggot that spits acid and you and damn, if it does not hit you and gets stuck on the floor for about 5 seconds. Dont walk on it or you take a ton of damage. The problem with this is that it caused me to die also a few times because I was focusing on the enemies upfront. Like the 50 enemies I mentioned above. A random maggot spits, or an elite makes a round house spit and you can get dunked on pretty fast.
The other points, one being "DLC for Online Multiplayer" have been resolved. It was meant to be tested but they wanted to give people the chance to use it anyways, even in the most unstable build. You could say that it isnt worth for a DLC but, eh. It was their decision, and not mine.
So far the game is ok. Its not good, it is not bad and it most certainly not a personal favorite or the best game I ever played. Undertale got that spot. No other game gets that. But jokes aside it wouldnt even be a close second. My point is: I dont like this game. However it is a game that people atleast have put effort into and a game that is decent enough to be played. And who knows: Maybe most of the mentioned points above are just me being an idiot ingame.
But that is about it. Thanks for reading.

Tell Tale games have done it again! This is the third (not counting TWD as two) of thier games I've played, the others being The Walking Dead 1 and 2 and Wolf Among Us. This one is based in the Borderlands world and it's great to be able to play the story in familiar places (more so from BL2 though). There are also old faces in there to chat with including Zero and Athena but the story is mainly based around 2 people, with two extra sidekicks along for the ride.
I'm not going to go too much into the story but a quick run over is that you are two, low level people in the world of Borderlands, trying to get out of the rut they're in by any means. He works for Hyperion and is sick of being stood on, she is a con artist, ready to fool anyone of their money. They meet up when a deal goes wrong and the story goes on from there.
The game is more of an interactive TV program than a full on action game. You watch the story, making choices about what's said and things they do with everything you do and say having a knock on effect at some point. It's not as cruel as The Walking Dead though, that would kill off people if you farted in the wrong direction. Every-so-often you'll take part in QuickTime events, where you'll have to press the right key, or mouse button in time to perform an action. if you get it wrong, it can change the whole story, or you'll die and be able to get another crack.
The writing is amazing, I would truly watch this is it was on TV. It's funny, sad, action packed and emotional with some great music and songs thrown in for good measure. The voice acting to makes it that extra bit special with every one of those involved being bang on the mark

I played this on a free weekend.
Even though I am giving this game a thumbs-down, I did enjoy playing it. The gameplay, at its core, is a fairly exciting party brawler (think casual Smash Bros.), with a good balance between close and ranged combat. Were it cheaper or free-to-play, I could very well see myself sinking a few more hours into it.
The graphics and music are excellent for an indie game.
The controls are good; although you have a lot of momentum and rolling going on, you have a lot of control too.
The characters ("forms") are rightfully goofy-looking for a goofy game.
You earn points for doing just about anything, including destroying random objects. Kills give the most points, but you can make up some difference with other methods.
But it has a laundry list of small problems, which I will now recite.
1. Look at SteamDB. There are sometimes zero people playing this online. Not good for a multiplayer game.
2. Soccer is a wasted game mode right now. Jumping with the ball makes you very difficult to hit. Not impossible, but difficult. The lack of ammo makes this the most powerful strategy.
3. Deathmatch has all the classic problems, like killstealing being the predominant strategy. Some of the powerups are extremely strong, even to the degree of one-shot kills. I'm not against it, per se, but it means the best killstealer and powerup-grabber wins over someone with good accuracy.
4. Low level players are very easy to defeat because you can pick them up and throw them off the edge for an instant kill; if you do it right, it's near impossible for a novice to escape. High level players remain very mobile, resulting in a lot of flying around and very little actual contact (except for shots with intent to killsteal, and powerups).
5. The only penalties for suicides are a little lost time and resetting any killstreak bonus. This is ripe for abuse, especially in 1 on 1 games. Anytime you get to red health with no healing around, just jump off the edge.
6. The three-round structure of deathmatch games doesn't really make much sense. There's this big pause every 2 minutes so you can select another character (which has zero gameplay impact) and class. Your score remains the same, so it's not "best 2 out of 3". Whoever's winning at the end of a round is still winning at the start of the next one.
7. Matchmaking is entirely random. High level players get put up against newbies with no thought given toward balance.
8. There is no mode for competitive play. There should be a 1 on 1 no-powerups mode, but there's not. Every game is a party.
9. The skill ceiling seems pretty low. I'm sure someone who's played 200 hours will win more than someone who's played 20, but there are only so many ways you can ram, shoot, and maneuver.
10. Lastly, a $30 price point plus microtransactions is very greedy for a game with three modes (near-identical deathmatch and team deathmatch, and the soccer I already mentioned). There are 5 classes, but they have the same moves (ram, shoot, throw, block). None of the characters or wearables have any impact on performance. It's like playing Smash Bros. where the only character is Fox McCloud.
Er, well... You know what I mean.

First things first: what this game is not.
It's not a shooter. While the Borderlands franchise is most well known for shooting things (and lots of guns) this is what I'd call a visual novel with don't-die quick time events. It's also not a choose-your-own adventure. While there are choices to be made in game they mostly change character motivations rather than the story as such. Whether this makes them important hinges on the characters being interesting and engaging. Which I'd say they are. But as I've stated before I may be biased.
Now on to what this game is.
It's a different view on the Borderlands universe. This time from the perspective of more of an ordinary Joe, trying to make it big (or just survive) in this dangerous world. Which is a nice turn from the main games, as now you can spend more time getting to know the world and people in it rather than getting to blow it all up. As is Borderlands tradition there is humor (although the Borderlands kind) and great choice of music.
TL;DR
- not much shooting
- much talking
- some clicking
- awesome music
- more Borderlands lore
- fun

My overall rating for Toren: 88/100
Clearly amazing game from an inpedendent studio. Swordtales proved us, that even with a low budget, the story can be narrated with lovely elements, tension and epic finale. Another great thing from Brazil! Let's see in a detail this lovely title, which tells us about pride of humanity, punishment for their crimes and a hope hidden within a girl's heart.
GAMEPLAY
+ Greatly designed platforms
+ Reasonably challenging puzzles
+ Lovely story
+ Lyrical symbols
+ Mystic, religion,
+ Meditiations
o Controller is an advantage
- Few texture glitches
It can be suggestive, that the main goal is to climb upstairs, but there is more in this. Whole story is a parallel to various legends, e. g. The Tower of Babylon, so on the route to release the moonlight and defeat an ancient enemy in form of a dragon, player have to encounter various pozzles, reveal hidden aspects from the story and find out ugly truth full of despair and hope. Puzzles are reasonably tough, they require a little of wits to solve them. Beautiful lyrical ending.
I encountered few texture glitches, what is not a big deal. In addition, you can play it on a keyboard, contoller is a bit of advantage, but not necessary.
VISUALS
+ Reasonably to ist price
- Some texture were not purely rendered
Visuals are as you can expect from game like this, with a specified budget. Lovely to eye, but some textures would need another rendering and polishing. So far, so good.
CHARACTERS
+ Fully used potentials
o Invincible dragon
Basicly, there are three characters to mention here. A girl,  for all of humanity, mage, knight. All of them have their vices and virtues, the second and the third are not playable, but equally important. They will tell us about tragic and failure of our predecessors.
I understand, that dragon must last until the end. and it has its meaning, but it might appear a bit frustrating to player, that it survived several mortal wounds.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Adequately designed
+ Lyrical tones
+ Great credits song
Vinicius Kleinsorgen is another composer I started to watch. After this game, filled with sensible, soft music and great credits song, there is nothing that can be complained about. Mariana Coelho did a great performance during the credits song, whatever player seeks, joy, despair, fight or victory, can be found there.
SUMMARY
I can not understand 58/100 from the Metascore. I admit, that this game requires a specific player to enjoy it, but it can tell something even to players out of the genre and I think, that it deserves twenty more points at minimum.
I can recommend it, it is short, yet tells more story than some of hard RPGs. And that is worth a shot.

As an old MMO player of DAoC, WoW and UO, testing a game like EVE Online was a rather huge step for me, however I quickly learned that EVE is nothing like I expected.
The game is completely controlled by players in every aspect. Everyone is playing on one major server and even though that might seem like it's insane, there are times where you will find yourself all alone in the universe.
You start as a new pilot with an endless list of things you can do in the world, you can become a miner, a pirate, a warrior, a corp leader and many more.
You can make yourself the richest in the game or just feel like destroying other people to annoy them and steal their cargo. You can build the largest corp or have a group of friends just mining and having fun.
Everything is your choice, there is something to do for everyone.
EVE is not like other MMO´s where you can just log in and play for 10-15 mins and log out, EVE takes a lot of dedication and time to master, the largest ship possible to fly takes 2 years in real time to just be able to fly and even longer to be able to use all its functions. Although your skills train even when you´re offline, if you want to be the best and the most powerful get ready to spend a lot of time in this game.
All in all a great game and a great MMO that stands out, don´t let the monthly fee scare you away from trying as you can use in game money to buy monthly game time if you are rich enough, this won't happen after a month or two, but I did make it happen after my 3rd month and never paid since with Real Life money.

This game is one of the best that I have ever played. It can be a real challenge, but it is always very fun. It is a constant struggle to survive, and manage food and resources, and the game gets progressively harder as your colony gets better, so it hardly ever gets to the point where your base is overpowered and nothing is a threat any more.
Even if the base game gets boring, or if you feel that it lacks in depth, Rimworld can be very easily modded, and the majority of mods out there are very well made, and fit in with the base game without unbalancing it, or feeling unnatural. The majority of Rimworld mods add or tweak small things, for example, one makes it so you can make prosthetics, rather than having to buy them from traders, and another adds a recipie for neurotramine. There are a lot of mods that tweak small things, or add things. So if there is something you dont like about the base game, or feel is unbalanced, you can easily mod it out.
Each playthrough is different and memorable: you have different colonists, all with different skills, traits, and backstories; Different events such as raids or toxic fallouts, or cold snaps effect each playthrough in a different way, and make it so that every playthrough has memorable stories. You can see what I mean by scrolling through the reveiws.
Don't let the fact that it is early acess put you off, as the game feels very polished, and is virtually glitch free.

Was hoping for a good platformer with some difficulty that rewards good platforming ability, with good levels, mechanics, etc, but this game was anything but that. This game is "difficult". But its one of those games thats hard for all the wrong reasons. I almost never felt death was my fault, and that is because it was usually due to poor game design decisions. First off, there are checkpoints, but there aren't enough. You will go through multiple really tough parts, and where a good game would reward you with checkpoints along the way, this game makes you repeat those sections if you die due to lack of checkpoints. This also doesn't help due to the tons of single pixel platforms and auto jumpers, usually stacked in a row, where if you aren't perfect you die. The platforming is decent, but you fall too fast and don't have enough control ability in the air. The game could have really used a double jump.
The music and visuals are pretty cool. The level design is horrible. First off, this game the level moves to the side or up at a predetermined fast pace, which makes it act like a runner or speedrun game, which is lazy design. You should be able to play a tough game at your own speed, forcing quickrunning through obstacles to increase death and repetition is stupid and unnecessary. In other levels the screen moves way too slow, forcing you to stand around while you get shot at, which once again is stupid for the same reasons above. You can kill enemies and rockets, but for some dumb reason, jumping on them doesn't work. You have to jump above them and then use a slam key to hit down on them. Especially in a game with forced speed running and level moving, this design decision makes no sense and is clunky and slows down the pace. The worst offense and design of the entire game is the missles. A well designed game would find tons of single pixel platforms, or even the forced speed running by level scrolling to be enough, but not for this game. Tons of levels have these homing missiles shot at you as you move across it. They can go through solid objects you can't (strike 1), they continually spawn even if you destroy them (strike 2), they go on forever, and never disappear (strike 3), they are faster then you (strike 4), and they shoot tons at once (strike 5). Its super stupid you can't avoid them to make them disappear or crash into platforms and they just keep coming, and you can't do anything about them besides use bad combat system. Dying to them never feels like it's your fault. Combine that with the decreased or super increased speed of level moving, and the lack of checkpoints, single pixel platforms, and its hard due to poor design for the sake of being "hard". Yes you die a ton so people who play it continuosly repeating the same sections tons of times due to cheap deaths and finally being perfect long enough to beat the level think theyre "hardcore", but who cares what they think. Anyone can make a game hard by poor design, but making a well made game where when you die its your fault, without superficial difficulty designed to force repetition and perfect runs, that is tough. Take a game like Mr. Bree. That was a well made game that is better than this game in every single way, and you should just play instead.
If you want a game where you die a ton due to poor level and game mechanic design, then pick this. If you want a good and fair game that rewards skill and is enjoyable to play and get better at, look the other way.

I have over 100 hours in this game. For starters, I think any game that nets you over 60 hours for 60 euro (AAA titles) is a good deal, because in my experience I can only get 30 hours at the very most from AAA titles. Rimworld is under half that price, and offers a potentially unlimited playing time - because there's one thing Rimwold has that other games don't - replayability.
Every single game will have a diffferent story. Every colony will develop differently. If you find yourself getting bored, all you need to do is up the difficulty to remind you just how flawed your strategy is. Every Alpha update adds a plethora of new content to enjoy, and it's obvious to see that this game is being loved and cherished by the development team.
With a thriving modding community since it's release, and developers who actively encourage them, it's a no-brainer to pick up Rimworld and enjoy it while in it's still in its Alpha, because I can easily see the price rising for full release to €40 euro - it'd be worth every red cent.
