Disclosure: I'm a fan of the Borderlands universe and I've finished Borderlands. Borderlands 2 and Borderlands the Pre-Sequel prior to playing this. I may be biased.
First things first: what this game is not.
It's not a shooter. While the Borderlands franchise is most well known for shooting things (and lots of guns) this is what I'd call a visual novel with don't-die quick time events. It's also not a choose-your-own adventure. While there are choices to be made in game they mostly change character motivations rather than the story as such. Whether this makes them important hinges on the characters being interesting and engaging. Which I'd say they are. But as I've stated before I may be biased.
Now on to what this game is.
It's a different view on the Borderlands universe. This time from the perspective of more of an ordinary Joe, trying to make it big (or just survive) in this dangerous world. Which is a nice turn from the main games, as now you can spend more time getting to know the world and people in it rather than getting to blow it all up. As is Borderlands tradition there is humor (although the Borderlands kind) and great choice of music.
TL;DR
- not much shooting
- much talking
- some clicking
- awesome music
- more Borderlands lore
- fun
Although pretty buggy and kind of annoying when it comes to playing the multiplayer with friends, the game provides a really good time, the multiplayer itself, when it works, is pretty fun.

I had this game on my wishlist for a long time, I missed the previous free weekend but watched videos and learned what I'm supposed to do and how to play before hopping in. Overall though, the game as it is does not feel worth money yet. The free Project Reality mod/game does everything this does and more, just with worse graphics and sound design. The visual aspects are good in Squad, though it's still very buggy. The same could generally be said of Project Reality, but it's free and this costs money. PR has helicopters and planes while this does not. There are also no MBTs in this game while there are in PR.
The vehicle request system is good in theory, but sketchy in execution. It mostly ended up vehicles just weren't used by our squad while others took them and many times drove right into an enemy base getting them blown up. There are more players in Squad (even regularly, looking at steam stats) but far more don't have a clue what they're doing in this game. PR has a smaller community, but they're much more cautious and willing to listen.
I also have utterly no idea how to score points in this game. I followed orders and helped capture points, but I guess I didn't do something very specific required to actually get any points. While it's true they don't really do anything for you, it feels very unrewarding to have few points after all the effort I actually put into my gameplay. As a test I flanked as a scout and picked off several enemy players and that too yielded basically no points. The overall concepts are simple enough, but if it's that hard to figure out what you need to do according to the game to get points it's really not enjoyable.
I would wait for this game to get further developed and see if it ever picks up, as of now I don't recommend it. When a free game is doing what your paid game is trying to do better, you're definitely not ready for prime time.

If you must, buy on sale and save it for a boring evening when you're in a contemplative mood.

I completed this game in one sitting and am left with... very mixed feelings.
The game has several pros. I particularly enjoyed hearing the mythology and symbolism in the game, which was different to what I've come to expect from this kind of fiction. The game had several particularly fascinating narrative moments, with the demonstrations of the Moonchild's reincarnation. The character designs too were innovative. It also goes without saying that the game looked very unique and beautiful. The aging of the character I do not believe was emphasised as much as it could have been which was a shame, but otherwise, this was some fascinating mythology.
However my enjoyment of these elements was dampened by several factors. The game was HIGHLY buggy. There were several moments when my character stopped responding to certain actions, such as jumping, and I had to reset to checkpoint in order to repair the problem. My character fell through the world several times while in the 'dream' sequences, and the environment clipped making specific locations difficult to find. The game instructions were fairly unclear which would have been fine if the aforementioned bugs made me doubt certain game mechanics that were SUPPOSED to happen. The game played very much like a pre Playstation One platformer - complete with sluggish commands and slow response times. Perhaps I was just very unlucky, and these are understandable problems from a newly minted company, but I hope Swordtales improve on these problems in future.
Some of the level designs were inventive (the mirror puzzle, for example), but others were intensely frustrating. I fail to see the appeal of making a player build a pattern of sand in complete darkness, with only occasional glimpses of light to inform their movements.
Overall I would probably give this game a 'no comment' if that were an option in recommendations. As it happens, I would recommend the game to anybody with an interest in atmospheric mythological storytelling and designs, but I would NOT recommend doing so at full price - the game just had too many bugs for me to fully recommend. Not a bad first Effort, Swordtales, but some of the flaws could be fixed, and I hope you listen to input from the players to fix these problems in future.

Where to start. Before I begin this review, let me start of by saying if you don't want to invest then don't play. This game requires an insane amount of dedication if you want to partake in those epic scale battles the game portrays. Up to the challenge? Then read on.
Graphics
EVE Online features a full HD adventure, as you travel around the many solar systems and other places in space. As you play, you'll notice the stunning backgrounds, whcih makes the game much more immersive overall. The only thing missing from this canvas of space? Your ship. Whatever ship you purchase or create will look fantastic wherever you go; if you're worried about how the game looks on an older computer, I myself use a Intel HD3000 Graphics Card on a 1.4Ghz laptop. Game still runs at HD with no lag.
Gameplay
The gameplay in EVE is not for everyone. While you can narrow it down to a  point and click adventure, it gets much more immersive the more you play. As you begin to partake in PVP or AI Battles, you'll start to feel as loose and well tuned the control scheme is. Everyday tasks are no different; you still have the same level of quality whether you're mining an asteroid or cruisin' round the system. With a deep story to boot, you'll either love or hate EVE's gameplay.
Overall
EVE Online is the World of Warcraft of space. while many tout it to be complex (Which it is, but for the sake of this review I've kept it simple), you choose how complex you want it to be. Want to PVP? You can just buy a good ship. Want to go deeper? Outfit it with the best stuff. Deeper? Look at stat bonuses for each item and create the perfect vessel. EVE is your game; you play your way. Everything is up to you, but it's up to you to begin the journey.

Personally I didn't think I'd enjoy the Telltale games as much as I did (I've only played Tales from Borderlands though) but it was a surprizingly good medium for storytelling. It's not so great if you don't have a controller though (Personal opinion) as you'll constantly have to sit with your keyboard and mouse incase something happens and you have to interact.
But wrapped up in a blanket, having it run on the tv with a controler in your hand, just lean back and enjoy the story. You feel like all the conversation options and choices you make actually have an impact on what happens throughout the story. And you get attached to the characters (No matter how annoying they might be) .
But as a game, it's all just quicktime events and conversation options. So you have to keep a bit of an open mind going into it.
Over-all, after finishing the game in about 12 hours (This includes ~2 hour breaks), I really, enjoyed my experience and the story. I got a lot more out of it than I was expecting, and the story made me laugh, smile, annoyed beyond comprehension and had me really depressed in some parts, making me truly regret the choices I made. So yeah, if you want to relax with a good story, I would truly recommend this. If you want to actually play a game, not so much.

Borderlands is a FPS mixed with RPG. It can be played singleplayer, but with friends you will have much more fun (max 4 people). Weaponry is composed by pistols, SMGs, shotguns, rifles, rocket launchers snipers and eridian weapons. There is also the chance to drive a car called Runner, which must be always used for moving in the different areas otherwise it becomes stressful going around on foot. The vehicle can be customized with 10 different colors and it can bring only two people: one drives and other one use the sentry, which can be a machine heavy gun or a rocket launcher. The car can be created on a Catch-a-ride station: you can create two of them. The difficulty can be easy at first but after finishing the main story you will unlock the "Hard mode", in case u want much more competition. Approximate time for completing the game with secondary quests included is 20-30 hours. Every character has his own special action (kind of super power) and a skill tree, which is divided in three subtrees:
Every skill tree give different power ups, which can go from special action power-up to weapon and melee damage to shield and health performance. You can choose how to set points but its recommended to follow a tree basing on your preferences. Points can be resetted to a customization station but you must pay for it so be careful. The station can be also used for changing the colors of your character. Last important thing about characters is the weapon skill. More you a particular weapon, more the skill weapon bar will increase. When you reach a new level, the damage, accuracy and stability with that type of weapon will increase permanently.
Models of weapons are a lot similar to each other: they can be distinguished by colors. Every color represents the material grade of a manufacturer, which give different buffs to a weapon.
Planet ambience goes from arid desert and lands to coasts, yards/hills of debris, snowy mountains, rivers and bandits-military bases, towns and caverns. A cool feature is the passages of the days (from night to day and from day to night).

Toren is an adventure game where an interesting story and concept are sadly marred by the actual gameplay.
-interesting,albeit cryptic,story
-very nice art style
-great soundtrack
-menus are clunky,no quick "back" button and it's somewhat difficult to understand what's highlighted
-clunky controls where turning, jumping and attacking often feel awkward and imprecise
-dream sequences remember what you've done game-wise but have no mid-checkpoints so if you fall you have to start from the beginning
-some annoying platforming sections, made worse by the aforementioned controls
-weak graphics overall, while the levels themselves are decent the char models and some effects are less impressive
-some noticeable screen tearing even with vsync on
-bland puzzles
-underwhelming and repetitive last boss fight
It's with a sad heart that I give Toren a thumbs down.
The story was interesting and the game concept is indeed nice, but I often felt that the actual gameplay was not only not adding anything to the game value, it was actually detracting from it and getting in the way of my fun...bland puzzles, slippery platforms paired with awkward jumping, boring combat all take their toll over the (short) game length.
Now,the game itself isn't a disaster or plain horrible and the dev team did manage to get some things right so I hope they can try their luck again with an higher budget and perhaps more time to polish their game.
I got it for 6$ on release day,for that price and despite my negative review I do not feel like I've completely wasted my money but I'd advise those wanting to experience the game story to wait for a sale.

14 years ago a small Japanese team created an exploratory puzzle-platformer called ICO that changed our perception of art in videogames and put Team ICO on the map. Since then more and more similar titles have come and continued the style, imitated the style, and even done it better. Brazilian studio developer Swordtales clearly aim to create 2015’s “ICO” with Toren, and while the heart, style, and intentions are there and righteous, the soul lacks just enough to prevent it from being an instant classic.
Casted in the role of Moonchild, you must ascend the mysterious tower you bore in as a newborn to slay the menacing dragon claiming ownership of the stronghold. A cyclical theme, Moonchild must continuously be reborn as the narrative necessitates. As you plant the seed for the Tree of Life by the wishes of your master, The Magician, various puzzles are required to be solved to prevail and help the tree grow along with yourself. Light on religious allegory, but playing a common role with the Tree of Life, the religious ideals of Kabbalah (wisdom that reveals how the universe and life work) help the player associate Moonchild’s goals of understanding and receiving the benefits of what one puts into the world.
Toren will not take much of your time, and it can be completed in an average of 3 hours, but like other games of this pedigree, it’s not the destination; it’s the journey and underlying message(s) found within. The density of Toren as to something like ICO might be more apparent as one plays, and it may not be as satisfying either; but as the credits roll you will have experienced something that’s not doing being done more often in the industry. Swordtales is presents a story that whisks you away to a world wherein your role is greater than you’d ever expect; something that is your destiny and is cryptically exposed as you climb the tower. The Magician likes to invade your dreams and never outright tell you your goal, but will acknowledge your strengths, push you forward, and ensure your objective is attained.
Toren, Swordtales, Versus Evil, Indie Games, Indie Gaming, Steam, PC, PS4, PSN, ICO,
Simplicity can be exceptional, even often times preferred, yet simplicity should still hold a message worth replaying or wanting to share almost immediately. Gone Home was a game many were eager to rush to forums and friends to discuss and learn of varying playthroughs. It was simplistic if you wished to get through, but also a depth that could be found and learned should you want to do that too. Very few playthroughs were ever quite the same, but Toren’s players will always tell the same tale no matter the decisions and exploration; Moonchild’s fate is already determined and cyclical no matter the player’s attempts. That’s completely subjective of course, and for one who like to ogle absolutely stunning graphics and treat their ears to majestically serene compositions, Toren grants that. Sweeping strings accompany dramatic scenes while somber songs flourish in discovering all the tower offers.

If you’re in the mood for a puzzle-platformer offering a story that satisfies but lacks an endearing finale, Toren certainly fills that hole. We will still talk of Toren come year’s end, and it will be played throughout the year, but we fear of the missed opportunity with Toren to create a bit more of a compelling narrative will hold it back from being a truly remarkable gameplay experience. Visually and audibly Toren is one of the strongest games of the summer, just not enough gameplay to make it a must own. Now, should you play it?

Borderlands is a FPS mixed with RPG. It can be played singleplayer, but with friends you will have much more fun (max 4 people). Weaponry is composed by pistols, SMGs, shotguns, rifles, rocket launchers snipers and eridian weapons. There is also the chance to drive a car called Runner, which must be always used for moving in the different areas otherwise it becomes stressful going around on foot. The vehicle can be customized with 10 different colors and it can bring only two people: one drives and other one use the sentry, which can be a machine heavy gun or a rocket launcher. The car can be created on a Catch-a-ride station: you can create two of them. The difficulty can be easy at first but after finishing the main story you will unlock the "Hard mode", in case u want much more competition. Approximate time for completing the game with secondary quests included is 20-30 hours. Every character has his own special action (kind of super power) and a skill tree, which is divided in three subtrees:
Every skill tree give different power ups, which can go from special action power-up to weapon and melee damage to shield and health performance. You can choose how to set points but its recommended to follow a tree basing on your preferences. Points can be resetted to a customization station but you must pay for it so be careful. The station can be also used for changing the colors of your character. Last important thing about characters is the weapon skill. More you a particular weapon, more the skill weapon bar will increase. When you reach a new level, the damage, accuracy and stability with that type of weapon will increase permanently.
Models of weapons are a lot similar to each other: they can be distinguished by colors. Every color represents the material grade of a manufacturer, which give different buffs to a weapon.
Planet ambience goes from arid desert and lands to coasts, yards/hills of debris, snowy mountains, rivers and bandits-military bases, towns and caverns. A cool feature is the passages of the days (from night to day and from day to night).

Basically, you build your own vehicle. You decide how large or small you want it, how many wheels, the type of cabin, combination of weapons and also support modules such as a radiator to reduce weapon overheating or a carjack to flip your car to it's proper position if you ended up upside down. There are many many MANY modules available to place on your vehicle, I've seen some badass builds.
I see many people complaining that this game is pay to win. Incredibly laughable considering that the most effective weapon in the game is the LM-Chord, the machine gun you can get on the first mission available to you. Spam as many as you can on your vehicle and you'll absolutely wreck drones, caucs, cannons or whatever the hell you're aiming at.
This game is very similar to world of tanks but strategies used in WoT often do not apply to this game. It is much quicker paced, much more variation on weaponry as well as much smaller teams and maps.
If you are having trouble in this game and you are starting to lean on the "This is pay2win" philosiphy, here is a few tips
1. STAY with teammates, regardless of what weapons you have, it is very unlikely that you can take 2 skilled opponents at once.
2. PAY ATTENTION to what is going on. Hold TAB to see the overall map.
3. When engaging an enemy, FOCUS their weapons. A vehicle without weapons can only suicide or cap, most will simply give up and suicide if you take out their weapons.
4. Do not put your damn fuel tanks and generators on the outside of the vehicle, when they are destroyed, they do massive damage to your vehicle. Hide them, don't show them
5. Drones are TOP priority, if you see drones flying or driving around, shoot them immediately. Machine Guns and Shotguns are ridiculously effective. Drone-users are useless without their drones.
I have spent only 3$ on this game but that 3$ was not needed. It is relatively easy to acquire coins. Once you have reached 3000 Powerscore on your vehicle, the "Get Wires" mission becomes available. Spam that mission and sell the wires you obtain. You'll have no problem getting coins. However, I would not recommend simply buying things from the market, it is much cheaper to build the weapons, cabins and other items yourself.
This game is incredibly fun and I see a great future for Crossout.

Gunpoint is good. Great even. Allow me to explain why.
When you boot up the game, you are greeted with a noir-detective-film kind of art style, jazzy music with a technological funk to it, and absolutely hilarious dialogue, featuring some of the best deadpan humour I've ever seen.
There's only one way to properly describe the gameplay: You have pants. That fling you into the air. Yeah, no time to explain that one - just roll with it. Oh, and you can climb walls, too. And you can hack stuff, rewiring light switches to doors, cameras, elevators, or elevators to light switches - anything you'd like.
When you have all of this the real fun starts: Stealth. Sneak through a level, rewiring everything in such a way that it works in your favour: Open doors which you previously couldn't, cling to walls as guards beneath you squirm in confusion as to why the light switch seems to be calling an elevator instead of turning on the damn light. Heck, knock the guard out by punching him in the face, why don't you?
If this doesn't sound - in any way, shape or form - fun to you... Well, too bad. If it does: Buy this, it's great.

With hopefully several more updates on the way as well as a thriving mod community, Rimworld stands out as one of the most fun and replayable games I've played in a long time.

I haven't played a game like Toren in quite some time. I don't expect to for quite some time, either. It's quite the experience.
Toren's story, atmosphere and music are stellar and I wish more games could take the approach that it does to weaving its narrative. Hinting at what's really going on with the world while leading the player to find out, it did a great job of hooking me into the story. The graphics, while not super hi-def, are very, very pretty. And the MUSIC, dear god. (If you're going to buy this game, do yourself a favor and get the soundtrack too, ESPECIALLY if you like strings.) All elements of the game's presentation work together to create a world that's captivating. I think my favorite part were the dream sequences, each of which had its own feel.
The game, while I enjoyed it, is far from perfect. The controls are pretty janky, and if you want to play the game without wanting to stab yourself in the face it's probably in your best interest to get a controller. I also encountered a lot of glitches while playing. (The most memorable one of these was when I picked up my sword right before getting killed by the dragon, and then every time I tried to use it thereafter it flew off into the air somewhere and you could see it wiggling around in the air while I apparently tried to punch the dragon to death. I had to reset.) Both of these issues are frustrating setbacks and had me pretty annoyed.
However, I'd still recommend this game. It's really something, and I don't regret playing it.

This little third person puzzle/action game is fairly mixed in my opinion. The visuals are great and the gameplay is not terribly bad. Keyboard controls can be classified as bad and I can imagine that even controllers can have issues with the automated camera, but there is a lot of room for errors so you can let it slide. The puzzles are childishly easy but even if you fail, the checkpoints are plenty.
The major flaw is the story though. The trailer and the description here on Steam explain more than what the game does which I found to be a huge flaw. There is an interesting story to be told somewhere in there, but your interest might have died even before the intro ends.
How can your interest die from just the intro though? Well, the quality is terrible in the opening of the game. It felt rushed and had some terrible animation sequences and straight up boring narration. It gets better soon enough after that, but for such a sort game I would have expected better overall quality for that price tag.
But still, it wasn't the worst thing ever. It's a fun little adventure that could almost classify as a fairy tale.. with a lot of emphasis on "almost". A kid would have been bored to death playing this.

I've been seeing keynotes and presentations from Swordtales about this game for quite awhile in game development conferences, since the team is from a Brazilian city close to mine. That said, I've been longing to play this game for about 2 or 3 years.
For some people that don't know the story of the development, or even how the industry is going in this country, it can be easy to bash on the small bugs and defects, and deem the game as a low quality small game that could be on mobiles on something like that - but let's be rational, this game is incredible!
Keeping things short, why you should buy this game:
+ It has great atmosphere, brought by nice graphics and level design, amazing soundtrack, and a story full of symbolism and philosophical references. At times, it reminded me of games like Dark Souls (for the architectures and somber scenes), and Shadow of Colossus.
+ The gameplay is simple, yet fluid and smooth. The game may have some clunky camera and controls, but you get used to it very early in the game.
+ It plays quickly, reminding the style of Journey, for it feels better to go through the entire game in one playthrough, as if seeing a film.
Why you may not want to play this game:
- It is very short and without many factors that would increase replayability.
- It is a simple game in terms of mechanics, don't expect much beyond some puzzles, exploration, and a boss battle every now and then.
- Sometimes you have to kill animals.

Proteus is an experience that's different for everyone.  It's a game that's hard to categorize but no less compelling because of it.  The charm it exudes as you wander through it's fantastical world cannot be denied, and as it grows on you, it opens up a part of you that you may have thought was lost from your childhood.  The world of Proteus is a musical one, and a living one.  The world reacts to you and sings to you as you explore it.  As the symphonies of rain drops and rustling trees combine, they start to make sense and melt together with the vibrant scenery into something beautiful and beyond description.  Proteus is a work of art, a tool for relaxation, a vibrant and ever-changing chorus, and so many other things that it feels futile to try to describe the sum of its part.  Simply put, the only thing you can do is play the game for yourself, and let it become your very own unique treasure.
If you're a fan of DBZ then I would recommend this game.

Have you ever heard the fable about the Emperor's New Clothes? It's the story of an Emperor who starts walking around outside in the nude and everyone around him has nothing but praise for his "new clothes". Basically each bystander knows that he's actually naked but they're too afraid of going against the crowd by acknowledging it publicly. That story is just like this game. All the reviewers I've seen say that it's "intoxicating" They say it's so good that it'll just suck the hours away with its immersive genius. I say this "game" is in fact a cynical practical joke made by the developer at the gaming community's expense with the explicit purpose of proving that people will buy *anything*. There is no interactivity whatsoever. The game consists of pixels of alternating colors (sometimes they move and sometimes they don't) accompanied by stereotypically surreal ambient music. I do get (and even appreciate) that sometimes developers push the boundaries of what a game actually is (Osmos, etc.) but under no circumstances... on no planet... could this title honestly be referred to as a "game". My experience consisted of walking around aimlessly for about 10 minutes until I realized that you can't do anything. Literally. A youtube video is more interactive than this (since you can at least pause it). I bought this game based on having read several reviews but now I seriously regret it. I want my $10 back. Selling this title on Steam without appropriate warnings, prominently placed, is tantamount to theft.
Update (01/13/14) -
Below is a snippet from a user review on metacritic that says it way better than I did:
"Proteus isn't actually a video game, it isn't even an interactive movie. I'd hardly even call it an "experience" let alone the digital Nirvana people claim it is. Proteus takes the "player" to an island which is supposedly randomly generated and it features a lot of pixelated objects passing for natural objects and animals. The player walks around using the WASD keys (W, mostly) and looks around with the mouse the music changes according to where you are walking and what you are looking at. Although the music will speak to New-Age electronic fans the game play won't. Neither will the graphics. Animals scurrying away and solid objects blocking your path is about the extent of your interaction with the world. There is supposedly an end to the game and I believe that "progress" is made by chasing certain objects in the world. This game is simply put an over-priced art-house project that one would expect to find on as a sort of attachment to a game developer's résumé. The odd thing is the high praise the game receives."

First and Foremost what you need to know about this game: “This Game is Paid to Win.”
Over two years in development with terrible balance in PVP, limited number of maps and mods for PVP and on top of it the game is pay to win. Laced with micro-transactions to take full advantage of players well before the game is being close to being finished, which the game is really far from it.
Now since that is out of the way, here is a small list of problems with the game.
1. P2W:
A. Problem: Players are able to buy high level items without reaching the required level to build it.
Solution: Make it to where if the player can not build the item they can not use the item.
Now I am not saying that the player can not own it, they can buy it to hold for trade to another player or to play the market and try to gain a profit.
B. Problem:  Renting workbenches is only attainable with credits either with real money or playing the market buy selling your reward items.
Solution: Game needs to offer one free workbench rent through completing Missions, jobs or even a season.
Offer 1 free workbench a week

2. Matchmaking:
A. Problem:  Power scores are meaningless.
High level player or Cash shop players against low level players or against new players
In-game bot fillers are ill-equip and the bot AI's needs to be adjusted.
Solution: A Fair and Balance fix is to make White items a tier 1 class so that players can face against other tier 1 players. Blue items would be tier 2, Purple items would be tier 3...etc.
When a player installs blue and purple item on their frame, the player will be put in the tier of their highest tier item regardless of the power score.
OR
Introduce blue frames for blue builds purple frames for purple builds ….etc and addition cabs for variety of power, structure and mass for the color frames.
A player can not install a blue part on white frame, but can install white part on a color frame if they so choose, but the player will still battle in that color frame bracket.

3. Limited Maps: Add a Snow wasteland, canyons or caves...etc
4. Limited Mods for PVP: need to add control point mod, capture the flag mod, bomb run mod...etc

Michael Todd Games’ Electronic Super Joy (2013) is unexpectedly one of the most relaxing hardcore platformers I’ve ever played. Design-wise, it initially presents itself as yet another hardcore platformer with both characters and stages being nothing else but simplistic, black and white pixel shapes with monochrome backgrounds, however, once booted up, the game starts to shine when the visual composition meets the soundtrack.
Health Warnings
Before considering playing this title, please be aware of two things: The camera and the flickering lights. In World One – stage 12, Pope 2: Hyper–Pope, the screen shakes at the beginning of the level. As I died fairly often, I felt nauseous after a couple of tries because of that. I felt similar unrest in World Three – stage 3, I Blame Your Mother, wherein the camera suddenly tilts clockwise by 90° only to tilt back a couple of seconds later. Another potential concern might be seizures as bright, rapidly flickering lights are a leitmotif in every stage.
With that said, anyone who has ever played a classic 8-bit platformer, will quickly comprehend Electronic Super Joy’s mechanics, namely: Any enemy that touches the protagonist kills him and the only way he can defeat them is by stomping on their heads. Also akin to “ye olde games” are the controls; one button to jump (in some stages also used to double jump or to flap the arms to fly), a different one to stomp, and a third one to quickly respawn from the last checkpoint, in case things didn’t turn out the way they should. However, though this is all easy to understand, the gameplay itself requires both experience in the genre and patience to get through and were it not for the last button and the many checkpoints, I doubt I would have gotten as far as I did.
As I am not too experienced with these types of hardcore platformers myself, it took me around seven hours to get through the 45 stages of the main campaign (Classic Electronic Super Joy) and so far, I’ve only beaten three of the 15 A Hot Sticky Mess DLC levels, none of the five bonus maps, nor any of the nine Micro Hell stages. During this playthrough, I never felt that any of the deaths were unfair, due to the controls being very well-balanced out and responsive, so that getting through was just a matter of trial and error and being observant. To spice things up a little bit though, in many stages the camera does not follow the protagonist, but instead scrolls by itself. That means that I frequently found myself in situations wherein I either had to react quickly or was required to stay in an enemy infested area for longer than I’d like to. Another noteworthy addition to the game were the occasional shoot ‘em up segments where players had to avoid an onslaught of projectiles while navigating the stage. But through all of it, I had a good time, which can be largely attributed to the rest of the titles presentation.
What got me hooked on the game was its juvenile sense of humor. The main antagonists motivation, for example, is to steal everyone’s butts and whenever the character respawns at a checkpoint either a male or female voice roars “Oh Yeah” or “Oh Là Là” in a hilarious, yet highly sexual fashion that is sure to make you blush uncomfortably when you’re playing this in the living room while your family is over for a visit. But in case that these utterances are a bit too much or you just feel annoyed by them, they can easily be turned off in the options menu under “PG”. Fitting to the sexy “Oh Yeahs” and entire atmosphere, the stages are accompanied by a strong house and techno soundtrack. Many of the enemies are even in sync with the music, which makes beating them that much more enjoyable.
Electronic Super Joy’s PC port does everything right. The button layout can be fully customized and the game features full keyboard as well as controller support and the menu can easily be navigated with a mouse. The game’s framerate is also unlocked by default and runs at around 230 frames per second (fps) with frequent drops to around 100 on my old toaster – an old, 32-bit desktop PC running on Windows Vista Home Premium, an Intel Core 2 CPU, an Nvidia GeForce 9500 GT, and 3070 MB RAM. However, even weaker models, like the Asus Aspire E1-410 laptop, can play the game without problems and framerate can be locked to 30 or 60 fps in the options menu.
If you’re not prone to nausea or seizures and are a fan of difficult platformers, this game is definitely worth picking up. The music is great, there’s tons of achievements (I only have 3/37 for completing the main story) and great music. The game also features a speedrunning mode and a global leaderboard. So, core gamers can rejoice.

The single best current fighting game available, especially on PC.
Why it's great:
-Extremely varied cast of unique characters, both in terms of visuals/themes and gameplay mechanics
-Easy to learn, ungodly hard to master mechanics, insane depth usually reserved for Japanese fighting games (but without the huge barrier of entry)
-Netcode is perfect, easily Guilty Gear/Blazblue quality
-Cross-play with Xbox One and Windows 10 versions on nearly every mode, meaning playerbase is not an issue
-Unmatched audio/visual presentation combined with gameplay pacing makes the game a joy to watch and makes you feel amazing playing it
-Some of the best audio I have ever heard in any game, soundtrack hits you like a truck and never lets off, reactive songs and effects almost dynamically turns the gameplay itself into music
-A huge amount of content including a strategy/RPG campaign to keep you busy even offline
-Shadow AI system is brilliant, accurately (and scaringly even) translates individual player habits into AI versions of themselves. Feels like you are playing online, best practice tool I've seen in any fighting game since the AI will actually replicate strategies used in the online meta and adapt.
-Tutorials and training modes are actually helpful when getting anyone into fighting games, including complicated concepts you often don't see represented in-game in other fighting games such as mixups and frame data (for every single move in the game)
What's not so great:
-Ranked mode is the only mode without crossplay for some reason in the Steam version. Don't buy it for this. (Though even on  Xbox most people do not play ranked as it's not very good, so you are fine)
-Some of the season 2 and especially season 1 ending unlock conditions for the story modes are ridiculously badly designed, such as Sadira's endings. You'll know what I mean if you try to go for them.
-The changes in development between each season leaves you with an inconsistent experience when it comes to story and other offline modes. Certain modes are only available to certain characters because of this. However the season 3 campaign features every character.
Overall it's easily becoming my favorite fighting game of all time, and on PC it's VERY underrated. Just get it.

The Grand Prix mode is 5 cups, containing the game's 20 (21 if you buy Metal Sonic & Outrun Bay) races. The cups are in this order: Dragon Cup, Rogue Cup, Emerald Cup, Arcade Cup, and Classic Cup. But wait, theres more.

I have more than 100 hours into the game.  I have received my money’s worth.
That said, this game has the potential to be great, but it’s just not there yet.  First, it has a very steep learning curve and even once you learn to play it, there are just things that don’t make sense.  Let me be clear, not mysterious, just flat do not make sense.
Second, it is not truly a sandbox game ... you are required to do things in a specific order and within a certain time frame or the AI will simply just defeat you.  It is sandbox only in that the game allows you to ignore the required steps so the AI can destroy you.
And that is part of the problem with the game.  It is a one-man development team and he seems to believe it is the task of the AI to beat you, rather than just making it challenging so you can try different things.  And his supporters will flat tell you in the forums "It’s fun to lose."
Personally, I don't find spending hours developing a colony, just to have the AI slam you with some event or catastrophe that results in the loss of all that work, fun.  Rather, I find it damned annoying.
You can certainly cheat and continue to reload saved games ... but that is not my idea of a "game".
Third, this game is HEAVILY focused on a "morale" system.  And just like with every other game that uses morale as part of the challenge, you reach a point where you just can’t satisfy your colonists … they start killing each other, killing your animals, burning your buildings/crops and just going on a walk-about they never return from.
The developer explains this in a round about way as a lessoning value derived from enterainment as the colonists get used to whatever you have offered them … but there’s only like 5 things you have at your disposal to offer them … even I can only watch one TV at a time, and yes, it does get boring.   I suppose you could put a plant or statue every 5 feet in your colony, but this again would be an example of it not really being a sandbox game ... but more a puzzle game.
Finally, the developer believes there was never a drug made (required here) the citizenry doesn’t get addicted to.  So the drugs you are required to research, grow, and manufacture, become a frustrating micromanagement scenario where you need to let them have access to them, but don’t let them have access too long, and make sure you keep them locked away, but don't forget they need it, and … /sigh.
So what turns out, at first, to be promising and refreshing new builder game, evolves into a click-fest that just becomes an exercise in frustration.
And yes, his rabid supporters, and there are many, will be in your face telling you, “IT’S ALPHA!”  Yes, it is … for more than a year now.   “It’s Alpha” has become the badge of immunity and cover for developers when their games are criticized.
I would wait until its released as a finished product and then wait for the reviews on that game.  Since developers seem to frequently ruin promising games as they approach release.  Or worse, never finish it for release.
This is just one man's opinion.

It's a mix between a beautiful dream and an experimental ambient electronica piece. If you prefer explosions and platforming, skip Proteus, but if you want to explore a procedurally-generated world and discover its secrets, this is well worth it.
It has a magic feeling to it. The graphics look very low-fi in the stills, but when the game is in action, the illusion is so complete, it all works. While people who don't give Proteus a chance and play it through at least once say otherwise, the game DOES have a beginning and end, and completing it once unlocks a few extra options (including allowing the terrain generator to get a bit crazier).
The save system is very clever. If you want to save a particular random seed because you like the island you're on, hit F9 to save a postcard. This postcard is a screenshot of basically your perspective at that moment, but it's more than that. The game visually encodes data into the image, and the image acts as a save state: Not only will you return to that island, you'll return to that moment.
If you can handle going 30 minutes in a game without blowing something up or killing a terrorist, you should take a long moment to consider Proteus.

Hello, everyone. Welcome to my review for Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed. Here, I will be reviewing each seperate part.
Lets start with the World Tour mode.
The World Tour mode is essentially a line of 10 (except for Sunshine Coast) races, with two characters (again, except for Sunshine Coast). You earn stars based on what mode you do and if you complete the challenge, and to unlock every character, you have to earn these stars. Doing it on Easy gives you one star, doing it on Medium gives you two, doing it on Hard gives you three, and doing it on Expert gives you four. This is how you unlock most of the characters, except for one...
Lets talk about that.
The Grand Prix mode is 5 cups, containing the game's 20 (21 if you buy Metal Sonic & Outrun Bay) races. The cups are in this order: Dragon Cup, Rogue Cup, Emerald Cup, Arcade Cup, and Classic Cup. But wait, theres more.
So, lets talk about the cast.
You have Sonic & his friends, AiAi and MeeMee, Beat, and plenty more. Want to be a part of the past? Choose AGES. Want a unique car? Wreck-It Ralph has you covered. Do you even want to play unarguably the most annoying character?! That would be the Yogscast! (even if I don't find him annoying, just good stats and annoy others that find him annoying even though you can play NiGHTS with the EXACT SAME STATS BUT BEARABLE TO LISTEN TO! Gee, its almost as if they dont WANT you to spend extra money on their game... oh wait, Metal Sonic and Ryo.)
Now, we should talk about multiplayer.
Multiplayer is really good, actually. You can play with any character you have, even if you cant get back in first if you get hit by... anything, really. Its fun.
Overall, I give S&ASRT a 'Yogscast has been eliminated!'/ten.

I picked up this game on a whim some weeks ago when I saw it on sale and have absolutely no regrets.  37 hours of gameplay logged and over 90% of the way to completing every task/challenge the game has to offer.  Great casual game for getting comfy and relaxing or just blowing off some steam after a rough day in the salt mines.
Pros
-Charming sidescrolling and puzzle solving gameplay that takes a rather tongue-in-cheek approach to the films and has a few nods to the literature.
-Easy to pick up and play.  Controller support is good and the content is suitable for all ages.
-Very, very humorous.  I had to pause the game quite a few times so I could finish laughing.
-Sizable overworld to explore.  Hobbiton is very charming.
-Lots of puzzles and secrets to search for in both the overworld and through replaying levels in Free Play mode.
-Useful treasures that emulate the abilities of other characters.
Cons
-Aiming can be slightly annoying at times with the bow when enemies or allies insist on standing in front of you.
-Gandalf's block puzzles can be rather frustrating at times with how precise you have to be.
-Camera can be a little wonky at times.
-Gollum is downright infuriating with his voice during the Dead Marshes level.
-Not a very difficult game, unless you plan to 100% it by finding all the secrets/treasures/quests/etc.  Then it becomes moderately challenging, but you're still not ever going to see a game over screen.  Like I said above, it's pretty casual.
-No online co-op, only local.
Overall, I'd say this is an 8/10 and a solid game to add to your collection whether you're a diehard LOTR fan or just someone who enjoyed the films.  TT Games definitely put a lot of thought into this and you can tell it was a labor of love from the end product.

Proteus is a interesting creation to me, It's clearly a video game but the it's nothing like I've played before, however saying that it does resemble some similarity to another game called "Dear Esther", the idea of both of those games is to explore and have a sense of adventure to progress to completing it. In Dear Esther however there is a narrator telling you bits of a story and it all pieces together when you finish the journey, in Proteus though there isn't a back story, or a plot, or an objective, there's nothing to do either,  it's very mysterious and from what I've heard from people they've seen and found thing I didn't see and vice versa.
You start the game by left clicking on the isles in the background, you spawn in the ocean next to the shore, you use the WASD keys to move and mouse to look around as the norm for most PC games, you must explore to continue the game and like I said before there's no object so do as you please, also the notice how the music changes depending on where you are, but it's not only the music you should notice, everything in the environment makes a unique sound of some sort. I remember chasing a frog for a while all because it makes a sparkly spring noise when it hops, everything makes a sound, and sometimes you have to wait until night time to hear some interesting sounds.
I found to continue to another part of the game, you have to wait until night time and find out where the these floating white partials are heading and follow them, you'll soon find a large cluster of them almost dancing in a circle, head inside the circle and you'll be taken into a new part of the game, it's easy to figure out what this game is basing its ideas on but all the same, you'll have to see for yourself, or buy it and have a go.
Not much else to say about Proteus with it being a sort game, I managed to finish just under an hour, but if you take your time and find everything you can find this game will easily last you more than a week. I urge  everyone who reads this to please try it out, over your mind to something bigger than your attachment to your comfort zone and try something new, it's won't hurt to try right? Thank you for reading!

Y’see, while Toren does its best to be visually appealing that’s all it really accels at. While yes the textures and poly distribution could use work it’s really the only highlight of the game. Had the team had better artists it could look better, but my main problem is the actual game itself.
While Toren will cost you around $10 it doesn’t really feel worth it because of how the game is structured as it’s only about and hour and a half long. With a game like Ico it’s $10 and the game can last around 7 hours. Journey is $15 and is 3 hours and honestly I feel like it’s worth more than 4x the amount because that’s how good it was. Toren feels more or less like it wants to be Ico in today’s new gaming world and it fails miserably at it.
One thing the game was supposed to feature was playing as the main character from her infancy to her adulthood. This might’ve been a misinterpretation of the game on my part, but it feels like it’s there for the sake of simply being a cool marketing feature. Within 30 seconds of getting control of your main character you’re practically shoved into being a teenager or at least a young adult via a time skip.
I feel like I either misinterpreted this part of the game or they purposely misled us. It feels more or less like the game expected players to take in the environment or be incredibly stupid and die a lot as the game is only an hour and a half. It feels like maybe the dev wanted it to be longer, but realized quickly the game was too short, therefore it tried to make certain areas just a bit harder.
There are some interesting moments, but they’re all pretty meh when compared to other games. When my friend saw what I was playing he claimed I was playing the final boss of Ico. The only boss in the game acts just like Ico’s final boss. He’ll shoot you with a wave of darkness or gusts of wind that kill your or send you back and your sword is the only thing to protect when you’re not near the blocks that you have to push around to reach your sword unharmed and when you land a hit they just knock your sword back again.
It feels like the whole game took its game design from Ico and just shoved it into two hours. See Toren tries to be art and you can’t be art for the sake of art. When a game does this it’s going to run into a lot of problems. It tries to entice you with its concept and art, but the music, or lackthereof, and gameplay just make the experience a dull little trek through typical modern indie game. There is a cool concept, such as dying when you’re turned to stone in order to use your previous incarnation’s husk as a shield or to progress through the level, but it only happens once during gameplay and the 2nd time it’s scripted.
The game barely has any puzzles too. What it does have are lines that you walk alone while spilling dirt and those are counted as puzzles. Not since the puzzles of Kirby have I had such an easy time with a game. Trying to fit a ball into a circular hole is harder than this! It’s all pretty pathetic.
It seems like the devs thought they had a hit on their hands and according to the Steam reviews they probably do. Yes, games can be short. ♥♥♥♥ing How Do You do It? proves that without a doubt, but at least that game was enjoyable. If you’re going to make a 2 hour game and charge me $10 I should feel like I got my money’s worth and less like a dev said “Sorry you’re so stupid for buying this game. Now bend over so I can ♥♥♥♥ you in your♥♥♥♥♥♥”
Thinking back to it there’s a really good Xbox Live Indie Game that shows off what it’s like to make a good game, charge a low price, and still have me feel like I got my money’s worth. It’s called I Made A Game With Zombies In It. Throughout the whole game you’re treated to a twinstick shooter while a hilarious song plays in the background. By the end of the 30 minute game, which develops from a game about zombie survival to a game about an acid trip with cats, you sit back and smile thinking to yourself “That was worth the whole ♥♥♥♥ing dollar I paid for it.” And I returned to it multiple times after to continue playing it because even without the song it was just that ♥♥♥♥ing good.
Toren made me feel gipped. There’s no replay value, but just to be sure I didn’t somehow skip 80% of the game I played through it again. I missed one or two things that padded on an extra 15 minutes, but even with the two hour playtime I still feel like I’ve been violated worse than your typical SJW when they complain that someone doesn’t agree with them.
Better yet, the character’s slow animations and movement speed feel like they’re done deliberately to make the game artificially harder, but honestly it’s still pretty easy. The game only has two enemies and one of them can’t even kill your, and if they can I’m pretty sure the game just didn’t realize it could.
The game even pulls a ♥♥♥♥ing Dark Souls II and says the cycle of the game’s story will constantly repeat so you might as fuggin’ well start a new file.
So is Toren worth your $10? ♥♥♥♥ no. Wait for it to go on sale if anything or if you have a friend with the game and pity them play it there so your friend feels like maybe they got their money’s worth. Or you could just wait for the game to be free on PS+. It doesn’t matter, even when it’s free you’re still going to feel ripped off.

It's pretty good. I'm writing this review about 2 weeks after I beat it, so don't expect a huge complex review because i'm for sure not playing it again.
It's one of those games where you play it to completion and then never touch it again, similar to Journey. If you're into a rich experience with a few things to discover along the way, this is the game for you. There isn't too much gameplay and the island is very small and hard to explore because you walk so slow, but the progression of the story runs on secrets so once you faff about enough you can eventually find the place to go to the next area. I'm not going to spoil anything but the game certainly isn't as pretentious as the trailer looks, it's just a simply relaxing experience with no hidden "message" along the way. that in itself may seem like an odd thing to say in a review, but it's one of the main things that almost stopped me from buying the game. I didn't quite like the ending, and although it was powerful it lasted way too long. The main part- the music, wasn't too special. It was relaxing but after a while it all started to sound too samey. It's possible that was the point though, as the whole island seems dreamlike at points and really chills you out.
Overall, while this game is extremely relaxing with a great atmosphere, it probably isn't for everyone. While I did find a few secrets along the way I do not believe there is any replay value or incentive to even start up the game again after completing it. You also walk almost as slow as "Dear Esther" so don't expect to be cruising around the island looking at things. The whole game takes time. I bought Journey for 15 dollars, beat it in an hour and didn't regret it at all due to the artistic quality and depth of the game. I bought this game for 10 and beat it in an hour as well, and feel the same way. Buying this game is like buying a ticket to an art gallery, just sit back and look at the paintings. If you're not into that, I would keep on walking as this game won't change your mind.

Mabinogi is unlike any game you could possibly experience, and has been primarily my favorite game (Console or otherwise) for several years now. Even eight years after the game's initial debut, not only has it withstood the test of time, but can directly compete with other "Innovative" game ideas. It literally transcends the normal spectrum of MMOs into something far greater.
The leveling system is comprised of your traditional numbered levels, but there is no actual cap for your characters, nor classes. Leveling gets you Ability Points, which you use to rank skills in a very Disgaea inspired fashion (Rank F to Rank 1) Every three weeks you can "Rebirth" which will set your level back to 1, while retaining all of the status bonuses and skill ranks you have been achieving through your past lifes. The result is you ARE ALWAYS getting stronger and there is no real endgame.  My own toon is now above total level 7000+ and growing.
Your character from the start can do anything they want from all available playing types. Talents serve as a very loose archetype for your play style, encouraging specialized play without taking away from t heir unique experience. Gameplay demands legitimate skill from it's players; attacks stagger and stun you, knock you down, and prevent you from retaliating. If Rock paper Scissors were turned into an action game, this is roughly what it would look like. All skills have ways to be counterracted, negated, blocked, or even avoided. It is up to the player to learn the complex knockback system to succeed. Even the lowest level fighters can complete endgame content with the right strategies. (It may take hours, but it's possible to not get hit even by the strongest foes in the game if you are really good.)
Quite possibly the best thing about the game however, is that it is not instanced, much like similar action title games like Dragon's Nest or Vindictus. You can explore this great vast world, fight field bosses, perform merchant commerce runs and more, all with your friends or strangers at the drop of a hat. There is a dungeon system catering to high level players and new players alike that is instanced. You can create parties or enter these dungeons yourself with passes you hunt from monsters or chests in the dungeons themselves for OTHER dungeons. There are also Hard Mode versions of each dungeon in the game which provide a greater challenge and better  loot, though a few are unreleased as of now. All in all, I recommend this to anyone who may be tired of cruddy MMOs as a whole. It will change your thoughts on what makes a good game, and good gaming world.

Indie developers at Zero Point Software were kind enough to share with me a review copy for Interstellar Marines, for which I am very appreciative.
Though it’s worth noting, as a brief aside, that a free copy does not necessarily elicit a flattering review – just see my Qora video for proof of that.
As always, I’ve gone into the game with little to no knowledge of the game or its mechanics, and given it a solid hour’s worth of play time in order to develop some first impressions of the title.
I had never heard of this game until the beginning of the week, but from what I understand, the game in question has been around in some guise or other since about 2005, when the developers involved first sought financial backing, finally hitting Steam Early Access in 2013.
I’m yet to decide exactly how I feel about the growing Early Access phenomenon. While it does operate akin to a long-term beta test, providing a customer base with an opportunity to give direct feedback and guide a game’s development, I feel uncomfortable with the need for financial outlay – particularly when a game can take a good many years to put together, running the risk of developers losing interest and moving on to other things.
Although set to feature a single player and co-op campaign comprised of four distinct acts, telling the story of man’s first contact with sentient life, all that’s been produced over the past nine years are four proof-of-concept demos and a mission entitled The NeuroGen Incident. Being a small outfit that, at this point in time is predominantly crowdfunded, it’s unclear whether the game will ever reach the high bar it’s set itself.
Based on my short playthrough of the NeuroGen mission, however, I very much hope it does.
Without any backstory, the mission drops you on un-named ship somewhere out in the depths of space. Everything around you is bathed in darkness, leaving you dependent on your torch’s narrow beam of light to navigate your way into the bowels of the ship and get the power up and running.
The mission itself is simple: to retrieve some research data and destroy all records. Although it’s unclear what the research is or why it needs to be destroyed, there are some strong Weyland-Yutani vibes -- of people in power having meddled in things they don’t fully understand.
Scrambling around in the darkness, crawling through claustrophobic air ducts, trying to bring the ship back to life, faint sounds of movement begin to echo all around you and a tense atmosphere begins to develop, the ship empty, apparently abandoned without warning but for the perpetual movement of faceless androids concealed within a shadowy labyrinth of tunnels.
It’s unclear whether they are friend or foe, showing little to no notice of you whatsoever provided you keep your distance. Antagonise them, however, and you have to act immediately. These things are fast, unpredictable and deadly. Think of the anthropomorphic androids from I, Robot and you’re pretty much there. You never know when they’re going to come for you, but when they do, you’d better be ready. They really are terrifying.
The ambiance for this mission was completely spot on in my book, and left me on edge throughout the entire playthough. It really did take me back to the first third of the very first Half Life game, venturing unaccompanied into a dangerous unknown, trying to piece together events for which you have only the smallest fragments of information. Stuff the co-op option, playing this thing alone is definitely the way to go.
I’ve seen people complain that the androids themselves are too powerful, killing you in just one or two hits. In my view, this is exactly how this kind of game should be. It makes them dangerous, puts you on the back foot, forces you to be cautious and plan your movements. Run and gun this♥♥♥♥♥♥and you’re in for a bad time.
As for guns, in my playthrough, all you have available is the very sub-machine gun you start off with. Now, some people might bemoan being unable to pick from hundreds of different shotguns and rocket launchers, with the developers themselves planning to eventually release 27 different weapons, but I liked the simplicity of it. The situation will no doubt change as new levels and environments get added, but on a small and enclosed ship, there was no need for anything more. And, as daft as it sounds playing a sci-fi video game, it added to the realism of the thing and maintained a pervasive feeling of vulnerability.
The visuals themselves are nothing special, but they don’t have to be. I’m a firm believer that, if the narrative and gameplay are sound, how a game looks should have very little do with your enjoyment of a game. That was very much the case here. After getting sucked in, creeping panicked around corners, inching deeper and deeper into the ship, the last thing on my mind was the lack of high-res textures and dynamic lighting and advanced particle effects.
Two points of note I will make regarding future development: first, when riding platforms that move vertically, the player’s character bobs up and down, as though clipping in and out of the platform’s floor. I’ve even seen mention elsewhere of people falling right through these platforms, so definitely looks like something the developers need to take a look at. In addition, the game seems to be pretty poorly optimised at present. Although I don’t have the fastest gaming PC in the world, the game was averaging around 15 FPS for much of my playthrough.
Those issues aside, this game was a very pleasant surprise. Though short and still far from finished, this small little taster holds a lot of promise. If the developers stick to their guns and play this right, Interstellar Marines could will be a worthwhile successor to System Shock. Watch this space and cross your fingers.

Age of Empires II is arguably a hidden gem in the RTS genre. The original game may be old, but it stood against the test of time. Most RTS games do not even have the same depth as AoE had established.
How good is it?
*The game allows players to adopt all sorts of different strategies. One can build walls and castles for defense, or focus on offense and pit enemies with swarms of knights or archers.
*There are multiple civilizations, ranging from the Britons to the Mayans, each with their own benefits and shortcomings. Every time a match is played, it's almost never the same thanks to the diversity.
*Gameplay wise, combat isn't the only aspect that is prioritized. The in-game economy is something to consider, as most resources are not infinite. Trees eventually deplete, food sources as well, and the same goes for stone and gold deposits. The fight for control over the sparce resources can be intense. It's also worth mentioning there's a degradation rate for wild animals, where it slowly decays and can be rendered useless after a set time has passed.
*AoE has a phenomenal soundtrack and goes well with the atmosphere of the game. The music starts off as calm when starting out and it gradually grows on players the more they compete in AoE.
*The Workshop addition and the map editor are great additions for AoE, where anyone can download custom maps, retextures, and other related materials, and even publish them.
Still, it does have flaws even for a great game.
*Running on an old engine means it cannot handle that many AI units at once. Even with a decent gaming computer, I have noticed units stutter and the game can lag when there are too many units in a large map.
*The Steam version lacks the option to set a video resolution and the ability to zoom in and out.
Even then, my only regret is not playing it sooner. Grab it now when it's at a sale.

Interstellar Marines is rich in story, development story firstly.
This is a game that was originally created in the Unreal Engine at the wrong side of the economic crash.
The outcome? A bankrupt studio and no way of affording the price of the then current Unreal pricing model.
So what did they do?
Give up?
Of course not!
They just shrugged it off and started in Unity Engine.
20 updates later and here we are at the Unity 5 update.
So what is this game all about in its current state?
What will it be like when it is finished?
Will it even be finished?
Why does everyone keep talking about sharks?
Is the IM community really that awesome?
Currently the game is all about the multiplayer, the single player and the co-op and most recently it is all about hellweek.
Multiplayer is fun, difficult, tense and frantic.
Single player is unnerving, tense and atmospheric.
Co-op is fulfilling and to be honest, a worthy challenge.
Hellweek is ambitious, sometimes cruel and unique.
When finished IM will probably be the best science fiction fps and I would go as far as saying it will probably be the bar that all other sci-fi games are judged on for single player story going forward.
Not even bankruptcy can put IM down so it seems safe to say that this game will get finished.
Sharks are scary enough at the best times but these abominations have legs. Have you even considered how scary it would be to get chased down in first person by a great white sprinting at you?
Some say that the IM community is the best community by far, all I know is that a game is only as good as its community when it comes to games with multiplayer.

Although it is "possible" to play this game for free, most players cannot afford to play for free with in-game currency.  If you think you are going to be one of the few playing for free, get ready when you discover how much time/effort is required to do that.  Get a real job if you are going to play this game and give up that fantasy of playing for free.
The good: Immersive, large galaxy, always something new to try out.
The BAD:
- new players are heavily targetted by veterans who want easy gains.  New players frequently lose everything they have and go broke due to ganks by 5+ year veterans of the game.  The developers not only allow this, but encourage it.
- 3rd person flight controls only
- The "player controlled economy" is a half lie: the devs can and do intervene in the economy of the game. Although player production does effect the economy, CCP has "adjusted" in game prices often.  Plex prices and supply, for example, have been manipulated by devs in the past and are subject to manipulation at any time.  The half truth is CCP usually allows player supply to drive the economy more than any direct price/supply manipulation by the devs.
-1 player per ship, no matter how big that ship is in game.  Absolutely no chance at multi-player crewed ships or boarding due to the limits of the game design.
- There are only 2 modes: 3rd person space flight or you are in your room in a station spinning your ships.  If you want more, wait for Star Citizen like the rest of us. ;)
- If you don't Pay 2 Win, it will take you a very, very, VERY long time to not be gank bait for veteran players in this game.
Play at your own risk.
If you like space combat and exploration, pass on purchasing EvE Online and check out Star Citizen instead.
P.S.  Oh yeah, I forgot to mention: scamming and griefing are allowed and heavily encouraged in this game. Don't cry when it happens... repeatedly.  I tried to warn you. ;)

This game has been labeled as an DIablo-style FPS, and I can't really think of a better way to describe it - it just says it all!
You start out choosing a class for your avatar, progress through story, earning XP, levels and climbing up the ability tree.
There are no saves to take into account, because a respawn system is in place, taking Your mind of that, and making sure that You just enjoy the game! You still need tactics and proper situation assessment, so it's not a "forgive-all" difficulty - You will still be punished for dying and enemies will respawn after time and regenerate lost hit health.
Each game has random loot, so no two games are exactly the same. It adds a nice touch and makes You think about how to (re-)distribute skill points for the current situation.
When starting out, just take Your time and if You ever feel frustrated, just do some research about some game mechanics/advanced settings. It's very well worth the time for this game :)
I do recommend this game wholeheartedly to anyone, not just the FPS loving crowd :)

genre : action/adventure
The story is about a young girl named Moonchild, whose goal in the game is to climb a tower known as Toren. As you progress you see the character age from infant to a grown woman.
+ beautiful art design, original score, although the storytelling is dark , the environments are colourfull and well designed (most of the time), Moonchild is also very nicely presented with some great animations, especially when seeing her age from infant to a grown woman.
+ excellent soundtrack, good voice acting from the narrator
+ gameplay wise the game is an adventure game in 3rd person with some puzzles and platform elements - the story is explained through scrolls of poetry - you enter in your dreams where most of the time gameplay is a mix between stealth (you have to avoid some ghosts/monsters) and platforming - the puzzles are simple and are usually solved by using the environment - there is also some light combat where you have to defeat the dragon.
+ although a controller is recommended , i played with mouse and keybort just fine
+ you might want to replay the game to understand it better
- although the presentation is nice, there are some bugs and glitches in the graphics (known from many games that use this unity engine), also some cutscenes are of low quality  reminding ps2 graphics
- no voice acting for the main character, which i guess is intentional and inspired by games such as ico, but i didn't find it fitting this game
- short duration, it's a 3-4 hours game even if you watch and read everything
- lots of bugs related to character's movement, like climbing invisible ledges , making platforming frustrating at times where it shouldn't and making you loose immersion
- stealth and puzzles are basic, lacking any challenge at all
It's hard not to recommend this game, only because it's obvious that the team behind it is very talented with some fresh ideas - on the other hand, games shouldn't be released early with so many bugs and glitches , they should have taken their time , the game seems unfinished both technically and story wise.
Still i recommend the game to those enjoying games like this (and it's exactly what you think it is from the description and trailers on the store page) and i encourage the developers to keep up developing unique games like this, maybe being more careful in the technical aspects this time.

I'm not sure this counts as a game, but it definitely is a piece of art.
The screenshots capture the mood of the game very well, you begin near an island which you head towards, then move across the island listening to dynamic 'music' as you approach trees, flowers, towers, stone circles and mountains. Each of these elements change slowly over time. Once night falls, you find a stone circle that will advance time to the next season. Once you have experienced Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter you will rise above the island and your experience will be over.
The islands are randomly generated, so each experience is slightly different.
Whilst I don't think this counts as a game, it is a beautiful and striking piece of art. It is slow and peaceful, something that takes time and patience, but there is something to appreciate here. Climbing a mountain above the morning mist in summer and watching the clouds roll below you is really quite moving, the stars spin away slowly at night and you can see comets streaking the sky on occassion. Small clusters of chickens run from you, conjuring up another layer of the dynamic music. Part of the charm of the game is moving near these small elements and seeing how they react, what they do, if anything at all. Sometimes just sitting and watching these elements reveals small surprises.
The graphics are simplistic, but there is a strength in their simplicity. The style brings to mind old text adventure game screens brought to life. The colour pallette is really striking and part of the strength of the games beauty. The sun sets and you see the sky and the clouds and the trees change from greens to browns to oranges, into the cool blues of night.
A walk through a virtual environment that may not be for everyone, but for those patient and willing to try, it is an experience unlike anything else.

Right now you're probably thinking "Oh god not another cheap zombie game."
Well prepare to feel bad about yourself.
It IS a cheap zombie game, but that's just the start. AZS proudly wears its indie status on its sleeve, with ultra lo-fi graphics consisting mostly of barely-animated 2d sprites and hordes of tiny dots, backed up by a tightly designed core gameplay that combines the best elements of RTS and tower defense games to create a truly unique experience. Randomly generated scenarios constantly force players to rethink strategies from one turn to the next, giving the whole thing an impressive amount of depth, while a variety of customizable gameplay parameters allow you to tailor the game to your particular tastes and skill level.
It's damned clever, highly replayable, and dirt cheap: buy this.

In this game you mine, build, craft, grow crops, breed animals, trade, form caravans, explore, fight, quest, research, slave-trade, do surgery, harvest organs, capture prisoners, "get some lovin'" (sometimes "x2," which, for a man my age, can be considered impressive) and the best part is: everything is well done, all of it works just fine and, as far as I can tell, the game is bug-free.
Your characters also interact socially with each other. They can become rivals, friends, lovers, or married (they can't have children though, at least not yet) so... there's also some The Sims to it... or rather some Big Brother--since some of them are pyromaniacs, drug addicts, alcoholics, lazy, psychopats or just plain A-holes.
Two things in particular are worth mentioning:
1 - Each of your characters' individual body parts can be damaged sepparately, and you can install prosthetics/bionic implants on them to substitute damaged limbs or otherwise just improve some of their weaknesses.
2 - The combat is fairly strategic and rather fun for a game like this. There's ranged and melee combat, and cover-usage. You can also unleash your animals upon your foes.
You roll the stats of 3 randomized characters to start the game with, then choose a starting location on a random-generated planet, build your base, buy/capture/rescue more people, raise their stats, research, trade, fight, craft/find/buy some gear, and have fun while you try to send your colonists back into space.
- Although the game is good, the price is rather steep for an EA, one-dev game.
- Not necessarily a con, but... I really don't get all the "story-driven game" stuff. I guess you can try to do a "farmers-only colony," a tribe of slave-trading cyborgs, focus on drug-dealing or whatever, but there's no real point in doing so. All skills/trades are useful, and you'll do much better just using all of them and playing always pretty much the same way.
You can choose one out of 3 "story-tellers" (databanks from which the random events that will happen during the game will be extracted) when you start a new colony-- and I've only played with the easiest one, true-- but said "events," at least at the moment, are just random raids on your base, materials falling from space, random people joining your colony... calling it a "story-driven" game sounds like a bit of a stretch to me.
Do not play in permadeath-mode (although it's the way "the game is intended to be played") until you know what you are doing. There are things you gotta try out to see if/how they work and, if they don't, there's a good chance you'll lose too much (or everything) and have to start over.
