Let's get one thing clear: this is not a bridge construction simulator. This is a puzzle game that has bridge-building as its conceit. What's the difference? A bridge construction simulator will let you build boring, practical, realistic bridges, and then challenge you to cut corners and make death-defying monstrosities (or go to the other extreme and build over-engineered sky-ramping masterpieces).
This is not that game. Bridge Constructor is a puzzle game, because it tightly limits your resources (funds, materials, and attachment points) to the point where a boring, bog-standard bridge is
on almost any level.
Overall, I still have to give this a thumbs-up, because it's not a
puzzle game. But it's not the bridge-building free-for-all sandbox you may be looking for.

I would recommend this game, although I'd recommend waiting for a few more patches first.
Some things that I love about the game: First, the lighting, omg it's insane. Utter darkness or bright daytime, it's done well. Only gripe i have is that they need to do a little better with the shadows although even those are fairly well done too.
Second, the guns (or the two that are out), actually do the damage that you might expect if you, say, got shot in the face. I don't know what other FPS games think, but taking a high velocity round to the head, if it didn't outright kill you, you're not getting back up let alone shooting back. And Instellar marines shows this well by most if not all headshots being instant kills.
Third, the environments so far. While most are kind of small, the rain, slight fog and lighting are incredible.
Finally, the HUD. It's ACTUALLY connected to you're helmet, instead of some games that it seems like it's just inside your eyeballs (CoD, wait what?). Basically you can shut off your hud by lifting your helmet with the H (default i think) key. This turns off the hud removes objective markers and you have to remember that allies have blue blips on their outfit. It also takes away the little rain droplets that would appear on your visor.
Alright. So those out of the way, things that I really think they could improve: First, instead of a flashlight, I would recommend nightvision that is short in range but allows you to see in the dark. The balance would be that there is a small green (or w/e color they might use) glow from the helm that any other player can see. Also, maybe don't remove the flashlight, but keep it in and a counter to nightvision is to turn the flashlight on and it blinds the person until they turn off Nightvision. The reason I bring this up is that these guys are INTERSTELLAR MARINES, you would think they'd have AT LEAST basic nightvision.
Second (although this is probably my biggest gripe), COOP!!! gimme gimme gimme. It boasts, rather claims but meh, that it has Co-op, but at this point it does not. I REALLY want to see what they have cooking up for co-op, especially because there are random announcements stating some very disconcerting things :D.
Third, vote-kick. In the current rendition, which consists of only team v team combat, there are a few people who go afk for some reason or another. Now I wouldn't mind near as much except that right now it prolongs the game and sometimes causes spawns to produce a worthless member until they get back. Personally I like to give people the benefit of the doubt that they'll be back in a minute or so and put a lock on vote-kicking until one of 2 conditions occur. First, two minutes of the game pass without the player moving or acting, or Two, someone kills a teammate within 20 seconds of the match starting.
Finally, movie mode. This is already in the game and what most people just starting don't understand is that it turns off your HUD even if your helmet is down. I personally like it, but in the current, and only, gamemode it's more detrimental than helpful. I would like there to be at least a description that pops up when you hover over the option that tells you what it does. Personally I would love to see the extent of movie mode in, say, coop, but until it's implemented I recommend keeping the mode off until; you know where all the cap points are and know how to tell friend from foe without any markers besides the ones on their suits.
I recommend this game because I see great potential in it, but I would recommend waiting for a few more updates (namely the update that brings coop) to come out before buying the early release/full game.

Below you'll find both a video and written impression of the game.
Interstellar Marines may come off as a generic tactical shooter upon first impressions, but once you start playing, you'll see that this game has a few interesting mechanics that helps separate this game from the plethora of other tactical FPSs on the market. The game features a very interesting, and realistic lighting system, where some times the map will put players into total darkness. This will force players to start using their flashlight which will of course give them away to enemy fire. Certainly an interesting take on a risk-reward system for a tactical FPS. The game also features mid-match dynamic level alterations. The game map will change, closing and opening new choke points and paths, mid match, in real time. This has a dynamic effect on the game field. Lastly the game features a ridiculous amounts of capture points in it's game mode. This came off as a negative, almost as a design flaw at first, but the more I played I saw what the designer had in mind. This tactical shooter encourages spiting up and covering ground, rather than the usual, 7 man in a choke point cluster F*** that the usual tactical shooter tend to lean towards.
The game's audio, and visual is impressive, and it's attention to detail as well as it's lighting is equally so.
The game is not with out it's faults though. In it's current stage of early access, there is no single player campaign, minimal tutorial, only one game mode, and only the default rifles hurt this game's variety. The game also has some net code issues as it has noticeable and undeniable bullet lag. Interstellar Marines also face the hurdle of developing a robust and active community, in the face of hundreds if not thousands of other tactical shooters, fighting for the same audience. Currently the game's community is active, but relatively small. Only 1-3 servers will any sort of population at any given time, or even less.
But overall, Interstellar Marines is a very enjoyable game that has a pile of potential! I think the game should change it's name as it's incredibly generic, and also promote it's unique light and dark play more to help interest more people.
Pros:
- Unique Light / Dark mechanic
- Unique mid-game battlefield transformation mechanic
- Impressive visuals, especially the lighting
- Very enjoyable and playable, even as an early access
Cons:
- Needs more variety
- Net code needs a lot of working out
- Needs to build a larger community

Positives:

- Hard puzzles
Negatives:
- Cliché storyline
- Only one type of monster + one boss
- Boss looks like the eye from lord of the rings ^^
- Some soundtracks are from sites with free music (in other words, not made by yourself)
- Some floating objects
- Very short, with no replay value
- Rushed ending
- Zero character development (I don't even know the name of the character I played as)
Conclusion:
Astray offers hard puzzles and horror, but lacks in everything else.
The level design is pretty good, but several objects such as books and mushrooms are floating in the air.
You made one single enemy (excluding the boss) and used it over and over again. It was very scary at first, but after encoutering it over and over again, I learned pretty quickly how it behaves and could easily avoid it with zero deaths after a few maps.
The storyline is yet another "we found a mysterious artifact with evil powers" we all have played a thousand times before, one of them being Amnesia The Dark Descent, but what really ruined it for me was the huge lack of character development. In fact, there aren't any. The main goal is to find my uncle, right? I found one dead body near the end of the game, not knowing if it was him or someone else from the expedition, and the character I played as showed no emotions about it what so ever.
I think this game puts too much faith in us as players, that we will take the role as the main character and react for him.
The ending was pretty weird and suddenly turned into a black screen with the credits printed on it. I hate when game developers don't put enough time with outros, and this game developer sure didn't.
But you did a good job with the puzzles and it was very scary for me. At least before I got used to the monster, but as I said earlier, it lacks in everything else. It doesn't offer much new to the table besides the puzzles and a few intresting level design ideas.

Greetings Everyone!  Still in memory lane…well kind of:  I decided to buy Uprising the expansion for C&C Red Alert 3 during the summer sale and I had a pleasant surprise.  I’ve never played this and C&C being one of my favorite franchises I was very happy with this!  So, is it worth purchasing right now in the ‘current year’?  Read on!
All Alone:  With the expansion there are several changes, some upgrades, some annoyances and others just different.  To begin with co-op AI commanders are gone (hazzah!) to my great enjoyment; though I did find that it felt a bit emptier on the battlefield.  Secondly there are some new units, most of which are your standard fare of expansion units but did include the harbinger which I felt was a bit too much: think of a Kirov but fast.  There were additional units as well:  Cryo units, archers, big robot ronin and a tank that just runs things over without a weapon.  Finally there were some adjustments, AI will no longer just stand there as you constantly bombard them with special abilities (sad face) which at times I felt invalidated many of the super abilities as the AI always knows when they are targeted.
Expansion Complete:  In addition to the above there is a new campaign, each faction has 3-4 missions along with an rpg style mission set that outlines the super character from the Rising Sun faction.  I enjoyed that part of the campaign the most and reminded me of the StarCraft 2 style (although it came first).  The rest of the campaign is kind of meh, lacking the character or flair of the main campaign; especially in the realm of the endings.
I was born ready:  One of the biggest additions to this game is the challenge mode, a clever mode that was before its time that allows you to slowly unlock new units for each faction through battles that are as much tactical as puzzle.  Each mission has a ‘par’ time which you are challenged but not required to meet; I despise timed things (especially in RTS) as I enjoy exploring and building up and playing around with un-optimized combinations, so I disregard it.  On the good side there are a lot of missions and the difficulty slowly ramps which created an overall pleasant enjoyment.  One thing I would have liked to see is more, just more period in the challenge mode.  It would have been interesting to only start with the ability to make one unit type from a single faction and nothing else and slowly unlock things.  Maybe even go as far allowing you to upgrade your units or even mix and match factions (it would work since you are playing as futuretech).
Overall, I enjoyed my time playing the expansion and happy to have caught it even if it was several years late.  But, do I recommend it to a new buyer?  For the current price I’d recommend against it; wait for a sale unless you are a very big C&C fan like me but you should really already know if you want this or not since you should have played the base game and I’ve provided enough for you to make up your mind.  Overall, your decision; I still had fun.

Definitely a B-tier production but what a game with decent attention to detail! The gameplay is fast paced but easy to play, hard to master. I would liken it to Super Smash Brothers in that it has a roster of familiar characters that are fairly unique (along with your created custom character) and the technical barriers to playing it are very low (no memorizing weird button inputs required for specials) such that it becomes a game that you can both jump in and enjoy flashy moves right away but also has a high ceiling for skill.
PvP is quite unbalanced as is but that's ok: the main attraction is the great story mode that mixes up the manga/show's storyline with hypothetical scenarios which your created character needs to fix and the "Parallel Quests" which are side missions based on events in the story that can be played in coop with up to 3 players.
The base graphics are a mixed bag where character models obviously had most of the love put into them while much of the backgrounds and props are very simple. The art style captures the feel of the DBZ show while doing its own thing. Many of the textures are very fuzzy and lose detail at a distance but forcing 16x anisotropic filtering in your drivers really helps clean up the game and, because it performs very well, you might even be able to play it at 4K at 60 fps which is what I'm doing on a single Radeon R9 280X.
Overall, an amazing brawler/fighting game that would be quite good even without the DBZ fan service but makes good use of the Dragon Ball universe. I'm looking forward to a higher budget XenoVerse 2!

So, hey!  This game is currently in an open beta.  But, is still set to launch as a free to play game when it's finished.  This game has been descrided as MAD Max, meets Roblocks.  I've never played Roblox, but i think the analogy still fits.  You are a survivor in a post apoc world, where vehicle battles are commonplace, and you gather scrap/weapons/car parts/money and other resources to build your ultimate battle rig.  You can choose a faction (5 as of now.  and 1 that you automatically are sided with from the start), and use their resources to help you build the best weaponized vehicle in the land!  You can mix and match peices from any faction to give you a truely unique ride (Literaly, almost infinite possibilities of vehicle creation)!  Take you creation into the waste and battle in an 8v8 pvp arena, or  try out the 4-6 player pve missions.  And don't forget races and free for all deathmatches.
This is a pretty good mmo so far.  Don't expect to win it big any time soon though, as the grindfest is real!  They have caps on the amout of resources that you can acquire.  Daily bonuses to xp help you level up.  But as soon as that runs out, you get almost nothing.  Oh, did I mention that there is a cap on the amount of xp you ca earn per match?  I don't know why.  The weekly scrap cap is o.k., since you can store more than the cap.  It just limits the amount you can gather for the week.  They are trying to slow progression down.  And it works.  And if you're thinking that this game sounds like a grind fest, you are correct.  You grind for everything.  Unless you want to spend real world money on in game currency or the available vehicle bluprints.  But, there are no items that you can't obtain, from just playing the game.  Semi-random loot is earned for each match, ranging from fuel, to scrap, to vehicle parts.  But only common items.  Any item that is considered "rare"  or "epic" (higher teir items in other words) has to be either bought on the open market, or built with the scrap/parts that you've gathered in matches.  And so that you can't just farm everything and build what you want in a timely fashion, you can't build for free.  You have to pay in game currency to "rent" a faction workbench.  And like I said before, you can buy in-game currency for this.  Or, you can sell the items that you've obtained through grinding, on the open market.  But, don't expect to become rich off of this.
The game itself is fairly fun.  Being in beta still, means that there are a few issues.  People taking advantage of balancing issues or crafting abilities.  All of which can be worked around.  Overall, it's enjoyable and worth trying out for free!

I'm just going to start off by saying that I've been playing Clone Drone on Itch.io since its inception, and it is HANDS DOWN, one of my favourite indie games of all time.
As a YouTuber, I go through games like your grandma goes through knickers. Ninety nine percent of the time, I'll never play any of those games ever again. If I do, it's only to make a video because "other" people seemed to enjoy it. Clone Drone in the Danger Zone is one of the very few games that I frequently return to to play for "myself". I absoulutely love this game.
So .. what makes it so good??
Well, when I'm searching for a game to play for my own enjoyment, there are usually a few main factors that I look for. Firstly, I want a casual game that doesn't require me to sit down and invest obscene amounts of time in order to get anything done. I want to hop on, be able to play for anywhere between 5 and 60 minutes, and come out feeling like I achieved something or that I simply had a good time. I want simple gameplay mechanics that are accessible to anyone, but also allow for deeper, more technical and strategic gameplay, for those that are more familiar with the game and are looking for a challenge. I want CUSTOMIZATION and UPGRADE trees! I want to be able to build my character in the way I want; adding the skills and abilities that I feel suit whatever approach I'm currently taking. I also want something that's aesthetically appealing, but most of all, I want a dopea$$ soundtrack to accompany this otherwise perfect concoction of game elements - and guess what?? Clone Drone has one of the BEST sountracks that I have ever heard in a game, EVER.
Even in its early stages over on Itch.io, Clone Drone has had unlimited replayability value since the implementation of its Endless Mode, and now with the latest update that brings Challenges and a whole bunch of other sweet bits and pieces, the future of Clone Drone is looking bloody brilliant. The developer is also insanely active in the community, regularly live streams the game's development as he does it, and is frequently adding new content to the game.
I honestly can't praise this game enough. Clone Drone in the Danger Zone is the bee's frickin' knees. Get it.

Best Game Ever!
And here is why:
Clone Drone in the Danger Zone is a fast-paced arena brawler featuring voxel destruction of your enemies and, less commonly, yourself. Armed with 3 weapons each with different play styles, you take on the killer robots awaiting you in the arena. As you progress, you gain upgrades like a jetpack, or a clone that help you more efficiently dispatch the increasingly difficult enemies.
Game Modes!
There is a developing story mode that is intriguing, but currently incomplete. (They are working on it, sometimes in front of you with dev streams) There are currently 2 chapters to play.
Endless Mode is what you probably will spend most of your time on. With so many levels, divided into 5 difficulties, you try and get as far as possible before your inevitable death. Can you reach Titanium?
I haven’t played the Challenges as of this review, but they contain various challenges to hone your skills. Hammer, Bow, Inferno, all of them provide a unique re-playability to the already awesome game.
Don’t forget Twitch Mode! That’s right, a mode designed for TWITCH STREAMING! This is, by far, the most difficult mode. So participate in killing the unfortunate streamer, or stream it yourself.
Clone Drone in the Danger Zone is always improving, with enemies, weapons and upgrades.  
TL;DR       Honestly it is the best game I have played and would recommend it to anyone.
        9.98/10

This game can be described in three words: Hide and Seek.  The easiest way to defeat the monsters, which by the way resembles the High Priest Imhotep (The Mummy), is to use only Method 1, which is to stay hidden somewhere and let the creatures pass you by, before going to the next room.
Don't you dare confront this creatures because you cannot defeat them.  I found a crowbar in the game, which I thought was a weapon, but it is useless against them.  Don't focus your flashlight on them, once they spot you, you're Dead.  If they hear you and try to get close to them, you're Dead.  The best way to deal with them is to use Method 1.
The most exciting and the scariest part of the game is when you and the monster are inside the same dark room and the flashlight's batteries  run low.   Suddenly,  you hear its footsteps and the creepy sound it makes.  You know it is getting closer and closer.  There is no chance to escape because you can't see anything.  That was freaking scary.

The game has potential, I give the developers that.  The setting is very eerie, which I thought at first was a mental institution, but it's not. The "No weapons only your wits" concept to defeat the monsters is a good idea in a survival horror game such as this.  I admit, it had its scary moments but it did not really give me a real satisfaction.  I bought it really cheap, so no real harm done in my wallet.  If you want cheap thrills, go ahead and buy it.  Otherwise, just avoid it.

Command & Conquer: Red Alert 3 - Uprising is a mini expansion to Red Alert 3. I'd suggest to play that before reading the rest of this review, and I will mostly talk about this game and not Red Alert 3.
Just read the points for the TL;DR, not the extra stuff after that.
Pros:
+New toys to play with! Each faction gets 4 (except rising sun) new units each
(USSR gets Grinder, Desolator, Reaper, and Motor Bikes)
(Allies get Cryo Legionnaire, Harbringer gunship, Pacifier FAV,  and Future tank X-1)
(Rising Sun get Steel Ronin Archer Maiden Giga-Fortress. No 4th unit!)
+New maps
+4 new missions for each faction plus an extra campaign about Yuriko Omega
+(somewhat) Interesting storylines
+More counters for faction that needed it (more AA for Rising sun, Even more variety for USSR, and Allies din't need anything to be honest, but still got the best units out of the bunch. Especially the gunship and Cryo Legionnaire. What are they supposed to do, make Allies even more annoying to fight? I guess they can help counter other land forces, especially when fighting the USSR's diversity of vehicles)
+Some of the new units (Rising sun) feel really powerful and are fun to play with
+The Campaign storylines have a the unique feel from RA3. The Rising Sun are♥♥♥♥♥hats, the USSR rise to the challenge and are the underdogs, and the Allies want to spread peace around the world.
+More commanders in this game in general
+Same people who brief you on the missions, but there's something different about them. Im not too sure what it is, but it makes it feel like there was a unique transition from RA3 to this game
+New maps look cool
Cons
-♥♥♥♥ing horrible voice acting for some of the new units. Almost none of the new units have any spirit or enthusaism at all. Its like they got a bunch of awful VAer's to try to sound like existing units but "cooler". Take a look at the USSR's naval units VA. They all sound genuinely worried that something is going to kill them and feel like they belong in the sea (look at the sub's and Stingray VA). The Dreadnaught is the exception, it knows its the biggest baddest thing in the USSR an shows it off in its VAing as a really proud vessel of the soviet might. Or the infantry in the USSR, which are (mostly) happy to be fighting and make jokes whenever they can. Now look at the new units. The desolator feels like its trying to be another Tesla Trooper, but its not. I can't stand him talking at all. Same goes for the the Bikes and Grinder.
-Yuriko Omega's campaign bored me to tears
-They substitute the campaign's short length for "challenges"
-The Rich (Allies) get Richer, and the poor (mostly the Rising sun) get to working status
-No Trading cards or Achievements
-The same price as RA3
-Some of the new units are completely useless except for some niche strats. USSR get a weak but highly mobile and cheap early game artillery (motor bikes. What else are you going to use them for?) which is useless after you get access to vehicles, or realize that infantry that cant get inside of building are useless unless they do something meaningful.
-Some of the missions aren't even difficult, just a war of dumbass war of attrition that almost takes forever to finish.
-You are referred to as a random Joe commander rather than the hero you were last game (makes sense most of the time though, but still)
Should I get it?

(I says have only 1 hour in this game, but it's about ~200 in total, since I was using nonsteam Crossout launcher)
If You love postapocalyptic games, Mad Max, and maybe even "Interstate 76" from 90s, then this is the game for you. "Crossout" is pvp oriented game, where you build your own vechicles from available parts and while some constructions simply work better then the others, you can still drive whatever your imagination dictate with any weapons combination that you like, which includes meele, shotguns, cannons, machine guns, turrets, missiles, drones etc.
Matches are quick, fast paced 3-5 min games, which make the game perfect if you want i.e. hop in, spend there 30min and logout.
Contrary to what other reviews are saying, this game IS NOT so called "pay-to-win". P2W simply means, that if you put real cash into the game, that give you advantage over nonpaying players, and that problem dont exist in Crossout. You can ofc pay and buy powerful toys, but then, the game will match you against people with similar powerful builds. Your vechicle have so called "Power Score" and every part you use to build your car will add to that PS - If you running with low level build you will be playing against people with similar builds, and although its possible to put 4 wheels, cabin and epic weapon which put you in lower tier, you will be essentially glass cannon that can be easily defeated.
The only game mode when there are no matchmaking tiers are 2 of 4 "brawls" mode, where you will be put agaisnt everyone who joined. However, winning in these mods don't give you much better rewards than normal matches.
You can progress naturally just by playing, but to be able to afford new toys and progress never, ever craft anything. After every match you will earn basic currency - "scraps". Sell it to the market, even with "quick sell" button. Sell everything you earn: scraps, fuel, bonus crates, and after few days of playing you will be able to buy your first "rare" weapon from the market itself. By using only the market you will be able to afford rares first, and after a month or 2 your first epic weapon, however, you might find playing in lower tiers more fun.
TL;DR Crossout is really good, vechicle PVP oriented free to play game, and you'll lose nothing to try it.

To sum it all up, button mashing with boobs and panties.
Gameplay wise, you're either fighting dozens of trash mobs who take no skill to defeat, or these erratic, cheap AI "bosses" all who have the ability to infinitely air juggle you to defeat if you don't know how to break out of it or avoid them. From the very first mission in the game, the AI reacts and behaves the same way, there's no noticeable ramp in difficulty or challenge.
The very last boss will play the same as the very first boss does. The only way to defeat these enemies is to cheese them out or exploit them back with undodgeable combos and attacks. Some fights are literally over in seconds, you can spam your powerful attacks and 1 or 2 shot the enemies. I don't see how there's any kind of skill in that. Combos are practically the same for every character too, you mash the attack button a couple times, launch someone in the air and follow it up with an air combo. Rinse and repeat for the dozens of missions throughout the game until you finish the whole thing.
The only challenge comes from the aforementioned 1 on 1 boss fights, where you've got no powerups from the get go and have to tap dance around the area avoiding the AI so it doesn't stun lock you and drain your entire health bar off in a cheap series of combos. Most of the time you'll level up mid fight however and be able to take the boss out in a single attack.
Outside of all that crap is a bazillion different useless cosmetic items to unlock, none of which are all that good visually.
I like T&A in my video games, I don't care if it's anime either, but the gameplay is so lopsided in this one that it makes the whole thing less enjoyable. The positive rating the game has received is easily from the content itself, than the actual core of the gameplay which is sloppy as all hell and completely unrefined.

The loot reward system is very bare bones because they want you to buy "packs" (& I did because I really like the game and wanted to contribute. I bought the $10 one.) 2a. Senran Kagura, infamous for its crude fan service, busty ninja girls, and over-the-top ability animations. The game runs very well, and I have had zero issues in terms of performance and framerate on my end, running on a rather below average laptop. Lots of characters, lots of customization, and a host of stuff to do to scratch anyone's completionist itch.
Pros
-Many playable characters (20+) that all have a unique personality and abilities.
-Expansive customization options. From hair styles, to clothing and accessories, there are a lot of options you can have with each character, and any item you unlock for one is available for any other. You can also fully manipulate the position, size, and angle of any accessory, allowing for some "interesting" options.
-Multiple playable stories. Each school has a playable storyline revolving around their respective 5 shinobi. While it tends to follow a story very similar to other schools, it is a nice introduction to each character and their individual and group goals.
-Many side missions. Each character has 5 "Shinobi Heart" missions to complete, afterwards unlocking additional cosmetic options and library assets. It can take quite some time to get through all of them,
-Fun over-the-top animations. Character abilities are very colorful and energetic, and it feels very satisfying to watch that combo meter go up.
-Very good as a "pick up, put down" game. If you only have a bit of time, you can do a mission or two before having to head out. It can also work well if you plan on sitting down for longer sessions.
Cons
-Characters start off somewhat weak. First few levels with any character means shallow combos, lower health and damage, and a tougher time in higher level missions. You may have to grind missions a bit with characters you are not as skilled with.
-Later missions drag on a bit. Bosses begin to have a lot more health, and use tactics that might make it a bit harder to take them down. Early missions can also be easily cheesed later on by abusing frantic mode.
-Some characters are overall a bit clunky to use. Characters like Mirai are difficult to play due to weak damage, and unreliable crowd clear without scrolls. Other characters may attack too slowly, and are easily interrupted mid combo.
-Story is "meh". Not really complicated, and each school is basically an alternate-world version of the others.
Misc/Other
-Humor and fan service is extremely hit or miss. I personally enjoy it, but some people may find it more or less detracting from the experience. It can be disabled in-game, however.
-The "Lingerie Lottery" is more or less just a time-consuming random-chance lottery to unlock 100+ pairs of different lingerie. There's also
achievement or unlocks tied to it besides the lingerie itself.
-It can be a little bit frustrating navigating between menus if you want to customize multiple characters.
-You can't play Shinobi Heart Missions as characters other than the one they are meant for, even after completion
-You will almost never use your ultimate shinobi art, as the requirements far outweigh the benefit. You must have 5 shinobi scrolls, and be at critical health to use it.
Overall, I actually really enjoyed Senran Kagura Shinovi Versus, and for more reasons than the fan service. The humor, while hit or miss, did make me laugh out loud at some moments, and the short-session method of slowly unlocking everything in the game made it a nice game to pick up and put down. I was able to obtain all achievements and unlock everything in game pretty reasonably, so it isn't too much of a challenge for any sort of completionist. Noticeable flaws would be that it can become a bit repetitive, and some missions begin to feel very similar to previous ones. Otherwise, I do definitely recommend this game, whether you are a fan of Dynasty Warriors-like games, or a connoisseur of fanservicey games.

"Short but sweet" pretty much sums this game up.  For only $6.99 one wouldn't expect too much from a game and that's certainly what you get with Astray.  It only takes about 2 hrs to beat and it looks nice and plays well, though there is some 'glitching', namely in the form of clipping = a few times while randomly standing in place to read a note, or while simply walking through a room, I suddently dropped through the floor and died.  It's an autosave game and whenever you die you're pretty much right where you last left off, which is nice, so don't worry about the minor clipping issue.
There is no inventory in Astary and you only need to find little more than a half dozen keys/items to complete it.  Besides the clipping issue, the only other odd problem this game suffers from is a pointless use of batteries for your flashlight -it recharges when not in use and yet the developers thought it necessary to place some stray batteries throughout the game, which really doesn't make sense (were they trying to bank on the success of similar/non-inventory games like Outlast, wherein batteries are paramount to your success in surviving).
Anyhoo, that and the clipping issue are about the only negatives I can come up with for this game.  The music/sound design works well with the pseudo-creepy museum the game largely takes place in and the handful of puzzles can easily be solved within minutes.  It's not exactly scary but it does have a 'Lovecraftian' theme to it, which is always good in my opinion. I would have preferred to pay only $4.99 for this, but still, it's nice to see more budget priced games like this on Steam.  Astray is worth a look if you have the money and a couple hours to kill.

Do you like indie horror games? are you reluctant to try this cause so there are so many crappy ones on steam? Well throw those worries away, because Astray is one of the best small-time Indie Horror games to come out on steam in awhile. It's well polished, with an interesting story, great atmosphere, unique enviroments,  decent puzzles, and a run-time of about 2-3 hours which makes it worthy of its asking price. Let me get into what i think are the pros and Cons of the game.
The Pros:
Presentation: Despite this not being a triple A horror game, it still feels very polished and well done. I encountered no bugs or glitches the entire game. The graphics were really good.  the lighting is good, the ambient noises were effective with headphones,
Story: An interesting story that progresses along well and takes a turn into Lovecraftian territory towards the second half. The notes you find pretty much tell the story, along with providing clues to solving environmental puzzles. Its to see the notes in a game to actually be useful for a change. The puzzles aren't to difficult, nor are they to easy, they seemed to be the right difficulty for this game.
The Setting: This takes place in a giant museum around 1909. You stroll along in different exhibit areas, where each one was totally different from the other, offering a good change of scenery. If this museum was real I would certain go check it out in person. (((MINOR SPOINLER --->> i don't want to spoil anything but later you go to explore other areas that lead you into depths that are pretty lovecraft-nightmare-like which were pretty freaky and cool.
The Cons:
- The monsters you encounter are pretty average, and once one gets up close and kills you, the fear factor drops significantly.
- There were some instances were sound was missing from certain enviromental interactions. I would move a box , or open a vent grate to no sound, it was kinda awkward.
In Conclusion, I def. recommend Astray. Its a well done first person horror game with light puzzles and a solid atmosphere, and for its asking price you cant go wrong. Oh, and for having been developed by only two people(as the end credits do suggest), i was thoroughly impressed, and can't wait to see what these guys do next.

Definitely a B-tier production but what a game with decent attention to detail! The gameplay is fast paced but easy to play, hard to master. PvP is quite unbalanced as is but that's ok: the main attraction is the great story mode that mixes up the manga/show's storyline with hypothetical scenarios which your created character needs to fix and the "Parallel Quests" which are side missions based on events in the story that can be played in coop with up to 3 players.
The base graphics are a mixed bag where character models obviously had most of the love put into them while much of the backgrounds and props are very simple. The art style captures the feel of the DBZ show while doing its own thing. Many of the textures are very fuzzy and lose detail at a distance but forcing 16x anisotropic filtering in your drivers really helps clean up the game and, because it performs very well, you might even be able to play it at 4K at 60 fps which is what I'm doing on a single Radeon R9 280X.
Overall, an amazing brawler/fighting game that would be quite good even without the DBZ fan service but makes good use of the Dragon Ball universe. I'm looking forward to a higher budget XenoVerse 2!

No doubt one of best FPS games of this decade. Wonderful art direction, intense combat that permits multiple play styles, and has alternate "timelines", a few simple diverging story paths that make replaying an already enjoyable game more appealing. No multiplayer though - unlike, say, another classic entry in the series, Return to Castle Wolfenstein, this is a purely singleplayer experience.
Anyways, the game takes place in a world where Nazis won the war using robots and lasers and other superscience bs. Now Beatles sing in German, there are swastika banners everywhere, and gasmask supersoldiers patrol the streets. Oh and the character you play as, Blazkowicz, got hit in the head during the Allies last ditch attempt to stop the Nazi war machine, so he spent like fourteen years in vegetative state. This early part in general is really, really cool - you firstly participate in an epic assault, and then you kinda fail to make a difference, and then get to explore this dystopian world while keeping a more or less low profile, almost all alone. Then you rescue some major resistance member, and then things start kicking off, as you begin taking on more ambitious acts to sabotage the Nazi regime. And the locales you visit are really cool, too - Gibraltar bridge, submarines, even the Nazi moonbase!
The combat is really fun - sometimes real tough as there are a few really nasty damage sponge enemy types that are lethal head on, but most of time you can dispatch of enemies pretty quickly, using some pretty standard FPS weapons - pistols, rifles, shotguns - but made significantly more fun thanks to ability to dual wield them and some very handy alt-fire/ammo modes. And you can also go sneaky beaky, taking on enemies with silenced pistols and knife throws, which is pretty easy to pull off in quite some situations, making it quite easy to cheese trough stealth-permissing sections once you get a hang of it. You can play this as a cover shooter or more classic one, but using cover seems worthless it's easy to destroy for both you and enemies, meanwhile running around is more engaging and you get to collect ammo supplies and other goodies instead of being a sitting duck. Grenades, strangely, play a rather specialized role as they're mor eefficient against mechanical enemies and can shut them off - but because regular enemies can dodge them, they have limited usability against larger groups of light soldiers - a bit counter-intuitive at first.
By the way, the sound and visual side of things is pretty great - while the ID tech engine has this weird habit of bluring out sections of textures once in a while, this is a momentary thingand seems to be less frequent on more powerful rigs. Still, the technical visual side has no match for art direction which is the king here. Sound is great too, as already mentioned, but... the scare chord when you kill an enemy steahily is weird, sounds like something that would play when you get detected, which ticks me off in the bad way when sneaking. Yet to play new Wolfenstein but hope they changed that one there.
So, uh, overall, definitely worth a try if you enjoy FPS games.

The graphics & sounds have been updated, two new characters & stages have been added, the play area has been widened for modern monitors, and more added features. The only things they removed are the Bonus Stages and the VS. mode, which were both just bare-bones shooting gallery mini-games anyway.
Comparing the graphics and such to the SNES, it's a vast improvement, or at the very least, more detailed. The music has been rearranged. If you prefer the classic sounds & music of the SNES version, you can unlock that option when you beat the game on any difficulty without using continues. The game plays well on both a controller and keyboard due to how minimal the controls were even on the original.
The general premise is incredibly simplistic, survive against waves of enemies until the time runs out, beat a mini-boss or two, and then eventually fight the end-stage boss. The faster/more you shoot down enemies, the faster the time runs out. It can get incredibly hectic if you don't shoot down enemies fast enough and this is especially the case on Hard mode.
Each stage only takes around 5 minutes to beat if you survive and there are only 6 total per playthrough, so finishing the game at the shortest takes around 30 minutes. There's no saving in between playthroughs so you'll have to dedicate a bit of time in completing the game as soon as you start. You get a few lives at the start and you get a 1UP for every 100,000 points you earn. You die in a single hit so dodging obviously becomes key. If you're confident, you can actually shoot enemy bullets with your own which can fill up a meter that allows you to be invincible for a short time. Losing all your lives in a stage means you'll have to restart that particular stage from the beginning, however you get an infinite amount of continues.
There are 4 characters to choose from; Clint, Annie, Doris, and Bullet.
Clint and Annie are the standard, original characters from the SNES version and in terms of how they play, they're not at all different from one another, pretty much making there only be 3 characters available.
Instead of using guns like the other characters, Doris just throws grenades, which do the most damage when used right. Holding the fire button allows her to charge up for more grenades to be thrown, but that doesn't necessarily mean more damage, however it does multiply her score the more she's got ready for throwing. She's the slowest character for obvious reasons but is also the fastest if you make use of her "dodging".
Bullet is a dog who uses a sort-of auto-aiming drone. He's probably the easiest to use because of that and his ability to move and shoot.
This genre of arcade-y gallery shooters is pretty unique. It's not exactly an on-rails shooter either as the Steam tag says, but rather a "Cabal shooter", thanks to a game of the same name that popularized this kind of gameplay. You can't move the character and crosshair individually and you can't shoot & move your character around either. You can move your crosshair while you're firing but you'll have to stay still until you stop firing. Bullet, the dog, is the only exception to all these rules. Because of this kind of gameplay, it can get a bit infuriating to get the hang of. At the same time, it makes it that much more of a skill-based game, testing you on how well you can play with its intended flaws.
There are a lot of i-frame options in the game with the most obvious one being the dodge ability, which is pretty long in itself but also has a relatively lengthy recovery time to offset that. Things that are less obvious for example are when you pick up & throw enemy dynamite and when you melee an up-close enemy. Doris' dodging has no i-frames whatsoever to balance out her fast sidestepping, so alternatives like jumping and simply moving out of the way are required.
There are 3 difficulty settings; Easy, Normal, and Hard. Hard is locked until you beat the game at least once. Each playthrough, regardless of difficulty, you go through a first stage, then a selection of 4 stages to do in any order you want, and then a final stage. For whatever reason though, they change the stages up depending on what difficulty you choose. Playing on Easy allows you to play the 4 original SNES stages during the stage select. On Normal, one stage is replaced for a new one. On Hard, another is replaced so there'd be 2 original stages and 2 new stages. So instead of being able to play all stages in every difficulty, or on Hard at least, they decided to keep the "4 stages to select" thing throughout the entire game.
A possibly major downside to this game is the multiplayer. It's local only, which is a shame because the game now features multiplayer of up to 4 players. The difficulties are also tied to how many players there are and is possibly made harder thanks to all players sharing lives.
The short playthroughs allow for easy replayability, which can also mean little time invested in the game. The only reasons to replay the game are to try out the different characters, go for the achievements, and just overall get better. Enemies spawn in patterns and their attacks are telegraphed, so it's possible to get that much better at the game in a short amount of time. You get a multiplier for most of the characters if you just stay still and shoot, like a risk & reward kind of deal for those who want the highest scores. There aren't any actual rewards aside maybe from unlocking the SNES sounds & music. You get a new color palette/skin each time you beat the game with specific characters but that's about it.
It's a great single player game if you can manage to work with this kind of gameplay, but is probably not worth $20 for such relatively little content.

This is actually the best part of the game, the offline content. It took me and my gf over 20 hours to play through the main mode 100%, before we moved to Grand Prix. This is also how I recommend playing the game, otherwise it's probably too easy. It doesn't matter which of the human players wins the race and that makes this game highly cooperative.
I've only read that the skill rating is brutal and connection issues are everywhere, which makes your rating drop if you drop out of a match. I tried to play this game online, but never found a match, so in my case the online game is dead. Again, YMMV. I wouldn't buy this game to play online, unless you get a good deal for a 4 pack or something with your friends.
The most important aspect of any racing game is how the controls work or how the cars (and planes and boats) handle. In car mode, it's quite okay and highly rewarding to combo boosts to get faster. But this is also where the game falls flat. The stats that the cars have are way inbalanced. Pick one of the most overpowered characters (like Gum or Alex Kidd) and you have an easy game, even in the highest difficulty. But if you have a favorite character and it has multiple handicaps stat-wise, good luck. Some of the maps and A.I. require near god-like performance to beat, plus the A.I. cheats. I'll write more about A.I. later.
Now, there are the plane and boat -modes too. Plane is okay, fastest of the three, but not really fun or challenging. You can air drift and try to cut corners, but otherwise this is the most boring of the modes. You can easily land shots even with the aim dependant weapons, the drones and wasps really f♥♥k the A.I. up in plane mode and it's just... boring. Plus some of the maps have invisible walls, so you need to take the long route even if you could easily just fly straight to your destination, because there are no obstacles. Not really annoying as it's so rare, but a "feature" none the less.
Boats... God I hate boats. Turning with a boat feels like you're playing with a 200ms lag. Plus you often overdo it, because turning just a bit feels like it's doing nothing. Then you overcompensate it to the other direction and you're head first at a wall, losing precious seconds and getting last. You can learn how to play with boats, but that takes a bit of the character variety out of the game, because if you learn how to do it with one character, the next might perform differently. Plus some of the maps just have the most ridiculous unfun water parts that you'll just be glad when you've beaten the map.
There are a lot of characters in this game, didn't bother to count them, but unlocking them makes the offline modes rewarding. Now one of the biggest cons in this game is how the basic stats of some characters are just irreparably underpowered. High handling is mostly useless beyond level 3 and some of the characters have like lvl 4+ handling and that is compensated with a slower car. It's ok in Drift challenges and maybe Ring Races, but in regular Races it's a recipe for last place.
If the first 2 stats (speed and acceleration) are low on the character, you might try to level them up and fix it with mods, but often it doesn't do enough. I understand that most of the variety in character comes from their stats, but it just makes some of the maps unforgivably hard in higher difficulties. Though, when you get better at the game, you can beat most maps with any character, like I did in my replay. I started over and only picked random characters for each race and didn't have problems. But sometimes you get Amigo for a Sprint race (beat the A.I.s best lap time) and you're in for a bad time. Overall, not a big con, any other game has better and worse characters, so it's just basic game design.
Some of the characters are just annoying and badly mixed voicelines break the immersion. Don't get the Yogscast DLC or you'll hate him everytime you play against him. Shadow and Joe Musashi (?) speak with their radio voice and that doesn't really fit in the sound design. That's a small annoyance, but one nevertheless. And don't bother playing bad with A.G.E.S because he'll comment every crash and burn like it's your fault, which might be true but god, does he need to turn the knife in the wound? :D
These need their own section. Bugs and glitches are so abundant in this game, that it's the main reason the game has turned into a swear-fest for me. It is just too frustrating having to restart a race over and over again, because either your character is prone to physics glitches (randomly getting flown up in the air, the car doesn't turn because it is considered being in the air etc.) or the map is glitchy. And none of these will ever be fixed for this version of the game. The last update was that Ryo character in 2014. So if you're getting this game, consider it glitchy from the get go. The maps are glitchy and the characters are glitchy. If you combine the two, you're in for a restart-fest. Otherwise you need to play the map all the way to the end and start again anyway. That is, if you want to unlock it all, like I do.
In lower difficulties the A.I. is super easy and slow, but in the harder difficulties expect to get hit from all sides with all kinds of weapons that makes you lose precious seconds. It's in the game design, yeah, but the A.I. isn't really fair in the first place. It would be ok, if the A.I. was affected by the same bugs as you, but no. They get overpowered boosts, they fly through tricky and tight corners with ease and sometimes they get so far ahead it's impossible to catch up. Start button, restart, choose difficulty, smash A will become a mantra when playing this game. You'll restart so often for the tiniest reasons just because the A.I. does stuff you can't counterplay. Sometimes they target you as a group and that means you will want to restart, again and again.
Mostly it's ok and fun, but the haunted house map is an example of annoying map design. 90 degree turns after a high jump? Doesn't really play well with the high speed feel of the game, having to slow down. Some maps have routes that are just super annoying and once you learn them you'll never go there again. Like the snowy map, you'll never want to go via the high route because it's one of the glitchiest parts of the map. Anyways, you'll have your favorites and pet peeves.
I don't know why I bothered to write such a long review for a 5€ game that is actually most of the time fun. The fun just gets undone if you don't get bored of the game before unlocking everything. The game becomes frustrating with all the issues and unfairness of the A.I. that will never be fixed. Without them, this would be near perfect kart racer for PC but we're left with an abandoned port that works with casual gamers. If Steam had other options than recommending a game, I'd happily give it something in between.
With stars it would probably be something like 3/5.

I bought the game because I like the genre, price had a big discount and it also has a GNU/Linux version. I have edited my review because they have been improving the game and I've been having some fun playing it occasionally.
Pros:
- Great graphics
- Variety of classes and scenarios
- Different take on the genre, real time action rogue-lite mixed with shmups
- High replayability
- You can keep your gear and level when you die
- Lots of randomness envolved (items and chests spawn inside the battlefield, random dungeons appear)
- GNU/Linux (or SteamOS) version available and working with the Xbox 360 controller (tested on Debian Jessie with xboxdrv package running as a systemd daemon)
- Online play (servers in Europe, USA, Brazil and China) with 4 people
Cons:
- Game might crash if you are playing on GNU/Linux with other applications running in the background, I noticed. There might be other reasons for the crashes. Playing with only Steam opened I have not been experiencing crashes lately.
- It was designed to be played with a controller, tricky to play with a mouse and keyboard combo or solely with a keyboard
- It seems there is a lack of polish in some places (I can't browse the leaderboards in the GNU/Linux version at least)
- Cool classes are locked by DLC expansions
- Game won't pause when you access menus, should pause in single player mode.
- Sometimes they have trouble compiling updates for the GNU/Linux and Mac versions, but the last few patches are up to date
The devs have been improving this game, now you can select the part of the level you want to restart it so you don't have to play boring easy waves all the time. They are trying to fix issues with random deaths. I can say this is a fun buy specially if it is discounted. If something is not working alright for you, you can ask Steam for a refund.
I don't like games with DLC, specially when they lock classes, so keep in mind that even if you get a good deal for the game, you might end up wanting to spend more.

This is one of those rare games that comes along every once in awhile that offers something a little new to the horror genre. With Astray, it's simply the setting. That's it. But it's the way the game presents itself that's interesting and is very much worth taking a look at.
Astray is a first person horror game with some light puzzles strewn about. Set in a museum for the supernatural, the game sets you off on a quest to find your missing uncle, who is the owner of the museum. The museum lobby is setup like a hub area, with a few doors leading to the different exhibits. There are 3 exhibits: Egypt, Atlantis, and Demonology. Demonology seems a little out of place compared to the other two, but it works. Each exhibit is modelled after what it's based on. Walking through the Egypt door, you are immediately thrust into what looks like an egyptian tomb. The walls are covered in hieroglyphics, scarabs, and the occasional torch. There's even a giant sphinx in one of the rooms, as well as a pyramid! The attention to detail here is top-notch.
Each exhibit has it's own puzzles to solve, and while they can be very easy, some players may have a little trouble with some of them. I had a bit of trouble with a puzzle in the Atlantis exhibit, for example. The end goal of each exhibit is to make it to the end and obtain the Exhibit Key. Back in the lobby at the far end is a giant door with 3 locks. Each Exhibit Key you obtain opens one of the locks, and behind the door is, well...I'll let you figure that out yoursef :)
The game plays out similar to other games in the genre. You move with WASD, jump with the Spacebar, Crouch by holding L-Ctrl, etc. You even get a handy flashlight for the really dark areas. In the bottom left of the screen a battery gauge for your flashlight is displayed. Every so often in a few areas you can find a battery laying around to refill your flashlight's battery gauge. This is kind of pointless though, as the gauge recharges on it's own slowly over time. There was a certain point in the Demonology exhibit where my full battery gauge instantly went to empty. Probably a glitch, and it wasn't gamebreaking, but it was very noticeable at the point in which it happened.
My only issue with this game is it's length. It's very short. If you find the puzzles to be fairly easy, you can finish this game in a matter of a couple of hours, maybe less. It can easily be expanded upon though, by adding more exhibits from different cultures and backgrounds, like the Mayans or the Greeks....just to name a couple. Simply add a hallway or two with more doors leading to the additional exhibits, perhaps even changing the big locked door to be sort of checkpoint, where unlocking it reveals more exhibits to be explored.
All-in-all, I highly recommend this game, especially for the price. It offers a really unique experience and has a different take on the horror genre. It may not be the longest game, but for it's price and content it's more than worth it.

Astray is a horror/puzzle game in first person. Set in a museum for the supernatural, you are tasked with finding your missing uncle. To do so, you must navigate through different museum exhibits, solving puzzles and carefully making your way through hazards. At the end of each exhibit you find a key. With all 3 keys in hand, you can then open a large, heavily locked door in the museum’s lobby, presumably where your uncle is kept.
THE GOOD
-----------------
*The game has nice visual intregrity. Environments are nice.
*Ambience is spot on, and appropriate for each exhibit.
*It can be very dark, which is great for setting up the game’s tone.
*You can explore each exhibit in whatever order you choose.
*A flashlight assists you in the darker areas.
THE BAD
----------------
*With only 3 exhibits to explore, the game is very short.
*The puzzles can be extremely easy.
*Little to no replay value.
*The battery gauge recharges over time, so batteries found are somewhat useless.
Astray offers a unique experience for it’s price point. At such a low cost of entry, there isn’t much to lose, even if you don’t end up enjoying the experience. It’s definitely worth checking out at least once, simply for the unique setting it offers.

If you're a fan of DragonBall, this is a definite should-buy. I've heard that it's similar to the original Budokai games, but having never played those myself, I'd have to say that it's more similar to the Raging Blast games mixed with a little bit of Burst Limit.
Pros:
-The character creation is amazing, and while not perfect, it's miles better than what they gave us in Ultimate Tenkaichi, and certainly exceeded my expectations.
-The story is a fresh take on the original, and for once isn't just a simple rehashing of the same old plot over and over again. Your character actually plays a big part in the central story, rather than just having their own little off-shoot.
-I'm using a keyboard, so I can't really talk about how a controller feels, but with a little bit of rearranging, the keyboard controls feel pretty solid. Personally, I'd advise setting Boost to F and Super Attacks to Shift, but really it's all up to how you feel the most comfortable.
-The sound effects and music are some of the best I've heard in a DragonBall game in a while, and while the main theme, Flow's rendition of Cha-La Head Cha-La, is getting a bit old (for my taste at least), the rest of the soundtrack is pretty dang beautiful.
-The visuals are nice and fit the style of the original series to a T. They can get a bit weird at times, but it's usually just a minor distraction.
Cons:
-The voice acting is, for the most part, mediocre at best, and complete rubbish at worst, with a few exceptions. Colleen's Gohan seems to have less heart than it did in previous games and Kai, and some of the writing isn't that great when compared to the previous games. That being said, the game does have a few gems of dialogue, Sean Schemmel and Chris Sabat do an amazing job as per usual, and Josh Greele performs a pretty good Demigra.
-The controls, while functioning, do feel a little stiff at times, and sometimes attacks won't hit or lock properly onto your opponent. As far as I can tell, this may just be a bug when running at 60 FPS, but I'm not sure.
-As I mentioned before, the visuals are nice, but they can mess up every once in a while, usually in cutscenes when someone uses an energy attack, like Ginyu's Body Swap. The character models also look a bit stiff at times, and if you're running on an older computer you may experience some lag.
-The servers are awful, plain and simple. It wouldn't be so bad if you could just play solo without having to connect to a server, but the game forces you into it as soon as you start the game. A way around this is to go offline from Steam, but this also prevents you from being able to stream and record for friends and spectators.
-The A.I. is extremely unbalanced. Usually in story mode missions where you need to protect your allies, they're the first ones to go down, and if even one ally is KO'd, the mission ends immediately. This is an especially big problem in the Ginyu Sneaking mission and the secret Bardock mission. The A.I. in free battle is also a bit odd, as sometimes the cpu will just fly around in circles, making it annoying to hit them.
All in all, Xenoverse is a definite step in the right direction, and it looks like patches are going to be released for a long time to come, so hopefully the more game-breaking things are resolved quickly. I wouldn't say this game is for everyone, and you're probably better off not getting it unless you're a die-hard fan of the series.
As a game on it's own, I'd probably rate this 6.5/10, 7/10 if I felt generous.

A very easy recommendation for anyone even slightly interested in fighting games.
:
+ One of the best ways to enter the fighting game genre as it has the most extensive tutorial I've ever seen, combined with an amazing AI system in the form of the "Shadow Lab", a system that makes a shadow version of yourself for you to practice against and send out to other players playing Shadow Survival. (think Sm4sh Amiibo's but online sharing compatable and extremely good at actually mimicing the actual player).
You can literally play against "yourself", punish your own mistakes and then have that same AI in the next round use the new punish you just found against you, which creates this infinite cycle of "getting gud". (also, I aint gonna lie, the fact you can see how your AI ruined someone's survival streak is amazing as you get a fully high detailed replay of it)
+ Varied and big roster, while most characters share the same input style (quarter circle + punch/kick motions) the way they end up fighting differs greatly: from the close range rushdown god that is Sabrewulf to the frustrating keepaway of Glacius to the straight up terrifying grappling of General Raam, it's all here.
+ Dynamic Music by Mick Gordon, the same guy that made the Doom soundtrack and it's just as amazing here.
If you need a good sample of what's ingame, personal recommendations would be Hinnamatoom, Inferno and I'm Back (to Rise), Thunder, Cinder and TJ Combo's themes respectively.
+ Amazing Netcode, and a reletively healthy playerbase thanks to crossplay.
+ Unique combo and combo breaking system, the definition of "easy to learn, hard to master"
:
- Unskippable win animations, no biggie in online but when running arcade or survival this gets repetetive fast, especially on characters with a lengthy win animation
- If you plan on playing a character that's not from the season 1 or 2 roster you won't be having an arcade mode, this is replaced with a "Shadow Lords" mode (which season 1 and 2 characters can also play), Shadow Lords is nice but the missing arcade mode for these characters is a bit odd
- Ranked mode does not have crossplay enabled for one reason or another.
- The free to play version is still being held hostage by Microsoft, which is a real shame considering how great it is at teaching how to play the genre as a whole.

People complain about how it is unfair to versus against people who are higher leveled than you and stuff like that. Seriously...if you are entering an online battle and you are level 30, you might as well quit now. Wait until you beat the entire storyline and complete a decent amount of the time quests. Also, make sure you train with many of the masters (like Andriod 18, Cell, Vegeta, and so on) in DBZ and master them to unlock very good moves. This is simple. Just be patient and wait until you are strong enough (like around level 55 or above) before even considering playing online. Unless you and a friend are just having a friendly, non-competitive fight.

I've put in several hundred hours into the Xbox One / Windows 10 version of KI, so ignore the finite Steam version in-game time.
Killer Instinct is one of the best fighting games of this generation. Season 3 overhauled the combo system, and Iron Galaxy has been relentless with well thought-out balance changes. They really listen to the community, and they love the game which is evident in each character design. The passion they pour into the game is immense.
It has the best netcode of any fighting game, and the community is strong and active throughout.
The Dojo (in-game tutorial) teaches you all of the mechanics in a meaningful way (great to learn about fighting games in general), and has hands down the best online resource available
for any game ever (easy reading, thorough explanations, tooltips, and gifs galore).
The combo system is an anchor of familiarity which allows you to more easily pick up a new character and explore various play styles. For example, I play Jago, Sabrewulf, Glacius, Arbiter, Sadira, TJ Combo, Omen, Riptor, Hisako, and Fulgore. Note the system can be as complex as you want to make it, allows for an additional layer of decision making, and supports a scope of what I like to call "calm" execution. It should not be scoffed at, and in my mind, deserves much praise.
Give this game an honest try, and I promise you won't be disappointed. Fight on!

We all grew up playing the Mario Kart games.  I remember playing split-screen on the Super Nintendo while others may have gotten their first taste with Mario Cart 64 or Double-Dash.  Its a fun twist on the racing genre and Sonic was long overdue for a spot in the limelight.  That is not to say to this is Sonic's first racing experience but its easily one of his best; it finally puts him on par with his rival.  A ton of different characters and tracks along with superb vehicle handling make this is a top-notch racing game.
Game play is key to any racing game and this one is exceptionally smooth.  This game is quite unique in the fact that you race across land, water, and in the sky.  Thankfully, the vehicles handle smoothly across all three modes.  The drifting is very satisfying and is quite easy once you get used to how it feels.  You'll be drifting a lot as you'll get a boost that varies in strength depending on the length of your drift.  If you need some assist there is an array of different power-ups at your disposal.  These range from homing RC drones, to big fat blow-fish, to snow balls.
The content in this game, especially in the career mode, is quite astonishing.  First and foremost almost everything can be played via couch co-op which is a rare find these days.  The career will have you compete not only in races but various challenges such as races that require you to constantly drift or races that require you to meet checkpoints while avoiding traffic.  The easier difficulties will make this game fairly accessible while the hard difficulties can be quite challenging.  All the game modes will reward your character with experience points for finishing racing.  These will unlock different mods you can use to change the stats on your vehicles.
Sonic is one of a dozen or so IPs represented in this game.  There is a bunch of characters from the Sonic universe including Tails, Knuckles, Amy, and Shadow.  You'll find them racing along the likes of Beat ( Jet Set Radio), Ulala (Space Channel 5), Aiai (Super Monkey Ball), Amigo (Samba De Amigo), Ralph (Wreck it Ralph), and many more.  You'll race across multiple tracks that represent just as many different games.  The character models look just as good as the tracks which are brimming with personality.  Some tracks feature each vehicle mode evenly while others focus one or two more than the others.  Almost all the tracks change each lap giving each race an exciting cinematic feel.
Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed is a successful modern twist on the classic kart racer genre.  The races are fast and frantic.  You'll feel great as you pull off tight drifts or knock out opponents sneaking up behind you.  There is a wonderful variety of much loved characters and locations featured in this game.  Bring a friend over to enjoy the robust co-op that is accessible across almost the entire game.  No matter how you play it or who you play as you're bound to have a great time playing this game.

This is the fighting game that you give to a friend who doesn't play fighting games to learn, the Steam Edition of Killer Instinct comes with all of the characters as well as the extra premium skins that were added into the game. Killer Instinct has arguably one of the best tutorial systems that I have played with in recent years, if not one of the best period. It allows you to learn at a reasonable pace each and every one of the specific features of the game, including assists so that people are able to learn what combo breaker they need to use versus specific attacks. Combo Assist in this is less a crutch or a hand hold mechanic and more of a guide when it comes to using combos, it will automatically add in linkers to combos so that people who are unfamiliar with the game aren't left mashing buttons and making a fool of themselves because they don't know what they are doing, it will free flow the fight as best as it can to help guide people toward what they need to be doing, showing off what specials people could be doing to link the combo together and maximize the amount of damage they could possibly get, and due to the combo meter it stops people from being locked into combos forever since once a combo ends you are forced away, either by the opponent's combo ender or the combo forcing itself closed.
The price that they ask for on Steam you will get more out of the game than you could expect from something this priced. There are two story modes specific to the first two seasons of characters that came out, then with Season 3, which brought back the two original bosses from the franchise, Shadow Lords, a seperate scenario style campaign in which you pick the team that you wish to take in your attempt to overthrow the Shadow Lord himself. That's without taking into account the Shadow Lab mode which allows you to train a Shadow of yourself, an AI that learns and builds off your own patterns to fight in a similar manner to yourself, these Shadows are used within its own unique survival mode, as well as special missions that can crop up within the Shadow Lord mode.
If you're after a fighting game to get into, or you're looking to get a friend into fighting games, this is the best one that you could possibly start with, since it will not only teach the specific mechanics to this one, but also allow you to learn in time a lot of the mechanics that other competitive fighters share, though this one, eases you into it, so that it is a less daunting experience, as well as being much friendlier to new players.

While I didn't have the fortune of seeing Wild Guns anywhere until the dawn of SNES emulation, the little I did see and played amused me lots. Back then I was in the "Sunset Riders" train and Wild Guns scratches that same Wild West itch that Sunset Riders did, while also experimenting with an idea that is similar to light gun and shoot'em ups, as you need to manually move out of the line of shot or shoot the bullets off the air, holding your ground for a time while taking down enemies to reduce that timer faster... It was all a fresh experience.
It still is.
This kind of gameplay isn't replicated often and, if it is ever replicated, most makes it so you can move AND aim AND shoot simultaneously, taking away the whole experience given by Wild Guns, so ever since I first saw Wild Guns I was looking all arouind for the SAME experience and could never find...
Not until last night, when this game popped up on Special Offers. I don't know why Steam never recommended me this game, I would have wishlisted right away to know when it goes on sale, or I would have bought ASAP on release day, I'd do ANYTHING to play this game ever again. The offer was very tempting, 50% off and I had enough on my Steam Wallet for this, but I had to think whether or not to buy. Almost one hour later, decided to "Ah, hell, why not" and bought it anyways.
So, onto Wild Guns Reloaded...
I spoke of that experience I missed since the days of SNES, and how many games failed to replicate it. Turns out that apparently many lacked the same dedication Natsume had in making it so unique, so true to itself. Apparently, it wasn't easy, or perhaps they all wanted their twist to it, but our Natsume had different plans: they wanted to make true justice to what Wild Guns was, to bring the same experience and make it even fresher.
The game in its essence is the very same, down to the very fact you move the cursor with the arrow keys or dpad, characters that have to hold their ground to shoot, but now so much more has been added! Stages, weapons and characters I've never seen! While the art appears to be the same, it was touched up nicely and new effects brings more light to the game without subtracting from the original experience. In fact, it made me even feel like I was playing some arcade game remix of it! And you can even play with 3 friends!
Of course, there are some things that are "lacking" and are understandable, and I will address them so none of you need to look further nor misjudge the game:
Mouse+Keyboard control would trivialize the entire game, and would also go against the general idea of how the game is meant to be played. The original game had no such thing as mouse aim or light gun, so the remake shouldn't either.
The lack of Online Multiplayer is understandable in that netcoding isn't simple, specially if no netplay was considered from the very start. It could happen someday, but until then we could be patient and enjoy as it is.
A thing I kind of wish it had is a Practice Mode, to practice stages you have been to and situations you have previously faced, and that's about it all.
If you liked Wild Guns then, you will love Wild Guns Reloaded now, no need to second guess yourself or hesitate. If a fresh experience with the arcade shooting is what you want and need, Wild Guns Reloaded will scratch that itch nicely. If reliving the past  games' difficulties is something you desire, you are in for one big treat, partner! This one does not disappoint!
