This game had a lot going for it, but ultimately cannot be recommended.
First, the good: The three-dimentional combat works remarkably well. The battles are generally fast-paced, and the ultra-moves are spectacular. The time-traveling setup provides an effective and interesting framing-device, and the resulting list of missions allow for a wide variety of scenarios. Fight alongside your favorite characters from DBZ... or change history by standing alongside the villains and securing THEIR victory. Lots of spectacular optional battles where heroes or villains from across the continuum join forces, too. Care to fight Super Vegeta 2, 100% Final Form Frieza and Powered Perfect Form Cell all at once? The game will provide you the opportunity to do that and more. Huge selection of fighters, including characters from outside the normal canon (Bardock, Broly, and several from DBGT, just for starters) and with it comes an equally huge selection of super-moves and ultimate moves, for all your ki-beam-throwing needs. The ability to create your own fighter and set him/her/it up just the way you like is as satisfying as promised - there's a huge variety of clothes and accessories to go with your carefully-configured character-appearance. Be a hulking titan, or a pint-sized powerhouse! Anything goes.
......BUT! And this is, as Zero Punctuation's Yahtzee would put it, a big, STINKY but. For all its advantages, it's got greater disadvantages. The combat works well... but you have to choose between 'interesting' and 'possible'. Meele combat is fast-paced and fun, but the useful skills are few and far between, and high-level enemies will devastate you without trouble, since they basically don't flinch - making them impossible to combo. Ranged combat (using 'Ki blasts') is extremely potent, but quickly gets really, really dull. Stand back while your allies distract the enemy, fire your favorite flavor of multicolored death at them (knocking off large chunks of the enemy's health-bar), then charge up your Ki again. Rinse and repeat until all enemies have fallen. That's it. That's ALL you're going to be doing for the last half of the game - well, that or constantly dying. Meanwhile, the huge roster of fighters has some glaring, obvious holes in it. Several familiar faces are missing, including Androids 16, 19 and 20. Intermediary forms of Frieza are missing, as is Cell's non-Perfected form.
And of course, there's the servers - the game has aspirations of MMO-ness, and while it CAN work just fine offline, it will stubbornly TRY to connect to the servers, often failing miserably and wasting your time in the process. If you DO connect, expect to get kicked off time and time again, returning to the main menu every time. Lose your internet-connection in mid-battle? The game will likely crash, taking your progress with it. This issue will probably be aleviated over time, as the dwindling number of players eases the pressure on the servers... also reducing the POINT of the multiplayer.
Several other niggling details tear away at the enjoyment. Randomness rules the day - enemies and allies alike may randomly drop pieces of gear or skills while you fight, and if you're trying to get your hands on a particular skill (either because it's awesome or because it suits your character perfectly), it can take a LOT of grinding to actually get it. Worse, the 'Ultimate Success' of side-missions is random too. To expand: Fulfilling certain requirements during missions (such as winning under a time-limit, keeping escort-targets from taking too much damage, or defeating enemies in a particular order) will activate 'Ultimate Success', providing an extension for the mission where new enemies appear, old ones ressurect and power up, or other interesting events occur... if you're lucky. If you're not, you can play the same mission over and over a dozen times, fulfilling the requirements each and every time, and still never see the special ending. Several of the missions are also frustratingly difficult to the point of impossibility, and while being ganged up on by constantly beam-spamming Super Saiyans can be handled with the right set of skills and a maxed-level character, there's no counter for escort-targets who can be one-shotted by the final enemy and constantly bounce right up in said enemy's face.
So no, I would not recommend buying it. In the final tally, it's got more frustrations than awesomeness. That being said, if you DO buy it, make sure to play it through to the end. The final, post-game chapter is ALMOST epic enough to make up for all the annoyance that went before. Almost.

(ESJ) is a platformer, distinctly of the indie variety. It has the simple pixel graphics, combined with trippy, colourful imagery, a notable soundtrack, and a sense of humour. I loaded up the game and was greeted with a message that warned that the game could cause seizures and motion sickness, as well as containing violence, sexuality, and blasphemy. Sounds like my kind of game.
Sadly, the game doesn’t manage to quite live up to that entire promise, at least, it doesn’t deliver as well as I’d hoped. You play as a character that’s had his butt stolen, and you set out to reclaim it. It’s silly, lighthearted, and amusing. The game has a silly streak, and there’s these simple characters that say simple, and funny things. They’re entertaining and have their charm.
Let’s get to the gameplay itself. I’ve often seen it described as the unholy combination of
and
, however I don’t think that’s too accurate.
features some fairly different platforming mechanics; they bear similarities in that they are both indie platformers noted for their soundtracks and difficulty. ESJ’s similarities to
include it’s colourful backgrounds, and it’s notability for its difficulty and it’s soundtrack, though they feature radically different gameplay. However, ESJ’s gameplay and soundtrack isn’t near as strong as SMB. ESJ’s music isn’t quite as strong as
, but it features a wider selection of tunes. ESJ also isn’t nearly as difficult as either of those two games.
Now, comparisons out of the way, let’s talk about the game itself a bit more. The gameplay mechanics aren’t anything too fancy. You run and jump, and have a stomp attack that can be performed from mid-air that will instantly bring you straight down to the ground. At one point in the game you’ll trade your stomp for a double jump ability for a few levels, and at another you’ll have no powers at all for a few levels.  Sadly, the double jump is only utilized in a scant few levels, which is a shame since it was put to good use in some of the stronger platforming segments of the game. A few levels feature lower gravity than normal. Some of the later levels of the game feature a flying mechanic, though it wasn’t as much fun as the normal platforming, and I didn’t entirely figure out how it worked.
Part of the problem with the game is that mechanics are sometimes introduced and removed randomly, and they aren’t always well explained. A bigger problem though is that while the game is fun, the mechanics aren’t particularly noteworthy either.
The game is often regarded as rather difficult, it doesn’t quite live up to that either. While I wouldn’t call it an easy game, and there are some difficult segments, it doesn’t have the same level of difficulty as many of the other games placed in the super difficult category (like the aforementioned
for example). Overall I’d rank the difficulty as slightly above average for the genre.
The game features an electronic soundtrack, and while it’s not my favourite game soundtrack around, there are some catchy tunes. It’s a bit uneven in quality, as a few of them I found rather uninteresting, there’re more good tracks than boring.
The main game will last about 3-4 hours, and I played through it in a single session when I was having a sick day and didn’t feel like playing a game that required me to use more than two buttons and directional buttons. (I opted to use a controller, but I don’t think it would be much different on a keyboard). I haven’t bothered to play the bonus content, as I wasn’t particularly enthralled with the game, (though I may go back and do it someday), so I can’t comment how long the game will last if you play through that.
In the end,
isn’t a must have game, but it’s still a fun few hours. If you’re a fan of platformers, especially of the indie flavor, then give this game a chance when it goes on sale.

This is the first Steam game I have ever refunded.
I already knew microtransactions were in this game, and usually that means no purchase from me. However, I read that they were aesthetic items only, and all can be earned in game through normal gameplay, so I gave it a pass.
What I didn't know is that Iron Galaxy and M$ put an obxnious "store" entry on the main menu (which does NOT have an OPTIONS entry, btw, you need to find it in submenus) with a bouncing "!" icon next to it that you apparently cannot disable. This is flatly unacceptable and a non-starter.
[update] According to someone who responded to my review, this annoying icon can be disabled by hitting "y" on the controller (and presumably a keyboard key) that I was not aware of. I tried clicking on the menu option to make it go away, it didn't. I'm still against it being there at all.
It also for some wierd reason defaulted to windowed mode while playing and set all graphical settings to minimal, even though I'm running a GTX 1070 (easily fixed, but annoying default behavior). In addition, the game delays letting you play while it syncronizes with their servers for "shadow lords" or something similar, which I can only presume is related to updating the aforementioned store content. It does this every single time you run the game and there doesn't appear to be a way to disable this behavior.
In regards to the actual gameplay, it is much as I remember it from the 90's. An approachable and entertaining button masher. I only played a few matches against the AI, so I cannot give much insight into the mechanics. I did enjoy seeing Rash from Battletoads make an appearance.
For me to ever consider coming back to this game, Microsoft/Iron Galaxy would need to either A. remove all store/microtransaction nonsense from the game, entirely. Or B. keep the microtransaction nonsense and make this a free to play game, as they've obviously modeled it after. I don't expect they will be doing either, so this will likely be the only time I ever play KI for steam.

Whilst I think this game is a pretty great example of an early access game done (mostly) right, I simply can't recommend it in good faith.
It's a good game with a bunch of really nice features, you've got animal taming, base building, it's easy to mod(taking a look at the workshop for Rimworld would pretty much convince you to buy it singlehandedly), it's even got imprisoning raiders and selling their organs for cash, pretty much everything you can imagine it's either been added or modded into the game.
Now to why i can't recommend it : It's broken.
Not in the traiditonal 'the devs are bad at building games and you can't take a step without falling through the floor' sense, but in a much MUCH worse sense.
Y'see, no matter how much money you spend on a good gaming rig, no matter how much you optimise and overclock everything, it'll run pretty much exactly the same as running it on a Playstation1 since the game is only capable of using one CPU core and the RAM is capped to a very low level(as with most other 32bit .exes).
'Surely it can't be that bad, if it's built to only take up that much then surely it simply doesn't need to take up any more'
Loading games that you've spent 50+ to 100+ hours(depending how you play) will completely crash the game, picking map sizes above the lowest two sizes (the recommended default is size 3 or above) will result in MASSIVE stuttering, dropped FPS and input lag after spending 20+ hours on the map, building a base that's any larger(or just more complex) than Riverwood in Skyrim will result in performance issues and possibly make the savegame too big to load.
I want to recommend this game, I genuinely do, but in it's current state I simply can't. The game's downfall is down to it having so much fun stuff to do which simply can't be supported by a game engine that can't run on anything except single threading and such minimalistic RAM. It's like Dwarf Fortress had a far more developed kid but it was still expected to run on the same spec caps as Dwarf Fortress

The title speaks for itself, really. This is Wild Guns, the good ol' SNES classic, remastered and -unlike a bunch of other remasters- with actual, added new stuff here and there, as well as some changes compared to the original (whenever you like them or not... Not everyone will be happy with the changes made to multiplayer, although I'm personnally okay with them for a few personal reasons).
This is really cool for both newcomers and veterans alike: the two OGs, Annie & Clint, play pretty much exactly like they were back in the day, while Doris and Bullet are actually new to the game and have a drastically different playstyle. Big props to the sprite art and all of that: both of them are created in the exact same style than the rest of the game, so much that you probably wouldn't be able to tell they're actually new additions if you didn't know.
attention to details.
Same stuff with the new stages: admittedly, I only played one of them, but it's included seamlessly with the rest of the original places,
introduced a new gimmick to keep things fresh.
Spriteworks and details are gorgeous for the 16-bit style, while staying completely faithful to the original game.
And don't get me started on the music... Can I have more of that Boss theme please?
All and all, an already great game made even better, and one that will keep you engaged for a while should you like Score Attack-style gameplay (with continues, you can admittedly clear the game pretty quickly, but most of the play-value comes from being able to 1-credit the whole thing, AND the different difficulty levels have different stages), whenever you go classic or try the new stuff.
Only recommandation: grab a pad. The game doesn't have mouse support for pretty good reasons (it would ♥♥♥♥ the whole balance out >.>), and playing with a keyboard is... Well, playing with a keyboard.

This quickly became one of my favorite fighting games of all time. And it has been only 2 days since I got the game!
This game has an amazing gameplay with possibly the best fighting/combo mechanics of all games, in my opinion. You don't have to spend weeks to learn a simple basic combo of a SINGLE character. You don't have to fight more to control your character and do their attacks, instead of focusing in the fun part: Fighting your oponent.
In this game it's really straightforward and simple to learn how to combo, but that doesn't mean the game is shallow. Not even close!
One of my favorite things in this game, is one of the Killer Instinct's signature: COMBO BREAKER. In other fighting games, when your oponent gets you in a combo string, all you can do is watch and wait as he juggles you around. Well, not in this game!
You have a chance to Combo Break his combo, and break free and fight back! And this is not an nearly impossible mechanic that requires weeks of training to get it right. It's as simple as pressing Kick+Punch in the same type your opponent is combo'ing you. (Ex: If he's using Heavy attacks, you press HP+HK, or Medium attacks you press MP+MK, etc.)
In this game there's always a way. There's always something you can do to fight back.
Not only that, all the characters are very nice, unique and they all act and feel different.
The sound effects, the announcer and the music are amazing! (The music was composed by none other than Mick Gordon. The same composer from Doom [2016])
Speaking of music, they are all dynamic, changing as the battle progress. Each character has it's own music theme, and they fit them really well.
The game has one of the best netcodes I've ever seen.
Amazing game modes, like the Shadow Labs, which the game will record the way you play and create an IA that plays like you, so you can fight agains yourself! (Or other IA created by other players).
Speaking of IA, the IA controlled opponents are very well done and challenging. It also has many difficulty levels.
This is a amazing game I can recommend for ANYONE, even those who are bad at fighting games (I'm one of those XD). It doesn't matter if you only want it for Singleplayer, or Multiplayer. You will have fun either way!

Well... it's mostly like Lego Batman 2. Lego LOTR uses an open world as well and follows the story of Frodo and his companions in order to destroy the One Ring.
Lego Batman 2 felt fresh because it didn't try to tell a story that had already been told. We all know the story of LOTR. We've all seen the movies by now, right ? While the gameplay is shallow but fun, it's nothing groundbreaking. And might I say I'm a big LOTR fan, so you can imagine my disappointment when I started playing this.
The classic Lego humor is still there, but mostly subtle though. And the gameplay is solid as always. But since it's a retelling you kinda know what to expect, making the whole thing... less exciting. Yeah yeah, there's no other way to have created this game, I agree. But still...
By the way, the low quality voice acting truly bothered me. It's like they ripped the sounds straight from a DVD or something.
Lego LOTR shows us that not every tale can or should be made into a Lego game (Lego Avengers does look pretty cool, however...).
For now, I think you're better off playing Lego Batman 2.

I've been playing Robocraft since it first hit Steam back in the Summer of 2014, and looking back on it, most of the changes are rather pleasing. From a game where you were forced to only use 1 type of gun on a bot with horrendous looking bots all around you due to the "tiering" system the Alpha started out with.
Fast forward to today and premium currency's died, endless weapon combinations can be used strategicially or just to have plain fun, Battle Arena matches don't take 30+ minutes and everything is accessable. The Epic Loot Update was definitely not their brightest hour, which is a shame because everybody became too up in arms over that abysmal update and began to ignore the fantastic gameplay still offered by the game. After it became obvious that the Epic Loot Update wasn't a shameless prank, and they started balancing out the rewards, I personally felt like Robocraft began to rise up again.
This game isn't perfect, but its been able to carve out a name for itself in this newfound (Destructable Vehicle Arena?) genre without going off the rails with blatantly P2W mechanics. You can buy premium to double crate output and get more from destroying items, or just buy more crates. It definitely sucked during the transition to loot crates before loot balancing changes and no possible way to get currency from crates, but FreeJam's listened to its community time and time again while not allowing the community to dictate the path they chose for the game.
In all I find myself having more fun today than I could have possible had 3 years ago during the grinding hell that was the Robocraft Alpha. I wish people could let go of the past and see the bright future this game has... provided FreeJam doesn't go full Gaijin on us....

Seriously, the best MMO out there right now, bar none. STO is great, WoW is meh. But Eve is magnificent.
Eve Online is essentially an economy simulator in space. You get a ship and you can fight things, but the crux of the game is money: how do you get it? What do you do with it once you have it?
You might be a miner, a freighter pilot, a smuggler, a bounty hunter, a mercenary, a security specialist or a CEO. One way or another, you make money in space.
And they add new stuff to the game all the time. And by that I don't mean content. There's not much "content" in the game in the form of "stuff to do." It's VERY sandboxy. The attitude of the dev team is "here's our game. Play it or gtfo." That's not to say that they don't listen to the playerbase, but they don't compromise their vision to the extent that Blizzard will with WoW.
I give Eve Online an A+. Seriously. This is one of my favorite games ever. I don't play it now because I have more important ways to spend 15 bucks a month.
And don't forget the first rule of Eve: if you can't afford to lose it, don't take it off the station. There is no such thing as "unfair" in Eve. Devs don't listen to complaints of "this dude stole my stuff." Well yeah. He's a pirate. Stealing is what he does. Shut up.
A corporation recently lost a large amount of real money (seriously, an amount of money that people get murdered over in real life) because their convoy got raided. They (of course) complained to the devs, who (predictably) said "tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ You knew the rules when you took that stuff out into space. You didn't get griefed; you got robbed."

This is DEFINITELY my favorite visual novel under the otome category. It may change in the future but for now this will be it. Yes this VN has a serious bug and some bad writing. But, in all honesty if you are going to let a small bug and bad writing influence you to write a bad review for this game in general, I think that's injustice. But regardless bugs should be FIXED by the developers- its a serious issue.
The whole story is about cakes, pastries, coffee and tea on the surface but beneath you'd find a sad depressive story on how a girl rises despite being an orphan to a wonderful pastry chef. Don't underestimate this VN, keep your wits ready as questions maybe asked randomly and there are various stat building activities. You need to plan things carefully and thoughtfully. This game is not JUST a VN it's pretty educational and makes you actually learn something new and interesting about food. I appreciate the efforts of the developers to do this valuable research.
There are many endings for some characters and I'll admit I did not get them all. The stories are bitter sweet: forbidden romance, tsundere romance, heated romance and unlawful romance. You can bake and make cakes according to the preferance of your bishi and also attend classes, eat at restaurants and also work in bakeries, gardens, palace and so many locations. Other than the main male characters for romance there are also side characters that you can develop relationships with- now thats interesting. There are so many events and activities and different roles for you- so many directions for any ending which is very commendable. There are also cute little pets that you can purchase that would ultimately feed you and boosts your stats- that's such a creative feature and something I haven't much experienced in VN's. Also when you are done with the main stories there are extra stories you can read for each character and for Lina as well. They were very cute and I loved them.
Art was very well done. But could have been improved. There were instances where the character would not look like the same in certain instances. Sometimes I felt the art were just renders and not fully furnished. I loved the work done with the backgrounds tho.
Special mentioning for the music since the lack of voice acting is present. The music undeniably suits the characters and makes the game very atmospheric. The characterization is incredible too- it's nothing totally fantastic but I feel like Christopher DM's route is my favorite and I loved him very much "kyaa"
-Would be awesome if it was voiced
-Please remove the bugs- although the writing didnt bother me much the bug is serious
-Maybe it should have been longer
-Improvement in art
-The achievements in the game should be put to steam (currently the achievements are only given to getting the endings)
Overall a very nice romantic game- that I would definitely play a few times.

A Great Game if You Want Something Different
Eve online is a game based entirely in space where you can create your own persona in an online universe, piloting different space ships and making allies.

Gameplay: The only thing you need to play this game is the mouse. Everything in the game including combat, mining, traveling, making trades, and constructing objects requires you to either point and click or right click and select the appropriate option. Now this sounds boring and impractical but the first time you fight multiple enemies at once, you'll find that not only is it intense, but it works well. The majority of the game will be spent either doing missions, mining materials, or managing resources (building stuff, and buying/selling objects). You get quests/missions while docked at space stations and can buy and sell stuff there as well in an auction house like style. The missions are fun and get harder as you train your skills up to use bigger and better ships.
The skill system is also unique to EVE online because you don't actually have to play the game to become the strongest character you can be. The way you train your skills in this game is by selecting it, and waiting for it to level up, there are 5 levels per skill and it takes longer for the skill to level up (training a skill from 4 - 5 can sometimes take more than a week). This is both a great and bad thing about the game.  The reason that this can be both is because if your a 12 year old or someone who has tons of time on their hands you'll feel like the developer is controlling how fast your character can level because there's nothing you can do to make your character level up faster. But if you're like me (a university stundent) or someone who has very little time to grind and do raids on a weekly basis, then having the ability to level up with minimal play time is good. You will need in game money to buy more advanced skills however, so this does force players to devote some time to playing the game.
There's a lot of customization with the ships, weapons, and various mods you can equip to your ship such as boosters (which allow the ship to go faster) and stasis fields, which can slow an enemy ship down. I should also mention that the game is PVP, meaning that any player at any time can kill you, and you can do the same. I found it to be an exciting part of the game but I can see how others would hate the idea. I should say that each system in the game (you travel from system to system to do quests and stuff) has different security ratings with 1.0 being the highest, were no-one can kill another player without getting the cops on their asses (and the NPC cops are tough) and 0.0 being the lowest were everything goes... this means even if you hate the idea of PvP, you can hang out in 1.0 space without too much to worry about.
Graphics: The graphics are great, they have been great for the past several years, and continue to improve as the developers upgrade them from DX9 to DX10 through patches. The vast space landscapes are beautiful and make the look and feeling of being in space believable. The graphics are great, but it does suffer from the same things as MMOs like the Matrix Online; Which is copied models being used over and over. Its not a big deal, but yes, every 10 or so missions you will see the same space station and randomized asteroid fields. There are 4 different factions in the game, so when you visit their systems and their stations you do get a sense of the environment being different.
Story: Unlike MMO's such as World of Warcraft, EVE online doesn't really have a story to speak of. All of the quests in Eve are given through text, and most quest line only last between 6 to 12 missions before shifting to a new quest line. During these however a minor story usually exists, and example of this would be the first few fighting quests you can get; they have you investigating and taking out pirates and at the end of this quest line you can either join the tyrant you have been fighting against (aka do pirate missions) or kill him (continue to do pro-civilized missions). Even without too much of a story, you'll be enthralled with the game play, and satisfied at least, with the mini stories you do get.
Sound: The sounds are great and work to make the space universe seem real. The thrusters on your ship sound real, the guns rail off shots and snap well, and when enemy ships blow up, the explosions sound good. There is music as well which fits the mood well, none of it licensed but it does sound like 80 SiFi films, much like John Carpenter's "The Thing" or music heard during the quiet moments of games like Mass Effect, which is good. There's also miscellaneous sounds when you're docked at stations sounds of stuff being moved and little touches like that, so it sounds good.
Overall: This is a good game, but its not for people who like grinding and questing for XP in games like WoW. You have to wait for your skills to level, and some people are not going like that aspect of the game. Some people will enjoy not having to devote hours a day to gain level however, which is good. The game looks great, plays great, and has a large following who don't want to go play WoW or any other MMO anytime soon. The game is updated on a regular basis with free expansions that come out around every 6 months. So with a good online community, lasting appeal, great game play, graphics and sound, this game is something that if you're at all interested in, should give a try.


Update November 2009 -
I read my review over again after I heard of the lastest expansion coming out, and I would like to clarify. Eve Online is not really a game for people looking for out-of-the-box fun. Eve Online really is better described as a space life simulator, in the sense that if you want to create an alter ego and create a well known company or become a feared pirate (not to NPCs but actual people) then you can in Eve, but it will require months of your life to do so. Alot of people play this game for one month and complain about the lack of fun they have, and fail to see that this is a game that requires a significant investment of time to really affect yourself or the game world. I also forgot to mention in my orginal review that (most definitly) 90% of the people who try this will be turned off by the game; I'm an interesting case because this was my first MMO that I tried at age 12... to give you an idea of how this MMOs difficulty is; I didn't even know how to move my ship the first day I played the game.

But after I got over that "minor" problem I realized the potential of the world in this game, its like the real world. You can fly up behind someone and blow their brians out or make contacts and trade routes to make money and become a powerhouse in the entire game world. I can say this without any question or doubt in my mind, this is the most advanced MMO out there, you can change the world, and I don't mean change the world WoW style by getting a purple sword or  killing a character, or some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like that, at the end of the day someone else has that sword too and the person (NPC or real) will respawn for someone else to kill. When you and a corp take on another corp and win a battle or when you get enough cash to control a trade route or material in the world you change how others must play (in either good or bad ways). If your in it for some quick fun, realistically, I should tell you to go play WoW, but if you want to build up yourself and make a difference in another world (it will take several months of devotion, no doubt) then give this game a shot; don't be afraid of this game, its like real life in that it has amazing opportunities...  but with lasers.

♥ Cute and engaging storyline.
Though it's a bit ironic for a person with massive food allergies (no chiffon cake for me!) to play a game centered around everything I can't have, I couldn't help but love it. The storyline is pleasing, a bit of mystery thrown in, and just enough side events to keep it interesting without taking away from the main story.
There is more dialogue than in other games, and the highlight of choices revolve around creating pastries, teas, etc. There seems to be an even split between baking and romance.
And yes, you will be quizzed on food. Harshly. I'm lucky that the in-game overlay works (thank you google, lol) and I had a culinary friend to help me. If you're looking for a pure romance game, I wouldn't suggest getting this - you need to be interested in baking, if not love it.
♥ Beautiful details.
Despite the problems with translations, it's clear that love was put into the other details. The graphics are beautiful, the pastries look positively d e l i c i o u s, and the music is charming.
I usually (if not always) play games on mute, leaving music/movies on in the background. Pastry Lovers is the first game in over a year I can remember /willingly/ leaving unmuted. Wonderful level of detail.
♥ Lots of playtime!
I bought the game for 49cents (USD) and spent more than seven hours playing. I earned all the achievements, though I still have 2 endings to explore with the 5 characters offered, along with further in-game achievements to earn.
I was pleased about the gameplay offered, especially as the story continues after you've chosen your internship -/- your lover's route. That was a nice change from other otome games that end once you've chosen your lover. I was grateful for the expanded storylines, and the various cutscenes/"secret" things to be unlocked.
I would have paid full price. Pastry Lovers is worth it!
✘ Wonky translations.
I know that otome games can be a mixed bag when it comes to translations. Some are seemingly translated by Google translate, others more care is put into. While Pastry Lovers has amusing translations and can be fairly well understood, there should have been more quality control.
I'm sure that plenty of people would have offered free translation help, in exchange for a copy of the game, a credit, etc. so it wasn't a situation of not being able to find help. I would rather wait longer for a game to be released and have superior quality than a quicker release -/- development shortcuts taken.
✘ Blatant sexism.
No, I'm not a cis-scum hating, tumblr loving person. I'm a normal, eighteen year old girl, who loves the romance genre more than she probably should. I'm used to the norm of female main characters, whether in books or games, that lack self-confidence and persue a fast, unhealthy relationship w/their love interest/s.
While this game offered more relationship development than expected, there were obvious, even blatant moments of sexism from working as a call girl (forgive me...hostess :') to the fan-service provided in the hot springs. The males offered the usual responses of wanting to protect Sakura, have her help them with /their/ dreams (except w/William's path and the teacher).
All of these things are seemingly the standard for otome games, and the romance genre as a whole. While it  didn't take away my enjoyment of the game (hello guilty pleasures!) it is a standard that should begin to evolve.
✘ No % progress in the internship path.
Once you choose your internship path, a few of the paths will require you to gain certain %'s in different categories to progress. While the menu provides a list of the %'s needed to advance, there is nothing that keeps track of your progress, beyond the chat screen that appears after you make choices. So while it shows you your progress after making choices, there's no log/record you can see of your % progress, before making choices. This can turn into a real pain, especially if you follow the pastry shop internship later on.

Killer Instinct on the SNES was one of the first video games I ever played, so the series is special to me.
I never owned an Xbox One and Windows 10 is cancer, so this was my first chance to play this game, and wow, I just can't believe how much content there is in this game.
Single player: It's sad to me that in 2017 I am surprised to see fully fledged out single player modes in a fighting game, but here it is. You have Shadow Lords, two different story modes, Arcade, two different types of Survival mode, a fully featured tutorial mode that is arguably one of the best ones out there, and an extensive practice that even allows you to take some of the practice mode parameters and use it in the other 1p modes. I did a playthrough of arcade with all of the hitboxes turned on just for fun.
For fans of Super Smash Bros 4, there is also a mode similar to how the Amiibos work, where you can train up a CPU character that has your fighting style and then it can earn you points towards unlocking skins, even when you're offline, when other players play through Shadow Survival mode.
Multiplayer: Netcode is flawless, but be wary that the crossplay feature is only available for lobbies and exhibition, so if you want to play ranked it will be kind of dead or you'll be fighting the same guy over and over.
Gameplay system: Easy to learn, hard to master. My favorite type of game. You can start the game up and within a few matches you'll have most of the basic mechanics down. Very new player friendly.
Sound: The sound design in this game is amazing. Between the musical menus, the background music being truely dynamic and syncing up to the action (or lack thereof) in a match, and how guttural and viscious each attack sounds, I just can't praise it enough.
Summary: Amazing fighting game, especially as a fan of the series. One of the best ones on the market right now. My only gripes are the fact that there's no f2p model so there won't get to be as many people to try it out, and the lack of the original 2 Killer Instincts that's on the XB1 version.

I've wanted this for a long time, and it's finally happened.
The dojo (tutorials) should be your first order of business because this quite the complex fighter. There are a lot of things to know about combo's, how you can link them certain ways, use shadow, enders, juggling, how to use the right combo breaker, etc. I'd say spend an hour or so in there to get up to speed.
Sound/Music - Everything from the announcer, to individual sounds characters make from just punches sounds awesome. The music is great. I even had a little fun just scrolling through the pause menu when I figured out the jingle it would make.. lol
Graphics - Yea, it's a 3 or 4 year old game at this point since it was released on Xbone release, but it still looks awesome. No complaints.
Controls - Tight. Out of any fighter I've played, I think this one would probably be the easiest for a casual to hop in, do some damage, and have fun. Special movies are easy and combo's are a fair challenge to string together into 20+ hits. If you've ever felt the absolute frustration of games like Street Fighter that seem to require you to master frame-by-frame analysis in order to string attacks together, then you'll be relieved to know it's not a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥like that.
Online - I played 3 matches so far. Matchmaking took maybe 20 seconds at the longest to find a match. They were fair and pitted me against people of my skill level and ranking. I may come back after I do my 10 qualifying matches and do another 10 or so to give further review on this.
Replay value - There is a lot here. Several different fighters with unique styles of play. Online play. Offline play. Story Mode and some strange shadow mode where you build a team, fight, collect items, heal your team, and ultimately save the world from what I can tell.. I haven't gave that much time, so I could be entirely wrong about it.
Bottomline - I got it on sale, but I think it's worth it's full price. There's a lot to enjoy here.

I've been playing fighting games all my life (not tournament-calibur however), and I think that this remake of KI is incredible.
I love the creativity and balance between all the characters (from what I've seen and heard).  That's really hard to achieve in a game.  Plus it runs butterly smooth on my 2-year old midrange pc, the loading is fast, and the sound and hits are really sharp and visceral.  You CAN tell that the facial detail isn't as good as that found in other AAA titles in the genre, but it doesn't make that much of a difference once you start spectating the action on the 2d plane where the fighting takes place.
While I do like how fast the game plays, I wish there were some "slow but rewarding if it connects" kind of moves too.  Think of the charge moves in the Soul Calbir/Tekken series.  Granted I haven't played KI for that long, but I think I've only seen one charge move from Sabrewolf, and when the streamer playing as him tried to perform it in an online match, he failed both attempts.  I know there are characters like Aganos too, but besides those few examples, it seems like the vast majority of attacks are super fast.  However that's just a minor gripe that draws itself from my days with SF2. The fighting game genre has evolved, and KI has moved with the times just fine.
There is of course other gripes like me STILL not being able to figure out how to get my Hori Fighting Commander 3 pad to fully work (in the meantime, I'm still playing on the keyboard), and the fact that I get a "Killer Instinct didn't shut down properly" message each time I exit.  But those aren't dealbreakers.
So far, KI offers so much in style, character creativity and balanced systems that really makes this game stand out from a lot of other fighters I've seen in modern times.  And the fact that it finally came out on Steam makes it possible for Windows 7 users like myself to play this gem for their first time.
Good job, keep it up!

Alright, so when i first saw this game on Steam, I downloaded it, read the reviews, and almost uninstalled. But I realized its unfair to judge the game before trying it. This game is a ton of fun. Queue times are fast. The vehicle customization is well done, the graphics are decent, and you can group up with friends fairly easily.
But this doesn't mean it's perfect. You'll have to grind for about 12 hours into the game until you get to level 10, and be able to chose a faction. Then you grind more to get to level 10 and so on with your faction. This would be fine-except for the fact that you can purchase coins with real money. Then use coins to by weapons/parts on the market. In this game your vehicle has a power score-a score that determines how powerful your machine is. Similar power scores will be paired up together. This
stop people who paid from being matched with people with worse cars. Unfortunately some weapons have a lower power score and players can create a very exposed vehicle in exchange for having 4 homing missiles coming after you.
The fix for this is easy; make them by cosmetics/cosmetic cases only. It would solve the "pay-not-to-grind" problem and the devs would still get the money to continue development for the game. This game is still in Early Access as of writing this and I'm sure there are many changes to come. My conclusion: Give it a try. If you don't like it, no harm done.

It's a crying shame that this game has a translation that appears to have been done by slightly blind and barely bilingual orangutans because the core game itself is surprisingly entertaining. You get to do everything from marry a prince to become the proprietor of an upscale gentleman's club -- c'mon, how awesome is that? Throw in a surprisingly feisty main character (you can get her to arrange beat-downs on her enemies!), some appealing love interests (the bad boy character is a special marvel and I love the "conniving prince" as well), and some startling changes in game-play... well, this game can entertain you for a good 4-10 hours, depending on how tolerant you are of a sometimes hilariously bad translation.
Pros: The baby boy character is seriously sexy; you can play the MC as a "bad girl" also; MC is pretty freaking awesome and great at standing up for herself; some of the art is lovely and polished; nice sound-track; a variety of different game-play modes; rather surprising story-line that finds nice ways of connecting across the different paths; you'll learn a surprising amount about pastry as well!
Cons: Hilariously bad translation; there are some weird art shifts; the story-line never quite reaches the heights it could simply because of awful grammar and pacing issues.
If you can get it on sale, it's definitely worth a play. Otherwise, at full price, maybe not.

After playing this game for a bit, I have to say that it's quite enjoyable.
What it does NOT have:  complexity, items with powers, story, background changes, tile image changes, a decent end level, qualities that the great match 3 games possess.
What it does have:  matching, charm, power-ups, fun.
It's really the ridiculous things this game does that other match three games do not do.  Probably not even intentionally.  The animation sequence for the game when tiles are matched and a cascade starts - the tiles disappear, they fall for a tiny bit, they stop and start shaking, and then the animation finishes.  It does this for every single row every time something disappears.  It makes me laugh.  It's like the tiles are actually afraid to fall.  The cartoon where the wolf runs over the end of the canyon, stops running, thinks for a second, feels around with one foot, and then ONLY starts falling once it realizes that, yes, it did cross over the edge.  The tile's parents warned them this would happen if they were careless about lining up in row.
At the start of each level, the game lays out the board, but sometimes there are matches there.  It will go ahead, do it's a-scared matching animations, and give you credit for all of the points that were matched.  I don't think I've seen a matching game do this, and I've played quite a few.  Well, thank you very much for those free points!
Also, no timer.  That definitely cuts out the stress factor.  It does have limited moves, though.
I did have to repeat levels to get three stars.  It does seem very random as to what you will start with.  Could be the board of death, or it could be a points cow.  I am not sure who the target audience is here.  Cutesy cuddle lust?  I guess the target audience is, well, me...  still .... it's fun.

So, what to say about the umpteenth TellTale's narrative-driven videogame?
It must be immediately said that, concerning the plot itself, the game is, as always, extremely well-written. There are many references to the Borderlands' franchise, the most evident one being having Handsome Jack play bad [again] obviously, but the plot also seems to start with a very assested rythm that, howbeit, then tends to accelerate alot, maybe even too much; evidently enough this is seen in Chapter 5. The player plays as Rhys and Fiona, the two protagonist, although it seems initially that the true main character would be Rhys for he's the starting point of the entire story, without which nothing could have started. The cast is incredibly good and each characters is given just the enough amount of space and time to be. That's an incredibly difficult thing to manage, especially when you have such a large supporting-cast.
It also seems that Tell Tale is not making any effort to not necessarily better, but at least change the gameplay of their games. There is no evident difference in gameplay among Tales from the Borderlands, both seasons of The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us. The mechanics are always the same, however they are usually employed in slightly different ways, as is the case of the final boss fight in Chapter 5 of Tales from the Borderlands (wherein the player has to put up with more complex combinations that resembles those of videogames like Mortal Kombat or Tekken {more like Mortal Kombat, actually}). Furthermore, one should not expect any kind of difficulty in the gameplay for there are no puzzles to solve, nor conundrums to keep in mind during the unrolling of the plot. Beyond dialogue's selection, meandering around and quick time events there isn't much else to technically do, ever. Hence it transpires that Tell Tale doesn't want to evolve necessarily their games' gameplay, that may eventually lead to a stagnation of the gameplay's mechanics. It would really be fascinating if Tell Tale could embark in an evolutionary process like Quantic Dream did regarding the incredible change from Farenheit to Heavy Rain and then Beyond Two Souls.
The OST it's partially well done. Exclusively regarding the Second Chapter the soundtrack is simply amazingly perfect as it ties flawlessly with what is shown, or rather "played", at the moment. In the next three chapters it can be heard that the soundtrack seems to get more discordant with the game's scenes. The music slowly becomes clashing with the ambience and atmosphere that the story seems to create and, whether or not this discordant music was deliberately made so to advocate certain feelings within the players, it certainly leaves an ambivalent reaction, which certain player may or may not enjoy.
The graphics are what one would expect from a Tell Tale's game. Cartoonish. Concerning Borderlands own graphic style one shouldn't see many problems within this choice; however such style leaves out certain visual effects and elements that could have contributed to the dramatization of the plot.
Tales from the Borderlands is an extremely beautiful, well-written, with an astonishingly good supporting music and ,last but not least, exceptionally fun game. There are lots of laughing moments of any kind of comedy: from pure sarcasm and irony to simpler childish "humour". The only real gargantuan problem is that the game lies to you. An assertion presented to the player just before the videogame starts recites more or less:
That is not entirely true. It is clear that to a certain extent it is impossible to make a game that truly develops and tailors after your actions as one of such nature would require a colossal amount of work and workfoce to metabolise such endeavour. Nevertheless, it also true that Tales from the Borderlands it is not, under any objective analysys, a videogame in which the player's choices considerably change the events (and this is valid for The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us, too). The plot's chokepoints never ever change. There is no purposeful variation at all. What changes, based on your dialogue choices and a couple of last minute decisions, articulated on a simple distich, incredibly (and maybe sometimes excessively exacerbated) overdramatized, is the position, mood, behaviour or presence of certain characters in certain chokepoints or important events/scenes. That is all. To some this less consequential changes may seem important and may bring to meaningful moments. It did to me, it always does, but the undeniable true is that these changes are minimal. One could say that it is not the player the controls the story, but the opposite, it's the story the controls the player, whose actions can only really affect so far the plot and the cast. Certain death's always happens, certain lines are always said, but to some players that can be passed over as long as Tell Tale is able to provide a strong and colourful plot as it certainly and undoubtedly did for Tales from the Borderlands.
It is sad to realise that certain things can never be said to Handsome Jack or that the Tell Tale's guys did not want to let us really control Fiona and Rhys' romance's options (which could've been taken as far as letting the player PLAY, deeply and thoroughly, a romance between the protagonists. Such freedom, while on one hand would have certainly required a lot of more hours of development, on the other it would've given the possibility to the player to manage extensively the relantioship, of any kind, between the two protagonists), notwithstanding there are many other moments within the game that stand in for these lost possibilities.
Finally, if you like Narrative-driven videogames without any genuine obstacles presented under the form of puzzles and conundrums, hell, what the heck are you waiting for? Tales from the Borderlands delivers very good extensive laughs and a well-written story, within which the player plunges into many funny and slightly grotesque predicaments, that even those who didn't play the Boderlands videogame could enjoy fully.
I don't like to give "marks" to digital games as a number does not really explain itself independently, however if it helps you in any way I'd give a fair 7.5/7.7.

One word on the devs before I talk about the game. They ♥♥♥♥ up. They ♥♥♥♥ up quite a bit with the game. They also treat the playerbase not always nicly.
HOWEVER (yes, there is one, and no, I was not paid to say that), they normally fix the♥♥♥♥♥♥they screw up. And the playerbase is sometimes quite toxic towards them. So as long as you look for a game without too much intereatcion, you should have little to no problems.
To the game. It's a sidewards top down RPG with roguelike elements. It's all made in pixelated art sytle and is quite gory.
So what did I like?
-Fast paced, even if walking feels slow at moments
-OP feeling (just admit it, that's what you're looking for too)
-Runs quite smoothly
-Lots of loot (relics and gear)
-Different classes
-Different maps, not random generated (the base that is)
-Not too easy, but also not too hard
-Different difficulties
-Single and Multiplayer, plus Co-op (local)
-Easy controls
-Quick to hop in and hop out
What I didn't like? Some things:
-Some DLC content, just 4 of 7 acts are playable from the start (base game)
-Sometimes a bit unfair (traps sometimes seem to insta kill you cause you didn't look)
I didn't play the multiplayer, so I can't give any words for that.
As for mucis/art, it's nice, but can get a bit repetitive after 2-3hs of non-stop playing. They are adequat though.
Also, your character dies, and then you have to restart the level. However, your gear and your character level stay, so you can level up by try-and-error. So if you are interested in it, you should enjoy the game.
You have the choice between melee and ranged characters, but IMO, the ranged ones are simply way better. You also can play safer with them.
So you start out in a map and defeat the waves of enemies that the game throws at you. After every so and so waves, you have to fight a bass and then progress to the next level. After 4 or 5 levels you then face the chapter boss, that you have to defeat to get acces to the next act. And so you grind your way out. After the first playtrough, you can then replay the entire part on a higher difficulty. After that's done, you can do it again, and again, and again until you are happy with what you achieved.
TL; DR and Rating
The game is very fun for singleplayer RPG roguelike action. I would absolute recommend this, especially if you are looking for a game for those 10 mins during and update, or when you have to leave soon again. It's similar to The Binding of Isaac, without that feel for "one more run".
So I would rate it a 8/10, leaning towards a 9/10, as it is very fun and a little game for inbetween

Trying to be as neutral as possible, I still find myself echoing many of the comments made by others. The game is a fast and fun roguelike with enough customization to be enjoyable without being overwhelming. It's good for a few hours of fun.
That said, it has gone through several changes to mechanics since I bought it, some of which affect balance and playability DRAMATICALLY. The mana system complaints are valid; it's frustrating to have high-level characters, into which you have invested much, suddenly become unplayable because their skills cost more than their maximum mana. The changes to skill synergies and itemization also significantly changed the game, though some may appreciate the changes. I enjoyed the speed of the game...the changes have increased the depth, which some players may like, but the game has lost its easy-going charm to me.
All that to say: the game has been fun in the past, and may continue to be so. Be aware, though, that MAJOR changes have come since release, and may continue to come, that may completely change your enjoyment of the game.

Electronic Super Joy is a precision platformer.
If you compare ESJ to genre rock star Super Meat Boy, you'll find a lot more conventional physics, and longer levels portioned by checkpoints. There's much emphasis on timing and a few gimmick levels. Tight controls, a unique stomp ability and lots of autoscroll make it a fast-paced experience.
The game has a hit-or-miss atmosphere. If you mind electronic dance music, flashing lights or corny sexual humour, you'll be annoyed. If not, you can have a good time.
Level design is pretty well thought-out, but there's some cheap shots and unintuitive segments.
The difficulty varies from moderately to very tough, and for a greater challenge there's incentives for no death runs, speed runs and collecting bonus stars.
If the premise doesn't put you off, you'll probably enjoy this game!
Get it when it is on discount. A wonderful game to play with friends!

This game is one of a kind, bringing RPG and Shooter together with its great art style and crude humor. You can choose between 4 different characters, all with different stats and abilities, and then you go on an epic adventure of loot and battles which will blow your mind and keep you busy for hours.
I would like to go over some problems the game has, though.
No FOV slider- If you want to change your FOV, you have to go into the files and add your own hotkey for changing it. This problem was resolved in Borderlands 2 +
No fast travelling to DLC areas- You can only fast travel to the starting area of a DLC, so if you are really far into the DLC you can't fast travel to your current quests are, you have to walk all the way there. This doesn't seem like a huge deal but when you are trying to farm bosses or something it gets super ♥♥♥♥♥♥. This problem was resolved in Borderlands 2 +
No official mod support- This is a problem with all Borderlands games, they are almost un modable. Borderlands 1 is probably the most modable of the 3, but even thats pretty eh. Hopefully the next game has official mod support.
Story- Most people complain that this game doesn't really have a story. I don't care since I don't spend the hundreds of hours I've spent in Borderlands for the story. But even then, it does have a story behind, the problem being that it tells most of it is told through text whenever you accept or hand in a quest. This problem is resolved in Borderlands 2 + though.
The challenges- This is another problem fixed within the new Borderlands. Borderlands has a challenge system, which is much better in Borderlands 2 + with its badass ranks and stuff. In borderlands 1 its only really used to earn extra xp, but some of the challenges are ridiculous to complete. Like, for example, Winning 1000 duels. This means that you have to sit there for hours, winning duels with another player over and over and over again just to complete it. Luckily there is no achievement to complete every challenge in this game.
Being someone who has played Borderlands since it first came out in 2009 (On Xbox), I think its fair to say that I am a pretty hardcore Borderlands fan. I would highly recommend every single Borderlands game to anyone interested in shooters or RPGs.

This was one of the best surprises I had this year. A great game with solid gameplay and story, and not many negative things to be said about it.
+ Great story and narrative. Characters are shockingly likeable, from the protagonist to the secondary characters. Two different timelines based on a decision made by the player at the beginning of the game increases the replay value as well.
+ A love story told in an interesting and mature way, not the "Will-They-Won't-They" cringefest you'd usually expect from couples in games.
+ Gameplay is solid, pretty straightforward, almost generic. No powers or gimmicks. You get to shoot people and dual-wield guns for extra coolness. It also encourages a more aggreesive playstyle since you sacrifice the ability to take cover in exchange for increased firepower.
+ Stealth action is not forced upon you. You can kill enemies silently with a pistol and silencer (not always), or you can kick the door and raise hell, your call. Useful to finish off commanders before they can call reinforcements.
+ Perks are acquired by completing specific tasks/challenges instead of simply buying them with XP.
+ Good level design with different routes to take and stuff to collect along the way.
+ Challenge on Hard difficulty is just right. The Very Hard difficult is still viable for people who like it rough.
- Enemy AI is laughably bad at times. Enemies will ignore dead bodies ("Oh look, a corpse, must be Tuesday") and bullets hitting walls 5 inches from them when you try to shoot them sealthly and miss.
- Gameplay might be TOO straighforward for people who are used to playing shooters. As I said there are no powers or anything to make it really different from so many other shooting games out there.
- Not that much enemy variety. You get to shoot regular nazis, improved nazis, super nazis, nazi dogs and nazi robots, and that's it (I think). There's like three bosses in the entire game, none of which are special in any way.
The story alone is worth the full price.

This isn't a negative review, but I cannot recommend Squad for this price at this time.
Squad has a lot of potential.  There is a lot to learn in it and the players I dealt with were very nice.  However, it just is not polished enough to warrant a $39.99 price tag as an Early Access Game.  I had picked it up during the Steam Summer sale for half that and I still requested a refund just because I do not think it is worth $19.99 as a sale at this point.  Not only are the game's components in need of polishing, but the graphics quality needs it too.  The screenshots look nice, but in-game the foliage and environment makes it really hard to see people that should be able to be seen. This meant that when my squad came under fire, it was almost impossible to locate where the bullets were coming from and see the enemy.
Obviously, as an early access game, I am sure it will become more polished, so my only real complaint here is the price; I just don't think at this time it is worth $39.99, or even a sales price of $19.99.

Let's get the basic points done first:
Pros:
- Nice art
- Decent stat-raising mechanic
Neutral:
- Story is okay
Cons:
- Translation and editing are bad
- Character development is non-existent
- Choices are basic, obvious and have no effect
When I say the character development isn't there, I mean it. You have the basic story, then you meet the four guys and then you pretty much have zero interaction with them until the end of the game. All you do is go to their room every night to feed them cake (which is a tedious thing to keep doing anyway) and their one line of dialogue when you go to see them eventually changes from "hey, how's it going?" to "holy ♥♥♥♥ I want to marry you and love you forever." All of them will do this if you raise all of their affection but you never actually have any other interation with them apart from a couple of short, pointless scenes so it's really weird when all of them are suddenly totally in love with you. At the end of the game, you choose a guy and get a small chapter 3 where you go off wherever with them and it almost becomes like a decent otome with actual time spent with the guy but...then it ends.
Should also note that with the exception of Haonan, all of the characters, including the MC, sound the same, have the same style of speech, there is nothing to distinguish them. They all have NO personality.
Also it amuses me that at the end of Christopher's route he asks her to please call him by his first name and she looks up at him and goes "Cheng..." Lololol, wtf Sakura, you suck. Such bad editing.
Also the choices are borderline worthless, they barely need to be there, and the story seems to jump around and not really get resolved. It's also so badly organised and worked into the game that you don't care about it, about the MC, about any of the characters.
Basically, this game is bad.

Interstellar Marines is basically a sci-fi shooter that takes place in the future. Now, a good thing about this game, it isn't a Starwars fad ripoff. You won't see flying people with lightsabers nor "pew-pew" guns. The Marines in this game wear their own, pretty unique and eventually customizable, armor including a visor you can even lift up. The guns are, currently, basically the same type of guns we use today with futuristic models. They still use solid bullets and have recoil so it is definetly relatable, The game's graphics aren't honestly that bad, and the game is definetly optimized, at least for my rig. One of the best parts of this game, it has that nostalgia of being an old school game with the benefits of modern technology. I personally have high hopes for the game.
The bad part? The game development is argueably slow, but the devs are extremely active and the piles of updates we have recieved so far is definetly an on-going trend. Each update adds more and more of what the devs promised, and many times they reveal "proof" of what they are working on. It is still an early acess game, don't let those who are under-educated try to tell you that unless the game has weekly updates, its bad. That is definetly not the case, and I hope to see more people in-game soon.
P.S. If you have high hopes for this great game like me, I recommend you buy the spearhead edition. That extra money really supports the devs and you WILL(as in the future when it is released) get rewarded with cosmetics.

Have you ever built something that was Pretty Good?  Not Perfect, but pretty good.  And you step back, look at it, and say to yourself "Oh, that bit's not quite right.  I can fix that, I can make it better."  If you had your friends there, they would pull you away and say "No, fix it on the next one; leave this one alone!"  But you're alone in the room.
And so you start poking, prodding, trimming, shifting, breaking, and glueing.  And somehow it's now worse than what you started with?  What was once a simple science fair project is now an 8 foot tall Paper Mache Volcano you can't even get out the door.  And where did that glitter come from?  Do I smell Bleach?
We all have.  This game, this game is where the Dev's have done that.  I would love to recommend this game.  And at several points during the game's life, I would have.  But noone's been there to slap the Dev's hands as they swoop back in to fix one last thing.
A tinkering here, a balance pass there.  Add an entirely new layer of stats. An accidental character wipe.  A purposeful gear wipe.  Break all the stats.  More tinkering.  Fix A, Break B!  Redo the stats again.  Redo the Gear again. Base a balance pass off of a very narrow range of statistics.  Be suprised when there are unintended consequences for the other 80% of the players.
If you liked the game a month ago, you won't recognize it now.
If you buy it and like it today, don't expect it to live in the current itteration very long.
Sure the game's cheap.  You'll probably get your money's worth if you put a solid week into it.  Just don't expect anything to work a month from now.
Edit:
I put this game down quite a while back for all the reasons I listed above.  Steam's front page redesign brought recent patches to my attention.  It appears all my previous gripes still stand as several of the last 4 patches are listed as having wild balance changes to various characters and specific portions of the game.

Command & Conquer Red Alert 3 Uprising not launching/working on Windows 10. after soo long trying to figure out some way to get the game to run on Windows 10, I FINALLY found a solution just when I was messing around in the display driver settings. First of all my laptop is the late 2016 Razer Blade with the GTX 1060 and Core i7 6700HQ. Okay here's how I got it to work on Windows 10, first, make sure the game is not running as an administrator and all the compatibility mode/settings are disabled, I know most people probably enabled these trying to get the game to work (including myself). Okay next, open settings, in the search bar type "device manager" then select it, next select "display adaptors" then "Intel HD Graphics" then go to "driver" and select "Roll Back Driver..." then just give it a minute, the screen may turn blue for a second or whatnot, and that's it! the game should run perfectly! you can adjust it to whatever graphics or resolution you want and you can use a dedicated GPU (if you have one). if this helped you please like this comment so others will see! :)

I won't pretend like it's the best fighting game ever, but it's definitely my favorite fighting game from the last few years. I think I've easily put over 100+ hours into the Windows 10 version and I'll probably put just as much, if not more, into the Steam version.
What can I say? This game just hits so many positives for me, I'm actually struggling to find many negatives. I'll try to list what I love about this game.
First and foremost, you get EVERYTHING and I do mean EVERYTHING, every character, every cosmetic skin (except for a few, more on that later) and it's an incredible port, it was released for the Windows Store and that version was an absolute delight, although a few things regarding the online interaction were a bit janky (fixed on the Steam version), but overall, the game doesn't need a powerful rig to run at it's best. The Steam version is the exact same game in terms of performance and content.
I've heard about a few people having trouble setting up their controllers, this shouldn't be much of an issue if you configure Xpadder or Steam itself to use whatever controller you want.
Content wise, you'll definitely get more than what you paid for, the Story mode is different for Season 1 and 2 characters, but for some reason, Season 3 characters never got their own story mode, BUT they definitely compensated it with the Shadow Lords mode.
Shadow Lords is like a hybrid between an RPG and a Rogue-like, you start with any character you want, Gargos is coming and it's bad news for the planet, it's inevitable, but you must prepare for his arrival or even delay it as much as possible. You create your own party of characters (3 in total) and you choose how to proceed in the playthrough, it's always different and it always changes with each decision you make. You get new items and boosts to fight against your oponents and if you choose, you can even play Multiplayer with said items and boosts.
I haven't even touched on the Shadow Labs yet, these are AI characters who replicate your very moves, your mannerisms and even your mistakes, the better you fight, the better your shadow gets. You can also fight against other players shadows and if you defeat them, they can challenge your shadow to a rematch and it can start fierce rivalries.
You win "Shadow Points" that you can use to purchase unique Shadow skins for your character, if you so desire.
There's also the survival mode, where you fight as long as you can, you can either play it offline with the regular AI, or you can fight against shadows.
And the multiplayer netcode is legendary, absolutely no lag to speak of, I only get laggy if someone is watching Netflix on my end.
Oh and make sure you also buy that soundtrack, it's from Mick Gordon, the same guy who did the DOOM soundtrack and it's just as bada$$ in this game as in DOOM.
I recommend setting the volume of voices, ambience and everything else to 60, the fight sounds to 80 and the music to 100.
So yeah, tons of polish, loads of content, wonderful soundtrack and a reasonable price, there's a lot to like here.

To start with I'll say that I am a Squad backer since before it's Early Access debut due to my love for it's spiritual predecessor, an amazing mod of perhaps one of the most classic multiplayer FPS games ever made: Project Reality for Battlefield 2. I simply love Squad and PR:BF2 so am definately biased coming into this review, so certainly read it understanding that upfront.

Being a person that typically prefers simiulated realism over the arcade or action type shooters I realize I'm part of a smaller percentage of the overall FPS playing population but I think the genre and the community is growing. Of course the modders that were private users of the software were the ones that created what is now Project Reality and other games that were created on the foundation of things already quite playable and great, so hats off to them.

I personally believe this title is meant to fulfill a need and a want in the multiplayer shooter community for a tactical/realism genre that necessitates the use of teamwork, communication, coordination and hierarchy to attain dominance of the battlefield ingame. Some people who played the vanilla versions of the Battlefield series and other classics were still left wanting, many of us wanted the unforgiving realism. I distinctly remembering one day while playing BF4 that everyone was just sprinting to wherever they thought they might get the most kills, and in most cases the use of audio communication was completely ignored except by small groups of friends.

Obviously the counter argument here is that it's a game but the lack of role playing in shooters while propelling your canon fodder against the enemy as if a real soldier would do the same has always bothered me because I prefer the realism. The following are some other elements of tactical realism that you can expect to experience in Squad:
- Some of the more experienced and veteran Squad Leaders may expect players to follow instructions not only for kit selection due to battlefield and logistics needs but also in regards to manuevering. For example, it's important to be concious of the formation and spacing used in certain situations and manuevers for many reasons. Here's a few particular reason it's important: a single, well placed grenade can take out a whole fireteam; a single VBIED can wipe out a Forward Operating Base; while on foot in an infantry unit, you may need to be tightly spaced and prone while maintaining trigger discipline because an operational objective may require that you don't give away your position by firing until a particular target has opened themselves to an attack. There's many other scenarios that can play out depending on the competence and cohesion of a squad that is generally decided within the first few minutes of a game.
-The bullets and shrapenel cause bleeding and not just health drop and death. From stamina simulation that's based on the class of soldier due to the gear required for the kit and it's relation to the environment (i.e. running uphill with an AR class is going to tire you out, so be thoughtful about your use of sprinting and cover). There is increased recoil and decreased targer aquisition timing with larger caliber weapons which feels natural and correct. As with the predecessor they introduced simulated suppression mechainic that was seen as critical due to the realworld use in combat as a tactical necessity. The snaps of enemy bullets in your general direction can actually be startling at times and if close enough will cause some visual limitation or blurring as it might in reality due to wincing/flinching and trying to cover yourself however futile the effort, the devs for PR:BF2 wanted a way to simulate that where it woulnd't make the use of suppression OP'ed. I think they found a good balance personally. Since that touches on sound some I'll state that the weapon sounds are all wonderfully powerful and sound great including the breaking of the sound barrier by high powered rifle rounds.
-In Mechanized Units and in some cases the Technical Vehicle Units/HUMVEE Units it can be important to utilize foot mobile infantry around the vehicles due to the realworld and simulated blindspots of these units. This mainly pertains to the armor. All it takes is an irregular with an RPG-7 at the right vantage point to end the lives of 8 plus soldiers. However the report of their heavy weaponry and the destructive power can be enough to cause whole rifle squads to run away, cower or ultimately be wiped out if used correctly. They are an asset to be leveraged while keeping the vulnerabilities in mind. The Squad Leader is the unit that approves the use of vehicles by other units from the map.
-The battlefield defenses building and logistics elements are other important factors. It's not uncommon in games with seasoned players to have whole squads dedicated to logistics and resupply as well as fire support in other circumstances. Another awesome teamwork component that is unique and adds depth to the tactical realism and strategy. The building mechanic is awesome and can advantage or disadvantage teams depending on how it's used. Sometimes it's not smart to build a bunch of defensive barriers and really dig into particular locations that you're capturing and sometimes it is. There's also instances where building in areas that you aren't capturing can be useful or provide a needed edge. All the general rifleman kits have shovels for building and the Squad Leaders approve the building plans in a radial menu.
I didn't plan to list every possible component of realism in the game in this review, because I plan on making a more comprehensive review for this game and others after some work to prepare. So another review of Squad and other games will be forthcoming from me in the future. In conclusion Squad is really shaping up as a project and it's my belief it will continue to do so. There is still a lot of content the developers plan to add and they've hit the mark consistently till now. I greatly anticipate the full release of this game whenever it should come.  There will be an Air combat component to the game as well as other exciting features that are planned in the developement cycle. I absolutely think this game is worth the money if you are a fan of tactical realism and strategy and want to see that implemented more in first person shooters. The people who enjoy more thoughtful experiences that don't reward Rambo wannabe's should see great opportunity and potential here!
