This otome visual novel by Chengguang Youxi（橙光游戏）, Shi Xiaonan（石小楠）and Forever Entertainment S.A. feature an orphan girl Sakura Asakusa who was raised and brought up at a monastery in a remote island on the western part of the Carseland Kingdom. Amidst the backdrop of pastry making and pastries being exclusive only among nobles and high officials within the kingdom, the emergence of St. Patras College as an academy to teach pastry making to all who enrol at the college regardless of social status with full scholarships being awarded to promising applicants and students who score S in their examinations, a mysterious notebook which details numerous pastry making recipes that was found with Sakura at the monastery and the support and encouragement by Sakura's close friends, neighbours and a visitor at West Island made Sakura decide to pursue her ambition to enrol at St. Patras College.
Over the course of this visual novel, Sakura will build up her attributes, learn and discover up to 8 new pastry recipes, obtain up to 4 pets and 10 treasures to help her, gain favourability with 4 main characters and 13 supporting characters, discover 5 clues about Sakura's origins, gain admission into St. Patras College and pass two semester exams and progress along a main character route
and obtain up to 13 optional in-game achievements.
The story and plot is written as a romance visual novel with a share of comedy, tragedy, mystery, drama and thriller. There are dating simulator and stat management mechanics with conditions for progressing further into the story clearly listed out in the tasks section of the menu. The visual novel also has plenty of general knowledge on numerous pastries, desserts, beverages and Eastern mythology references. Background music, artworks and CGs are great with pleasant background music to match the main characters and settings in the game and nice chibi artwork on Sakura's pets and main characters. Highly recommended for those who like a medium-length(Between 10-30 hours) visual novel with stat management and dating simulator mechanics and random facts on a large variety of pastries, desserts, beverages and Eastern culture and mythology.
The game is also sometimes at discount with up to 90% off coupons being available from badge crafting, trading section of the game's discussion forums and from coupon gifting Steam groups(eg. Coupon Dumpster) at the time of this review.

Though I usually don't review games, I am inclined to post this review because of some of the overwhelmingly negative and incorrect things I've read amongst the 'most helpful' comments. Things like "they are no closer to a campaign and coop today than they were when the game came on steam almost a year ago", "they barley [sic] release any updates" and "IT IS A RIP-OFF AT ANY PRICE!!". A lot of this is simply false, yet those reviews are still hurting the chances of this game simply by being there. So if you've read those reviews and are now doubting whether or not you'd like to buy Interstellar Marines, allow me to address some of the misconceptions that those reviews are propagating.
Firstly, contrary to what some reviewers who've played less than two hours of this game say, this game is extremely close to receiving co-op. The developers have recently stated that co-op play will be arriving in the next update, aka before August. Since this co-op is part of the game's overarching campaign, this means that work on the campaign is now bearing fruit and we will have a single-player campaign to play sooner rather than later (unlike, as some knowledgeable commenters might have you believe, in five years minimum). Moreover, this game has multiplayer. It isn't polished or as complete as AAA titles like CoD or Battlefield, no question about that, but it's still quite enjoyable. Besides, that's why we call games like this alphas...
The accusation that the developers barely release any updates is also false. Major title updates (e.g. an entirely new gamemode, new maps, an overhaul of the HUD and damage systems) are released every one to two months. Intermediate progress updates are usually not shown on the site, which is why some people may get the impression that no progress is being made, but development progress can be monitored on twitter; the developers tweet updates quite regularly and are excellent at interacting with the community.
Finally, this game is not a rip-off. There's a reason why this game is in the 'early access' section of Steam and has "Early Access Game" stamped on it in big, bold letters. Right now, you're not paying £13.99 (£8.39 with summer sale) for a finished experience. You're not even paying it for a game that has more than two guns or for a game where there is any sort of single-player. You're giving the developers your money because they have an idea that you want realised. An idea for a sci-fi shooter that doesn't follow the cliched approach of CoD or Halo, one that feels like true hard-sf rather than the rehashed "Big bad aliens are comming to kill us! Quick, call Doom Gu- I mean Master Chief!". The fact that the devs have stuck with this game since 2005, even though the majority of their plans were foiled in 2008 by the recession just as the game was about to release, just shows that they're still dedicated to bringing us this product and the idea that lies behind it. So don't think of it as paying £13.99 for an alpha. Think of it as buying a £13.99 bond the return from which is an AAA title in a year or two.
Overall, this is a very promising game. It even has crouch now! On a serious note though, for a team that has less developers than your hand has fingers, this game is very impressive. They have built a working multiplayer that, bar the optimisation issues and current lack of weapon customization, is almost as polished as CoD ever was. They are on the cusp of releasing the first part of this game's campaign along with co-op and have built a graphically-impressive shooter in Unity3D, a game engine I used to mainly associate with free-to-play online games. Taking into account the hardships they've faced, their progress is quite impressive and now is the perfect time to buy into the game. It's on sale, it's about to receive co-op along with a campaign and the pace of development seems to be picking up. So if, like me, you want to play a shooter that does things differently from the status quo, I suggest you buy this game. The more people that do, the greater a chance this game has of becomming something truly stunning.

This game is one of a kind, bringing RPG and Shooter together with its great art style and crude humor. You can choose between 4 different characters, all with different stats and abilities, and then you go on an epic adventure of loot and battles which will blow your mind and keep you busy for hours.
I would like to go over some problems the game has, though.
No FOV slider- If you want to change your FOV, you have to go into the files and add your own hotkey for changing it. This problem was resolved in Borderlands 2 +
No fast travelling to DLC areas- You can only fast travel to the starting area of a DLC, so if you are really far into the DLC you can't fast travel to your current quests are, you have to walk all the way there. This doesn't seem like a huge deal but when you are trying to farm bosses or something it gets super ♥♥♥♥♥♥. This problem was resolved in Borderlands 2 +
No official mod support- This is a problem with all Borderlands games, they are almost un modable. Borderlands 1 is probably the most modable of the 3, but even thats pretty eh. Hopefully the next game has official mod support.
Story- Most people complain that this game doesn't really have a story. I don't care since I don't spend the hundreds of hours I've spent in Borderlands for the story. But even then, it does have a story behind, the problem being that it tells most of it is told through text whenever you accept or hand in a quest. This problem is resolved in Borderlands 2 + though.
The challenges- This is another problem fixed within the new Borderlands. Borderlands has a challenge system, which is much better in Borderlands 2 + with its badass ranks and stuff. In borderlands 1 its only really used to earn extra xp, but some of the challenges are ridiculous to complete. Like, for example, Winning 1000 duels. This means that you have to sit there for hours, winning duels with another player over and over and over again just to complete it. Luckily there is no achievement to complete every challenge in this game.
Being someone who has played Borderlands since it first came out in 2009 (On Xbox), I think its fair to say that I am a pretty hardcore Borderlands fan. I would highly recommend every single Borderlands game to anyone interested in shooters or RPGs.

Just as a preface and a tl;dr, this is a good game (Don't let my time fool you if it says .5 hours or something on my record, it's actually about 16). If you like Dragon ball Z, you should look into this.
That being said, there are a few minor issues I have with the game:
-Some events/characters were changed or left out of the main story. Obviously, they can't have everybody in the game, but characters like Android 16 would have been a great addition to the android saga missions. There is also a lack of Bulma and Chi Chi, I want my domestic abuse simulator, dang it (Please don't hate me, I was only kidding ;~;)! Although, as side characters, I understand their omission from the main story.
-Some moves cannot be used outside of 1v1 matches. That feels incredibly restrictive. The only move I've come across (and it may be the only, correct me if I'm wrong) that does this is Body Switch, which would be awesome to use in missions. I realize that it's cheap, but that's what Captain Ginyu taught me to be! Maybe only being able to use it in already cleared missions would be a middle ground?
-Character creation feels limited. Don't get me wrong, it's amazing, but your character either becomes mostly physical or mostly Ki based. There is little room for the middle and still being able to clear missions easily enough. Also transformations are limited outside of the Saiyan class.
-I don't know why this one bothers me, but if my character just finished, let's say, the Buu saga, and did a 1v1 against Hercule, why should he stand a chance? I realize that balance is needed in a game like this, but if I want to destroy someone utterly, I should be able to. Again, not sure why that bothers me.
-Time to get drops. It can take HOURS to get a drop you are looking for. Typical of this genre, but might want to be shortened a bit.
There is quite a bit of good, however:
-A decently long story. Anywhere from 9 – 14 hours on the main story alone, based on your skill level as a player.

Quick Review:
I haven't even seen all the characters, let alone played as them. I've spent most of my time as Hisako, but dabbled with a few others. I'm by no means a master at the game, but I (think I) understand the mechanics, which IMO are the most important part of a fighting game. The game is deep, and in very surprising ways. A lot of the back-and-forth of other fighting games has shifted *into* the combo system here. You still throw pokes and there are mix-ups aplenty, but landing a hit and going into a combo is only the beginning of the mind games due to the intricate combo and combo breaker system. It's really refreshing to actually be encouraged to freestyle combos, rather than just learn "the best" combo and fish for a hit to play a rhythm/memory game. Don't get me wrong, I love many other fighting games from Arcana Heart 3 to Marvel 3, but the uniqueness of KI is refreshing.
The graphics are great, with over the top designs and ridiculous amounts of effects and particles. It's kind of garish to be honest, but I do like the aesthetic.
Soundtrack is awesome, I highly suggest buying it with the OST if you like heavy, epic, electro, metal music.
About a year ago I played the free/demo version on the windows store and I had to turn down a bunch of settings to pass the online test (to prevent system slow down causing problems), but it seems they have done LOTS of optimisation since then as I can run it at max settings, 1080p with the exact same computer. For reference, I'm playing on a laptop with:
Nvidia GTX 1060 6GB
16GB RAM
Windows 10
Using a MadCatz Street Fighter 4 SE Stick, Xbox 360 version
The online allows for crossplay between Xbone/Windows Store/Steam play, EXCEPT in ranked, where it is Steam only. I do hope they integrate ranked in the future, but I've always been able to find matches and for the most part they run very smoothly. One of the better fighting game net codes I've experienced.

Whilst I think this game is a pretty great example of an early access game done (mostly) right, I simply can't recommend it in good faith.
It's a good game with a bunch of really nice features, you've got animal taming, base building, it's easy to mod(taking a look at the workshop for Rimworld would pretty much convince you to buy it singlehandedly), it's even got imprisoning raiders and selling their organs for cash, pretty much everything you can imagine it's either been added or modded into the game.
Now to why i can't recommend it : It's broken.
Not in the traiditonal 'the devs are bad at building games and you can't take a step without falling through the floor' sense, but in a much MUCH worse sense.
Y'see, no matter how much money you spend on a good gaming rig, no matter how much you optimise and overclock everything, it'll run pretty much exactly the same as running it on a Playstation1 since the game is only capable of using one CPU core and the RAM is capped to a very low level(as with most other 32bit .exes).
'Surely it can't be that bad, if it's built to only take up that much then surely it simply doesn't need to take up any more'
Loading games that you've spent 50+ to 100+ hours(depending how you play) will completely crash the game, picking map sizes above the lowest two sizes (the recommended default is size 3 or above) will result in MASSIVE stuttering, dropped FPS and input lag after spending 20+ hours on the map, building a base that's any larger(or just more complex) than Riverwood in Skyrim will result in performance issues and possibly make the savegame too big to load.
I want to recommend this game, I genuinely do, but in it's current state I simply can't. The game's downfall is down to it having so much fun stuff to do which simply can't be supported by a game engine that can't run on anything except single threading and such minimalistic RAM. It's like Dwarf Fortress had a far more developed kid but it was still expected to run on the same spec caps as Dwarf Fortress

Killer Instinct -- an enjoyable fighting game in keeping with Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat.
The steam edition is on par with the definitive edition otherwise offered on the Windows store and Xbox. As such, all characters are fully unlocked. Although there are micro transactions, these are entirely optional--as all skins/badges et al. are accessible via regular game play/grinding and are all totally cosmetic.
The major two complaints with this iteration of Killer Instinct are as follows:
1. Cross platform play for Ranked Matches is blocked between Steam and Win/Xbox player bases. This seems arbitrary and very short sighted on the part of M$.
2. The online performance test, which is required for online ranked matches, can prohibit players from participating in ranked matches if their system is deemed to be below certain undisclosed thresholds. This "black box" testing is unacceptable as several instances of otherwise viable rigs have been reported as failing this test. However, the feedback afforded from the ingame diagnostic does not give any viable information/suggestions as to what is causing the respective low score (It simply gives a score with a minimum threshold of 1000). This can result in systems, which can run the game perfectly well in unranked matches and single player, being unable to participate in the ranked system.
Overall the game is fun and fits well with the original coin-op iterations of KI1 and KI2. However, for online play, due to the opaque performance testing and segregated ranked player bases, cannot be fully recommended. Simply put, the design and implementation of these two elements are abject failures and seem highly arbitrary.
Purchase the game for solo play or online unranked play.
Do not purchase the game for online ranked play (as you may well be blocked from participating by the game itself).
Do not purchase the game if you are keen to complete all achievements -- as several require access to online ranked matches to which you may not have access.

I recommend this game even though it will take me quite some time to conquer the control physics.  This game is not for amatuers..... I have some real life riding experience and know that I cant just expect to jump on a 1000cc race bike on some track and expect to be instantly good at it.  This game requires experience and knowledge of bike control ie keeping the bike stable using weight transfer via correct braking and acceleration techniques.  You can be an absolute gun at car racing games but do not think this will make you instantly good at this game, the only skills transferrred here are knowledge of racing line; controlling your vehicle is much more complex here.  The difficulty in mastering bike control is as with all racing games not being able to feel the virtual traction but on top of that you are unable to feel the virtual weight transfer making it a constant learning experience corner to corner.  If you have some track experience on motorcycles or extensive road biking you will be able to adapt your skills/knowledge in this game but as I have found
still may struggle to ajust to virtual physics: THIS WILL TAKE TIME TO CONQUER!!!
LOVE the burnout dynamics ;D  If your the kinda racer who gets frustrated stack after stack, take a breath, get back on the bike and let roar with some AWSOME smokin' of the back wheel letting loose into some stompin "wheelies" and finish up mastering the "Stoppy" for some side fun.  Adds more thrill to sometimes frustrating "neck-break" racing.
I congratulate the dev team for the bike control physics; NAILED IT!!! Possibly as close as you will get without actually real world biking.
To those who have given a negative review for reasons such as control........ READ ABOVE and understand this game requires EXTENSIVE BIKE knowledge, maybe sit for a real world learners permit to help understand bike control.
For anyone with real world biking experience this will be a blast and give you an avenue for letting loose riding like you never should on the open roads unless you have a death wish of course.
Constant practice in this game may even help for real world riding giving that you can open the throttle all the way without the risk of death or wrecking your beloved road beast, ultimately getting a feel for high speed track control.  All without needing a track permit and a billion bucks to afford the costs of racing.
This game is for anyone who is a bike enthusiast and wants a more life like gaming experience.... Riding in this game is not at all like jumping on the many bikes of GTA or SAINTS ROW........
For anyone who just loves racing games, give this game time.... practice, practice, stack and more practice.  I definately will be..... saves stacking in the real world :D
SOME TIPS:
* Change views,  Ive found that the on bike first person view is more forgiving for cornering control.....
* REMOVE majority of riding assists, really get full control of the bike,  also doing burnouts is heaps better :p
* Use of both brakes is important for getting the correct shift in weight transfer as is the weight transfer on stick (JOYSTICK)
* XBOX controller recommended for the analogue acceleration and braking..... Could not imagine attempting with the digital touch of the keyboard
* Ride MANUAL, who in the real world races with an AUTOMATIC!!! If you want full control this is a must...
* YOU ARE NOT VALENTINO ROSSI, dont expect to win every race..... be persistant with racing and accept track position if you stack, get back on the bike an finish the race.  Winning will come with practice... (I really need to follow my own advice here, Stack, restart race, stack, gain good position, stack, F***, restart race)

To start with I'll say that I am a Squad backer since before it's Early Access debut due to my love for it's spiritual predecessor, an amazing mod of perhaps one of the most classic multiplayer FPS games ever made: Project Reality for Battlefield 2. I simply love Squad and PR:BF2 so am definately biased coming into this review, so certainly read it understanding that upfront.

Being a person that typically prefers simiulated realism over the arcade or action type shooters I realize I'm part of a smaller percentage of the overall FPS playing population but I think the genre and the community is growing. Of course the modders that were private users of the software were the ones that created what is now Project Reality and other games that were created on the foundation of things already quite playable and great, so hats off to them.

I personally believe this title is meant to fulfill a need and a want in the multiplayer shooter community for a tactical/realism genre that necessitates the use of teamwork, communication, coordination and hierarchy to attain dominance of the battlefield ingame. Some people who played the vanilla versions of the Battlefield series and other classics were still left wanting, many of us wanted the unforgiving realism. I distinctly remembering one day while playing BF4 that everyone was just sprinting to wherever they thought they might get the most kills, and in most cases the use of audio communication was completely ignored except by small groups of friends.

Obviously the counter argument here is that it's a game but the lack of role playing in shooters while propelling your canon fodder against the enemy as if a real soldier would do the same has always bothered me because I prefer the realism. The following are some other elements of tactical realism that you can expect to experience in Squad:
- Some of the more experienced and veteran Squad Leaders may expect players to follow instructions not only for kit selection due to battlefield and logistics needs but also in regards to manuevering. For example, it's important to be concious of the formation and spacing used in certain situations and manuevers for many reasons. Here's a few particular reason it's important: a single, well placed grenade can take out a whole fireteam; a single VBIED can wipe out a Forward Operating Base; while on foot in an infantry unit, you may need to be tightly spaced and prone while maintaining trigger discipline because an operational objective may require that you don't give away your position by firing until a particular target has opened themselves to an attack. There's many other scenarios that can play out depending on the competence and cohesion of a squad that is generally decided within the first few minutes of a game.
-The bullets and shrapenel cause bleeding and not just health drop and death. From stamina simulation that's based on the class of soldier due to the gear required for the kit and it's relation to the environment (i.e. running uphill with an AR class is going to tire you out, so be thoughtful about your use of sprinting and cover). There is increased recoil and decreased targer aquisition timing with larger caliber weapons which feels natural and correct. As with the predecessor they introduced simulated suppression mechainic that was seen as critical due to the realworld use in combat as a tactical necessity. The snaps of enemy bullets in your general direction can actually be startling at times and if close enough will cause some visual limitation or blurring as it might in reality due to wincing/flinching and trying to cover yourself however futile the effort, the devs for PR:BF2 wanted a way to simulate that where it woulnd't make the use of suppression OP'ed. I think they found a good balance personally. Since that touches on sound some I'll state that the weapon sounds are all wonderfully powerful and sound great including the breaking of the sound barrier by high powered rifle rounds.
-In Mechanized Units and in some cases the Technical Vehicle Units/HUMVEE Units it can be important to utilize foot mobile infantry around the vehicles due to the realworld and simulated blindspots of these units. This mainly pertains to the armor. All it takes is an irregular with an RPG-7 at the right vantage point to end the lives of 8 plus soldiers. However the report of their heavy weaponry and the destructive power can be enough to cause whole rifle squads to run away, cower or ultimately be wiped out if used correctly. They are an asset to be leveraged while keeping the vulnerabilities in mind. The Squad Leader is the unit that approves the use of vehicles by other units from the map.
-The battlefield defenses building and logistics elements are other important factors. It's not uncommon in games with seasoned players to have whole squads dedicated to logistics and resupply as well as fire support in other circumstances. Another awesome teamwork component that is unique and adds depth to the tactical realism and strategy. The building mechanic is awesome and can advantage or disadvantage teams depending on how it's used. Sometimes it's not smart to build a bunch of defensive barriers and really dig into particular locations that you're capturing and sometimes it is. There's also instances where building in areas that you aren't capturing can be useful or provide a needed edge. All the general rifleman kits have shovels for building and the Squad Leaders approve the building plans in a radial menu.
I didn't plan to list every possible component of realism in the game in this review, because I plan on making a more comprehensive review for this game and others after some work to prepare. So another review of Squad and other games will be forthcoming from me in the future. In conclusion Squad is really shaping up as a project and it's my belief it will continue to do so. There is still a lot of content the developers plan to add and they've hit the mark consistently till now. I greatly anticipate the full release of this game whenever it should come.  There will be an Air combat component to the game as well as other exciting features that are planned in the developement cycle. I absolutely think this game is worth the money if you are a fan of tactical realism and strategy and want to see that implemented more in first person shooters. The people who enjoy more thoughtful experiences that don't reward Rambo wannabe's should see great opportunity and potential here!

I think it needs to be said that the game does fail as a physics based puzzle game, in that I've had at least one moment where simply running the simulation a second time without changing anything achieved a different result than it did the first time I ran it (a part did not break at the homestretch of my bridge, netting me both the win for the level and the Pinocchio achievement).  I can only report this happening once because I instantly came here to point this out in a review, and before now I hadn't even tried such a boneheaded maneuver when things went wrong (I only did it this time to reevaluate what was wrong with the bridge!).  I'm having trouble recommending a physics based puzzle game where you can get different results by trying the same thing more than once (isn't that the definition of insanity?), so I will have to give this a thumbs down.
However, I would also point out to prospective buyers that the game actually is a lot of fun, so I'm hitting "no" on a bit of an edge case.  If the game seams appealing to you, you probably should still buy this, it just cheapens the experience a bit to realize that there may be an (indeterminable amount of an) element of pure luck involved here.

Summary:
The game has a well thought out story and it is incredibly immersive, especially the opening level! There is a bit of a cliche antagonist but I think it is more light-hearted and silly over serious, so I will give that a pass. Gameplay is fun and rewarding, I feel as if it needs to be played on the hardest difficulty to be a challenge, anything lower and I think I would find myself being a bit bored. Levels are well designed, as with the enemies.
All in all the game has fulfilled its duty of some rock solid entertainment, I found myself enjoying almost every bit of this game and I would highly recommend this to anyone who either likes futuristic stories, WW2 or just a good story driven FPS. Also I liked the little sub-plot between BJ (lol) and Anya.
Verdict: 8/10
Gameplay:
Gunplay is fantastic bar one thing. The weapons are fun to use, sound great and there is a weapon/ammo combination for everyone. The steady unlocks and upgrades are good, but I feel there is too much of a focus on the LKW, which is a laser rifle you get later on in the game. This coupled with the fact laser weapons in the game are pretty much essential later on make it so you are really locked to only about 2 weapons. Not to say you couldn't use anything else, but you would be putting yourself at a major disadvantage. Grenades in this game I found to be something I hardly ever used, they are really not too useful at all, they only really come into play when you are battling a boss.
Enemies:
Great variety and perfect scaling through the game. Only downside is there is an enemy type later on in the game which spawns with the rest of the grunts, he can be a massive pain, particularly towards the final levels. Yellow guy with a shotgun that ricochets off walls. This guy will be the bane of your existance.
Level Design:
Well made levels, multiple routes, cover well placed, secrets are challenging but not impossible to find.
Performance:
Ran on a 1070, i7 4700 and 16gb of ram. 1440p and med-high settings. This game ran well apart from the 60FPS cap, and when removed it speeds up, so that sucks. Also due to the cap I noticed a bit of stuttering here and there but V-Sync fixed that issue. Overall not many issues on the performance side of things.

Electronic Super Joy is a 2D Platformer that centers around challenging microstages  while listening to amazing electronic-themed music.
The story is about a lone, wandering hero who's fought in many battles and wars, losing many limbs including, most importantly, his butt. This entire journey is to find and defeat the one that took his butt. The story is really simple, and is told through quick dialog that's thrown out to you as you go through the level. It doesn't take itself seriously, it's very silly, and you'll get some laughs out of it.
Gameplay is very addictive. It mostly involves around precision platforming, an endurance race outrunning the screen while dodging obstacles, or surviving an onslaught of missles which you need to get rid of. There are 5 worlds with 20 stages each, lasting any time from 10 seconds to a couple minutes; with the exception of World 4). It sounds short, but it's a hard game. A very hard game, later on. You need to bring your platforming A-Game if you want to survive the difficulty it brings.You can think of it as Super Meat Boy, but a little less extreme. As you can tell, this game would be ideal for platforming lovers and gamers who love a good challenge, and I'm both of those. Achievements further reward your skills with painful goals such as earning zero deaths on each level, or beating all the time trials. If you love challenge, and want to be tested, this is for you. For other game modes, there's Infinite Love Mode, where you try and go through as many microstages as you can in a row before you fail. There's also No Checkpoint Mode for the most hardcore players out there.
The soundtrack is one of the highlights that everyone keeps talking about, and rightfully so. The game offers many tracks to keep your spirits high and your ears a lovely taste of music with each step. For most people, it's what keeps them going, and offers motivation to move on  to continually hear the amazing beats this game pulls out. I suggest you find the soundtrack when you can.
Overall, Electronic Super Joy is a fantastic difficult platformer with stellar music and a hearty challenge that platforming enthusiasts would surely love, and achievement hunters will get a run for their money.

The first thing that made me think so much less of this game was the way turbo boosts get charged. In the last game, each racer, depending on their turbo stats, would charge turbo in a different span of time and recieve a different amount of speed for it. But even for the characters that take longer than the others to charge turbo, it charges within a decent margin.
For example, for the duration of a level 1 charge, you can drift to charge another turbo boost just before or just after the first level 1 turbo boost ends.
But in this ♥♥♥♥ing game, every character seems to take the same amount of time to charge a turbo boost, and they changed it so it takes so much ♥♥♥♥ing longer to charge it. it takes about 10 or so seconds to charge a level 3 boost, and it isnt as easy as it was in the previous game either. When you drift in a direction for a certain period of time in this game, your vehicle starts to cave in on the drift and turn itself into whatever direction you're drifting in, even if your pointing your control stick the opposite way so you can spread the drift wider to keep it going. So to keep your boost charge, before you hit a wall because the drifting in this game sucks, you have to let the drift go and immediatly drift in the opposite direction without banging into the road walls or obstacles, just to even attempt a lv 3 turbo charge. So with turbo being something harder to obtain, you have to rely more on weapons to ♥♥♥♥ up your opponents gain and the speed boosts on the course itself.
The great thing about games like Mario Kart 8 and the original all stars racing is that you can chain your turbos nicely if you know what you can get away with in a course. And it doesnt take much time to get to lv 3 charge. When you know how to string your turbos through multiple turns, you gain a huge advantage. Even if the AI Rubberband in the original All Stars Racing, you can keep a good 5-10 second lead. But with this game, you dont get that, its much more chaotic and random with opponents catching up to you and hitting you with homing weapons just so you lose your lead. Then you get to use your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ turbo to try to catch up while using either homing weapons or using well placed snowball or rocket skillshots to attempt to catch up.
And then there's the boat and air segments that suck and dont work, trying to make this into a overdone version of Diddy Kong Racing. The Boat segments make my controls seems sluggish like im playing a bad version of Wave Race. And Navigating the air leaves much to be desired. I much prefer the way mario kart 8 handles air segemts with a glider over a small span of the course. While some courses in ASRT have entire laps in the air, leaving you to essentially have dog fights in the air because using the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ drifting to catch up while in the air is just aweful. And I have never been a fan of Dog fighting games like War Thunder.
The things I can say that are actually good about the game are the amount of characters, the mods for them, and the way stunts work. The original game had a nice cast of characters (with a guest appearance from Banjo & Kazooie in the xbox version only unfortunatly). But this game has a lot of Guest characters for the pc version and in general. And while some of them are a bit weird like General Winter and Footbal Manager, I love the fact that Wreck-it Ralph and 3 members of TF2 are playable.
The maps are also visually appealing and the atmosphere of the courses are great. And while I miss challenge mode, world tour isnt that bad either.
TL;DR
Turbo in ASR Transformed is utter ♥♥♥♥ing garbage aswell as the boat and air segments. And while the maps and aesthetic of the game are better looking than the original ASR, the original ASR plays much better and you feel in control of what you're actually doing.
While this game has multiplayer and the original All stars doesnt, almost no one plays online so its not really worth it for that reason. Buy the original All Stars Racing for a better "Kart Racing" experience.

This game deserve a few minutes of reviewing. First of all I'm not a big console fan and I prefer simulation racing game to arcade ones. I enjoyed Mario Kart on the SNES back in the days but the further iterations were just "meh" to me because I haven't felt any great improvement over the years. I bought this kart racing game on sale to increase my Steam library and to have a casual game to play with some friends online. I'd never tough I'd get hooked like this. It actually beats Mario Kart in every aspect thanks to it's diversity, freshness and style. The artwork quality is outstanding compared to other arcade PC games and I run at a constant 60fps on a low-midrange card with everything maxed out; it's that well optimized. The gameplay is fast, responsive and the tracks are very diversified. The levels are all themes of different Sega games in history from Sega Master System up to Dreamcast along with some brilliant remastered music. If you’d prefer a video review: Now, I’m not a very big fan of comedies. I don’t really like the idea of a movie or video game story, that only exists to make you laugh. On the surface, Tales seems like it’s just that. But underneath the superbly written layer of humour, is, a host of charming characters, and surprisingly dark, and tender moments. Sure, the engine still has those moments where it just seems to seize up and snap like an old hard drive, and for much of the game the choices don’t matter, it carries with it the same luggage that other Telltale games do, but there’s so much it does that separates it from it’s siblings.

Presentation

The art-style is borderlands-y, which seems to be Telltale’s forte recently. I personally think it looks great, but I know that there are people out there who are tired of Telltale’s comic book look. The thing about the presentation that has blown me away this time though, is the creative direction they have taken with the cinematography. You’ll notice the camera whizzing around, sections of slow-motion, and the action is captured extremely well. The designs of the characters are distinct and unique, and the environments lend themselves into that. Where the presentation falls flat is on the technical side of things. On the console I know that there are some frame-drops in areas, and on both the console and PC, the engine tends to run quite poorly. There’s a lot of stuttering in places, and while this isn’t presentation related,; I heard there were some save file losses for people on PC. The score is fantastic, there’s awesome licensed music to go with the wonderful episode intros, very little not to love.

Plot

I mentioned that choices don’t really matter. Like any other Telltale game, they don’t affect the way the overall plot pans out. That said, really more than any other Telltale game before it, I felt like I got the best payoff from the sum of my actions. In the fifth episode, there is a particular moment where some of your choices can open up options that change the way the moments leading up to the ending pan out. That sounds like an odd way of putting it, but I’m dancing around spoilers here. Your choices will not change the ending, but they affect enough elements in the final episode to make you feel like your experience was fairly unique. Other than the final episode, though, your choices are there only to make you feel like you have control over the action when, in reality, you really don’t. But if we’re talking about the plot when it comes to the set story? Incredible. There is very little for me to criticise here. One thing that may have detracted from the stakes, is the fact the story is being told by the two main characters. It means that there is very little to worry about when it comes to them, because you know that, somehow or another, they will survive. Granted, this restriction isn’t placed on any of the other characters, so they certainly could be killed off. The thing is, the story being told this way is so integral, in my opinion, to the curve of the narrative, that the lack of dread for the two main characters was a worthwhile sacrifice. But overall the plot is extremely engaging. Parts of it can be predictable, but then again there were moments I didn’t see coming at all. It ends conclusively with some hints of a sequel, but satisfying none-the-less. Most importantly though, near the end the thing that the characters were fighting for resonated with me entirely. At the end of the game I felt so in line with the characters and their motivations, that I felt myself cheer on the inside for them to win. That’s a really difficult thing to do, and the only other time that Telltale did this for a lot of people was in the first season of The Walking Dead, when Clementine was your motivation, and many many people could get behind that. It’s an extremely powerful thing, when you agree relentlessly with what the characters of a story are doing.

Characters

And of course, the characters need to be incredible in order to form that kind of a connection between the player and the walking pixels on screen. Every single character in Tales is extremely likeable. Some are better than others of course, but even the most boring characters in Tales have charm to them. And I think it’s the humour. I think it’s the way the characters act with one another, and the fact that the writing is so good I found myself in stitches, that really makes it feel like you're hanging out with an old group of friends when you play this game. And so, when one of them is in trouble, you as the player feel entirely emotionally invested in saving those characters. The two weakest characters are the two main characters that you play as. I also think the next weakest are their respective sidekicks. It’s interesting that the characters closest to the player felt the least interesting and compelling to me. They’re not bad characters, and they do interesting things and say funny stuff [STOP], but pale when comparing them to the huge number of colourful side-characters. The four core characters just lack the distinctness of the others. That said, I want to mention again that they are still very much likable, but their character types aren’t massively fresh. When it comes to the side characters, who are introduced slowly as the story progresses, it’s impossible to accurately convey how wonderful they are without experiencing it for yourself. And even more than that, many of the characters I am labeling “side-characters” become increasingly more important as the game goes on, so calling them just side characters is kind of hard to justify.

Verdict

Frankly, this is one of the best games of the year, and that’s saying a lot because 2015 has been an insanely good year for gaming. And even more so, the more I think about it the more it becomes one of my favourite games of all time, and one of my favourite stories of all time. The criticisms I have brought up in this review, while valid and certainly true, took a long time for me to come up with. I really really love this game and I urge you to play it if you value a good story. And this is coming from someone who openly says that he doesn’t like comedies, because Tales is so much more than that. It’s drama first, comedy second and action third. So, if you threatened to gouge out my eye and realise I wasn’t really dead, I’d absolutely recommend this game, 100%.

I'll try to keep this as short as possible because there's a lot to say about this one. If you're a Dragon Ball fan, you're gonna want to buy this. It's probably the greatest DBZ game in years, if not ever. The biggest selling point and the biggest reason why it's so good is the character creator. You can choose between 5 different races: Majin (male or female), Saiyan (M or F), Earthling (M or F), Namekian, or Frieza Clansman. It's really difficult to choose, not only between race and gender, but between all the different appearance options available and will keep you busy for quite a while. That's the nature of a good character creator. Every single special move in the game can be unlocked and equiped by your character, allowing a lot of possibilities. Iconic costumes and other equipment can be bought or unlocked to personalize your character. RPG elements allow you to level up the way you want to by putting points into different stats.
The fighting system can best be compared to the Budokai Tenkaichi series. You can move/fly around freely in an arena and lock on to opponents. It's fun but probably not too deep, though there is room for creativity with the custom move sets. There's an interesting story mode that puts a new spin on the all too familiar storyline of DBZ. It's great to see them doing something original with a story that has been done to death in practically every game in the series. It doesn't go over everything, only important fights, so some characters you may have expected aren't present. That being said, the character roster isn't huge like Tenkaichi 3's, but your custom character is probably the only one you'll end up using most of the time.
Toki Toki city, the game's central hub is a bit cumbersome to traverse. Instead of using a menu you have to use the "services" in this city to access things like online battles and quests. Some faster movement speed or more streamlining would have been nice. Speaking of quests, the game employs an RNG system with item drops, turning the game into a grind sometimes. Each quest has certain possible items as rewards, but since it's random you'll end up playing the quest again and again until you get what you want. You either hate or tolerate this. If you don't mind this Monster Hunter-esque grinding it's probably not a big deal. You'll have to grind for experience anyway, since some of these quests and missions are brutally difficult, sometimes unfairly so.
The biggest problem right now is the Xenoverse server. It's unreliable and goes offline at the drop of a hat. I've been able to play offline most of the time, but I've frequently been booted back to the main menu because the server went offline (luckily this only seems to happen while in the hub area and not during quests or missions) . I've also been stuck on the "logging in" screen 2 or 3 times. It's an issue I hope will be fixed. I don't see why I need to be logged in on the server if I want to play offline. Online matches work decently in my experience, some annoying lag sometimes, though you can do online battles even when you're in the single player lobby. You can also do online co-op for the quests (not the story), which is great!
Graphics and performance wise there's nothing to criticize. It looks and runs great. Maybe some more AA would have been nice, but oh well. I noticed putting the glare to high eats up the framerate a bit, but I found it to be painful to the eyes anyway.
I could go on and on about the things I would have liked to see more of, like bigger roster, voice acting for the custom character, more destructible terrain etc. Maybe a possible sequel will deliver that. What's here is totally worth full price if you're a Dragon Ball fan. Gave me a serious fangasm for sure. And trust me, I didn't talk about everything that makes this game so awesome. You'll have to see for yourself.

Extended info:
Despite this game having great customization which you can find in both equipment and the way your character gains strength as you level up. (You gain status points which you can use to increase their offensive or defensive capabilities like you see in many rpgs.) It fails on a few key elements.
First and foremost, there is the AI in dragonball xenoverse. You'll often hear people complaining about the difficulty of xenoverse, and where in some games this comes from a dangerous but fair AI (-read 'Dark Souls'-) in xenoverse the difficulty comes from the unbalanced power of the AI opponents.
All fighters in xenoverse have a stamina bar, and if you want to use evasive moves, or block incoming attacks, your stamina will drop. The problem is that many of these evasive moves also inflict damage on the attacking enemy.
In a player versus player match this would not pose a threat but the AI seems to have a different stamina bar that regenerates ridiculously fast in comparison to that of a player. This means that the AI is going to spam these evasive moves to get out of a players combo. When sooner or later you yourself run out of stamina and your opponent doesn't, be prepared to take in damage despite having the upperhand. This damage will be magnified if there is a level difference between you and your opponent. Did I mention many strong opponents can't even begin to be combo'd unless they lose stamina first?
Another issue is the hub world.
I understand what the developers wanted to create, but they made some mistakes here. For one the world is far too big for what is actually in it. The running around is boring and annoying in an otherwise fast paced game. This is made worse by the fact that after each mission you'll be dropped at a difference place than where you accept missions. This should be easily fixable by adjusting 3 lines of code however.
Another thing I should mention is that there is a transformation that is only available to the saiyan race. This transformation called super saiyan, unlike its effect in the dbz universe, presents the player with a 'limited' time of being able to spam ultimate and super attacks. While this will not pose a problem in pvp to experienced players who can dodge these attacks, it does seem to be the best way to counter the unbalanced AI. This ends up demoting the at first difficult AI to nothing more than silly target practice.
Despite all of this, you can have a lot of fun teaming up with up to two friends simultaneously to tackle missions and grind for equipment. Which brings me to the last problem of this game.
Many rpg games, including this one will give you slightly random rewards. This is a great way to add replayability and fun, trying to get that one special item. The problem here however is how xenoverse handles this. Instead of only rewards being random, some events that give you these chances to obtain rewards are also random. Quite a mouthful, right? Let's rephrase that, you'll have a random chance, to obtain a random chance, to obtain your item. This is simply bad design that leads to frustration. Especially considering some of these random events, aren't random, but need to be triggered by certain hidden objectives that are nowhere mentioned in the game. This way you never know if that event that might give you your desired item happened by chance, or by some random teammate's health being below a certain point when you finish the mission. William "B.J." Blazkowicz doesn’t have much luck with the Nazi’s. He has been captured, tortured, escaped from prison and killing them for years and still can’t get a break. After an assault on Deathshead fortress to turn the tide against the Nazi’s goes wrong, BJ is left in a vegetative state after suffering serious head wounds. Mistaken for a German soldier and cared for in a psychiatric asylum in Poland for over a decade he snaps out of his coma when they come to kill everyone and burn the place to the ground. This is where the fun begins, as you start your new mission to try and take down the Nazi regime.
Nazi controlled Europe looks intimidating and dark. Everything in this game does a wonderful job of warping the 40/50's style to what it may have been like under the Nazi regime. All the buildings are foreboding, super concrete structures, which make them imposing to look at (super concrete being one of the weapons they used to win the war). Even though this is an alternate reality, I’m happy they managed to stay away from zombies and other undead creatures in this game. Because of all the giant dog robots, super soldiers, advanced armour, moon missions, and other crazy weapons the game has a retro-futuristic feel to it which i think they nailed.
The missions are well designed and aren’t as linear as most shooters, as you can explore the mission grounds fairly well and there are plenty of collectables, upgrades and hidden weapons and ammo to find. Depending on your moral choice at the beginning of the game the route through missions you can take, upgrades available and some collectibles will differ, as will resistance fighters in your home base you interact with. This effects everything including any new games that you start (as your previous collect health/armour upgrades carry over to the new game), which I thought was a nice touch and adds some replayability into the game other than just making the missions harder (while its much the same, there are subtle differences)
Graphicly the game looks great - it’s dark and sticks to bleak tones but you are mainly assaulting checkpoints, bunkers, fortresses, running through sewer systems so it’s all appropriate. The resistance fighters and other refugees become NPC’s that you actually want to try and help out, something that hasn’t been done well in previous Wolfenstein games (or at all) and again shows how war effects those displaced by it.
If you are chasing 100% achievements then it’s possible, but you will need to do a few runs (which is worth it to see how things play out with your moral choice)

I really enjoyed Red Alert 2 and was craving  a good RTS, so I got excited when I remembered this was in my steam library. The excitement was very short lived - heres why.
My PC can run almost any game at 60 fps on the highest settings. In this game, I have to run it on medium just to get 45 fps. This was the first bump in the road, but I figured the gameplay would still be good. Oh how wrong I was...
The campaign opens up with some cutscenes that, due to acting and set and some video editing, are comical in appearance - I believe this is intentional. The rest of the campaign is also comical - not intentionally. Let me make this clear: if you are looking for a real RTS, maybe coming from SupCom or another great game, this game is NOT for you. The campaign more closely resembles a point and click adventure than a real RTS game. Move from location A to B. Oh no, enemies, fall back and wait for reinforcements. Move to B. Move from B to C. Oh no, enemies, fall back and wait for reinforcements. Move to C. And on and on and on and on. NO effort WHATSOEVER put into developing a good campaign.
Here's another point in which they made huge mistakes: superweapons. These add to the removal of need for strategy in a strategic genre. These weapons allow massive destruction, killing of units, bombing runs, etc etc, without need for Line of Sight, units in the area, or any other balancing factor. Basically, they all have a charge time and it becomes a time bomb. This forces you to throw troops into battle just as soon as they're made, or deal with the consequences when the enemy's super weapon comes online in 2 minutes. No time for planning, or an army, or strategy. Just go go go before you get hit by Russia's massive bomb or their magic vacuum that sucks your units up into space forever.
Speaking of which, let's talk about Russia. If you play AS Russia, you win. If you play AGAINST Russia, you lose. Yup, that's all I have to say about Russia.
They started out with a great game, but completely half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the campaign and added some "features" that remove the need or the ability to use strategy in the game.
If you are looking for a visually appealing game in which you get to watch two armies (but not really because you can't POSSIBLY build a force big enough to call an army without a super weapon wiping it out) constantly duke it out in small skirmishes, with the occasional dramatic wipeout of one, then this game is for you.
If you are looking for a game focused on strategy, balance, and, well, basically an RTS game, this is NOT for you. Go find another game.

I do not think you should buy this game as of now.
While most the positive reviews are for the most part, correct, I still don't think you should buy it.
My reasoning? The AI. It's rather difficult to use.
If a colonist has something they want to do, you can't really stop them. You can prioritize other things, but they'll do that and instantly go back to what they were doing, and when for the most part you're playing on 3X or 2X speed, it is annoying. To try and do one tile at a time while the colonist is trying to wander off to pick up granite on the corner of the map is fustrating.
The AI is minorly buggy, and doesn't like to respond sometimes, or does something that is really dumb, or even go against your rules. Now, wether the last one is a feature or not, I don't know.
A specific problem that happens way too much when I'm extrememly low on food: I have a dead animal in a fridge room. I've got meat in there as well. I've got a eight guys hungry as hell and four dogs even more hungry.
I set my cook to cook some simple meals, expecting the AI is smart enough to wait. Instead, the cook and five others go into the fridge, grab meat and some rice, and another grabs a ♥♥♥♥ing turkey corpse. I put all the colonists on draft, and the animals aren't allowed in the fridge already. I un-draft the cook, but then he goes and eats raw stuff and wanders off. He didn't respond to anything but draft after that, and the others once un-drafted ate raw food and one even ate a goddamn turkey corpse.
And, as I play more I experience more. Got a guy with a malaria. Needs tending, but nobody will heal him. Nice one, Rimworld.
Now, I have played it quite a while, and I have more problems. The cooks won't cook sometimes, even though there is only raw stuff. I'll disable jobs, and even set areas restricting them to the fridge and the stove.
In short, AI is sometimes unresponsive, buggy, and fustratingly hard to use.
And, as the game hinges on the AI being good, I think you should wait for either a sale, or for when it gets a bit better/goes into beta. Though, it is super ♥♥♥♥ing addicting.

Disclaimer: I was provided a copy for my unbiased review.
Playing "An Occasional Dream" was like stepping back into time.  It brought me back to my younger years of JRPGs, when the voice acting wasn't something that could make or break a game and you could just enjoy the story.  This very much hit all the nostalgia buttons for me and I truly enjoyed playing this game.
The story and the characters felt pretty fleshed out.  I enjoyed the nod to the genre in the sense of the main character figuring out he is in an RPG by recognizing all the tropes (why are all the doors always unlocked and why does no one ever care when you bust in and take their stuff?  I have been wondering this for AGES).  I even liked the slight romantic element to the game, though I would have enjoyed maybe exploring that a little more.  I won't get into the ending (though I did like it and thought it was a little bittersweet) but I really would have liked to have some time to really get into the dynamic of the relationship.
The battle system was well done as well.  It was easy enough to figure out and I liked the points to spend on abilities take for leveling.  The monsters looked great and I liked the added visuals for spell casting.  I was pretty happy to see that when I got the next level of the spell or ability that it was reflected in the game by the visuals.
The map I thought was great and it reminded me of my old Secret of Mana feels.  My favorite area ended up being the snowy one.  The minimap is such a great tool as well and I was happy to see it on here.
When I play JRPGs I am one that really lives the grind it out part.  I spent a lot of time leveling and grinding up the characters.  This game definitely delivered when it comes to this and I am sure it is something I will do on my next play-through as well.
I did dabble a bit in the end game content but I haven't gotten that far through it yet.  I did beat the main story and I look forward to seeing if there is a part 2 (I sure hope there is!).  Bottom line, this game is well worth the price and if you are a fan of the genre you shouldn't be disappointed.

hehehehehe....boobs.........joking aside lets do this review. I will be going over the game in a pro/ con style and end it with my final thoughts on the game. I will try to be as detailed as can.
Pro:
The game is nice looking. I really enjoy the battle scenery and i like the pictures used in the VN text dump sections. The models for the characters are solid though there are moments where there is come clipping or Z fighting but it is small and not really a big deal.
The music is fantastic, the sad song that plays at those moments of deep sorrow is on point. Really catches the entire mood of the situation as well as combat music is nicely varied so theres alot to listen too. Also if you want there is also voices of the characters you can listen to if thats what you want to do....i dont speak any other language besides english soo i dont understand it....dont remember if it is englished subtitled for the voice recordings.
The game story is good. Well to be fair most of the game has a good to great story. At the worst possible scenario aka the gensson squad or however you spell it; i didnt like their story. It just was not that interesting but besides that the rest of the game is great.
Characters are great. Theres a lot of different characters that have different combat styles so you can never get tired from the repetitive fight till enemy hp reaches 0 moments because the game in story mode switches you up between 5 girls that are on their respetive team. Most are pretty nice to play as but there are a few that when you are forced to play as the combat is such as drag and i say that for the slow hitters and the weak attackers.
Character dialog is solid. I did find a good ammount of characters i enjoyed in the game and i am petty so if their combat sucked in the game i immediantly hated them as a character but in the VN sections the remaining characters were on a spectrum of ok to very enjoyable. Most were very enjoyable except the Gensson squad, shiki was the only good one i enjoyed because her dialog was fun to read and her combat was really cool.
Theres different costumes, hairstyles, and acessories to use. Technically you can dress up any character how you want them which is really nice. I didnt do that often but i got to say i enjoy rin alot that the leader of hanzo has her shinobi costume. I didnt change anyone's hair styles because i was never interested in that because all i wanted to do was fight and enjoy the story....not play dress up but hey the option is there if you want it.
Rpg elements. I dont know why but i always enjoy in RPG games that when i level up i feel stronger and here i do feel stronger whether i take more hits, visually see my hp bar get progressively bigger, or deal more damage to end fights faster. I like feeling like a badass. As you level up you gain more attacks to chain in the combo which is awsome to have a more flashy combo but with exp gain you also gain exp for your mastery skills. They act as passive abilities but i dont really focus on them and never saw anything really amazing or must have.
Con:
Enemy AI is cheap. Many times when fighting the goons especially the ravens or bird like enemies. They always spawn in with an attack off screen so it maks the dodge slim to none. Its not fair that they get a cheap shot like that. Also the AI shinobi's always act cheap the further you are in the story mode. They spam cheap attacks and stun lock you pretty easy. Sure you can get out with a limit break but it is frustrating to see that everytime you get one hit on them they get 20 on you because of cheap tactics.
The frame rate is horrible. The game is not well optimized, the ingame combat is super sluggish probably hitting 10fps if even that unless if you have a nivida card and set it to high processing or whatever it says. Then the game will run alot better frame wise. It might not be that big of a deal but why make it so the player needs to work around it?
Conclusion:
Honestly i thought the game was great and was tons of fun from the story, music, gameplay, and characters. It is realy hard to choose what character i truely enjoyed that is how much i enjoyed of many characters provided. Also i forgot to mention that their was battle damage on clothing so you slowly strip away clothing of your oponents. Thought i should mention that. Sure i had frame rate issues at first till i fixed it because the hyperdimension neptunia rebirth 2 game had the same issue with the frame rate. There are so much good that this game provides that it is hard not to reccomend the game to friends or to other players in general. The game is more than eye candy with boobs and what not. With the developing characters it adds an understanding of a character's struggle in a given situation and hopefully the player feels attached through the story and invested in the characters through the journey.

This is, in my humble opinion, the greatest visual novel ever written.
If you are like me and watched the anime first, you may be wondering, "Why bother buying this game?" I always felt the same. The anime is a stellar adaptation and I give it a ten out of ten. I loved everything about it and I didn't think anything could beat it, even if the game came first and it had considerable acclaim.
I was very wrong. I ended up buying this game on a whim, and once I started playing it, I couldn't put it down.
What is there to be said? Everything about it is incredible. It has one of the most captivating plots I've ever experienced, with perfect pacing and interesting, likable characters. The soundtrack moves me to tears, the voice acting is stacked with emotion, and the artwork is unique and beautiful. Even the scientific aspects (something that isn't touched on much in the anime) are extremely well researched.
Even if you've seen the anime, I'm certain you'll find something new in this game. There are 5 routes that weren't adapted (Suzuha's, Faris', Lukako's, Mayuri's, and Kurisu's) and numerous new scenes, all narrated by one of my favorite protagonists ever, Okabe Rintaro.
A tremendous game. I'd give it an 11 out of 10 if I could. If you were only able to play one visual novel in your lifetime, I would recommend this one.

To quickly judge whether you'll enjoy Titan Souls or not, play the demo. If you enjoy the demo, you'll enjoy the game. If you thought the demo was irritating, too difficult or not fun, you can safely avoid Titan Souls.
I really enjoyed my playthrough of Titan Souls; the repeated treks from the checkpoint/savepoint to the boss wasn't nearly as irritating as the negative reviews make it out to be, if not only because I took a more patient approach to this game than a rapid-fire speedrun approach.
You can fight the bosses in (almost) any order you want except for the first four and the last two. When you're not in a tense fight to the death, you're exploring and traversing a beautiful calm world with a fitting ambient soundtrack that changes depending on your location.
I think what I liked the most about Titan Souls was that each boss felt unique and memorable in their own way. All of them are puzzle bosses, and the only time I ever needed a guide was on the Final Boss since I genuinely thought it was next to impossible.
After you beat the game once, there are additional modes available that add for replayability, which are as follows (marked spoilers in case you want to find them out for yourself):
I recommend Titan Souls because I enjoyed the challenge it provided and it felt both very challenging, but also very possible with a clear feeling of progress and accomplishment after defeating a boss. However, it is rather short (I completed my first casual all-boss playthrough in about 3 hours) and I do not think the amount of content it provides is worth $15 USD. As such, I would definitely get it when it is on sale.

Warning to potential buyers: This game has some bridges that won't be solveable with the only structures the game shows you, you'll have to make some weird sh** up and I know this because I had to look up the answer after failing some of the bridges over and over. The game does little to show you which structures you should be thinking about (other than triangles), and often you might not really see if something is working that 10% better than your other builds, and that's often a crucial difference. It also doesn't really explain what materials might fare better beyond the absolute basics of (steel is stronger than wood), and it would've been awesome if they did more to show how the rope can help to support tight budget bridges by connecting along the underside of your bridge from end to end. I only know it distributes weight better this way because some walkthroughs used it. Other materials can be a bit fiddly with load distribution depending on how you've arranged them.
I have played through a bunch of this game and BC: Medieval and while I like both just for the physics puzzle challenge, I find the Medieval one's solutions end up making more sense than this one. It still barely guides you but at least those structures kind of make sense.
In this version you can build diagonal roads (which might be the only way to solve some of these bridges, it's certainly the only way I could find for some) and they end up letting you hold them up with ropes from nonsense structures on the sides because the stone pillars are too expensive or not available.
I still recommend it because I've enjoyed it either way, the physics are simple but pretty consistent, and it's a good little brain work out, but if you want a well-paced puzzle game with some actual help on what to do, this game fails a little on that front. I personally looked up a few answers and still enjoyed trying to figure the level out before I gave up.

Having not played a Dragonball Z game for quite literally the better part of ten years, it was a combination of nostalgia, a PC release and the create-a-character feature designed plot that drew me to this. I bought the game as a pre-order on a bit of a gamble, and I'm happy to say that while at the time of this writing that the online's still busted, the singleplayer game is a real fun time-sink. The long and short of the story is that the typical Dragonball Z canonical story is being changed by sinister forces, and you're summoned to help save the day by going back in time and interfering in the bigger battles in DBZ with odd twists due to the aforementioned changes.
Let's get the biggest drawbacks out of the way from the outset; besides the online issues, some difficulty spikes, some questionable voice acting, subtitle errors and all number of smaller quirks, this game was a joy to play. The graphics are solid, fitting the design of the original works in good, sharp 3d. There's an arena based on Namek's impending explosion that's a real treat to look at. The create-a-characters do look a bit on the generic side, but that's just the nature of the beast; All create-a-character games suffer from this, but thanks to the sharp cell-shaded graphics, your avatar certainly looks the part, especially when you get the right outfit.
Sound-wise, the game certainly has the full breadth of the Dragonball effects; flying, charging, impacting blows all sound hilariously old-school, but in a way that works to the games benefit as a fan-focused title. That said, especially playing as a melee focused character, longer combos would trigger the heavy-impacting sounds which in fast-striking combos would make a real racket. Like I mentioned earlier, voice acting is quirky in all the ways DBZ and anime as a whole can be. The Japanese and English Voice casting is good though, pulling a lot of old talent back to reprise roles, but be warned; while the Japanese voices sound better as a whole, part of the joy of the game is the banter that occurs in-combat, and when you're fighting for your life, reading subtitles is less than ideal.
Let's get onto the real meat of the game; the gameplay. Having not played a DBZ game for a while, I know a lot of people took issue with what's considered a 'simplified' combat engine but I felt it was fine. You're essentially given a three-district city-hub; an industrial/shop area, a side-mission and online central area where you both do offline and online vs battles and 'Parallel Quests', which consist of the small 'what if' missions that don't factor in to the main plot.
The last area is an odd one; consisting of where you make wishes with the eponymous dragonballs, enter an area where the main story advances and you can re-do old story missions, and an area for local vs combat and another online 'World tournament' stage.
Fundamentally, you start the game, do a few of the canonical bigger fights as Goku vs the villain of that arc with a gradual interjection of the plot's time-changing aspect triggering, before the plot allows you to make your avatar. You only have one slot to begin with, so be sure to give some thought as to what you want to play as, and it can be worth doing a little research about what races, and indeed genders, have what effect on your ability to fight. That said, as someone who played as a female saiyan (apparently one of the worst melee types in the game), who went out of his way to make as balanced a character as possible, with some specialising in melee late game, I never felt too hampered by my choices; indeed, with a blank outlook to start with, I learned how to handle the melee combat and only very rarely abused any of the games less balanced aspects.
Being predominantly a fan-focused game, your avatar can be equipped with a lot of character specific outfits, as well as some new ones that are colour customisable, and a great deal many of the more (and less) famous moves in the game. Ever fancied having both a kamehameha AND the gallick gun? Go right ahead. Part of the fun of the game, and an aspect that detracts in a point I'll make later, is learning and adapting based on the skills you know and find as the game progresses. It took me a while to learn how to get good at the melee game in Xenoverse, but sure enough by the time I hit level 50 or so out of 80, I had some attacks that I kept for the rest of the game and I could fight off pretty much any enemy with ease, and smart tactics let me win when outnumbered.
As mentioned though, you only get one character slot to start with. Once you finish the story, THEN you get the other slots, of which there are enough to make one of each race, and of each gender if the species allows it. The problem I had in this regard though was you have no option to re-do the actual story from scratch with a new character. While you can in fact replay these missions, the fact you have all the outfits and moves unlocked really dampened my will to do another 'play-through'. I'm sure there's a way to reset your save, but I don't want to lose my initial female saiyan character, I just want to learn and develop like she had me do rather than starting as a low stat master with the best skills.
Still, while I don't know the exact time I played this game for, as I had to play with Steam in offline mode to play the game due to the broken online, it lasted me a fair long while. Part of this is because of the randomness of some of the gameplay aspects. It's both a blessing to some and a curse for all. Side-missions have extra objectives that vary from task to task, commonly things like beating it in a short time-frame or beating certain characters in order, but both generally improve the items you get from a mission (special moves, clothing, items you can use to make buffs and healing items for tougher missions and z-souls, items that grant unique abilities in particular circumstances, like buffs when low on health or slow health regeneration and the like). Thankfully few missions use the full extent of the typical 15 minute time-frame, but considering I still have, at the time of this writing, a side mission where I cannot get the bonus objectives to trigger despite doing it to the letter. I've tried this mission some 20+ times to the point where trying it now, the mission is hilariously easy to beat but the frustration of it never triggering the extra objectives leaves a bitter taste in ones mouth.
The story missions are thankfully a fair bit easier, if only because they're pretty straight-forward. So long as you dedicate some time to do all the parallel missions a couple of times each I found my levelling met the pace of the plot quite handily. Make no mistake though, if you so choose, you can grind relentlessly until even battles against the most powerful villains of the Dragonball world are weaklings. I much prefer it this way; even if I didn't use it, you never know when someone might struggle and having an ability to reward patience with a slightly easier shot at the mission by becoming more powerful is a useful tool. Odds are even if you don't explicitly enjoy grinding, you'll likely accidently do it due to wanting a particular move or outfit.
All in all I recommend this game, although I would advise caution due to the presently broken online, and the nature of the game being guilty of the usual anime-game trappings with the voice acting and not being for the typical player-base, fighting games or otherwise. If you're interested in a longer-term, slightly grindy fighting game with cool visuals, enjoy developing a character into powerhouse suited to your own play-style, and enjoy a unique Dragonball Z plot with you as the hero fighting alongside the majority of the heroes and villains, then I'd certainly recommend it.
